en: *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle One.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asvabhāva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
I prostrate to the Greatly Awakened Tathāgatas, To the Unsurpassed True Dharma, and the Noble Assembly;
For the benefit of self and others, and so that the Dharma may long endure, I shall provide a brief commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
The treatise states:

In the *Abhidharma Mahāyāna Sūtra*, prior to the Bhagavān, for the sake of revealing the greatness of the essence of the Mahāyāna, it was spoken by Bodhisattvas who were already well-versed in entering the Mahāyāna.
The commentary states:

One wishes to encompass all essential points of the Mahāyāna through ten meanings; since those meanings can reveal that the nature of this treatise is the sacred teaching (āgama), they are used as the gateway for its exposition. Thus, one speaks of the *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-sūtra* and so forth, because it is the cause for the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) or because it is commonly understood.
In the Abhidharma, "saṃjñā" (conceptualization) serves as the defining characteristic.
The Mahāyāna sūtras state this to distinguish it from other contexts. To provide a brief explanation:

it is called the Mahāyāna because it is both a vehicle (*yāna*) and great (*mahat*); or, it is called the Mahāyāna because it possesses the nature of being great. This is due to the greatness of its cause and fruit, and the greatness of its activity and equipment. As for the fruit, it refers to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

To explain it in detail: because it is associated with the seven kinds of greatness—namely, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), the perfections (*pāramitā*), the trainings (*śikṣā*), and the characteristics of retention (*dhāraṇīlakṣaṇa*)—and because it pierces through and sews together [the teachings], it is called a *sūtra*.

In this context, it is precisely that which accords with the eight periods of time; its essential nature consists of the appearance of what is heard as being either direct or indirect speech, gathered and manifested upon the consciousness of the listener.
If this is so, how can a bodhisattva speak in a way that is not [merely] the consciousness of the listener?
This is stated because he is capable of speaking it and because he is its predominant cause;
for example, through the predominant power of deities and others, one may obtain treatises, mantras, and so forth within a dream.
If it were separate from consciousness, how could the Buddha have spoken the phrases of the various sūtras?

To claim that speech is the intrinsic nature [of words] is unreasonable, because it is unreasonable for individual syllables to be able to express meaning; furthermore, as they arise sequentially, they do not abide simultaneously and lack a collective assembly. Thus, their intrinsic nature cannot be established, and since speech would have no movement [of transition], this is unreasonable.

Furthermore, it is not the case that there is no phoneme (*akṣara*) such that even a slight name (*nāman*) could function as a signifier; therefore, the claim that various sūtras are called "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is also unreasonable.
Consequently, it is certain that, according to the sūtra as it has been taught, [the designation] "intrinsic nature" is logical.

In this *Abhidharma-mahāyāna-sūtra* thus explained, the term "Bhagavān" refers to the Blessed One; he is called Bhagavān because he destroys all Māras and is able to destroy the four kinds of great demonic adversaries.

Regarding the four kinds of māras: first, the māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*); second, the māra of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*); third, the celestial māra (*devaputra-māra*); and fourth, the māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*).

By relying on the *samādhi* of emptiness, one is able to destroy all the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of the māra of afflictions, abide in the state of the transformed basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), and accordingly realize immeasurable roots of goodness.

Furthermore, by relying on the power of diligence and wisdom, one can destroy the māra of the aggregates; by relying on the meditative concentration of loving-kindness, one can destroy the celestial māra; and by relying on the cultivation of the bases of psychic power, one can destroy the māra of death.
Because he is able to destroy these four great māras, he is called Bhagavat.
Furthermore, because he is endowed with qualities such as mastery (vaśitā), the Buddha is therefore designated as Bhagavat.
Why is this so? Because it is intended to proclaim the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

In that context, "before him" signifies that the Buddha has authorized it as fit for wide circulation, since there is no discrepancy with what was spoken directly to the Great Master, as in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
Regarding those who have already been able to skillfully enter the Mahāyāna: they are either distinguished by their virtuous traces (*guṇa-vastu*) or are known collectively.

That is to say, because they have already been able to skillfully enter the Mahāyāna, or because they have already entered it most excellently within this very [teaching], they are called "those who have already been able to skillfully enter the Mahāyāna. This reveals that they have attained the merits of various *dhāraṇīs* and eloquence (*pratibhāna*), being able to uphold and expound the meaning of the Mahāyāna; thus, based on this significance, such a name is spoken.

Regarding the term "Bodhisattva": one is called a Bodhisattva because the *bodhicitta-sattva* (the being of awakening) serves as the object of focus (*ālambana*). Thus, the designation "Bodhisattva" is established based on the words of the great vow.

Furthermore, it is observed elsewhere that names are spoken based on the object of focus; for example, when impurity (*aśubha*) and so forth serve as objects of focus, the two samādhis are termed "impurity" and "emptiness."
Alternatively, one is called a bodhisattva because that very mind possesses both the aspiration and the capacity to seek awakening.
Regarding the phrase "to manifest the greatness of the essence of the Mahāyāna": it is great because it is profoundly deep, lofty, vast, and unsurpassed.
The essence of sound refers to its intrinsic nature and function.
As it is said in the world, "fire has heat as its essence" or "poison has harm as its essence"; because this essence is great, it is called the "greatness of essence."
"Manifesting" means to reveal that which others have not yet understood.
"Acting for" means desiring [to benefit them].
The treatise says:

That is to say, based on the Mahāyāna, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten aspects of the most excellent and supreme discourse: first, the most excellent and supreme discourse on the basis of the knowable; second, the most excellent and supreme discourse on the characteristics of the knowable; third, the most excellent and supreme discourse on the entry into the characteristics of the knowable; fourth, the most excellent and supreme discourse on the cause and fruit of that entry; fifth, the most excellent and supreme discourse on the distinctions in the cultivation of those causes and fruits; sixth, the most excellent and supreme discourse on the superior morality within such distinctions in cultivation; seventh, the most excellent and supreme discourse on the superior mind within this [superior morality]; eighth, the most excellent and supreme discourse on the superior wisdom within this [superior mind]; ninth, the most excellent and supreme discourse on the abandonment which is its fruit; and tenth, the most excellent and supreme discourse on the gnosis which is its fruit.
By these various scriptural passages spoken by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, it is demonstrated that the Mahāyāna is truly the word of the Buddha.
The commentary states:
"The term 'sound' (*śabda*) is a brief designation for the meaning of the ten superior bases (*daśa-viśeṣa-sthāna*) that have been explained."
For those who rely on the Mahāyāna, that which is practiced and that which is taught is neither the Śrāvaka-yāna nor the mundane.

Furthermore, the Mahāyāna is cited as the definitive meaning to clarify what is relied upon; it is this alone and nothing else. This is because that which relies on the mundane differs from the Buddha’s word due to other characteristics, as a verse says:
"Truthful speech without anger, giving little without seeking reward," and so forth.
If one relies on the Śrāvaka [vehicle], it differs from the Mahāyāna by virtue of other characteristics, as a verse says:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing," and so forth.
Therefore, the Mahāyāna is again cited as being consistent with reason.
Regarding the phrase "there are ten [categories]," the number is used to manifest the number.
This preeminent word of the Buddha establishes the body of the treatise.
"Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the lineage (*gotra*).
Because these [characteristics] are mutually distinct and unmixed through their successive differentiation, they are called "excellent" (*viśiṣṭa*).

Alternatively, because they are vastly superior to the dharmas of the śrāvakas and others, and because they are preeminent (*adhika*), they are called "excellent," for they are capable of bringing forth great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
Because these ten characteristics are preeminent, his speech is preeminent; therefore, it is said that there is "preeminent speech characterized by ten forms of preeminence.
As for the Blessed One, he has exhausted both defiled and non-defiled sleep of ignorance.
Because he has the meaning of awakening the wisdom regarding all that is to be known, he is called a Buddha; it is like a man waking up, or like a lotus flower opening. As it is said:
"The meaning of awakening and opening; sometimes the activity of the Buddha-realm," and so forth.
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, how is this [meaning] made manifest?

Because these ten points, as here explained, have never been seen taught in the Śrāvaka vehicle, but are seen taught in various places within the Mahāyāna; that is to say, the ālayavijñāna is designated as the essence of the "basis of the knowable" (*jñeyāśraya*).

The three natures—first, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); second, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); and third, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)—are designated as the essence of the characteristics of the knowable.
The nature of consciousness-only is called the essence of entering the characteristics of the knowable.
The six perfections are called the essence of the cause and fruit of that entry.
The ten stages of the bodhisattva are called the essence of the distinctions in the cultivation of that cause and fruit.
The bodhisattva vows are designated here as the essence of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*).
The various samādhis, such as Śūraṅgama and Gaganagañja, are designated here as the essence of higher mind (*adhicitta*).
Non-conceptual wisdom is designated here as the essence of superior insight (*adhiprajñā*).
Non-abiding nirvana is designated as the essence of its fruit, which is abandonment (*prahāṇa*).

The three bodies of the Buddha—the first being the essential body (*svābhāvika-kāya*), the second the enjoyment body (*sambhogika-kāya*), and the third the transformation body (*nairmāṇika-kāya*)—are designated as the essence of its fruit, which is wisdom (*jñāna*).

By means of these ten points thus explained, it is shown that the Mahāyāna differs from the Śrāvaka-yāna and is further shown to be supreme; for the Blessed One taught them solely for the sake of bodhisattvas. Therefore, one should know that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess ten kinds of most excellent and preeminent speech based exclusively upon the Mahāyāna.
The commentary states:
It is called "the knowable" (*jñeya*) because it is that which ought to be known.

"Basis" (*āśraya*) refers to the support; this term "basis" specifically selects the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)—both defiled and purified—which depend upon it, and does not include the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), because the latter lacks the sense of being a basis.
The basis is precisely the ālayavijñāna, because it is the cause of that [consciousness] and because it can induce it, as is appropriate.

If this is so, then the object of knowledge is itself the basis of the object of knowledge; there is no contradiction, since the maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna) is of the nature of an object of knowledge.

This basis of the knowable is itself sublime; because it is sublime, its expression is also sublime—namely, that which was previously described as the speech of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, which accords with all circumstances.
Regarding the characteristics of the objects of knowledge (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*): it is because the intrinsic nature of the objects of knowledge is that which is characterized (*lakṣya*).

It is explained through the operation of dependence (*āśraya-karma*), wherein many *lupta* (elided) terms such as "objects of knowledge," "that which is to be abandoned," and "that which is to be realized" are supplied.

Alternatively, it is explained through the operation of possession (*samanvāgama-karma*), for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) lacks both the characteristic and that which is characterized, thereby signifying its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is its universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), while the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is its particular characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), because the consciousnesses of "self," "sentient being," and "object" are mutually distinct.

This is like the earth element and so forth, which take hardness and so on as their manifesting characteristics; although there is no difference in their essence, they are spoken of as characteristics.

Furthermore, just as the marks of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*) are taught, or the various marks such as those of a Śrāvaka and so forth according to the Sautrāntikas and others—by virtue of these causes and conditions, that which is known is itself the mark, or it is the mark of that which is known; thus it is called the "characteristic of the knowable" (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*). This is also to be understood accordingly, because it is taught that there is no difference in nature, and because difference and non-difference in nature are absent.

"Entering the characteristics of the knowable" means that this [treatise] is either the means for entering the characteristics of what is to be known, or it is the entry into the characteristics of the knowable itself.

"Entry" refers to the realization (abhisamaya) of entering the characteristics of the knowable, which is the nature of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā). This is what is preeminent; because this is preeminent, the words are also preeminent.

Regarding "the cause and fruit of entering that": this refers to the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), which is designated as "entering that" during the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*).
When practicing the preparatory applications (*prayoga*), the mundane perfections (*pāramitā*) that are not yet purified are called the "cause of entering that.
Once one has already attained entry, they are the supramundane perfections; because they are subsumed by the purified superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), they are called the "fruit of entering that."
That entry into cause and effect is itself sublime; because this is sublime, the discourse is also sublime.
Regarding the distinctions in the cultivation of those causes and effects, they refer precisely to the causes and effects of the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).
Because one repeatedly practices this, it is called "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*); because there are distinct stages, it is called "differentiation" (*viśeṣa*).
This nature of the differentiation of cultivation regarding the cause and fruit of that entry is precisely the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
This is indeed preeminent; because this is preeminent, speech is also preeminent.

Within the specific cultivation of the perfections (pāramitās) across the various stages (bhūmis), one diligently practices further in order to fully embrace them. Taking this as the basis, the three trainings (śikṣā) are established:
first, the training in higher ethics (adhiśīla-śikṣā), which refers to practicing with right diligence by relying upon ethical discipline; therefore, it is called the training in higher ethics.

That is to say, within the various stages (*bhūmi*), the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline (*saṃvara*) consists of the three types of pure precepts: distancing oneself from all evils, benefiting sentient beings, and encompassing all virtues.

The *śīla* thus undertaken protects past and present bodily and other actions that have already arisen and remain; because it thoroughly restrains and governs them like a skilled trainer, it is called "discipline" (*saṃvara*).
Thus, because one trains in the correct practice by relying on this higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*), it is called "training" (*śikṣā*).
This higher ethical discipline is itself preeminent; because it is preeminent, the speech [concerning it] is also preeminent.
Second is the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*), which refers to the diligent cultivation based upon the mind; therefore, it is called the training in higher mind.
Its nature consists of various samādhis, such as the *ākāśagarbha* and others.
The term "and so forth" includes other samādhi-kings such as Bhadrapāla.
Furthermore, regarding the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*), it is said:
"The Great Teacher has declared that all these samādhis are the mind."
Because it is painted by the mind, it is like the work that has been performed.
The third is the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*); that is, relying upon wisdom, one diligently practices and trains, and for this reason it is called the training in higher wisdom.
This nature is precisely non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which serves as the antidote to all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
Among these, it is the basis for the preparatory non-conceptual wisdom, and this fundamental non-conceptual wisdom itself is the basis for the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
Such a basis is not what was stated in sequence.
These three trainings—of ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom—are the essential nature of the Path.
Their fruits are twofold: first, abandonment; second, knowledge. Because these are preeminent, the discourse regarding them is likewise preeminent.
Regarding "the abandonment of that fruit": the fruits of the various trainings are termed "that fruit," and the abandonment of that fruit is termed "the abandonment of that fruit.
This nature is precisely the dissociation from adventitious obstructions, which is *tathatā* (suchness), liberation, and non-abiding *nirvāṇa*.

Because one perceives that quiescence, saṃsāra is itself nirvāṇa; taking that very state as a condition, one remains free from defilement and attachment, yet this is not the nirvāṇa-realm without remainder.
Therefore, non-abiding is preeminent, and because it is preeminent, its expression is also preeminent.
Regarding "the wisdom of that fruit": the fruits of those various trainings are termed "that fruit," and the wisdom that constitutes that fruit is called "the wisdom of that fruit.
This nature consists of the three bodies of the Buddha:
first, the *svābhāvika-kāya* (self-nature body), which is stainless and unimpeded wisdom; this is the meaning of the *dharmakāya*.
Now, what is the distinction between this and that non-discriminative wisdom?

Since discriminative thought does not function in either of these two types, the former has an antidote and something yet to be accomplished, whereas this [latter] is its fruit, for which that which was to be done has already been completed; such is the distinction.

The second is the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), which is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Precisely because of the extraordinary power of this wisdom, it partakes together with a multitude of sublime great bodhisattvas in the uncommon, subtle joy of the Dharma and accomplishes such activities of enjoyment; therefore, it is called the enjoyment body.
If such external pure wisdom did not exist, the remaining provisions cultivated by the bodhisattva would not be fulfilled.

The three transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) are the specific manifestations of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); that which is capable of transforming is called the "transformation body," and it is the manifestation through the sovereign power of this wisdom that constitutes its specific differentiation.

That is to say, by means of this, one subdues the arguments of others, shares the joy of the Dharma with all bodhisattvas without interruption, and accomplishes the tasks to be performed by bodhisattvas at the stage of initial practice as well as by śrāvakas and others.
For example, just as visual consciousness perceives various forms, if that [consciousness] were non-existent, this [perception] would also not exist.
This [teaching] is therefore superior; because it is superior, its expression is also superior.
Regarding these ten points thus explained, they refer to the general meaning of this and other Mahāyāna teachings.
"Points" (sthāna) has the sense of "matters.
They differ from the Śrāvaka vehicle because those [points] are not taught therein.
Furthermore, it reveals the most excellent [teaching], because it definitively proclaims the path to the fruit of Buddhahood.

If the World-Honored One were merely teaching for the sake of bodhisattvas, one should have stated here that "the bodhisattva teaches only for the sake of bodhisattvas. However, because he teaches based on what the Buddha has directly perceived and what the Buddha has authorized, it is called "the teaching of the World-Honored One," as in the *Daśabhūmika* and other sūtras; therefore, the term "Bhagavān" is mentioned first.
The Commentary says:

Furthermore, how is it that by means of these ten marks of excellence, the speech of the Tathāgata is shown to be truly the Buddha’s word regarding the Mahāyāna, while the Śrāvaka vehicle is excluded from being of the nature of the Mahāyāna?
These ten points have never been taught within the Śrāvaka vehicle, but are found taught everywhere in the Mahāyāna.

That is to say, these ten points are most capable of inducing the nature of great enlightenment; they are well-established, consistent, and non-contradictory, serving as the means for realizing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñājñāna*).
Regarding this, there are two verses:
The basis of the knowable and its characteristics, Its entry, its cause and fruit, and its various cultivations, The three trainings,
their fruits, abandonment, and knowledge— Subsumed within the Supreme Vehicle, these are its excellences.
This teaching explains what is seen and what is not seen elsewhere;
because it is the most excellent cause for supreme enlightenment, the Mahāyāna is accepted as the true word of the Buddha, being distinguished by its exposition of the ten topics.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, as for the question "How is it by these [factors]?"—this objection is raised because [the interlocutor] has not yet attained faith and understanding. Why is this?

It is not that the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) and so forth have never been taught within the Śrāvakayāna; rather, they are seen taught here and there in the treatises of the Vaiśeṣikas and others.

Even if one were to grant that the treatises of the Vaiśeṣikas and others are truly the word of the Buddha, the previous response already accommodated such an objection; therefore, he subsequently provides a comprehensive rebuttal.

This means that these ten bases are most capable of inducing the nature of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*); it is called "great enlightenment" because it is both awakening (*bodha*) and great (*maha*), or because it awakens to the nature of greatness, and is thus termed "great enlightenment."

This great awakening has the excellence of wisdom and abandonment as its defining characteristic; as it is said, through the abandonment of the afflictive and cognitive obstructions, one attains stainless and unimpeded wisdom by virtue of that abandonment.
These four types are collectively termed "bodhi.

It is that which is most capable of inducing [enlightenment], meaning these ten bases are the means for attaining it, rather than the six categories of Vaiśeṣika or the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and so forth; therefore, that treatise is not the true word of the Buddha.
"Being well-established" means that these ten bases are followed by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as will be determined in detail below.
"Conforming" (*anuloma*) means being oriented toward [the goal] and having the sense of being in accordance with it.
Regarding the statement "there is no contradiction," this is because such faults do not exist.
It is not like the false cognitions of the six categories of Vaiśeṣika or other systems, nor like the Śrāvakayāna, which possesses defects that are incompatible with the fruit of Buddhahood.
Regarding these two verses, they summarize the meaning already explained and that which is yet to be explained.

As for the statement, "This is taught here, whereas it is not seen or taught elsewhere," this refers to the sublime discourse on these ten points, which is found throughout this Mahāyāna, but has never been seen or taught in other Hīnayāna vehicles.
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, why are these ten topics explained in this specific order?
It is because Bodhisattvas must first become proficient in the causes of all phenomena before they should attain skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Thereafter, one should skillfully master the characteristics of all phenomena produced from conditions, for this enables one to effectively distance oneself from the two extremes of the faults of superimposition and denial.
Subsequently, a bodhisattva who has thus cultivated skillfulness should correctly penetrate the well-grasped characteristics, thereby bringing about the liberation of the mind from all hindrances.

Thereafter, having attained mastery over the characteristics of the objects of knowledge, one should further perfect the superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) through the realization of the six perfections (*pāramitā*) previously practiced during the stage of application, so as to attain purification.

Thereafter, one should diligently cultivate the six pāramitās subsumed under the pure intention (*śuddhāśaya*), with their specific distinctions across the ten stages (*bhūmi*), which requires passing through three incalculable great eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Thereafter, one should bring to fulfillment that which is to be trained in regarding the three types of enlightenment (*trividha-bodhi*).
Once these are fulfilled, one should manifest and realize their fruits: nirvāṇa and unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Therefore, the ten bases are taught in this specific sequence.
Furthermore, within this teaching, all Mahāyāna systems reach their ultimate consummation.
Commentary:
To clarify how one proceeds toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*) by means of this, he further reveals the sequential methods and the necessary causes.

That is to say, Bodhisattvas must first attain skillfulness regarding the cause before they can attain skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). They must know that such-and-such an effect arises from such-and-such a cause, and furthermore, they must know that such-and-such an effect necessarily depends upon such-and-such a cause. Therefore, it is not possible to understand that cause through teachings apart from this [present] cause; that very cause is the *ālayavijñāna*.
By stating this, one abandons the views of causelessness and unequal causes.
Subsequently, regarding all phenomena produced through conditions, one should understand their characteristics in order to remain far removed from the extremes of superimposition and denial.

To forcibly establish what is non-existent and causeless as being existent is called "superimposition" (*samāropa*); to forcibly deny what is existent and causeless as being non-existent is called "denigration" (*apavāda*). Both such superimposition and denigration are described as "extremes" (*anta*), in the sense of falling away; when these two operate, they destroy the Middle Way.

By virtue of having well-cultivated the contemplation of reality through repeated practice, one becomes skillful in distancing oneself from these two extremes. Regarding the purely imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), there is only the fault of superimposition (*samāropa*) and never the fault of negation (*apavāda*), because it does not exist at all; for negation can only arise with respect to that which exists.

Regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there is no superimposition (*samāropa*), because it possesses substantial reality; for superimposition occurs only with respect to that which does not exist.
Nor is there any denial (*apavāda*), because it exists solely as a false appearance.
Regarding the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), there is no superimposition (*samāropa*), because it truly exists; there is only negation (*apavāda*).

Precisely for this reason—or rather, in this regard—one who is well able to avoid the faults of the two extremes of superimposition and negation is one who, with respect to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), superimposes a non-existent imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and negates the truly existent perfected nature.
Furthermore, as it is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:
"Maitreya, what do you think?"
Among all those things that are conceptually constructed, that which lacks real existence— is it form or non-form? "No,
World-Honored One."
"Within all that is dependently originated, there is only the nature of designation through names, concepts, and verbal expression; is it form or non-form?
"No, Blessed One."
"Among all perfected natures (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), is that emptiness and selflessness form or non-form? "No,
World-Honored One."

Maitreya! By this gateway, you should understand it thus: all thoroughly imagined natures (parikalpita-svabhāva) are definitively non-existent; all dependent natures (paratantra-svabhāva) exist only as designations, conceptualizations, and verbal expressions; and the emptiness and selflessness that constitute the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) are truly existent.
Based on this, I have spoken with intentional meaning that those [phenomena] such as form are "without duality. Thus, one is liberated from the faults of the two extremes.

Having attained skillfulness regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), one should thoroughly penetrate the characteristics of the knowable through the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).
"Entry" refers to thorough penetration and realization, or that by which one is able to accord with such penetration.

Subsequently, regarding the six perfections practiced within the entry into the essence of the thorough penetration of the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), they should be further realized from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and the pure intention (*śuddhāśaya*) should be further embraced.

Desire (*chanda*) and resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) are termed "intention" (*āśaya*); although these two do not increase in number at that time, they are described as "pure" because they are subsumed under the "purities of verified clarity" (*avetyaprasāda*).

Subsequently, within those same [stages], during the ten stages (*bhūmi*), because one diligently trains in the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) and practices them repeatedly throughout the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), they should be brought to fulfillment.

Subsequently, as for that fruit: the two obstructions of afflictions and the cognizable must be eternally severed, and the stainless, unimpeded knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) must further be realized.
Thus, the sequence of skillful means and the necessary causes as analyzed herein demonstrate that these are conducive to the nature of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
Precisely by virtue of this explained sequence, there are exactly ten points, neither more nor less.

Having thus explained both the *Mūla-śāstra* and the *Anu-śāstra*, one should therefore know that it is unreasonable to claim that the path of the Śrāvaka vehicle is identical to the path of the Buddha vehicle;
for if that were so, there would be no distinction between their fruits.
Furthermore, within all the Śrāvakayāna systems, there has never been a place where the path of the Buddha was extensively taught for the sake of bodhisattvas.

Moreover, it is not admitted that there is no difference between a Buddha and a śrāvaka, for otherwise the distinction between teacher and disciple could not be established; therefore, it is said that there is a distinction between two paths.
Therefore, it is said that this is called the "Compendium of the Mahāyāna" (*Mahāyānasaṃgraha*), because there is no separate exposition of any of the essential outlines of the Mahāyāna.
**Part 2: The Basis of the Knowable (*Jñeyāśraya-vibhāga*)** *Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Part Two, Section One: The Basis of the Knowable. The treatise says:
Herein, first of all, the basis of the knowable is explained; that is, the ālayavijñāna.
In what place did the Blessed One speak of the *ālayavijñāna* by the name of *ālayavijñāna*?
It was said by the Bhagavat in a verse of the *Mahāyānābhidharmasūtra*:
"The element (*dhātu*) from beginningless time, The common support of all phenomena..."
"From this arise the various realms of existence, as well as the realization of nirvāṇa.
Commentary: This citation from the Āgama proves that the ālayavijñāna is designated as the "basis of the knowable" (*jñeyāśraya*).
"Beginningless time" means that there is no initial limit.
"Element" (dhātu) means cause; it is the seed.
Of what is this the causal seed?
This means that all phenomena are exclusively defiled and not pure; therefore, it will later be stated that the basis for the cultivation of hearing is not subsumed within the *ālayavijñāna*.
Just as the ālayavijñāna functions as the seed— such as that which arises from correct mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*) and appears as phenomena and their objects—
it is the support for all those phenomena because it can sustain them, and not because it is their causal nature.
The meaning of "capable of supporting" is the meaning of "basis," not the meaning of "causal nature," because the natures of the basis and the based are distinct.
If it were otherwise, the term *dhātu* (element/realm) alone would suffice, and the word "basis" (*āśraya*) would be redundant.
Regarding the statement that "by this there are the various realms of existence and the attainment of nirvāṇa," this shall be analyzed in detail as it appears in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*.

That is to say, the defilements of birth and so forth, such as those in the hells (*naraka*) and other states—if these births and so forth were to exist apart from the *ālayavijñāna*, they could not possibly occur.
The ultimate cessation of all afflictions (saṃkleśa) is called nirvāṇa; this cannot be realized apart from the ālayavijñāna.
The treatise states:
Furthermore, regarding this very point, a verse is spoken:
"Because it stores all phenomena, The consciousness of all seeds Is therefore called the ālaya; This I have revealed to the Victors. Commentary:
Furthermore, citing the scriptural teachings, it is proven that the *ālayavijñāna* is named *ālaya*.

That which "is able to store and conceal all phenomena" means it is that which is perfumed and constitutes the sense of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), rather than being like the *mahābhūtas* or other manifest phenomena.
Within the *kośa* (the most excellent treasury), the manner in which the *ālayavijñāna* contains and stores all phenomena is likewise.
To distinguish this specific meaning, it is further described as the "consciousness of all seeds," because it arises and ceases simultaneously with all seeds.
Because the *ālayavijñāna* and the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) serve as mutual conditions for one another, they mutually contain and store [seeds];

therefore, it is called the *ālayavijñāna*. It is not like the "Most Excellent" (*jina*), which is of a manifest nature; because it manifests itself by distinguishing itself from the inferior, it is further stated: "I reveal it to the 'Excellent Ones' (*jināḥ*). This means that because Great Bodhisattvas possess the requisite capacity, they are called "Excellent Ones"; it is for them that it is revealed, and not for others who are inferior.
The treatise says:
Thus far, we have cited the Āgamas as proof.
For what reason, moreover, is this consciousness called the ālayavijñāna?
Because all phenomena belonging to the category of defilement that have arisen are stored within this [consciousness] as its fruit-nature,
and because this very consciousness is stored within them as their cause-nature, it is therefore called the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Alternatively, because sentient beings grasp and conceal this consciousness as a self, it is therefore called the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
The commentary states:
"All that has birth" refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
The dharmas of the category of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) are distinguished from pure dharmas.

Non-pure dharmas are of an afflicted nature; they are comprised within the essential nature of the seeds that constitute the treasury of all afflictions, because [the pure dharmas] are able to counteract them.

It is not the case that being mutually contradictory constitutes the nature of cause and effect; rather, this is the correct principle. Nevertheless, it can serve as a basis, because wherever there is that which is to be remedied, there is also that which remedies it.
Regarding the term "that which contains and stores" (*saṃgraha*), this indicates its capacity to maintain habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

It is not that only habitual tendencies are called the *ālayavijñāna*; rather, it must be that which can maintain habitual tendencies, just as it is said regarding the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Alternatively, for those sentient beings who grasp and conceal this consciousness as a self, it has the sense of "clinging.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, this consciousness is also called the *ādāna-vijñāna* (appropriating consciousness).
Regarding the *āgama* in this context, as stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*:
"The appropriating consciousness (*ādāna-vijñāna*) is profound and subtle;
Containing all seeds like a torrential stream, I do not reveal it to the foolish and ignorant, Fearing they would conceptually grasp it as a self."
The commentary states:
Furthermore, by citing other teachings that employ alternative names, the *ālayavijñāna* is revealed and established so as to be made perfectly clear.
It is called "profound" because its depths are difficult for even the most intelligent and wise people to fathom.

Regarding the statement that it is "extremely subtle": because it is difficult for the śrāvakas and others to comprehend, this consciousness is not revealed to them; for they do not seek the subtle knowledge of all-knowledge (sarvajñajñāna).
"All seeds are like a torrent" means that they continue in an uninterrupted succession from moment to moment, just like a rushing torrent of water.

"I do not reveal this to the foolish and ignorant" means that I do not disclose it to those who harbor the view of a self (*ātman*), for fear that they would conceptually construct and cling to it as a self.
How could such categories of beings maintain their conceptual constructions and attachments until the very end of saṃsāra?
For their mode of activity is of a single type, remaining without change.
The treatise says:
For what reason is this consciousness also called the *ādāna-vijñāna*?
Because it appropriates all material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and because it is the basis for the grasping of all personal existences (*ātman*).
Why is this so? Because there are material sense-faculties which, through this appropriation (*upādāna*), remain without decay or destruction and persist throughout one's lifespan.
Furthermore, at the moment of linking rebirth within the continuum, one appropriates a physical body by taking up that birth.
Therefore, this consciousness is also called the *ādāna-vijñāna*.
The commentary explains:

"Because it appropriates all material sense-faculties," and so forth; this indicates the reason for the application of the term. Because it is able to appropriate all material sense-faculties, such as the eye, and because their security and peril are shared and it persists throughout the duration of life, it is therefore called the *ādāna-vijñāna*.
If it were not so, it would perish immediately like a dead body, because it is the basis for the appropriation of all personal entities (*ātma-bhāva*).
The word "etc. refers to all such things, whether singular or plural, that possess the nature of being the basis for the appropriation of personal entities.
If the faculties such as form have not yet arisen, or if the self-body of the formless realm arises, this is called "continuity" (*saṃtati*).
Because it appropriates that [existence], it is termed "correct linking of birth" (*pratisaṃdhi*); because one undergoes that birth and because of the union of semen and blood.

It is not that there is no ālayavijñāna while there is the appropriation of a self-body for the duration of a single lifetime; it is, for example, like a house or courtyard encompassing light, because this self-body for a single lifetime is permeated by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The treatise says:
This is also called "mind" (*citta*), as the Blessed One has said:
"Mind, mentation (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—these three."
In this context, there are two types of intention (*manas*):

first, it serves as the basis for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*); that is, consciousness that has just ceased can serve as the generative basis for mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

The second is the afflicted manas, which is always associated with four afflictions: first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); second, the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*); third, self-love (*ātmasneha*); and fourth, ignorance (*avidyā*). This is the basis for the defilement of consciousness.
Furthermore, consciousness arises from that first basis and is defiled by the second; it is termed "mind" (*manas*) in two ways:
because it cognizes objects, and because it has the sense of being the immediate antecedent (*samanantara*) and the sense of deliberation (*manana*).
The commentary states:
This is also called "mind" (*citta*); furthermore, by citing other teachings to establish alternative names, this [concept] is made firm.
Regarding the second, the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭamanas*), it is so called because it is defiled by the four afflictions, beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Among these, the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) refers to the firm attachment to the nature of "self" and "what belongs to self.
By the power of this [attachment], one gives rise to the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*), and relying upon "self" and "what belongs to self," one exalts oneself.
Because these two exist, craving for a self arises; this is termed "self-love" (*ātmasneha*).
All three of these take ignorance (*avidyā*) as their cause.
What is called ignorance is precisely a lack of knowledge, as it is that which is counteracted by clear knowledge (*vidyā*).

This is precisely the basis for the defilement of consciousness; it is not in contradiction with any state—whether determinate or indeterminate, wholesome or otherwise—because it is constantly active.
In what manner is this so?
This means that even at the time of a wholesome mind, one still clings to a self.
It arises based on the first [basis] because it arises from the immediately preceding ceased mind (*manas*).
It is defiled by the second because it is associated with the four afflictions; for the mind, by conceiving of a self and so forth, is able to produce defilement.
"Because it discerns the meaning of objects" means that it is capable of apprehending objects and appearing as those objects; this explains the name "vijñāna" (consciousness).

"Because it has the meaning of immediate succession" and "because it has the meaning of cogitation"—these two explain the name "manas" (mind). If one does not employ the principles for explaining the etymological meanings of words, one will ultimately be unable to cause others to achieve understanding.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, how is it known that there exists a defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*)?
It is because if this were non-existent, the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) could not exist, which would result in a logical fallacy.
Furthermore, the five [mental consciousnesses] possessing the same nature [as the sense consciousnesses] cannot exist, as this would result in logical fallacies.
Why is this so? Because the five groups of consciousness must necessarily have the simultaneous supports (sahabhū-āśraya), such as the eye and the other sense organs.
Furthermore, the etymological definitions [of these states] would be untenable, resulting in logical fallacies.
Moreover, there would be no distinction between the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), which likewise results in a logical fallacy.

This means that the non-ideational attainment (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is manifested by the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*), whereas the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is not. If this were not the case, there would be no distinction between these two attainments.

Furthermore, it would entail the error that there is no affliction during the course of a single lifetime in the Heaven of No Perception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), provided that self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) and the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) do not exist therein.
Furthermore, the activity of the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*) is perceptible at all times, occurring within minds that are wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
Were it otherwise, only unwholesome minds would exhibit the activity of the afflictions of "I" and "mine" (*ahaṃkāra* and *mamakāra*) through association with it, and not wholesome or neutral ones.
Therefore, if one posits that they function as co-existent (sahabhū) but not as associated (samprayukta), this fault does not arise.
Regarding this, the verse says:
If it were non-common ignorance (*avidyā*), And shared the same characteristics as the five [aggregates],...
Regarding the two [points] of the instructional verses on definitive distinction: if [the self] were non-existent, both would result in faults.

There would be no Lord of the Unconscious; the persistence of the grasping at a self would become a fault, as that grasping would constantly follow [the person], yet it would not exist in any way whatsoever.
If the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) did not exist, there would be a contradiction regarding the [simultaneous] presence of two or three [minds].
Since it does not exist in any state, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) should not occur.
It constantly acts as an obstacle to the arising of the mind that realizes the true meaning (*tattvārtha*).
It accompanies all factors; this refers to the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).
Because this manas is defiled, it is of the nature of obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and is always associated with the four afflictions.

Just as the afflictions of the two entanglements—those of the form and formless realms—are subsumed under the category of obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) nature, because the entanglements of the form and formless realms are concealed by śamatha, and because this manas follows along subtly at all times.
The commentary states:
In order to lead to the correct principle for establishing the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), the verse is again briefly cited and explained directly.

That is to say, "If this did not exist, the non-common ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) could not exist," and so forth; for if the afflicted mind were not said to exist, then the non-common ignorance could not exist.
The characteristics of non-associated ignorance shall now be explained: it is the delusion that acts as an obstacle to the arising of true knowledge.
This cannot be said to exist within the five sensory consciousnesses, because there is no antidote present in those states.
Wherever there is an antidote, there is that which is to be countered; however, the antidote does not exist within the five consciousnesses, because the Path of Seeing does not arise therein.
It does not exist within the non-defiled mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because if it were there, that consciousness would consequently become defiled.
Nor does it exist within the defiled mental consciousness, because when it is associated with other afflictions, the designation "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇikī avidyā*) would be untenable.

If it were established that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) becomes defiled by virtue of those afflictions, then it would follow that it must be definitively of a defiled nature; consequently, states of mind such as generosity would not be wholesome, because they would be constantly associated with the characteristics of those afflictions.
Furthermore, if it were said that those afflictions coexist with a virtuous mind, then they would be exclusively associated with it, and no others could exist therein.
It would be illogical for such a defiled mental consciousness to induce its own antidote.

If it is said that there exists a distinct wholesome mind co-arising with the afflicted mind (kliṣṭamanas), such that because the antidote capable of counteracting it arises, the object to be countered is extinguished, this conforms to correct reasoning.

If that were so, then the "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇikī avidyā*) you have established would also not be tenable, because it is always associated with other afflictions such as the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Your objection is unfair; I do not say it is called "unshared" because it is not associated with other afflictions. Rather, I say it is called "unshared" because that particular delusion does not exist elsewhere, just as, for example, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) are so named.
The previous statement that [a cognition] associated with other afflictions is not established was made to demonstrate the faults in the opponent's position through analysis.

Furthermore, regarding the fault that the five [sensory cognitions] would also fail to be established due to their shared nature (*sādharmya*), this refutes the claim that the six consciousnesses arise solely from two conditions—the six [objects] and the six [faculties]—and asserts instead that the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, share a common nature with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

That is to say, it arises from two conditions; if that afflicted manas did not exist, it would be contrary to this, because there would be no distinct simultaneous dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) upon which it depends.

Furthermore, the visual consciousness and the other consciousnesses each possess two conditions and are all of the nature of consciousness; such natures of consciousness all have distinct bases that arise simultaneously with the eyes and so forth, which serve as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) alone and not as causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the like.
This serves as the illustrative analogy.
It is the same for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); it too must have such a distinct basis.

Although the *ālayavijñāna* is the co-emergent basis of the mental consciousness, it should not be established as this specific basis, because it is a common basis and its nature is that of a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The Sautrāntika position that matter (*rūpa*) serves as a distinct, co-arising support for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is untenable and does not accord with reason. This is because,
in relation to the conceptualizations of investigation (*abhinirūpaṇa-vikalpa*) and recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*), [the mental consciousness] would necessarily be non-conceptual at all times.

By this reasoning, the position established by other schools—that there is a material entity within the chest serving as a distinct support for the mental consciousness—is also not tenable, because the aforementioned faults persistently follow it.
For example, just as the various consciousnesses depend upon the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*), such difficult points should be extensively analyzed and resolved.

Furthermore, regarding the etymological derivation (*nirukti*), there would otherwise be the fault of its non-establishment: as previously stated, the meaning of the term *manas* is based on its nature of "deliberation" (*manana*). If a defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) were not established, what would this [term] depend upon?
The six consciousnesses, having already ceased, cannot constitute the *manas*, because their substance has perished and no longer exists.

Furthermore, regarding the distinction between the absorption of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), there would be the fault of making them indistinguishable. If one were to establish the existence of a defiled *manas*, does this exist or not exist in the continuum of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and in the continuum of noble ones (*ārya*)?
In this sequence, the principle for the distinction between the two meditative attainments is established.

If it were otherwise, there would be no difference between them regarding the existence of mental activity despite the cessation of perception and feeling; nor could one say that they are distinguished by their respective levels—the fourth dhyāna and the level of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra)—or by the difference in their desire for liberation and peaceful dwelling. Thus, the distinction between the two attainments is proven.

Since there is no distinction between the two in terms of their intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), what difference is there in the simultaneous cessation of the mind and its mental factors (*caitta*)?
This present determination is made because it is somewhat closer to the position of the Sautrāntikas.

According to the tenets of that school, the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) do not exist as substantial entities; how then could there be a real distinction between the two meditative attainments?

Furthermore, it would entail the logical error that during the course of a single lifetime in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) would no longer arise.
Regarding the term "non-conceptual" (*asaṃjñin*): it refers to those born within the Heaven of Non-conceptual Beings (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*).
There, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) cease; at the moment of initial rebirth, they arise momentarily, and from that point onward, they continue in a continuous succession.

If the existence of a defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) were not admitted, there would be no grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*) throughout the course of a single lifetime; yet it has never been observed that one possessed of afflictions could remain entirely without grasping at a self for the duration of a single lifetime.

Furthermore, because all noble ones (ārya) likewise censure and loathe it, it is not the case that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arising at the moment of birth is the basis for the grasping of a self (*ātma-grāha*). This is because [the self-grasping] is projected by the force [of previous habituation]; thus, it is said that "self-grasping has not been permanently severed. This is consistent with reason, just as in the case of those suffering from epilepsy and the like.
Because both the basis of the grasping at a self and [the self] itself have ceased, and because there is no further basis for the momentum of its projection, [your position] is illogical.
Furthermore, it is also unreasonable that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the grasping at a self should persist within the continuum of the body.
It is not logical for material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) to be perfumed, as they lack such capacity.

Furthermore, the Sautrāntika masters do not assert that matter alone is designated as mental phenomena (*cittadharma*), because the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is absent in matter, and because mind and mental factors are fixed as having four conditions.
If one asserts that there exists a distinct, eternally co-arising mind which serves as the basis for the grasping at a self, this would be without fault.
However, it is not logical that the grasping at a self should persist in all moments [of consciousness].
That is to say, if one does not posit the existence of the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*), it would be inconsistent with the facts at all times.

Even in virtuous states such as generosity, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) constantly follows along; one thinks, "I am able to practice generosity," and this does not occur apart from the accompaniment of the grasping at a self rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*).
Ignorance does not exist apart from its basis, for it is a mental factor (*citta-dharma*).
This basis, moreover, cannot possibly exist apart from the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*).
It is not logically tenable that a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*) itself is the basis of ignorance.
As it is said:
"In this way, the afflicted mind (kliṣṭamanas) is the support of consciousness;
as long as this is not extinguished, consciousness remains bound and can never attain liberation."
"Non-dual" refers to the unique ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*) and the five factors common to it.

"The three constitute contradictions" means that the etymological derivation, the distinction between the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and the persistence of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) among those born in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*)—these three all constitute contradictions.
Having previously briefly mentioned the unique ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyā*), it is now explained in detail; thus, the true meaning is stated:
"the mind is about to arise," and so forth, which refers to that which can obstruct the vision of the true meaning (*tattvārtha*).
If that [seed] were presently existing, this [result] would not arise.
"Accompanying all states" means that it constantly follows and operates throughout the states of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
The treatise states:
Regarding the third [aspect], the substance of mind (*citta*), if one were to exclude the *ālayavijñāna*, no other distinct entity could be found.
Therefore, it is established that the *ālayavijñāna* constitutes the substance of mind; with this as its seed, the *manas* and the [six] consciousnesses evolve.
The commentary states:

Regarding the third [aspect], the essence of mind—if nothing else were obtainable apart from the ālayavijñāna—it would mean that the term "defiled mind" (kliṣṭamanas) refers to the manas, while the term "immediately ceased mental consciousness" refers to the six types of evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna).
Thus, neither mind nor sound can be found to have an intrinsic nature apart from those two; yet it is not the case that there is no intrinsic nature while there exists that which expresses it.
Nor are they distinct categories, for the consciousness and the two sounds express different objects.
In this context, the term "essence" (*tattva*) is intended to signify that which is expressed.
Therefore, the phrase "establishing the *ālayavijñāna* and so forth" demonstrates that it is a definitive principle that the *ālayavijñāna* is that which is expressed by the term "mind" (*citta*).
The treatise says:
For what reason is it also called "mind" (citta)?
Because it is accumulated by the seeds perfumed by various phenomena (dharma).
The commentary states:
"By means of various dharmas" refers to the various categories of dharmas subsumed under the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
"Seeds of perfuming" refers to the specific functional capacities established through perfuming.
That which is "accumulated" refers to the accumulation therein of various kinds of things.
"Hence" (*gata*) has the meaning of "gate" (*dvāra*) and the meaning of "basis" (*āśraya*).
This demonstrates the cause for the arising of mental verbalization.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, for what reason is this mind not taught in the Śrāvaka vehicle under the name *ālayavijñāna* or the name *ādānavijñāna*?
It is because it is subsumed within a sphere that is profoundly subtle.

Why is this so? Because the śrāvakas do not operate within the sphere of all objects and knowledge; therefore, although they could attain wisdom and achieve liberation even without this teaching, it was not taught to them.
If bodhisattvas are certain to engage with all objects and states of knowledge, it is for this reason that this is taught.
Apart from this wisdom, it is not easy to realize the knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*).
The commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "because it is comprised within this profound and subtle object," this indicates that the *ālayavijñāna* is both profound and subtle, and is thus an object of knowledge (*jñeya*).
Because it is profound and subtle, it was not taught to the *śrāvakas*.
Because they are objects of knowledge that are coarse and superficial, being suitable for those to be converted; thus, profound and subtle wisdom provides no benefit to them.
That "the śrāvakas do not operate within the sphere of all objects and wisdom" reveals that they lack the capacity or aspiration for such a domain.

Therefore, regarding the phrase "even though for them this teaching is absent," it means that although the *ālayavijñāna* is not taught to the Śrāvakas, they are nonetheless able to permanently sever all afflictions by correctly observing coarse and superficial objects such as form (*rūpa*), the nature of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), and the characteristics of impermanence (*anityatā*).
For this purpose, he diligently practices the holy life (brahmacarya) in the presence of the Blessed One.
As for the term "coarse and superficial," it refers to the fact that the essential characteristics (lakṣaṇa) of all material phenomena (rūpadharma) are coarse.

Furthermore, phenomena such as sensation (vedanā) and so forth have objects of perception (ālambana) and modes of activity (ākāra) that are easily distinguishable, because their modes of activity are coarse.
Contrary to this, the ālayavijñāna is described as "deep and subtle" according to its specific characteristics.

As it is said, "I do not say that there is even a single dharma that has not been reached or fully known," this is a statement of intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-vacana*). It refers to the state of non-abandonment of the afflictions by using a term for a specific characteristic to express a general characteristic; it does not mean that the various afflictions are abandoned individually.
Alternatively, because they apprehend common characteristics such as impermanence and so forth, it is not taught that the *ālayavijñāna* exists; yet there is no fault in this.

If bodhisattvas definitely engage with all objects and the sphere of knowledge, this reveals that bodhisattvas possess the power of their spiritual lineage (*gotra*), for they are endowed with the complete correspondence of functional capacity, aspiration, and the sphere [of practice].
The nature of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) is the goal to be attained; apart from this, one cannot accomplish the welfare of others. Why is this so?

Without omniscience, there is no capacity to understand the inclinations and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of others, nor their spiritual elements (*dhātu*), faculties (*indriya*), and degrees of excellence or inferiority, nor their capacities and incapacities, nor the distinctions of time—all of which are required to fully accomplish the welfare of all others.
Such matters as these are what the bodhisattva seeks; therefore, the *ālayavijñāna* is taught.

Regarding the phrase "if one is separated from this wisdom," it means that if one is separated from the *ālayavijñāna*, wisdom cannot permanently sever the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) regarding objects.
Because that [grasping] is not severed, non-conceptual wisdom cannot arise, for one clings to the existence of objects imagined by the parikalpita-svabhāva.
Due to these causes and conditions, it is not easy to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Why is this so? Because while one can realize the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all that is knowable, this is the object of conceptualizing wisdom (*vikalpa-jñāna*) which cognizes the imagined nature (*parikalpita-artha*). Since the distinctions of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) differ from one another and are infinite, it is certain that no one can fully realize them all.

If one knows that these [appearances] manifest as objects, sentient beings, and a self solely through the power of the transformation of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) produced by the *ālayavijñāna*, then at that time one realizes the non-existence of the apprehended object (*grāhya*). Likewise, one can also know the non-existence of the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*). Thereby, one attains non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), and subsequently, through the wisdom attained after [meditation] (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one penetrates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) according to what has been practiced.

Revealed by the common characteristics of all phenomena, suchness is of a single flavor; thus, one knows all phenomena and can easily realize this in a single instant, for the objects and wisdom of all things are not infinite.

Furthermore, as for the statement that one must pass through three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), this reveals that only by accumulating vast provisions (*saṃbhāra*) can one realize the subtle wisdom of the fruit that possesses all modes of appearance (*sarvākāra-jñatā*), which is both vast and supreme.
The aforementioned provisions for sublime wisdom are not separate from the realization of the object that is the selflessness of phenomena.
Therefore, it is said in verse:
Without severing the conceptualization of grasping at objects within the entire range of the knowable, [one cannot attain this wisdom].
And is able to realize all-knowledge; Therefore, he proclaims the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Because they do not properly comprehend such principles and teachings, there is a verse that says:
"By virtue of their mental continuity possessing such capacity, One should know that they consume everything, just like fire."
In this way, one must admit that the Omniscient One is capable of knowing all things and knowing everything.

Therefore, regarding whether or not this *ālayavijñāna* is known, those who seek to realize or fail to realize the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) should certainly base their assertions on this school [of thought].

One who does not know that all phenomena are without self is not called "All-Knowing" (*sarvajña*); although such a person possesses all-knowledge, they do not possess the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle One;
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle Two.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asvabhāva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part Two of the Second Section: The Basis of the Knowable. The Treatise says:
Furthermore, within the Śrāvakayāna, the ālayavijñāna has also been taught through various indirect methods and intentional terminology (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
As it is said in the *Ekottarika Āgama*:
"The sentient beings of the world love the ālaya, delight in the ālaya, rejoice in the ālaya, and find pleasure in the ālaya."
In order to sever such an ālaya, when the True Dharma is taught, one listens with reverence, dwells in a mind seeking understanding, and practices in accordance with the Dharma.
The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is thus a most marvelous and rare occurrence; such a True Dharma appears in the world.
In the Śrāvaka vehicle, within the *Tathāgatotpattisambhavanirdeśa-caturguṇasūtra*, the ālayavijñāna has been revealed through this intentional terminology (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
Furthermore, in the Āgamas of the Mahāsāṃghika school, it is also taught through intentional terminology as the "root-consciousness" (*mūlavijñāna*), just as a tree depends upon its roots.
Within the Mahīśāsaka school as well, this is referred to by another synonym with intentional meaning as the "skandhas that exhaust saṃsāra.
There may be occasions and places where form and mind are seen to be interrupted, yet within the ālayavijñāna, their seeds are never interrupted.
The commentary states:

Regarding the statement that "within the Śrāvakayāna, the ālayavijñāna has also been taught through various indirect methods (saṃdhāya)," this is mentioned first as a general introduction to show that the ālayavijñāna is like a great royal road, established in common by other schools.
As stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, this is the teaching of the Sarvāstivāda school.
The phrase "those who love the ālaya" is a general statement referring to those who are greedily attached to the *ālayavijñāna*.
"Delighting in the ālaya" refers to delighting in the ālayavijñāna of the present life.
"Rejoicing in the ālaya" refers to rejoicing in the ālayavijñāna that has already arisen in past lives.
"Delighting in the ālaya" means delighting in the future arising of the ālayavijñāna.
Because this nature intensely aspires toward that [arising], and because it takes pleasure and joy therein, it is collectively termed "craving for the ālaya."
"Regarding the phrase 'for the sake of severing such an ālaya,' it means for the purpose of permanently destroying it.
Regarding 'when the true Dharma is being taught,' it refers to the teaching of the true doctrine.
Regarding 'reverence,' it refers to the desire to hear [the teaching]."
"Applying the ear" means listening with a firm vow; this refers to the wisdom resulting from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
"Abiding in a mind seeking understanding" means seeking certainty regarding the meaning as it has been heard; this refers to the wisdom resulting from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

Regarding "one who practices in accordance with the Dharma" (*dharmānudharmapratipanna*): that which is realized is called the *dharma*, while the Path is called *anudharma* because it conforms to it.
Furthermore, the supramundane path is called the *dharma*, and the mundane path is called *anudharma*.

As the practitioner practices that, his own mental continuum increases those [images] because the tree has increased them; since he causes them to manifest and attain mastery, this refers to the knowledge produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).

Regarding the statement in the *Tathāgatotpattisambhavanirdeśa-sūtra* that the ālayavijñāna is revealed through this implicit intention (*samdhāya*) by means of a particular method: it refers to how that sūtra proclaims that the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world possesses four kinds of praiseworthy qualities.
Regarding the *Āgamas* of the Mahāsāṃghika school and others, this consciousness is established therein as being like a great royal highway.
The fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is the cause of the other consciousnesses, just as the root of a tree is the cause of the trunk and so forth.
Regarding the Mahīśāsaka school and others, within that school there are three kinds of aggregates (*skandha*):
first, the aggregate of a single moment, which refers to phenomena that arise and perish in a single instant;
second, the aggregate of a single lifetime, which refers to phenomena that persist and follow one throughout until death.

Third is the aggregate that exhausts birth and death (*ātyantika-saṃsāra-skandha*), which refers to those phenomena that continue to function until the attainment of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).

If this were excluded from the *ālayavijñāna*, it could not exist elsewhere; it is merely another name for the *ālayavijñāna*, just as the term "aggregates" (*skandha*) definitely does not apply to that which exhausts birth and death.

If one asks, "In what way? this answer states that "seeing occurs in certain places and at certain times. "In certain places" refers to the realm (*dhātu*); "at certain times" refers to specific phases (*avasthā*). This means that in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), all forms are interrupted; and in the Unconscious Heaven (*asaṃjñisattva*) and during the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), all mental states are interrupted. It does not mean that forms and the seeds of mind are interrupted within the *ālayavijñāna*.
Until the path of counteraction has arisen, there is an interval during which [the state] should not be conceptually imputed.
Since the correct meaning exists as it ought to exist,
it is unreasonable to conceptually impute a secondary meaning that contradicts the correct meaning.
The treatise says:

Thus, regarding this basis of the knowable, it is taught that its nature consists of the *ālayavijñāna*, the *ādānavijñāna*, the mind (*citta*), the *ālaya*, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and the aggregates that persist until the end of saṃsāra (*āsaṃsārika-skandha*).
By this alternative formulation, the *ālayavijñāna* becomes the great royal road.
The commentary explains:

"Etc. refers to the fact that within the noble Sthavira school, this consciousness is also spoken of by the term *bhavāṅga* (the constituent of existence), because the *ālayavijñāna* is the cause of existence (*bhava-hetu*), just as it is said that the six consciousnesses neither die nor are born.
Death may occur either through the *bhavāṅga* (the constituent of existence) or through contrary conditions; one is then born from the resultant consciousness-element (*vipākavijñānadhātu*).
Since it is only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that can thus project [a new existence], it is said:

"The five consciousnesses have no discernment regarding phenomena; they are merely projected. The same applies to the mind-element (*manodhātu*): it merely seeks, while the visual consciousness merely illuminates.
Regarding "pervading equally": it refers to the establishment of definitive wisdom, which is capable of initiating verbal discrimination.

The six consciousnesses can only follow along with the performance of deportment; they cannot receive wholesome or unwholesome courses of action, cannot enter meditative absorption, and cannot emerge from meditative absorption. Their functional power, however, is capable of initiating all such activities.
Because it can induce awakening from sleep and, by its functional power, observes the events of dreams,
and so forth, the Vibhajyavādins also call this consciousness the "constituent consciousness" (bhavāṅga-vijñāna).
Because the various scriptural authorities of these schools serve as valid criteria, the ālayavijñāna is like a great royal highway.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, there is a certain class [of scholars] who claim that the terms *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* have the same meaning despite differing expressions.
This argument is not established, for a distinction between the two meanings of *manas* and *vijñāna* can be perceived; therefore, one should know that the meaning of *citta* must likewise differ.

Furthermore, there is another class [of teachers] who claim that what the Blessed One said—"sentient beings are attached to the *ālaya*"—and so forth at length, refers here to the five appropriated aggregates (*pañcopādānaskandha*) being designated as the *ālaya*.
Others again claim that the feeling of pleasure associated with craving is the *ālaya*.
Still others claim that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the *ālaya*.
These various teachers hold such views because they are ignorant of the *ālayavijñāna* both through scripture and through realization.
Establishing the name "ālaya" in this manner is also inconsistent with the principles established according to the Śrāvaka-yāna.
However, for one who is not deluded, if they grasp the ālayavijñāna and establish it by applying that name "ālaya," such an establishment is the most excellent.
What is the most excellent [explanation]?

If the five aggregates of clinging were called the *ālaya*, it would be illogical for them to be that which is grasped and stored (*upādāna*), because when one is born in the miserable destinies—a place of uniform suffering—it is utterly loathsome and repulsive; sentient beings never give rise to affection or delight therein, and since they constantly seek to abandon and leave it behind, it is unreasonable for it to be the locus of appropriation.

If the feeling of pleasure associated with craving were called the *ālaya*, it would not exist from the fourth dhyāna upward; furthermore, sentient beings possessing those states would always feel aversion toward it, and thus it would be illogical for them to harbor [the seeds] within it.

If the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) were called the *ālaya*, then those who have faith and understanding in this True Dharma and constantly feel aversion toward it would find it irrational to maintain a sense of appropriation (*upādāna*) within it.

Although the ālayavijñāna is comprised within the nature of an internal self, and even when one is born in the miserable realms—a place of constant suffering—one seeks to escape the aggregates of suffering, yet that [seeker] is always bound by the attachment to the ālayavijñāna as a self and never seeks to abandon it.

Although those born in the fourth dhyāna or above constantly feel aversion toward the pleasure associated with craving, they are nevertheless perpetually bound by the love of self toward the ālayavijñāna.
Although those who have faith and understanding in this True Dharma and who loathe and oppose the view of self may still be constantly bound by self-love toward the *ālayavijñāna*.
Therefore, establishing the name *ālaya* for the *ālayavijñāna* is most excellent and definitive.
The commentary states:
