Furthermore, there is a certain class of people who claim that "mind" (*citta*), "intellect" (*manas*), and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) differ only in expression while having the same meaning; this reveals their erroneous attachment, for they assert that the names "mind," "intellect," and "consciousness" as explained all refer to one and the same thing.
If this meaning were not established, it would be an irrational position.

That the two meanings of "consciousness" (vijñāna) and "mind" (manas) can be distinguished is because the two sounds and their two meanings—the signifier and the signified—possess distinct intrinsic natures (svalakṣaṇa).
That is to say, the six groups of consciousness that have passed away immediately prior are designated as "mind" (manas), while the discernment of objects is designated as "consciousness" (vijñāna).
Just as there is a distinction between the names and meanings of "mind" and "consciousness," so too should there be a difference in the meaning of "mind" (citta).

Furthermore, there is another class who say that what was taught by the Bhagavat [refers to something else]; this indicates that other teachers hold divergent interpretations regarding the *ālaya* and so forth.
To say that the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are called the *ālaya* means that all sentient beings grasp them as a self.

Regarding the statement that "the feeling of pleasure accompanied by craving is called the *ālaya*," this means that the aggregate of feelings co-arising with craving is collectively termed the *ālaya*, because this feeling is the locus where the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of craving increase.
Alternatively, each [of these views] may individually be called *ālaya*, because the points of attachment differ.
As for the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) being called *ālaya*, it is because one grasps that [aggregation] as having the nature of a self.

As for these masters who, due to ignorance regarding the ālayavijñāna through both scripture and realization, hold such a view: it means that those masters possess flawed scripture and flawed realization, and thus they are ignorant of the ālayavijñāna.
Alternatively, because those masters lack a personal teacher and lack their own understanding, they are deluded regarding the ālayavijñāna.
Even the principles established according to the Śrāvaka vehicle are inconsistent; furthermore, even according to their own school, it is not logical.
The "substances" (*dravya*) and so forth established by the Vaiśeṣika and other schools are not supreme, because they are subject to faults.
That which is established in this manner is supreme, because it is free from faults and possesses excellent qualities.
In order to reveal the faults of that conceptual attachment, he asks again:
"What is most excellent?

If one establishes the five appropriated aggregates (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as the *ālayavijñāna*, then those born in the realms of evil destinies where there is exclusively suffering are called "born in evil destinies. Because they possess only suffering and because suffering appears [there], these are called "places of exclusive suffering. These refer to birth in the hells (*naraka*), the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*), and the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Because it has never possessed even the slightest pleasure, it is most loathsome;

because it is characterized by manifold suffering at all times, sentient beings never give rise to affection for it. It is not that there is no sense of being "unloved," but rather that it lacks the meaning of being "appropriated" (*ālaya*), as it is incompatible with the sense of appropriation.
It is unreasonable to maintain that [the ālayavijñāna] is stored therein, because those who constantly seek to abandon it quickly are always lamenting over the aggregate of suffering, thinking:
"How might I be free from this aggregate of suffering?"
It is not reasonable to maintain that [the storehouse consciousness] is sought for the sake of swift liberation, because such a claim contradicts correct principle.

In the fourth dhyāna and the higher formless realms, the feeling of craving-accompanied pleasure is perpetually absent; rather, there is constant aversion, because these states are the cause of such aversion and are inherently loathsome.

Regarding the statement "possessing that," sentient beings in the fourth dhyāna and above possess that type [of mind]; therefore, it is also illogical to maintain that those places are the locus of appropriation (*upādāna*), because such a mind does not exist there.

Those who possess faith and understanding of selflessness within this True Dharma constantly and intensely loathe the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because it is that which must be abandoned.

Since such a view does not exist for one who sees selflessness, and since they merely take up faith and understanding while constantly seeking its abandonment, it is also illogical for [the ālayavijñāna] to be grasped and stored therein.
Having thus revealed the faults of the opponent's position, one must now further demonstrate the superior qualities of our own school.

Regarding the statement that the *ālayavijñāna* is subsumed under the nature of an internal self (*ātman*): sentient beings falsely grasp it as the substance of an internal self. Nevertheless, the use of two terms [“internal” and “self”] serves as a double negation to prevent others from making such false conceptualizations.

Those in the hells and other such realms are said to be born in the evil destinies, places of unrelenting suffering; although they constantly seek to distance themselves from the aggregate of suffering, they are nonetheless perpetually bound by the noose of self-love toward the *ālaya-vijñāna*, never escaping its grasp.
One never gives rise to craving for non-existence therein, because it is associated with equanimity and is therefore neither loathsome nor repulsive.
Why is this so? Although one may have such aspirations:
"How might I bring it about that these aggregates of suffering are entirely non-existent?
Yet, regarding the self, one has never sought to abandon the view of a self, because no antidote has yet arisen and there is no other realm of existence [to turn toward].

If there is a longing for the aggregates, this is due to the power of the ālayavijñāna; it is not logical that such self-love exists in the manovijñāna, because [the latter] is constantly associated with painful sensations in the miserable realms.
By this principle, even in other realms of existence, such aspirations are likewise inappropriate.
Although those born in the fourth dhyāna or above constantly feel aversion toward the pleasure associated with craving, they remain bound by the underlying attachment to a self that never departs.

In this way, my craving functions in dependence upon others; it depends upon the ālayavijñāna and not upon the mental consciousness (manovijñāna), because the ālayavijñāna functions without change until the path of the antidote has arisen.

Mental consciousness is not like this, for it is interrupted in the attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation; thus, it is not the case that mental consciousness exists while feeling does not, as both would then necessarily exist together.

Regarding those who have faith and understanding in this True Dharma concerning selflessness, although they constantly detest and oppose the conceptualized view of self (*parikalpita-ātma-dṛṣṭi*), they are still bound by the innate view of self (*sahaja-ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Where does this reside?
This means that when they suddenly hear a sound, they immediately grasp at an internal self within the ālayavijñāna, because fear and dread arise.
For what reason do you not allow that self-love exists precisely with respect to the aggregates?

If there were self-love toward that [state], it would be the *ālayavijñāna*; for the four formless aggregates, which can be distinguished by their objects and modes of activity, do not continue in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) or in the two mindless meditative attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*).
If that were so, then even though Arhats loathe and oppose the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), they would still possess it.
[To this we reply: "Because my craving has been severed, it does not exist. Since the Arhat has eternally severed all views of a self, there is no such fault.
Therefore, it is said that for an Arhat, who has already transformed the ālayavijñāna, this craving for self no longer exists.

Consequently, the establishment of the name *ālayavijñāna* as *ālayavijñāna* is definitively accomplished; it is free from all faults and possesses all supreme virtues. For this reason, it is said to be "accomplished in the most excellent way."
The treatise says:
Having thus explained the various designations for the establishment of the ālayavijñāna, how is its characteristic to be understood?
Briefly, there are three ways to establish its characteristic.

First, the establishment of its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); second, the establishment of its characteristic as cause (*hetulakṣaṇa*); and third, the establishment of its characteristic as result (*phalalakṣaṇa*).

Among these, the establishment of the specific characteristic of the ālayavijñāna refers to its being the generative cause for all phenomena belonging to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśapakṣadharma*), by virtue of its capacity to maintain the corresponding seeds (*bīja*).

Regarding the establishment of the causal characteristic (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) of the ālayavijñāna herein: it refers to this very ālayavijñāna, which consists of all seeds, acting at all times as the cause for the manifestation of those phenomena belonging to the category of defilement (*saṃkleśa-pakṣya*).

Regarding the establishment of the resultant characteristic (*phalalakṣaṇa*) of the ālayavijñāna herein: it refers to the fact that the ālayavijñāna arises in continuous succession, based precisely upon the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of all those factors belonging to the category of affliction (*saṃkleśapakṣa*) that have existed since beginningless time.
The commentary states:
Thus far, the establishment of the various categories has been explained; next is the establishment of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Since this consciousness cannot be fully discerned through its name alone, it is necessary to subsequently explain the characteristics that correspond to its own nature.

Briefly stated, there are three [aspects]: by analyzing the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of this consciousness into two types based on the difference between cause and effect, such statements are made regarding the self-characteristic of consciousness.

This refers to the latencies (vāsanā) based upon all factors belonging to the category of total affliction; that is to say, greed, hatred, and so forth are termed "all factors belonging to the category of total affliction," and because they arise and perish simultaneously with their perfuming agents, they become seeds.
This very capacity, in relation to that which is about to arise, acts as the productive cause (*janaka-hetu*).

Because it is capable of maintaining the association with the seeds, the third turning is spoken of in the fifth location; this is because it signifies the meaning of maintaining the association with the seeds.

In this context, "corresponding to the maintenance of seeds" means that because there is the simultaneous arising and simultaneous ceasing of phenomena that are subject to birth, perfuming (vāsanā) is established; such perfuming, which maintains the seeds, accords with correct principle.
Because this is associated with it, it can produce that; it is not [produced] by the most excellent [cause], such as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and so forth.

As for the association that maintains the seeds as described, it is also not the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and so forth; although those can provide support, they are not the most excellent cause, because they are not associated with the maintenance of the seeds.
As for the supreme cause, it is the seed *ālaya-vijñāna* that is able to sustain this; therefore, it can act as the generative cause for that [result].
It is not merely by way of grasping (*parigraha*) that it serves as the cause, but rather because it acts as the cause precisely through sustaining the perfumed capacity (*vāsanā-śakti*).

The causal characteristic (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) is the activity of intensification; the capacity of perfuming (*vāsanā*) can function as the cause because it is able to produce defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) when manifested.

The resultant characteristic (*phala-lakṣaṇa*) refers to those various defiled phenomena, such as greed and so forth, which are comprised within the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and are maintained by the perfuming; this is termed the resultant characteristic.
Since the causal relationship of the ālayavijñāna is not fixed, it should be stated as follows:
"Produced by the perfuming of speech, all dharmas arise from that [perfuming];
the ripening consciousness and the evolving consciousnesses arise through mutual conditioning."
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, what is called "perfuming" (vāsanā)?
What is the referent signified by the term "perfuming"?
This means that based on those phenomena, there arises and ceases simultaneously with them a causal nature capable of producing them; this is what is meant by the "signified.

It is like the perfuming of a flower within a *śirīṣa* seed: the *śirīṣa* seed and the flower arise and cease together, and thus those *śirīṣa* seeds are produced carrying the causal factor capable of generating that fragrance.

Furthermore, as for those established as practitioners of greed and so forth, the latencies of greed and so forth depend upon that [mind] which arises and ceases simultaneously with the greed; this mind arises bearing the causes for the production of those [latencies].

Alternatively, one who is "learned" (bahuśruta) is so called because the perfuming of learning arises and ceases simultaneously with the mental attention based on hearing; this mind is produced bearing the causal seeds of that [learning], and because it is able to sustain them through this perfuming, such a person is named a "holder of the Dharma."
The principle of the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the *ālayavijñāna* should be understood in the same way.
The commentary states:

Furthermore, as for the question "What is called perfuming, etc.?"—this is posed with great emphasis in order to definitively ascertain the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of perfuming, because it is difficult to understand.

This means that based on those dharmas, there is simultaneous arising and simultaneous ceasing; herein, there exists the causal nature capable of producing them. That is to say, this perfumed [basis] and those perfuming [factors] arise and cease simultaneously, and through their mutual dependence, there is the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) of the fruit-dharmas belonging to the same category as the perfuming factors, which accord with and are capable of producing them.
The word "both" (俱) serves to distinguish it from different times;
"arising and ceasing" (生滅) serves to differentiate it from permanence (常住).
This demonstrates that the characteristics of perfuming (熏習) differ from other [erroneous] theories.
"Dependent upon" (*niśritya*) means "due to" (*hetu*).
One establishes such a causal condition (*pratyaya*) based on this cause, as when one says, "It rains because of the clouds.
By citing its nature as a cause, it is shown that within this [condition] there exists the essence of a cause capable of conforming to the production of a result.

Regarding the phrase "as with the perfuming of flowers within a *kārṣika* seed," this cites a metaphor commonly established by others to illustrate the tenets of one's own school, because, according to what [the Yogācāra] perceives, the *kārṣika* seed and the flower are both transformations of the mind.

Just as that *kustumburu* seed arises and perishes simultaneously with various fragrant flowers, and by virtue of this cause, it subsequently gives rise to successive moments of *kustumburu* that continuously carry the fragrance of the flowers; so too is this case.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that for those who practice with greed and so forth, there is the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of greed and so forth: this cites the perfuming established in common by other schools as a metaphor for the meaning of our own school.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, do the seeds of the various categories of defiled phenomena within the *ālayavijñāna* abide as distinct entities, or do they not abide as distinct entities?
It is not that there exists some distinct, substantial entity called a "seed" residing within this [consciousness], nor is it non-different from it.
Rather, the ālayavijñāna arises in such a way that it possesses specific functional capacities capable of producing those [phenomena]; this is termed the "all-seed consciousness."
The commentary states:

The seeds of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are specific functional capacities (*śaktiviśeṣa*) of the ālayavijñāna. Just as the activity of a phenomenon and the essence of that phenomenon are neither identical nor different, so it is with this as well.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, how can it be seen that the ālayavijñāna and those various defiled phenomena act as mutual causes for one another simultaneously?
For example, in a bright lamp, the flame and the wick arise and burn simultaneously,
acting as mutual causes for one another. Again, just as bundles of reeds support each other so that they do not fall simultaneously,
one should observe that the principle of mutual causality here is likewise.

Just as the ālayavijñāna is the cause of all defiled phenomena, so too do all defiled phenomena serve as the cause of the ālayavijñāna; it is solely on this basis that the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) is established, for no other causal condition can be found.
The commentary states:

For example, at one and the same moment, a bright lamp’s wick and its flame stand in a relationship of mutual cause and effect—the flame arises while burning the wick, and the wick serves as the cause for the flame.
The nature of the *ālayavijñāna* and the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñānas*) is likewise: at one and the same moment, they stand in a relationship of mutual cause and effect.

In this way, a bundle of reeds supports one another so that they remain standing without falling; at the very moment that this one supports that one to keep it from falling, at that same moment, that one supports this one to keep it from falling.
"Establishing the causal conditions only in this manner" means that it refers to what was previously explained as being associated with the maintenance of seeds, and not anything else.
"Because other causal conditions cannot be found" means that other phenomena are not associated with the maintenance of seeds.

If one speaks of five causes as being the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), this is merely a different way of describing the three causes of the *ālaya-vijñāna*: the homogeneous cause, the omnipresent cause, and the ripening cause.
This is because it would be inconsistent [to claim that the *ālaya-vijñāna* is the causal condition] apart from its nature as the cause of the perfuming that sustains [the seeds].
If perfuming were to exist apart from the ālayavijñāna, it could not possibly occur.

As for the associated cause (saṃprayuktaka-hetu), the mind and mental factors depend upon one another; they possess their own functional capacity for the experience of objects, just as a caravan of merchants cannot exist apart from its functional capacity.

The *ālaya-vijñāna* functions as the simultaneous cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) for the arising of seeds; that is to say, if the *ālaya-vijñāna* and the various evolving consciousnesses were separated from such inclusion within the simultaneous cause, no other causes and conditions for internal or external seeds could possibly be found apart from the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
The Treatise says:
How can perfuming (*vāsanā*), which is itself undifferentiated and unmixed, serve as the cause for those various phenomena (*dharma*) that are differentiated and mixed?

It is like a cloth being dyed with various mordants (*rañjana-upakaraṇa*): at the moment of dyeing, although no distinct, mixed, or multi-variegated categories are yet perceptible, once it has entered the dye-vat, thereupon upon the cloth appear variegated, mixed, and multi-variegated patterns of interwoven colors.

The ālayavijñāna is likewise: it is perfumed by diverse and heterogeneous perfuming agents. Although at the time of perfuming no diversity or heterogeneity can yet be perceived, once the result—the vessel of defilement—has manifested, there is indeed diversity and heterogeneity, and dharmas of immeasurable categories appear.
The commentary states:
Regarding the question, "How can there be no difference in the perfuming? this is raised as an objection based on principle.
To resolve it according to that principle, it is said:
It is like various dyeing implements;
the dyeing process and the implements used for dyeing consist of differences in color and texture, yet at the time the cloth is being dyed, no distinct or variegated patterns can be perceived.
Because the arising of the fruit is itself the vessel for defilement, it is called the "vessel for defilement that arises as the fruit.
Because it is embraced by conditions, it is called "entry.
The *ālaya-vijñāna* is like the cloth to be dyed; just as various images appear when dyeing, so do all phenomena manifest.
The treatise says:
Such dependent origination is extremely subtle and profound within the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, to state it briefly, there are two types of dependent origination:
The first is the dependent origination of the discrimination of self-nature; the second is the dependent origination of the discrimination of the agreeable and the disagreeable.

Among these, the arising of all phenomena based upon the *ālaya-vijñāna* is called the dependent origination of the discrimination of self-nature, because it functions as the causal nature by being able to discriminate various self-natures.

Furthermore, there is the twelve-linked dependent origination, which is called the "dependent origination that differentiates the agreeable and the disagreeable," because it serves as the causal nature for differentiating the various types of individual existences—both agreeable and disagreeable—within the happy and miserable realms of rebirth.
The commentary states:
Thus, that which is extremely subtle within the Mahāyāna dependent origination refers to its being difficult for the world at large to comprehend.
That which is profound refers to its being difficult for the Śrāvakas and others to fathom its depths.

Regarding "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*): it means that there is an arising based on a cause; thus, one should understand that the term *pratyaya* (condition) is placed after the root *pad* (to go/arise) with the suffix *ktvā*.
Regarding "discrimination of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-vikalpa*): it is called discrimination because it possesses power over discrimination, or because it is required for discrimination.
The *ālaya-vijñāna* is able to differentiate its own nature because it can analyze the nature of all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and defiled (*kliṣṭa*) phenomena, rendering them distinct.

Regarding "differentiating the agreeable and the disagreeable," this refers to the twelve links [of dependent origination], such as ignorance (*avidyā*), which serve as the most predominant conditions for the arising of various distinct individual existences—whether in happy or miserable destinies, and whether pleasant or unpleasant—when the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth arise from the *ālaya-vijñāna*. This is because, through the power of ignorance and the other links, there are distinctions among merit, non-merit, and the imperturbable (*āniñjya*).
The treatise states:

Regarding the first dependent origination within the *ālayavijñāna*, there are those who are deluded and conceptualize intrinsic nature as the cause, or conceptualize past karma as the cause, or conceptualize the transformations of Īśvara as the cause, or conceptualize a real self as the cause, or conceptualize that there is no cause and no condition.
If one is deluded regarding the second dependent origination, one further discriminates that "I am the agent" and "I am the experiencer.
It is, for example, like a group of many blind men who have never seen an elephant, and someone else speaks of and points out the elephant to them.
Among those born blind, some touched the elephant's trunk, some touched its tusks, some touched its ears, some touched its feet, some touched its tail, and some touched its backbone.
Some people may ask:
"What are the characteristics of an elephant?
and some might say: [as follows].

The elephant is like the handle of a plow; some say it is like a pestle, some say it is like a winnowing basket, some say it is like a mortar, some say it is like a broom, and others say the elephant is like a rocky mountain.

If one does not understand these two types of dependent origination, then ignorance is likewise like being born blind; some conceive of inherent nature (*svabhāva*) as the cause, some conceive of past actions (*pūrvakṛta*) as the cause, some conceive of a sovereign lord (*īśvara*) as the cause, some conceive of a real self (*ātman*) as the cause, some conceive of no cause and no condition, and some conceive of a self as the agent and the self as the experiencer.
The self-nature, causal nature, and resultant nature of the ālayavijñāna are like one who does not understand the true nature of an elephant.
The commentary states:
This is due to delusion regarding the meaning of the two kinds of dependent origination, being like those born blind.
Some may hold the view that past actions (*pūrvakṛta*) are the cause [of existence]; because this negates human effort (*puruṣakāra*), it constitutes a false attachment.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, to state it briefly, the ālayavijñāna has the nature of the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) containing all seeds; it is capable of encompassing all individual existences (*ātman*) and all realms of rebirth (*gati*) within the three worlds.
The commentary states:
In order to clarify the nature of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as it discriminates its own essence, it further says, "Furthermore, if summarized," and so forth.

This means that throughout successive births, due to the perfuming of various wholesome and unwholesome karmas, and through the conceptual attachment to the grasped and the grasper, the *ālayavijñāna*—which has the nature of the maturation (*vipāka*) of the basic substance of sentient beings produced from seeds—is its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), serving as the seed for all defiled phenomena.
That which can encompass the three realms is able to encompass the entanglements of the desire, form, and formless realms.
That which encompasses all individual existences is able to encompass the continuums of all sentient beings.
"All destinities" (*sarvagati*) and so forth refers to that which can encompass the heavenly destinities (*devagati*) and others.
"Can encompass" means the characteristic of constant continuity. Why is this?

Just as the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) have interruptions in their continuity depending on place and time, the ālayavijñāna is not like this; for it persists throughout all states until the antidote arises, constantly maintaining everything everywhere.
The treatise says:
Herein are five verses:
"The external and internal are not clearly manifest; these two kinds exist only conventionally."
The seeds of the ultimate truth should be known to be of six kinds:
they are momentary, co-existent, perpetually evolving, determined,
dependent on various conditions, and capable only of producing their own specific results.

That which is stable, indeterminate, and capable of being perfumed, And which is associated with the perfuming agent— The object perfumed is not other than this; This is the characteristic of perfuming.
The six consciousnesses lack such association, Due to three distinctions and contradictions.
Two moments of mind do not coexist; by this analogy, other cases would also incur error.
Furthermore, one should know that seeds—both external and internal—are capable of both producing and projecting.
Withering and death occur due to the projecting force, just as [a movement] ceases spontaneously after its momentum has spent itself.
The commentary states:
Previously, all seeds were explained in general terms. To clarify the specific distinctions among these seeds, five verses are further presented.
That is to say, external things such as rice, barley, and wheat are called external seeds, while the *ālaya-vijñāna* is called the internal seed.
That which is not clearly discernible is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
As for the "two kinds," they refer to the external and the internal, or alternatively, to the effect and the cause.
Both of these are merely consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), because they evolve as the two dharmas of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) by maintaining the nature of causes.

Regarding the statement in the root verses, "in both," one should understand that in terms of cause and effect, external seeds such as barley are designated as conventional because they are manifestations of the *ālayavijñāna*.

Regarding the term "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*): the ālayavijñāna is the actual seed, because it is the actual nature of the causal condition for all seeds and because it constitutes their very substance.
These two types of seeds are distinguished by six kinds of differentiation.
Regarding momentary cessation: because they perish immediately after arising.
A permanent entity cannot constitute a seed, as it would lack differentiation at all times.
Although it perishes moment by moment, it is not yet extinguished. Why? Because that which has already perished cannot coexist [with its effect];
for it would be illogical for something already extinguished to produce a fruit, just as a dead chicken cannot crow.
Therefore, one must admit that the seed and its fruit coexist simultaneously, because their coexistence with the fruit is not contradictory, as in the case of a lotus root.
Although they exist together, they do not persist for one, two, or three moments, being rather like a flash of lightning.

Why is this? It should be understood that this [consciousness] functions as a constant succession and evolves moment by moment, because it functions as a constant succession throughout a long period of time. Why is that?
Because the increase or decrease of the root applies equally to the branches and so forth.

If [the mind] always functions in accordance [with the seeds], and you do not admit that even a slight degree of pleasure can serve as a seed, for what reason would everything not arise simultaneously from everything?
To avoid this difficulty, it is said that [the seeds] are determinate (*niyata*).
Although they constantly evolve together, because the functional capacities of the various seeds are fixed, everything does not arise simultaneously from everything.
Even so, why is it that [the cause] does not always produce its fruit at all times?
To avoid this fault, it is said that it "waits for various conditions.
Since the various conditions do not assemble at all times, there is no error.
Now, whose seed is this seed?
To answer this question, it is said:
it is that which alone can project its own fruit.
Regarding the term "only" (mātra): if at this time it can produce its own fruit, it is then designated as a "seed. This is because both the seed and that which possesses the seed are beginningless.

By the word "only" (*eva*), it is excluded that the continuum (*saṃtāna*) and so forth constitute the essence of the seed; for the nature of the seed as described is incompatible with them. Rather, the natures of the "seed" (*bīja*) and the "possessor of the seed" (*sabījaka*) are established only when there is a mutual correspondence between the perfumed (*bhāvya*) and the perfumer (*bhāvaka*).
The qualities of solidity and so forth are mentioned in order to distinguish that which is perfumable (*bhāvya*).

If a phenomenon continues in a series, remains stable, and persists—such as a mustard seed—it is then perfumable; it is not that which does not remain stable, such as sound and the like. Furthermore, it must not only be stable but also neutral (*avyākṛta*) in nature to be considered perfumable.

It is like a neutral fragrance that undergoes perfuming (*vāsanā*), rather than an extremely fragrant substance such as aloeswood or musk, nor an extremely foul-smelling substance such as garlic or leeks.

Regarding what is called "capable of being perfumed" (*vāsya*): if a substance can be perfumed or is capable of receiving perfuming, and if these qualities are mutually blended through successive stages, it is then termed "capable of being perfumed."
Substances such as metal or stone cannot receive perfuming (*vāsanā*), because they cannot be intermingled part by part.
Not only must something be capable of being perfumed, it must also be in association with that which perfumes; only then is it called the "perfumable" (*bhāvya*), not when it exists separately.

Simultaneity in the same location, being neither identical nor separate, is called "concomitance" (*saṃprayoga*). Possessing these various qualities, it may be termed the "perfumable" (*bhāvya*); nothing other than this qualifies.
The negation of "sound" is intended to exclude all evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) from having the nature of being perfumable.
Because it would contradict the meaning explained above:

the essence of the ālayavijñāna is firm and stable, continuing in succession until its antidote arises; its nature is exclusively neutral (*avyākṛta*), being neither wholesome nor unwholesome; its nature must be susceptible to perfuming or capable of receiving perfuming, because it is not permanent and because it arises and ceases simultaneously with the perfuming agents.
This constitutes perfuming (*vāsanā*).

Regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*): because it is that very dharma, the perfumed (*bhāvya*) serves as the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), while the perfuming (*vāsanā*) serves as the characterized (*lakṣya*).
Furthermore, the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are certainly not perfumable, because those six consciousnesses lack stable association (*samprayoga*).
Why is this? Because the three distinctions are mutually contradictory.

If the six evolving consciousnesses were necessarily co-existent [with the storehouse consciousness], then their three aspects—the support (āśraya), the object (ālambana), and attention (manasikāra)—would not be distinct from one another.
Because they are distinct from one another, the six types of evolving consciousnesses do not necessarily arise simultaneously.
Because they do not arise simultaneously, there is no fixed association (*samprayoga*).
Since there is no association, how could there be the nature of that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*) and that which perfumes (*bhāvaka*)?

If it is claimed that a preceding thought perfumes a succeeding thought to constitute habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), this argument is untenable, because these two thoughts do not exist simultaneously.
This also demonstrates that since two moments (*kṣaṇa*) do not coexist, there can be no fixed association between them.
Because there is no association (*samprayoga*), there is no nature of that which is perfumed (*bhāvya*) or that which perfumes (*bhāvaka*).

If one speaks of the meaning of the category of "dependence" (*āśraya-jāti*), then either the six types of evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) share the same class of consciousness for two moments, or there is no distinction between their momentary classes.

Because they belong to different categories, it is unreasonable to claim that either that very consciousness or those specific moments possess perfuming (*vāsanā*) while others do not; for such a distinction would lead to logical fallacies when applied by analogy to other similar types.
The mind of an Arhat does not emerge from the category of consciousness; it too should be perfumed by the unwholesome, because it belongs to the same class of phenomena (*dharmas*).
Alternatively, "if one were to establish a fault by analogy with others" means that there is a logical error in applying this analogy to other categories.
What is the meaning of this?
It means that the sense organs such as the eye, which are of the nature of pure matter (*rūpa*), are all followed by their respective categories of faculties.
Consequently, the mental faculty (*manas*) would also have to be of the nature of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), because the definition of a "faculty" is the same for both.

Furthermore, there are various alternative theories regarding such perfuming (*vāsanā*): some claim that the six consciousnesses mutually perfume one another; others claim that a preceding moment perfumes a succeeding moment; and still others claim that perfuming occurs within the seeds of a single moment of consciousness. All such views are unreasonable.
Therefore, it is a correct teaching to say that only the ālayavijñāna is that which is perfumed, and not the other consciousnesses.

Thus, both external and internal seeds serve as causes for production (*janakahetu*) and causes for projection (*ākṣepakahetu*). Specifically, with respect to the sprout, the external seed is the cause of production; conversely, with respect to the stalk and so forth, it is the cause of projection.

The ālayavijñāna is the internal seed; in relation to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), it is the direct productive cause (*janakahetu*); in relation to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), it is the projecting cause (*ākṣepakahetu*).
The productive cause (*janana-hetu*) has been explained; what, then, is the projecting cause (*ākṣepa-hetu*)?
To answer this question, it is said that [seeds] "wither and perish" by virtue of being the "projecting cause.

If these two types of seeds were merely productive causes and not projecting causes, then seeds such as barley stored in granaries would not continue in a similar succession over a long period of time.
After death, since the corpse undergoes states such as turning blue-black and so forth, its sequential transformation should not occur either.
Why? Because it ought to perish and disintegrate immediately upon death.

How so? It is like that which ceases spontaneously after having arisen; for example, when an arrow is shot, the force exerted by the release from the bowstring acts as the generative cause, causing the arrow to leave the string and not fall immediately.
The force of drawing the bow serves as the cause for inducing the arrow’s forward motion, enabling it to travel a great distance before reaching its destination.
It is not merely the release of the string that causes the arrow to move; if the force alone could produce motion, the arrow would simply fall immediately.
Nor is it a momentum of motion, for if it were so, it would not fail to fall as it successively impels itself forward.
Since it travels far once released from the bowstring and reaches its destination, we know that within this there are two forces of motion: the power to produce and the power to draw forth.

Regarding the verse stating "because it ceases spontaneously later," that [author] directly employs reasoning to augment the cause of projection (*ākṣepahetu*) rather than providing an illustration. Why is this so?

When the oil and the wick are completely exhausted, the lamp-flame ceases gradually and spontaneously at the end without depending on external conditions; it does not cease immediately at the beginning.
By this principle, it must be concluded that there exists a capacity for inducement whose power has not yet been exhausted.
Internal conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) should likewise be understood in this way: they possess a seed-like potency that can successively induce them so as to remain uninterrupted.
The treatise says:
To demonstrate that internal seeds are not like external seeds, two verses are further stated:
One should know that external [seeds], which may lack perfuming, Are not like internal seeds.
Without the permeation of hearing and so forth, the arising of the fruit is not logical.
Because of the faults of losing what was done and gaining what was not done, contradiction is established.
External seeds serve as conditions for the internal, by virtue of depending upon that permeation.
The commentary states:

Thus far, it has been demonstrated that the nature of external and internal seeds is similar in its gross characteristics; however, to reveal their differences, it further states that external seeds may lack perfuming (*vāsanā*), and so forth.

Alternatively, to distinguish the indeterminate meaning: external seeds may be either perfumed or unperfumed, as in the case of charcoal, cow dung, or wool, from which, respectively, mustard seeds, blue lotus roots, and so forth are produced.

Furthermore, things such as reeds—which are not of the same nature as *śaṇa* hemp and so forth—arise and perish simultaneously with charcoal and other such substances; they are produced from those [substances] through mutual perfuming (*vāsanā*). Thus, external seeds may be without perfuming.

Just as in the case of the *kṛsara* grain and so forth, which arise and perish simultaneously with flower garlands and the like, fragrances and other qualities are produced through perfuming (*vāsanā*); in this same way, external seeds may also possess perfuming.
Thus, external seeds are indeterminate when analyzed; for this reason, it is said that they "may" exist.
Internal seeds, however, are the perfumings of all phenomena within the ālayavijñāna; one should know that such seeds necessarily exist due to perfuming.
Why is this? Because if there were no perfuming by hearing and so forth that serves as a support, the fruits of extensive learning and the like would not be observed to exist.
Furthermore, regarding external seeds such as rice and the like, some may be sown yet subsequently perish, while others, such as weeds and tares, may grow even without being sown.
Why is it that internal seeds do not incur the fault of arising whether they have been produced or not produced, as external seeds do?
Therefore, the next response states:
"Consequently, there is a contradiction."
Because internal seeds and external seeds are of different natures, they are said to be "contradictory.
If there were a distinction between external seeds and internal seeds, how would this not contradict the previous statement that the ālayavijñāna is the true seed of all phenomena?

To avoid this difficulty, it is said that external seeds have the internal as their condition, and so forth. This is because external seeds, such as those of rice and other grains, are all seeds of karmic perfuming for sentient beings' experience and enjoyment; they are manifested through the power of the *ālayavijñāna*. Therefore, external seeds are not distinct from the internal.
As a verse says:
Heaven, earth, wind, and space, Ponds, pools, and the vast ocean— All are created within the True; Discrimination does not exist without.
There are immeasurable verses of this kind.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, the remaining evolving consciousnesses universally [arise] with respect to all self-bodies and realms of existence (*gati*).
It should be understood that this is designated as the "experiencer.
As stated in a verse in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*:
"The first is called the object-condition consciousness, The second is named the experiencer."
"Among these, that which is capable of experience, And that which discriminates and investigates, are mental factors.
The commentary states:
"The various destinies" refers to the destinies of devas and so forth.
The "capable experiencers" are the six evolving consciousnesses, because they function as the agents of experience;
they arise from conditions, for their objective spheres are subject to conceptual differentiation.
To clarify this meaning, a verse from the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* is cited as authoritative testimony (*āptāgama*).

Regarding the phrase "in this context": among these various consciousnesses, that which is capable of experiencing is the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha); that which is capable of conceptualizing is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha); and that which is capable of motivating is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha). Volition (cetanā) motivates the mind, for it is the most predominant factor in directing the mind toward various objects.
It is said that these three aggregates are all able to assist the mind in experiencing its objects; therefore, they are called mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
The treatise states:
These two consciousnesses serve as mutual conditions for one another, as stated in a verse from the *Mahāyānābhidharmasūtra*:
All phenomena reside within the storehouse consciousness, and the consciousness likewise resides within phenomena;
they are mutually the nature of each other’s effects, and also eternally the nature of each other’s causes.
Explanation:

In this context, in order to demonstrate that the ālayavijñāna and the various evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñānas) serve as mutual conditions for one another, and to reinforce this by citing the Āgamas, it is said: "All dharmas are stored within the consciousness," and so forth.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* section of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the ālayavijñāna functions as two types of conditions for the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*):
first, by serving as their seeds; and second, by serving as their support.
Regarding their being seeds: this means that when all virtuous, non-virtuous, and neutral evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) evolve, they all take the ālayavijñāna as their seed.

Regarding "serving as the basis," this means that because the ālayavijñāna appropriates the material sense organs (*rūpindriya*), the fivefold group of consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*) functions in dependence upon them; it is not without such appropriation.
Furthermore, because the ālayavijñāna exists, the manas can exist; based on this manas as its support, the manovijñāna arises.
It is just as the five groups of consciousness arise based on the five sense organs such as the eye, and not in the absence of these five organs.
The mental consciousness is likewise not without the faculty of mind (*manas*).
Furthermore, the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) act as two types of conditions for the ālayavijñāna:
first, because they can nourish its seeds within the present life; second, because they gather and plant those seeds so that it may arise in future lives.

Regarding the nourishment of those seeds within the present life: this refers to how, based upon the *ālayavijñāna*, when the wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral *pravṛttivijñānas* (evolving consciousnesses) evolve, they—in such and such a manner—arise and perish simultaneously with that single basis, thereby perfuming the *ālayavijñāna*. By virtue of these causes and conditions, the subsequent evolving consciousnesses of wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral nature evolve further increased, evolve more intensely, and evolve more clearly.

Regarding the phrase "in a future state, for the sake of its arising, it gathers and plants its seeds": this refers to the category of that perfuming which is capable of inducing and gathering the future neutral *ālayavijñāna* of maturation (*vipāka*).

Thus, for the sake of being their seeds, for the sake of being their support, for the sake of nourishing the seeds, and for the sake of gathering and planting the seeds, one should understand that the establishment of the ālayavijñāna and the various pravṛttivijñānas as mutual conditions is intended.
The treatise says:

If, within the first dependent origination, these two consciousnesses serve as mutual causes and conditions for one another, then in the second dependent origination, what kind of condition do they constitute?
This is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Of how many conditions are these six consciousnesses produced?
They are produced by the dominant condition, the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

These three types of dependent origination—namely, that which extends to the limits of saṃsāra, that which pertains to pleasant and unpleasant destinies, and that which pertains to experience—possess four conditions.
The commentary states:
"Regarding the first type of dependent origination" refers to the dependent origination of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Regarding these two consciousnesses being mutual causes and conditions, it is as explained immediately above.
"In the second dependent origination" refers to the dependent origination of the distinction between the agreeable and the disagreeable.

Regarding its being the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*): because it is preeminent, through the dominant power of ignorance and the other [links], it causes the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth to bring about the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) in the good or evil destinies.

Regarding these six consciousnesses arising from three conditions: herein, for visual consciousness, the eye is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), visible form is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the immediately preceding ceased consciousness is the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Just as it is said that visual consciousness arises from three conditions, so too each of the individual evolving consciousnesses, such as auditory consciousness and the rest, arises from its own respective three conditions; the principle of their arising is equal to that of the aforementioned visual consciousness.
The nature of conceptualization arises solely from causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), because the other three conditions do not truly exist [as independent entities].

Regarding these three types of dependent origination—such as that which extends through the cycle of birth and death—it should be understood that while they may possess all four conditions in certain contexts, it is not the case that each one individually possesses all four; rather, it is specifically the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) that possess all four conditions.
The treatise says:
Having thus established the various synonyms and characteristics of the ālayavijñāna,
how is it known that these synonyms and characteristics apply exclusively to the ālayavijñāna and not to the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna)?

If one were to distance oneself from such an established ālayavijñāna, neither defilement nor purification could be established; that is to say, because the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*), the defilement of karma (*karma-saṃkleśa*), and the defilement of birth (*janma-saṃkleśa*) would all fail to be established, as would mundane purification and supramundane purification.
The commentary states:

Having already established the existence of the *ālayavijñāna* by citing the authoritative scriptures (*āgama*) of both our own and other schools, it is now necessary to establish it with due gravity through correct reasoning (*yukti*). Therefore, these brief questions and brief answers are presented, for both scripture and reasoning each possess their own specific capacity [to prove the point].
As a verse says: The sacred teaching and correct reasoning Each possess their own distinct function;
For the sake of generating faith and wisdom, There is not one that fails to accomplish this.

Since, if one were to exclude this ālayavijñāna and attempt to establish such synonyms and characteristics elsewhere, neither defilement nor purification could possibly exist, we know for certain that the ālayavijñāna definitely exists.
"Defilement" (saṃkleśa) means turbidity, murkiness, and impurity.
"Purity" (vyavadāna) means freshness, cleanliness, and cleansing.
There are three kinds of defilement:
There are three [types of] defilement: first, that produced by afflictions; second, that produced by karma; and third, that produced by birth.
There are two types of purification:
first, mundane purification, which consists in the temporary suppression of manifest afflictions through the path with outflows (*sāsrava-mārga*); [and second, supramundane purification].
Second is supramundane purification, because through the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are ultimately and completely eradicated.
The treatise asks:
Why do the defilements of affliction (*kleśa-saṃkleśa*) not come to be?

Because it is illogical for the substance of those seeds—produced by the perfuming of the primary afflictions and secondary afflictions—to reside within the six groups of consciousness. Why is this so?

If one maintains that when visual consciousness arises together with afflictions and secondary afflictions such as greed, it is by those [afflictions] that seeds are perfumed and not by anything else—and yet this very visual consciousness has already ceased and been interrupted by other consciousnesses—then both such perfuming and its basis would be unobtainable. Consequently, it would be illogical for a visual consciousness that previously ceased, was interrupted by other consciousnesses, and currently lacks an existent entity, to arise again together with those [afflictions] like greed, because that [past consciousness] currently lacks an existent entity.
It is not logical that the maturation fruit of karma arises from a past action that currently lacks substantial existence.
Furthermore, the latencies (vāsanā) co-arising with this visual consciousness, such as greed and so forth, would also not be established.
However, this perfuming does not reside within greed, because that greed is a dependent phenomenon and is not stable.
Nor can it reside within the other consciousnesses, because their bases are distinct and they do not necessarily arise and perish simultaneously.
Furthermore, it cannot abide within its own substance, because that substance is definitively devoid of simultaneous arising and ceasing.
Therefore, it is unreasonable for the visual consciousness to be perfumed by afflictions such as greed, as well as secondary afflictions.
Furthermore, this consciousness is not perfumed by other consciousnesses.
As it is said regarding visual consciousness, so it is with the remaining evolving consciousnesses; this should be understood accordingly.
The commentary states:

Furthermore, based on the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), it has already been established that afflictive defilement (*kleśasaṃkleśa*) cannot be accounted for; therefore, it is said: "If one posits the expression 'eye-consciousness' and so forth.
This very eye-consciousness refers to the eye-consciousness permeated (*vāsita*) by craving and the other afflictions.

Regarding those instances interrupted by other consciousnesses—such as being interrupted by auditory consciousness and so forth—because such perfuming and its supporting consciousness have already ceased and perished, they are all unobtainable.

Regarding the claim that visual consciousness arises simultaneously with craving and so forth: it is illogical for visual consciousness to subsequently arise in conjunction with craving, hatred, and delusion because there would be no cause, as that past visual consciousness lacks substantiality and cannot function as a cause.

Regarding the point that it is illogical for the maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) to arise from a past action that lacks a present entity: according to the Sautrāntika masters, since the past has no entity, its maturation fruit is induced by a present perfuming (*vāsanā*).
The Vaibhāṣika masters maintain that [the fruit] arises from the maturation of past karma;
this should not be accepted. Why?
Because the past does not exist.
By this analogy, it is not logical for desire and other mental states to arise [simultaneously].

Thus, having already explained that one provisionally accepts that eye-consciousness arising together with desire and other states is perfumed by those very desires and so forth, while other consciousnesses arise in the interim, it is not logical for eye-consciousness accompanied by desire and other states to arise again at a later time.

Now it shall be further explained that the habitual impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by this very visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) arising simultaneously with greed and so forth cannot be established; therefore, the phrase "and this visual consciousness, etc. is stated.

Regarding the statement that "this perfuming does not abide within greed," the word "however" (*ran*) signifies a sequential order; that is to say, for the time being, this perfuming cannot abide within greed, because greed depends upon consciousness.

Attachment is bound to consciousness, yet consciousness does not depend upon attachment; it is not logical that consciousness—which is the dependent—should be perfumed by the support of attachment, because [attachment] is what perfumes.
As for the phrase "because it is not firmly established," this specifically excludes desire-attachment from being of the nature of the perfumable.
"Nor can it abide in other consciousnesses" means that it cannot abide in the consciousnesses of the ear and so forth.

Regarding "because their bases are distinct": the bases refer to the ear and so forth; because they are distinct, the consciousnesses are distinct. How could a consciousness based on the eye-faculty infuse a consciousness based on the ear and so forth?

Furthermore, because they do not exist simultaneously, that which is not simultaneous cannot possess the nature of being perfumed (*bhāvya*) or being a perfumer (*bhāvaka*); this demonstrates the absence of the characteristic of perfuming.

Moreover, regarding the phrase "it cannot abide within its own substance," this means that visual consciousness itself cannot perfume visual consciousness, as this would entail the fallacy of confusing the perfumer with the perfumed, or the agent with the action.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "this consciousness is not perfumed by other consciousnesses," this means that this visual consciousness is not perfumed by auditory or other types of consciousness, because their respective bases (āśraya) are distinct, as has already been explained previously.
Only such a principle can be established; all other [positions] are entirely unreasonable.

As for how this should be understood, one should know that the principles for establishing and refuting the remaining *pravṛttivijñānas* are to be understood in their entirety according to what is appropriate.
The Treatise says:

Furthermore, when one dies from the higher realms such as the Realm of No-Thought (asaṃjñika) and is reborn in this world, the initial consciousness at that time is defiled by afflictions and secondary afflictions; yet this consciousness would have no seed, because both its support and its perfuming have already passed away and lack present existence.
The commentary states:

Those who pass away from the higher stages, such as the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*), and are reborn in this world, are those who pass away from the upper realms and are reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
At that time, the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) refer to greed, hatred, and so forth.

The "first consciousness that is defiled" refers to the first consciousness of the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisandhi*); this is because it is defiled by all the afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to its own level.

It is not the case, as the Sautrāntikas maintain, that once the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) have been severed, the past afflictions and mind can still be apprehended as existing and subsequently manifest from them again.
It is not logically tenable that the mind at the moment of death serves as the basis for this [the intermediate state], because that mind at the moment of death is itself not established.
If that is so, why do you not simply refer to it directly?
Because that [state] is not necessarily defiled,
and because there is no distinction between this and that, what difference is there ultimately between speaking of that and speaking of this?
The treatise says:

Furthermore, when the consciousness that serves as the antidote to the afflictions has arisen and all other worldly consciousnesses have ceased, it would be illogical for the seeds of the remaining afflictions and secondary afflictions to reside within this antidotal consciousness if the ālayavijñāna were absent. This is because the nature of this antidotal consciousness is liberation itself, and it does not arise or cease simultaneously with the other afflictions and secondary afflictions.

Furthermore, at a later time, when worldly consciousness arises, if it were apart from the ālayavijñāna, those various perfumings and their basis would have long since passed away and would currently lack substantial existence; thus, there would be no seeds for it to arise again.
Therefore, if one were to be separated from the ālayavijñāna, the defilement of afflictions (kleśasaṃkleśa) could not be established at all.
The commentary explains:

"If the consciousness that serves as the antidote to the afflictions has already arisen," and so forth; this means, for example, when one is first directed toward the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), the path that serves as the antidote to the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing arises, and all other worldly consciousnesses have already ceased.

At that time, if the ālayavijñāna did not exist, upon what would the latent dispositions (anuśaya) of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation depend? It is not logically tenable that a consciousness which serves as an antidote should carry those seeds, because such an antidotal consciousness is by its very nature liberated; that is to say, it possesses the meaning of being intrinsically and utterly pure.

Regarding the phrase "because it does not arise or cease simultaneously with other afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)," this indicates that the antidote and the object to be countered are mutually contradictory—just like light and darkness—and thus demonstrates that [the ālayavijñāna] is not associated with their seeds.
"Furthermore, at a later time" refers to the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) following the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
"Because it has long since passed away and lacks a present entity" refutes the establishment of the past as having real existence.

The Vaibhāṣika masters’ [theories regarding] the acquisition (*prāpti*) of afflictions and so forth have already been refuted by the Sautrāntika masters; therefore, they will not be refuted again here.
However, the Sautrāntikas' position that the basis for perfuming (*vāsanā*) lacks any substantial entity is accompanied by logical fallacies and is therefore untenable.
Therefore, if the defilement of afflictions cannot be established apart from the ālayavijñāna, this concludes the reasoning determined by the preceding discussion.
The treatise asks:
In what way is the defilement of karma not established?
Because consciousness conditioned by volitional formations would be inconsistent;
if this [consciousness] were absent, then existence conditioned by grasping would likewise be inconsistent.
The commentary states:

Regarding the statement that "volitional formations (saṃskāra) cannot serve as conditions for consciousness (vijñāna) because they are dissociated [from it]," this explains that the karmic defilement (karma-saṃkleśa) within the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna) would not be established.

That is to say, if one were to claim that the various consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, which arise simultaneously with craving and other [afflictions], are accepted as the member of consciousness (vijñāna-aṅga) conditioned by volitional formations—this would be unreasonable, because there is an authoritative scriptural statement (āgama) that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is conditioned by consciousness.

Why is this so? Because the various consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, perish with extreme rapidity in a single moment; it is logically untenable for them to serve as the condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) after they have long since ceased.
If, fearing this deficiency, one were to allow that the consciousness at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*) constitutes the member of "consciousness," this too would not be correct.
At the time of rebirth, since meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations have long since ceased, it is not logical that these should arise again from what has long ceased.
Furthermore, the mind at the moment of rebirth is not of a neutral (avyākṛta) nature, as it is accompanied by craving and aversion;
since it is not neutral, it is unreasonable for it to take formations as its condition.

If it is said that the evolving consciousnesses are associated with formations, and that by virtue of these being their conditions, the ālayavijñāna is able to maintain the perfuming and is thus designated as the "link of consciousness," this accords with correct reasoning.

If this were non-existent, it would also be inconsistent for grasping (*upādāna*) to serve as the condition for existence (*bhava*). This refers to the stage of perfuming (*vāsanā*), where the seeds of various karmas, having matured and manifested, are designated as "existence" (*bhava*); or alternatively, they are called "existence" because they have acquired the functional capacity to produce future fruits.

If the consciousness perfumed by the formations were not established, where would the seeds of those karmas be situated, such that one could further say that they produce fruits which manifest and function, being designated as "existence"?
Therefore, if one is separated from the ālayavijñāna, this defilement of karma also cannot be established.
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle Two;
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle Three.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asvabhāva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part Two, Section Three: The Basis of the Knowable. The treatise says:
Why is it that the defilement of birth is not established?
Because it is incompatible with the moment of linking the continuity [of existence].
The commentary states:

Now, it is demonstrated that if the ālayavijñāna did not exist, the very substance of the defilement of birth could not be established; therefore, it is said that [the process] is inconsistent at the time of the linking of rebirth.
The treatise says:

If one dies in a state that is not in meditative equipoise (*asamāhita-bhūmi*) and is reborn, the defiled mental consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manovijñāna*) arises based on the mind of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to effect the continuity of rebirth. This defiled mental consciousness ceases within the intermediate state, and the consciousness (*vijñāna*) then merges with the *kalala* in the mother’s womb.

If the mental consciousness itself were to conjoin with that [intermediate state], then once conjoined, it would rely upon this consciousness for the mental consciousness to arise within the mother’s womb.
If that were so, there would necessarily be two mental consciousnesses arising simultaneously within the mother’s womb.

Furthermore, it is not logical that the consciousness which is conjoined with those [afflictions] is of the nature of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it relies upon defilement, because its occurrence is uninterrupted, and because the objects of the mental consciousness cannot be found therein.

If the consciousness of conjunction were simply the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), then this mental consciousness of conjunction would have to rely upon the all-seed consciousness as its support, while the other mental consciousnesses produced from that [all-seed] consciousness would themselves be the all-seed consciousness.

If this combined consciousness (*saṃhatavijñāna*) is the all-seed consciousness (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*), it is precisely the ālayavijñāna, which you have established under the different name of "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*).

If the dependent consciousness (*āśrayavijñāna*) were the all-seed consciousness, then the supporting causal consciousness would not be the all-seed consciousness, while the supported resultant consciousness would be the all-seed consciousness; this is illogical.

Therefore, that which accomplishes this harmonious consciousness is not the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), but rather the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), which is the consciousness of all seeds (*sarvabījaka-vijñāna*).
The commentary states:
"The non-equipoised stage" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Non-existence" refers to death.
Regarding the state of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), it means relying on the transitional consciousness that occurs between the two existences of death and birth.
That which arises as defiled is accompanied by craving and aversion, because of the presence of cognitive distortions (*viparyāsa*).
Regarding the term "mental consciousness," it is because at that time all other consciousnesses have long since ceased.
It is called "continuity" (saṃtati) because it maintains the connection of birth; it is called "linking of birth" (pratisaṃdhi) because it takes up the birth.
This defiled mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises because it conditions the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*).
That which ceases within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) must cease; for if it did not cease, there would be no arising of the existence of birth.

Regarding the mutual blending of the consciousness and the *kalala* within the mother’s womb: this means that at the time of its cessation, the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) within the mother’s womb shares the same security and peril as the red and white elements, causing them to blend together and form the *kalala*.
As the Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, if consciousness were not to enter the mother's womb, it would not coalesce with the kalala to form the essential nature of the kalala."
"If it were the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)" means that this is not the *ālayavijñāna*.
"Once they have combined" means once birth has been taken.
"Depending on this consciousness" means depending on the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

Regarding "the transformation of consciousness with mental objects": there is a distinct evolving consciousness, namely, the discriminating mental consciousness that evolves in successive stages, associated with faith and so forth or greed and so forth, and accompanied by feelings of pleasure or pain.

If that were so, there would necessarily be two mental consciousnesses functioning simultaneously within the mother’s womb: namely, the resultant body—the fundamental substance of the sentient being—which functions without depending on present application of effort.

The indeterminate mental consciousness and the mental consciousness associated with discernible objects, modes of activity, and feelings of pleasure or pain—these two types of mental consciousness would have to arise simultaneously within a single body;
however, this must not be admitted, as it contradicts the sūtras.
Thus the verse says:
It is impossible and there is no occasion for two consciousnesses of the same body and the same kind to arise simultaneously, neither before nor after.
Furthermore, one should not admit that these two are identical, because their intrinsic natures are distinct.
Moreover, the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) should not be subject to interruption, for after the continuity has been joined, it must undergo rebirth in another location.
Furthermore, the nature of the maturation (vipāka) is exclusively a constant continuity that does not transition into other destinies.

Moreover, it is illogical for the consciousness that is conjoined with that [maturation] to be of the nature of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it would depend on defilement and its occurrence would be uninterrupted. This is demonstrated by a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) that reveals a contradiction with the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of that phenomenon: namely, if it were established as being mental consciousness, it would not depend on defilement in all places, in all modes, or at all times, just like the mental consciousness that occurs at a later time.

Thus, at the moment of linking rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*), consciousness—in all locations, all modes, and all times—is invariably associated with defilement; that is, it is subsumed within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Taking the final mind as its support, this supported mind arises with the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*) as its object; for in all locations, all modes, and all times, it is defiled.
The consciousness that serves as the support is not the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it transcends the nature of the mental consciousness.

Some say: "The mind that is constantly associated with the four afflictions is called the defiled support. [To this we reply: A mind that has already entered into a continuous stream would then have to be defiled; however, this is already established, for it is admitted to be of an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature, specifically that of maturation (*vipāka*).
Because its nature as maturation (*vipāka*) is uninterrupted throughout time, this also excludes it from being of the nature of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Regarding the phrase "because the object of mental consciousness cannot be apprehended," this meaning further reinforces the exclusion of the causes for it being mental consciousness.
If it were the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), its own objective sphere would necessarily be perceivable—just as it is in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

However, the objective sphere of the final mental consciousness, which is the mind that has already entered into the continuum of rebirth, cannot be perceived; therefore, it is not the mental consciousness.

One should not raise an objection based on the mind dwelling in the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), for we do not admit that this [mind] is of the nature of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Thus, in this context, it is only said that the object of perception (*ālambana*) is unobtainable because it is difficult to discern; it is not that it is entirely non-existent.
At that time, it is not that phenomena do not exist; although they do exist, they cannot be known.

From the statement "if consciousness were merely the aggregate" up to "it is simply the maturation-consciousness, the consciousness of all seeds," the text employs a double-layered interrogation to establish the correct view and refute the erroneous, thereby concluding by returning to the fundamental meaning.
The text is easy to understand and does not require extensive explanation.
The Treatise says:

Furthermore, once the continuity of rebirth has been established, if one were apart from the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), the appropriation of the material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) would also be impossible; for the other various consciousnesses each have their own distinct bases and are not stable, and thus these material sense-faculties should not be separated from consciousness.
The commentary states:
"Having already undergone the continuity of rebirth" means having already acquired a personal existence (*ātman*).
"If separated from the maturation-consciousness" means being separated from the *ālayavijñāna*.
"Appropriation" (upādāna) means that which is able to grasp and maintain.
"Material sense-faculties" (rūpīndriya) refers to those excluding the mental faculty (manas).
"Also cannot be obtained" means that the other evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) are all incapable of appropriating the material sense-faculties.
Why is this? Because the other various consciousnesses each have their own distinct bases.
This demonstrates that among the six sense organs, such as the eye, there is not a single dharma capable of universally appropriating [the body].

For example, visual consciousness relies solely upon the eye; likewise, the remaining consciousnesses, such as auditory consciousness and so forth, rely solely upon the ear and their respective bases. If something is the basis for a particular consciousness, only that consciousness can maintain it; if something is not the basis for a particular consciousness, that consciousness cannot maintain it.

Regarding the phrase "because it does not abide firmly": this refers to the fact that [the mind] is repeatedly interrupted and arises independently; furthermore, because there is interruption in states such as the non-percipient realm (*asaṃjñika*), at those times the eyes and other faculties lack any capacity for grasping, and thus there should be no sensation or perception.
Some say that the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is the "appropriator" (*upādātṛ*) because it pervades the entire body.
This interpretation is incorrect, because the body-faculty is itself also something that is appropriated (*upādeya*).
Even if this body-faculty were the appropriator, it could not be established as such, for there would be nothing else remaining to appropriate it.

Furthermore, the Buddha should have stated that death occurs at the moment one abandons the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), rather than saying it is when vitality (*āyuṣka*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) depart.
Since such [factors] would already be abandoned at the time of leaving the body, it is illogical for the body-faculty to be the faculty that maintains [the body].
The treatise says:

If one were to exclude the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), the mutual dependence of consciousness and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)—which proceeds like bundles of reeds leaning against one another—would likewise be untenable.
The commentary states:
As the Blessed One said:
"Consciousness conditions name-and-form."

In this context, "name" refers to the four aggregates that are not form, while "form" refers to the nature of the kalala; both of these take consciousness as their causal condition. Furthermore, consciousness evolves in a continuous succession of moments based upon them, and this evolving consciousness does not exist apart from the ālayavijñāna.
