Why is this so? Since the term "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) already includes the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), what further would be included by mentioning the word "consciousness" again?
Furthermore, as the Sūtra says: "Up to consciousness, there is a turning back."

"Consciousness" refers to the ālayavijñāna; because its own substance serves as the support for the uninterrupted transformation [of the subsequent moments], it is therefore said that this name-and-form has consciousness as its condition.
Furthermore, as it is said in a sutra: "Ānanda!"
Whether it be a man or a woman, if consciousness were to be severed, destroyed, and extinguished, would name-and-form attain growth and expansion?
"No, World-Honored One."
Such being the case,
it is logically impossible to establish these [phenomena] apart from the ālayavijñāna.
The treatise says:
If apart from the ripening consciousness (vipākavijñāna), the nutriment of consciousness for sentient beings already born would not be established. Why is this?
Because among the six consciousnesses, it is impossible to find even one that can perform the function of nutriment for sentient beings already born within the three realms.
The commentary states:

As for the fact that the food of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*) is not established for sentient beings who have already been born, it is because the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are of a nature such as being wholesome and so forth, and thus lack the meaning of constantly and perpetually nourishing all forms of existence (*bhava*).

Furthermore, because [these] do not exist in the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) or in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), the food that is consumed does not pervade the three realms. Nor can the various mental states and mental factors associated with entering meditative attainment be called "food," for it is not so stated in the Sūtras, and because they have already ceased and no longer exist.
The cessation of mind and mental factors is also not nutriment, because the categories of nutriments such as *kavaḍīkāra* (edible food) have already been definitively established.
The treatise says:

When one dies from this state and is reborn in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-bhūmi*), the continuity of rebirth is linked by a non-equipoised, defiled mental consciousness. Since that non-equipoised, defiled mind is subsumed under that [equipoised] stage, no other entity of seeds apart from the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) can possibly be found.
The commentary states:
Thus, it has already been demonstrated that within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the continuity of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhi*) cannot be established if the ālayavijñāna is excluded.
It shall now be shown that this is likewise impossible in the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*).
"If one passes away from here and is reborn in a state of meditative equipoise" means the time of death in the desire realm and subsequent birth in a higher realm.
"By a non-equipoised, defiled mental consciousness" refers to its association with afflictions such as craving for the flavor of meditative concentration belonging to that [higher] level.

Apart from the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), the substance of other seeds cannot possibly be found: for the mind bound by the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) does not possess that seed-substance, because arising and ceasing do not coexist;

nor is the mind born in the meditative states (*samāhitabhūmi*) the seed-substance of that [desire-realm mind], because it is inconsistent for the nature of a seed to exist within a single momentary mind;

nor is the mind bound by the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and so forth, previously acquired in another birth, the seed-substance, because there is no other consciousness present to maintain its perfuming (*vāsanā*).
The continuity of form (*rūpa*) cannot serve as the substance of the seed, because it lacks the necessary causes and conditions.
Therefore, it must necessarily depend upon the *ālayavijñāna*, wherein there has existed from time immemorial the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of this mind, comprised within that respective stage.
The Commentary says:

Furthermore, regarding birth in the formless realm, if the all-seed maturation-consciousness were absent, defiled and wholesome minds would lack seeds, and defiled and wholesome minds would lack a supporting basis.
The commentary states:
"Those born in the formless realm" refers to those who have already attained birth in that realm.
"Defiled and wholesome minds" refers to the minds that experience relish (*āsvādana*) and meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
"Should there be no seeds" means that the consciousness possessing seeds would not exist.
"Should there be no support" means that the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) would not exist.

At that time, all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) would necessarily be non-existent; therefore, one must admit that the consciousness containing all seeds and the ripening consciousness definitely exist, because their causes and supports must necessarily exist.
The Commentary states:

Furthermore, regarding that very state, when supramundane consciousness is directly present, all other mundane minds are completely extinguished; therefore, at that time, one should indeed be extinguished and depart from those realms of existence.
The commentary states:
"Furthermore, 'in that very place' refers to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
'Supramundane mind' refers to the untainted mind (*anāsravacitta*)."
That which is present before one refers to the arising of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
As for the remaining worldly minds, they are [also] untainted.
That all others are extinguished means that everything is eternally ceased.

At that time, one should extinguish and depart from those destinies because the maturation (vipāka) subsumed within those destinies no longer exists; thus, by means of natural spontaneity rather than through effort, one should attain nirvana without remainder, for all that is to be remedied has been forever severed once the remedy is present before one.
The treatise states:

If one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception or the sphere of nothingness, when a supramundane mind manifests before one, both destinies should be entirely extinguished and abandoned.

This supramundane consciousness does not take the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its basis, nor should it take the sphere of nothingness as its basis, nor does it take nirvana as its basis.
The commentary states:

"If one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," etc., means that when one is born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and seeks to abandon the afflictions of that stage, because perception (*saṃjñā*) is so subtle and weak, there is no path belonging to that same stage; rather, the stage of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is clear and sharp.

When that untainted mind arises and becomes present, at that time both destinies should be extinguished and abandoned—namely, the extinction and abandonment of the two destinies of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). At that time, sentient beings would necessarily undergo death, because the bases for those two destinies would no longer exist.
Non-outflow dharmas (*anāsrava*) are not included within the destinies (*gati*), because they are unconditioned by the realms of existence and because they are the antidote to the destinies.
Furthermore, nirvāṇa is not that which serves as a basis for a destiny, because one abides in the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
Furthermore, because all realms of existence (*gati*) are eternally extinguished and transcended, nirvāṇa is called "the realm that is no realm.
Thus, being entirely devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and karmic maturation (*vipāka*), it can serve as the support for supramundane consciousness.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, at the time of death, whether one has performed wholesome or unwholesome deeds, the physical basis (āśraya) gradually becomes cold from either the bottom or the top.
None of this would be possible if the ālayavijñāna did not exist.
Therefore, if one were separated from the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) containing all seeds, the defilement of this birth could not be established either.
The commentary explains:

"At the time of passing away" refers to the moment of death; for one who has performed virtuous deeds, the lower parts of the body gradually grow cold, whereas for one who has performed non-virtuous deeds, it is the opposite.
If one does not believe in the existence of the ālayavijñāna, this [argument] is not established. Why is that?

At that time, the manovijñāna has no locus and does not exist; whereas the ālayavijñāna does have a locus and exists, because it abides by depending on a locus and manifests as the appearance of spatial dimensions.
The treatise says:
How is it that mundane purification is not established?

It refers to one who has not yet abandoned the greed associated with the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-saṃyojana*) and has not yet attained a mind associated with the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). Such a person, for the sake of abandoning the greed associated with the realm of desire, diligently practices the preparatory application (*prayoga*) by means of a wholesome mind associated with the realm of desire.

Since this preparatory mind associated with the desire realm does not arise and cease simultaneously with the mind associated with the form realm, it is not perfumed by the latter; therefore, it is illogical for it to serve as the seed for that [form-realm mind].

Furthermore, since the mind bound by the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) has been separated from the present moment by many past lifetimes and other intervening states of mind, it cannot serve as the seed for the present concentrated mind, as it no longer exists.

Therefore, it is established that the *vipākaphala-vijñāna* containing all seeds, which has been transmitted through successive generations, serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the present concentrated mind, while the preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
In this manner, it should be understood that all stages of detachment from desire are likewise [inapplicable].
Thus, such worldly purification cannot logically be established if the maturation consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) containing all seeds is absent.
The commentary states:

Having thus already demonstrated that the three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) cannot logically be established in relation to the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), we now wish to further demonstrate that worldly purification (*viśuddhi*) likewise cannot be established. Therefore, it says: "those who have not yet abandoned the greed and other [afflictions] bound to the realm of desire."

Because the preparatory wholesome mind (*prayoga-kuśala-citta*) associated with the two entanglements of desire and form lacks the sense of arising and ceasing simultaneously, it is illogical for it to function as either the perfumed (*bhāvya*) or the perfumer (*bhāvaka*).

Furthermore, the mind entangled in desire is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and thus cannot be the perfumed; because its stage of existence (*bhūmi*) is distinct, it cannot serve as their causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

The virtuous mind associated with the realm of form (rūpāvacara) obtained in other lifetimes throughout beginningless saṃsāra is not the seed for the present virtuous mind associated with the realm of form, because it has been interrupted by many intervening moments of mind associated with the desire realm (kāmadhātu) over the course of many past lives.

The masters of the Sautrāntika school [hold that] past non-existence lacks a substantial entity; thus, it is unreasonable for it to serve as the seed for wholesome minds bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

Therefore, the phrase "is established" and so forth concludes the aforementioned subtle reasoning regarding functional capacity, proving the definitive existence of the *ālayavijñāna* as their causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Furthermore, it serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the preparatory wholesome minds bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) at present, because it is the uncommon cause and its power is superior.

Regarding the phrase "in their respective order, all such [states] in the stages of freedom from desire should be understood accordingly": one should understand that for each of the higher stages, the wholesome minds of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the specific freedom from desire likewise refute the false and establish the correct, as appropriate, in accordance with what has been explained above.
The treatise says:
Why is it that supramundane purity is not established?
It is because the World-Honored One has said:
Based on the sounds of another’s speech and one’s own internal individual appropriate attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), right view arises with these as its causes.
Do these—the sounds of another’s speech and the appropriate attention—infuse the ear-consciousness, the mental consciousness, or both?

If one reflects upon those phenomena in accordance with reality, at that time auditory consciousness cannot arise, and mental consciousness is likewise interrupted by various other scattered cognitions.

If, at the time it arises in conjunction with appropriate mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*), this consciousness perfumed by hearing—which, having long since ceased in the past, certainly lacks any substantial entity—how can it again serve as the seed capable of producing the mind that subsequently arises in conjunction with appropriate mental attention?

Furthermore, this mind associated with correct mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*) is a worldly mind, whereas that mind associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is a supramundane mind; they have never arisen or ceased simultaneously. Therefore, this [worldly] mind is not perfumed by that [supramundane] one.
Since it is not perfumed, it is illogical for it to serve as their seed.

Therefore, supramundane purity cannot be established if it is separated from the resultant consciousness that matures all seeds (*sarvabījaka-vipākaphala-vijñāna*), because it is inconsistent for the cultivation of hearing (*śrutavāsanā*) therein to contain those seeds.
The commentary states:

Now, wishing further to demonstrate that even supramundane purity cannot be established for the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), it says, "How could there be the supramundane," and so forth.
The text is easily understood; there is no need for further elaboration.

Regarding the phrase "because it is inconsistent with the appropriation of those seeds," this refers to the previously mentioned point that it is illogical for the appropriation of supramundane pure seeds [to occur within such a consciousness].
The treatise asks:

Furthermore, how can the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), which possesses all seeds and serves as the cause of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), also serve as the seed for the supramundane mind that acts as its antidote?
Furthermore, because the supramundane mind has never been practiced in the past, its perfuming must certainly be non-existent.
Since there is no perfuming, from what seed could it arise?
Therefore, one should answer as follows:
"Arising from seeds of correct hearing and cultivation that flow forth from the most pure *dharmadhātu*.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, as for the question of how [it could arise] even from seeds of a pure mind, this demonstrates that it is ultimately impossible; one has never seen poison become nectar.
The ālayavijñāna is like a poisonous drug; how could it give rise to the supramundane, nectar-like, pure mind?
Furthermore, as for from what kind of seed the supramundane mind arises, this indicates that the pure mind has never been attained before; how could it arise suddenly without a cause?
The phrase "from the most pure up to that which is produced from seeds" indicates that this pure mind has its own distinct seeds and is definitely not produced from the seeds of the *ālayavijñāna*.
What is the distinct seed?
It refers to the permeation of correct hearing that flows from the most pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
As for the "most pure dharma-realm," it is the dharma-realm of all Buddhas, because it is forever free from all adventitious obstructions (*āgantuka-āvaraṇa*).
Regarding the term "outflow" (niṣyanda): it refers to the teachings arising from the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). Because one listens to such teachings without error, it is called "correct hearing.
The perfuming (vāsanā) produced based on this correct hearing is what is termed "perfuming."
This very perfuming, which is capable of producing supramundane, untainted mind, is called the seed.
Such a seed is not the ālayavijñāna, because it has never before been attained.
The treatise says:
Is this perfuming by hearing the nature of the ālayavijñāna, or is it not the nature of the ālayavijñāna?
If it were the nature of the ālayavijñāna, how could it be the seed of its antidote?
If it were not of the nature of the ālayavijñāna, how could the basis for these seeds of the perfuming of hearing be perceived?

Up until the realization of the bodhi of all Buddhas, these seeds of the perfuming of hearing abide in whichever one of the bases they are associated with, dwelling within the vipākavijñāna; they evolve in conjunction with it, blending together like water and milk.
Nevertheless, they are not the ālayavijñāna, because they are of the nature of seeds that serve as its antidote.
The commentary states:

Regarding the question of how this "perfuming by hearing" (*śruta-vāsanā*) and its basis are to be perceived, this constitutes a series of successive inquiries and challenges intended to demand a specific basis.
The phrase "up until the realization of the bodhi of all Buddhas" means up until the attainment of the basis for the stainless and unimpeded gnosis (*jñāna*).
This "perfuming of hearing" refers to the perfuming induced by the unerring hearing of the teachings of the sūtras and so forth.

"Whichever one of the various bases it may abide in" means that it resides within the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), depending on whichever one of the various streams of continuity it abides in.

Regarding the phrase "harmoniously combined and evolving together like water and milk": although this perfuming by hearing is not that [ālaya] consciousness itself, it dwells within that consciousness and evolves together with it.

However, that which is not the *ālayavijñāna* refers to this perfuming by hearing (*śrutavāsanā*), which is the seed of supramundane consciousness; it is neither the intrinsic nature of the *ālayavijñāna* nor its seed. Nevertheless, it is accepted as being "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) insofar as it functions simultaneously and inseparably [with the *ālayavijñāna*].
"Because it is the nature of the seed that serves as the antidote to that" means it is the cause of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is the antidote to the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

This meaning is like a storehouse where various substances are mixed together; or like an elixir of immortality (*rasāyana*) mixed with various poisons; or like taking an *agada* medicine for many illnesses, which, although it coexists for a long time with foul poisons, is neither of the nature of those poisons nor the seed of those poisons.
The seeds of this cultivation through hearing are likewise so.
The treatise states:

herein, based on inferior-grade cultivation, one achieves medium-grade cultivation; based on medium-grade cultivation, one achieves superior-grade cultivation; for by extensively practicing through hearing, reflection, and meditation, one attains correspondence [with the path].
The commentary states:
The expressions "inferior, middling, and superior" regarding the perfuming (*vāsanā*) and so forth are clear and easy to understand; there is no need for further explanation.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, it should be understood that these seeds of the perfuming of correct hearing—in their inferior, middling, and superior grades—are also seeds of the *dharmakāya*. They are contrary to the *ālayavijñāna* and are not subsumed within the *ālayavijñāna*, because they are of the nature of an outflow from the most pure supramundane *dharmadhātu*. Although they are mundane, they possess the nature of seeds for the supramundane mind.

Furthermore, although the supramundane mind has not yet arisen, it is already able to counteract the entanglements of all afflictions, is already able to counteract all perilous and evil destinies, and has already performed the counteractive treatment that causes all existing evil karma to decay; moreover, it can accord with and serve all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Although these belong to the mundane realm, one should know that what is attained by a bodhisattva who is newly engaged in practice is also subsumed within the dharmakāya, whereas what is attained by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is subsumed solely within the vimuktikāya.
Furthermore, this perfuming is not the ālayavijñāna, but is subsumed within the dharmakāya and the vimuktikāya.
As the perfuming increases gradually through the stages of inferior, medium, and superior, so too does the maturation-result consciousness decrease gradually, whereby the basis is transformed.
Once the basis has been transformed in every respect, the maturation-consciousness and all seeds proceed without seeds, and all seeds are forever severed.
The commentary states:

Furthermore, the statement that "this correct hearing, up to and including what should be known, is also the seed of the dharmakāya" is a brief enumeration; the following sections provide a detailed explanation.
Regarding the phrase "contrary to the ālayavijñāna and not subsumed within the ālayavijñāna," this is because it does not possess the same intrinsic nature as that [ālayavijñāna].
Although these belong to the mundane realm, they appear as if they were with outflows (*sāsrava*);
yet, because they possess the nature of seeds for supramundane mind, they constitute the provisions (*sambhāra*) for the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) mind.
In this context, the characteristic of realization is called the *dharmakāya*.
It is termed "worldly" because it arises in dependence upon the world, as it functions in mutual interpenetration and coexistence within the *ālayavijñāna*.
To demonstrate the superior capacity of this perfuming (*vāsanā*), it is said that even when the supramundane mind has not yet arisen, and so forth.

For one who has already been able to counteract the entanglements of the various afflictions (*kleśa*), this homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) continues in succession; its momentary power is capable of acting as an antidote, just as fire consumes by burning.
Regarding the ability to counteract all perilous and evil realms of existence, as a verse says:
"In whatever world-systems there may be, Those with the highest degree of right view,
Though they pass through a thousand births, Shall not fall into the evil realms."

Because the force of previously committed unwholesome deeds may cause one to fall into the evil destinies, it is next stated that there is a "remedy for the decay" of all unwholesome karma already created. The power of this cultivation through hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*) damages the efficacy of unwholesome karma accumulated since beginningless time; therefore, it is called the "remedy for decay."
Regarding inclusion within the *dharmakāya*, it is because that [liberation] is its cause.
The same should be said for inclusion within the *vimuktikāya*.

As for the distinction between the *dharmakāya* and the *vimuktikāya* herein: the *vimuktikāya* merely consists in the eternal separation from the bonds of the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). It is like a person from a village who, having been freed from shackles and all other fetters, has the cessation of various sufferings, yet lacks the association with supreme, preeminent, sovereign, and abundant bliss.

As for that *dharmakāya*, it is liberated from the two kinds of obstructions—those of afflictions and those regarding the knowable—along with all residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); it is adorned by a multitude of immeasurable, rare, and wondrous qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); it is the basis for all wealth, happiness, and mastery; and having attained the foremost and most supreme sovereignty, it acts according to its pleasure.

For example, it is like a prince who, having previously received the consecration, is imprisoned for a minor offense; as soon as he gains his release, he is endowed with the foremost, most excellent, sovereign wealth and happiness.

Regarding "the transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): it is like taking elixirs of immortality to transform the physical body; although there is no death and rebirth, there is the relinquishing of the inferior and the attainment of the superior.

Regarding "transformation without seeds": one should know that the ripening-result consciousness (*vipākaphala-vijñāna*) is devoid of all seeds of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), and for this reason, it is said to be "severed."
"Permanent severance of all seeds" means the severance of all categories of seeds.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, why is it said to be "like water and milk"?

The non-ālayavijñāna and the ālayavijñāna do not function simultaneously in the same location; rather, while all seeds of the ālayavijñāna are exhausted, all seeds of the non-ālayavijñāna increase, just as a swan drinks milk from water.

Furthermore, just as in the world when one attains freedom from desire, the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the non-meditative states gradually diminish while the latencies of the meditative states gradually increase, whereby one achieves the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
The commentary states:

For example, it is like a swan drinking milk from water, or like the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) through the transcendence of desire in the world; these passages are easy to understand and do not require further elaboration.
The Commentary states:
Furthermore, it is taught by the Noble Ones that when one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), consciousness does not depart from the body.
In this context, the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) must be what does not depart from the body, for this attainment does not arise as an antidote to it.
The commentary states:

Having thus already explained that the principles of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) would be untenable [without it], it is established with certainty that the *ālayavijñāna* exists.

Furthermore, by citing the fact that the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) would be untenable as a supporting reason, the previous argument is reinforced; therefore, the words "and entering the attainment of cessation," and so forth, are spoken.
Except for Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, those who have attained the fruit of Non-returning, and Bodhisattvas at the stage of non-retrogression, others are unable to enter it.
To clarify the distinction between the meditative attainment of cessation and death, it is said that this consciousness does not depart from the body.
Consciousness does not depart from the ālayavijñāna. Why?
Because the meditative absorption of cessation cannot counteract it.
The meditative attainment of cessation is not produced for the sake of counteracting this [consciousness], because its object and mode of activity are difficult to discern.
Nor is it entered into the attainment of cessation for the sake of counteracting non-manifest consciousness, because its lack of tranquility is difficult to discern.
Therefore, the meditative absorption of cessation cannot counteract the ālayavijñāna; if there were no counteraction, it would not cease.

This absorption arises specifically to counteract the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna), because their objects, modes of activity, and lack of tranquility are easy to discern. Consequently, this absorption only ceases the evolving consciousnesses, while the ālayavijñāna is not ceased within it.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, this consciousness does not arise again upon emerging from meditative absorption; for once the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) has been interrupted, it cannot be regenerated without the reconnection of the continuum.
The commentary states:

There are those who maintain that although the various consciousnesses cease during meditative absorption, consciousness arises again upon emerging from it; therefore, they say [consciousness] is not separated from the body.

To refute this view, the text says, "Furthermore, it is not the case that [it arises] upon emerging from absorption," and so forth. This passage is easy to understand and requires no further explanation.

The Commentary states: Furthermore, if there is an adherence to the view that because of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), there is mind during the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), this mind is untenable for the following reasons: because the attainment itself would not be established; because its object and mode of activity (*ālambana-ākāra*) cannot be apprehended; because it would entail the fault of being associated with wholesome roots; because it would be illogical for it to be unwholesome or neutral; because it would entail the fault of the manifestation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedanā*); because contact (*sparśa*) would be obtainable; because it would possess functional capacity within meditative concentration (*samādhi*); because it would entail the fault of being merely the cessation of perception; because it would entail the fault of the manifestation of volition (*cetanā*) and wholesome roots such as faith (*śraddhā*); because it would be illogical to extract the supported [mind] from its support [the body]; because there is a supporting analogy; and because, unlike the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*), it would not exist [in all states].
The commentary states:

Furthermore, if there is one who maintains that because of the presence of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the meditative attainment of cessation possesses mind, yet this mind cannot be established—meaning that the consciousness which does not depart from the body within this attainment is certainly not mental consciousness.

Regarding the phrase "because meditative concentration (*samādhi*) would not be established": this means that perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) would both fail to cease. Since the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is never dissociated from the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), and because both perception and feeling would thus fail to cease, meditative concentration could not be established.
Furthermore, the consciousness herein is certainly not mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because its object (*ālambana*) and mode of activity (*ākāra*) cannot be apprehended.
All mental consciousnesses are never found apart from the apprehension of an object and a mode of activity; since these are absent here, that [mental consciousness] does not exist.

Furthermore, the consciousness herein is certainly not the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), for that would entail the error of the manifest activity of wholesome roots; therefore, this concentrated mind is certainly neither unwholesome nor neutral (*avyākṛta*).
What is exclusively wholesome?
It means that this wholesome mind cannot possibly exist apart from non-attachment and so forth, because it is associated with them and because wholesomeness is their defining characteristic.
Since the wholesome roots are present, why do the two types—perception and feeling—not manifest?
Furthermore, since non-attachment and the other [wholesome roots] are certainly never dissociated from contact, contact is established.
Contact produced by meditative concentration has pliancy as its characteristic and is conducive to pleasant and equanimous feelings; therefore, feeling must arise simultaneously with contact.
Since the Noble Ones have taught that there exist sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth, there should be no absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

Alternatively, it may be argued that one enters this absorption because one feels aversion toward perception and sensation as if they were an abscess or an arrow; thus, within this absorption, only perception and sensation cease.

To refute this view, it is further stated that there is efficacy and so forth within samādhi; that which is capable of being brought to revulsion within samādhi is not limited to this [cessation] alone.

Why is this? Because within the state of the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), there would be the fault that by the power of the preceding preparatory concentration (*prayoga-samādhi*), there should be the cessation of only the perception (*saṃjñā*).

If that which is to be loathed were only this [perception], then prior to the attainment of non-perception one would only loathe perception, and within the attainment of non-perception only perception should cease; however, you do not admit this.
Furthermore, if that which is supported ceases, that which depends upon it necessarily ceases; therefore, within this state, the mind should also cease.
If the mind were not to cease in such a meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), then wholesome faculties such as reflection and faith would have to be manifest.
If that [support] were to cease, the mind would necessarily cease; therefore, it is not logical that only the supported should cease.
Since there is a support, it is unreasonable to extract the supported from it.

Regarding the phrase "because there is an analogy," it means that the state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) serves as the analogy here; just as it is illogical for that [state] to be extracted [from the body], so too must this [mind] perish together with it.
Alternatively, there are analogies based on the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*upādāyarūpa*), because they are mutually inseparable from one another.

Furthermore, since the wholesome (*kuśala*) and other such factors are not universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), being fixed as distinct [categories], they need not be present in all states of mind.
Since the two factors of perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), they necessarily abide within the category of omnipresent factors.
Therefore, it is illogical that these two should not exist whenever consciousness is present.
To clarify this point, it is further stated: "Because this [consciousness] does not exist, it is not universal.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, for those who maintain that there is mind within this meditative absorption due to the presence of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), such a mind—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—cannot be established; therefore, their position is irrational.
The commentary states:

Furthermore, within this meditative absorption, the cognition that does not depart from the body is certainly not mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it cannot be established as being of a wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral nature.

That is to say, if it were determined to be mental consciousness, it would necessarily be either wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; however, this mental consciousness cannot be wholesome, for it would entail the fault of being associated with the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). As previously stated, how could a wholesome mind exist apart from non-attachment (*alobha*) and the other [wholesome roots]?
How should these be separated from contact (*sparśa*)?
Furthermore, how should they be separated from the omnipresent mental factors (*citta-dharma*), such as feeling (*vedanā*)?

Or again, there is the view that the meditative mind (*samāhita-citta*) is wholesome because it is induced by wholesome preparatory effort (*prayoga-kuśala*), and not by the power of association with the roots of wholesomeness (*kuśalamūla-saṃprayoga*).
This contradicts that treatise, which establishes that the mind becomes wholesome through the power of association.
Furthermore, what fixed condition exists here such that the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) is wholesome simply by virtue of being associated with non-attachment and so forth?

This is because [the mind in question] is neither a mind that is the outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*) of this meditative absorption, nor is this mind inherently wholesome (*svabhāva-kuśala*), since only those things such as the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) are included in the category of the inherently wholesome.
Furthermore, this wholesome mind is not ultimately wholesome; only liberation is definitively so.
Alternatively, some may say that if there is a conjunction [of conditions], it is called "conjunction-contact" (saṃprayukta-sparśa).
Not all contacts are capable of producing a conjunction.

In this present context, contact lacks the capacity to generate feeling, because at the time of meditative preparation (*prayoga*), one has already cultivated weariness toward those feelings and so forth.

The refutation of this false attachment has already been explained as before; namely, that one should simply extinguish these [afflictions], and therefore it is illogical for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) to be without feeling (*vedanā*) in this state.

Furthermore, what is the reason here that when the verbal formations of vitarka and vicāra cease, speech no longer proceeds, whereas when the mental formations such as saṃjñā and vedanā cease, the mind still continues to proceed?

One cannot state this as a universal rule; for instance, while bodily formations (*kāya-saṃskāra*) have ceased, the body still persists. Therefore, when mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*) have ceased, the mind should likewise persist.

Since the Blessed One has taught that apart from bodily formations there are other causes that allow the body to remain—namely, food, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—it follows that even in the absence of inhalation and exhalation, the body can still persist.
Apart from perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedanā*), it has never been stated that there exists a distinct mental formation (*manosaṃskāra*).

Therefore, it is illogical to establish the existence of a mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) apart from perception and feeling within this state; thus, the consciousness in this meditative absorption is not mental consciousness.
Furthermore, the consciousness within this state is not unwholesome, as it is necessarily wholesome.

Since even in the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) one does not admit the presence of any unwholesome states, how much less could there be unwholesome states within the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)—which occurs during the meditative progression toward liberation through successive transcendence?
Furthermore, at this present time, activities such as craftsmanship cannot possibly exist; therefore, all three types of neutral states (*avyākṛta*) are absent here.
If one were to allow for the existence of the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) within this state, it would be tantamount to establishing the *ālayavijñāna*.

Furthermore, if it is asserted that there is a distinct type of non-retribution (*avipāka*) activity that functions as a fifth kind of indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), such a tenet is merely a matter of names and concepts; it cannot avoid all the faults previously mentioned.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, if there is an adherence to the view that matter and mind arise in immediate succession as the seeds of all phenomena,
this cannot be established, as has already been explained previously.

Furthermore, it would be illogical for one to pass away from the formless realms or the realm of non-perception, or to emerge from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth.
Moreover, the final mind of an Arhat could not be established, as there would be nothing but the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) to accommodate it.
The commentary states:
"If there are further proponents" refers to the Sautrāntikas who hold such a position.
"The uninterrupted arising of form and mind" means that various forms and minds arise in a continuous succession, one after another.
That which is the seed of these phenomena is the causal nature capable of producing all conditioned things.
This refers to their tenet that the matter of a subsequent moment arises immediately and without interval from the matter of the preceding moment.
From a preceding momentary consciousness, the subsequent momentary consciousness and its associated mental factors arise without interval.
Since the principle of cause and effect is thus established herein, what need is there to further postulate the *ālayavijñāna* as the cause of all phenomena?
To refute this attachment, it is stated next that "this cannot be established, as previously explained.
As it was said that two moments of consciousness do not exist simultaneously and so forth, what further fault would there be?

That is to say, when one passes away from the formless realm and is born into the realm of form, the principle that the seeds of prior form can produce the present form cannot be established, because they have been severed and extinguished for a long time.

Likewise, when one passes away from the state of non-conception and is born with the arising of mental consciousness, or when one emerges from the meditative attainment of cessation and the arising of mind occurs, it is in all such cases unreasonable to claim that the seeds of prior mind can produce the subsequent mind, because they have been severed and extinguished for a long time.

Furthermore, if one were to set aside the principle of the simultaneous arising and ceasing of seeds through mutual grasping, and instead maintain that only the preceding moment of consciousness can act as a seed to project the immediately succeeding moment of consciousness, then the final mind of an Arhat would be untenable; he could not enter the sublime realm of Nirvana without remainder. This is because the final mind, acting as a seed and an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), would necessarily give rise to another mind. Consequently, the sublime realm of Nirvana without remainder would not exist.

Therefore, as form and mind arise sequentially from one another, there can only be the *samanantarapratyaya* (immediately preceding condition) and the *adhipatipratyaya* (dominant condition); there is no *hetupratyaya* (causal condition).
The treatise says:
"In this way, if one were apart from the resultant consciousness (*vipākaphalavijñāna*) which contains all seeds, neither defilement (*saṃkleśa*) nor purification (*vyavadāna*) could be established."
Therefore, it is established that the ālayavijñāna, possessing the characteristics previously described, definitely exists.
The commentary states:
Thus, if one were to exclude the maturation-result consciousness (*vipākaphala-vijñāna*) which contains all seeds, it would be pursued by the various faults as previously explained.
Although there is no desire for it, because its own function is weighty, one must nevertheless admit that the ālayavijñāna definitely exists.
This is called the principle of counter-interrogation (prcchā-yukti).
Within this, there is also a reasoning that establishes the point, because it reveals the underlying characteristics through skillful means.
By means of the general characteristics of the non-deceptive *saddharma-śāstra*, it is established that the Mahāyāna is truly the word of the Buddha.
This means that the Mahāyāna teachings are truly the word of the Buddha because they do not contradict the selflessness of persons (pudgala-nairātmya) in any respect.
Furthermore, the teachings that express the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) correspond to the meaning they signify, for they were spoken by the Buddha.
As it is said regarding such statements as "momentary and swiftly perishing," which are like other words of the Buddha;
furthermore, all Mahāyāna teachings are certainly superior because they do not contradict the Dharma or its phenomena, just like the teachings on profound dependent origination and so forth.
The remaining extensive analysis, including the resolution of objections and the formulation of challenges, should be understood according to reason.
The treatise says:
Herein are three verses:

If the Bodhisattva, in a pure mind, remains far removed from the five consciousnesses and undergoes a transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) without any remaining [defiled] mind, how could you possibly achieve this?
If it were a transformation of the basis through an antidote (*pratipakṣa*), it would not be established, because [the defilements] would not have been severed.
If there were no distinction between cause and fruit, it would result in the fault of [the path] being eternally severed.
If one were to assert that the absence of seeds or the absence of a substantial entity constitutes the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
such a transformation would be illogical, because those two absences do not exist.
The commentary states:

Furthermore, if one does not believe in the existence of the *ālayavijñāna*, the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) while abiding in the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) cannot be established.
This is demonstrated through three verses of summary and inquiry, namely: "When the Bodhisattva, regarding the pure mind... and so forth.
"Regarding the pure mind" refers to wholesome consciousness (*kuśala-vijñāna*).
"Distant from the five consciousnesses" refers to the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).
The term "without remainder" means that, excluding the unwholesome and the indeterminate, there is no remaining contaminated (*sāsrava*) wholesome mental consciousness.

This means that because one is free from other contaminated states within the uncontaminated, it is called "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*); it does not mean that the proclivities to be abandoned exist within the antidote itself.
"The transformation of the basis of the mind" refers to the transformation of the basis of the mind.
How could you effect this transformation? If you do not believe in the existence of the ālayavijñāna, how could you bring about this transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti)?
If you allow that the antidote itself is the transformation of the basis, that is logically untenable, because that [antidote] is not a total abandonment [of the defilements].
That which is not the counteragent is itself the permanent abandonment. What is the cause of abandonment?

It is because permanent abandonment is the fruit of the counteragent and is the essence of the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*). If one were to allow that the counteragent is identical to permanent abandonment, then there would be no distinction established between cause and fruit, since the cause—the counteragent—would be the very same as the fruit—abandonment.

If one were to accept that the absence of seeds or the absence of a substantial entity constitutes the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), this would reveal their specific position; therefore, it is said: "Either various seeds of affliction (*saṃkleśa*) accumulated in the mind [constitute the basis], or the absence of those seeds is accepted as the transformation of the basis, or the non-existence of the substance of the seeds is accepted as the transformation of the basis."

Regarding the claim that the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is illogical because those two do not exist: if those two were present, one could speak of them as being "without seeds" or as being "without substance"; however, it is not the case that when those two are absent, one can say they are "without seeds" or "without substance."
When the supramundane mind is actually present, that [mundane state] cannot be found; how, then, can it be said that its seeds are absent or that its substance has been severed?
The treatise says:
Furthermore, what are the distinctions of this ālayavijñāna?
In brief, it should be understood that there are either three or four kinds.

Regarding these, the threefold division refers to the distinctions among the three types of perfuming (*vāsanā*): first, the distinction of the perfuming of linguistic designations (*nāma-kāya-vāsanā*); second, the distinction of the perfuming of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi-vāsanā*); and third, the distinction of the perfuming of the members of existence (*bhavāṅga-vāsanā*).
The four types are: first, the distinction of manifestation; second, the distinction of maturation; third, the distinction of causal characteristics; and fourth, the distinction of appearance.
The commentary states:

regarding the question of what the distinctions of this *ālaya-vijñāna* are, it refers to one who has already gained faith and understanding of the meaning of the established characteristics of the *ālaya-vijñāna*, yet further inquires about its distinctions.
Answer: It is either threefold or fourfold, and so forth.

Regarding the differentiation of the perfuming of names and words (*nāma-vikalpa-vāsanā*): because the names and words for the self, phenomena, and their functions are manifold, there are distinctions in the perfuming of such things as "human" or "divine," "my eye" or "form," and "past" or "future. Due to this, the functional distinctions that cause the various consciousnesses to arise—manifesting as the shadows of these selves, phenomena, and functions—are produced.

Regarding the differentiation of the habitual tendencies of the view of self: it means that due to the power of the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within the mind (*manas*) defiled by the four afflictions, there exists within the ālayavijñāna a differentiation of habitual tendencies capable of grasping at a self.

Regarding the distinctions in the perfuming of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*): it refers to the distinctions in the perfuming of [the links] from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) within the various realms of existence, such as the heavens, due to the predominant power of meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
The treatise states:
Regarding the distinction of "inducing" (*ākṣepa*) herein, it refers to the newly arising perfuming (*vāsanā*).

If this did not exist, the conditionality of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) for consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the conditionality of grasping (*upādāna*) for becoming (*bhava*) would be impossible to establish.

Regarding the differentiation of maturation (*vipāka*) herein: it refers to the differentiation of maturation within the various realms of existence (*gati*) conditioned by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and becoming (*bhava*). If this were non-existent, there would be no seed, and the arising of the phenomena of future existence (*punarbhava*) would consequently be impossible.

Regarding the distinction of the objective aspect (*nimitta*) among these, it refers to the objective aspect of the grasping at a self within the manas. If this did not exist, the objective referent (*ālambana*) for the grasping at a self within the afflicted manas would be impossible to establish.
The commentary states:
Three types [of differentiation] shall be explained; for now, we explain four types, which is why the terms "inducing" (*ākṣepa*) and so forth are mentioned here.

Regarding "the differentiation of induction," this refers to the newly arisen perfuming (*vāsanā*); that is, the perfuming first produced by linguistic expression (*nāma-kāya*). This is called the differentiation of induction because it induces and brings about [subsequent states] through this perfuming.

If this [ālayavijñāna] did not exist, it would be impossible for karma to serve as the condition for consciousness and for grasping (*upādāna*) to serve as the condition for existence (*bhava*). That is to say, it is precisely this ālayavijñāna that, depending on the power of the various latent afflictions (*anuśaya*), arises and abides in the present; this is what is designated as "existence."

Regarding the differentiation of maturation (*vipāka-viśeṣa*): this refers to the differentiation of maturation within the various realms of existence (*gati*) conditioned by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and becoming (*bhava*). This means the differentiation of maturation projected by those [formative forces].

If this did not exist, then the arising of the various phenomena of future existence (*punarbhava*) would not be possible from seeds; that is to say, if one were separated from the root, there would be no branches and so forth.

Regarding the distinction of the objective aspect (*nimitta*): that which is the objective aspect for the grasping at a self within the manas refers to this very *ālayavijñāna*; it is the objective aspect for the grasping at a self when the defiled manas arises through the power of the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and grasps at a self.

If this did not exist, the objective referent (*ālambana*) for the grasping at a self within the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) would be impossible to establish; that is, if this specific aspect of the ālayavijñāna as an objective referent did not exist, the objective referent for the grasping at a self within the mind would not be established.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the distinctions among these characteristics, it means that this very consciousness possesses both common characteristics and non-common characteristics, as well as characteristics of seeds for non-experiencing rebirth and characteristics of seeds for experiencing rebirth, and so forth.
The common characteristic refers to the seeds of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
The individual characteristic refers to the seeds of the respective internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
The common characteristic is the seed for birth without sensation; the individual characteristic is the seed for birth with sensation.

When the antidote arises, it is exclusively of an uncommon nature; when that which is to be countered ceases, its common nature is perceived as pure, being maintained by the conceptualizations of others.
Thus, for a yogācāra, various resolutions and various perceptions regarding a single object are all established.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
"Difficult to sever and difficult to fully know, They should be known as common fetters;
The minds of practitioners differ Because external signs are so vast."
Although the pure is not extinguished, one perceives purity therein;
likewise, the Buddha-fields are purified because the Buddha perceives them as pure.
Furthermore, there is another verse which establishes that the various resolute convictions (*adhimukti*) and various perceptions previously cited are all validly established.
When various practitioners of yoga have different resolutions regarding a single object, their various perceptions are all established;
therefore, one knows that what is apprehended exists only as consciousness.
If this [storehouse consciousness] did not exist, the various distinctions in the arising of the receptacle world and the sentient world would be impossible to establish.
The commentary explains:
"The distinctions of characteristics are of many kinds and not uniform, meaning the various differences such as common characteristics and so forth."
Among these, the "common characteristic" (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) refers to the seeds of the receptacle world; it is the cause for the manifestation of the consciousness that reflects the receptacle world.

Furthermore, regarding the common characteristic: by the dominant power of the maturation of similar individual karmas, for all those capable of experience, there arises a manifesting consciousness that reflects a similar [world].

Furthermore, regarding the "unshared characteristics" (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*), which refer to the seeds of the respective internal bases (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*): they are called "respective" because they are the objects of the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). They are called "internal bases" because they exist within the internal body as the various bases such as the eye and so forth. Because they signify the cause of these respective internal bases, they are called "seeds."

Regarding the statement that "the common characteristic (*sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is the seed for the non-experience of birth": this refers to the cause capable of giving rise to the basis for that which is neither painful nor pleasant, being neither harmful nor beneficial; it does not refer to the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), because the vessel-world does not possess matters of harm or benefit such as pain and pleasure.

Furthermore, the "unshared characteristic" (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*) is precisely that which possesses the seeds for the arising of sensation; this is because it serves as the causal basis for the production of feelings such as suffering and pleasure.
"When the antidote arises" refers to the time when the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) arises.

Regarding the cessation of that which is countered by the unique characteristic (*asādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa*): this refers to the cessation of the seeds within each individual internal sense-base (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*), because they are mutually contradictory.

Regarding that which is held by the conceptualization of others based on the common characteristic (*sādhāraṇa-lakṇa*) and is seen as purely clean: since this common characteristic constitutes the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), although the practitioner’s own internal sense-base conceptualizations have been eternally extinguished, it remains held by the conceptualization of the mental continuums of others; thus, one can only realize and see its purity therein. One contemplates that purity as being like pure space—neither rotted by water, nor supported by earth, nor burned by fire, nor blown away by wind.
How does one attain the purity of vision regarding that which possesses meaning?

Fearing potential objections from others, it is subsequently stated: "Just as a yogin has various resolute convictions (*adhimukti*) toward a single object," which means according to the various distinct resolute convictions regarding gold, silver, grass, and so forth.
Regarding "various things seen": it is only the objects that are seen which are designated as "the seen," because the term *luta* (seen) is frequently used in relation to karma.
"All are established" means that according to what is seen, the various distinctions such as gold, silver, grass, and trees are all established.
Regarding "difficult to abandon and difficult to fully know": that which ought to be abandoned is called "abandonment," and that which ought to be fully known is called "full knowledge.
Since these acts of abandonment and full knowledge are not accomplished even through the greatest exertion and hardship, they are said to be "difficult."
"Knot" (saṃyojana) refers to that which is difficult to sever, just like a physical knot. Why is this so?
Because it is shared; this is the meaning of being a common cause.
Regarding the statement that "minds differ," this is because their various inclinations (*adhimukti*) are each distinct.
Regarding the phrase "due to the magnitude of external signs," this refers to the vast and extensive arrangement of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).
"Pure" refers to that which has already undergone the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
"Though not extinguished" means that because other sentient beings continue to maintain conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) with respect to this very [basis], it cannot be entirely extinguished.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that a pure buddha-field is purified by the vision of the Buddha: it refers to the very same place where ordinary beings—who have not yet severed their conceptual discriminations of form and so forth—perceive a muddy, sandy, stony, uneven terrain of mounds and hollows, stumps, thorns, impurities, and filth; therein, the Tathāgata—who has already severed such conceptual discriminations of form and so forth—perceives a pure buddha-field composed of various jewels such as gold and silver, just as one situated on a filthy sandbank might see a pure grove of gardens.

"If this were non-existent" means that if this ālayavijñāna, characterized by both common and uncommon aspects, did not exist, then the various distinctions in the arising of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) and the sentient world (*sattvaloka*) would be impossible; that is, the distinctions between purity and impurity, as well as the distinctions between suffering and pleasure, would all fail to be established.
The treatise states:
Furthermore, there are the characteristics of heaviness (dausthulya) and the characteristics of pliancy (praśrabdhi).
As for the characteristic of heaviness, it refers to the seeds of the afflictions (kleśa) and secondary afflictions (upakleśa).
The characteristic of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) refers to the seeds of contaminated wholesome phenomena (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*).

If these were absent, the resultant maturation (*vipāka*) would lack functional capacity (*karmanyatā*), and the differentiation of the basis (*āśraya*) that possesses such capacity could not be established.
Furthermore, there are the characteristics of the exhaustion of sensation with remainder and the characteristics of the exhaustion of sensation without remainder.
The characteristics of the exhaustion of sensation with remainder refer to the seeds of wholesome and unwholesome karma whose ripened fruits have already matured.

The characteristic of the exhaustion of experience refers to the seeds of linguistic proliferation (*nāma-vikalpa-vāsanā*), which are the seeds for the circulation of various conceptual proliferations since beginningless time.
If these did not exist, the exhaustion of the fruits of the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—already performed would be impossible to establish.
Furthermore, the arising of new linguistic designations (*nāma-vikalpa*) through perfuming (*vāsanā*) would be impossible.

Moreover, there is the characteristic of being illustrated by analogies; that is to say, this ālayavijñāna is illustrated by the analogies of a magical illusion, a mirage, a dream, and a visual impairment.
If this did not exist, then because it would lack the seeds of unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*), the correspondence with inverted conditions could not be established.

Furthermore, there are complete characteristics and incomplete characteristics: those who are bound by all fetters are said to have complete characteristics; those in the world who are free from desire are said to have diminished characteristics; Śrāvakas in training (*śaikṣa*) and Bodhisattvas are said to have the characteristic of having partially and permanently eradicated [the afflictions]; Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas are said to have the characteristic of having completely and permanently eradicated the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and the characteristic of having completely and permanently eradicated both the afflictive and cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), as appropriate.
If this did not exist, the sequential cessation of such defilements would be impossible.
The commentary states:

Regarding the characteristic of *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness), it is called "coarse" because it is evil; it is called "heavy" because one becomes submerged by its acquisition. It refers precisely to all the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
If this were non-existent, the state of being heavy and lacking capability (*dausthulya-akarmaṇyatā*) would not be possible.
As for the characteristic of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), it is the opposite of what was described: being light, peaceful, and possessing capability is the characteristic of pliancy.

Regarding the statement that "there is the characteristic of the exhaustion of sensation," which refers to the ripening of the fruit of maturation (*vipāka*) and so forth: once the seeds of good and evil have matured, they cannot ripen again, because their experience has been exhausted; this is just as a seed, once it has produced a sprout, cannot produce another.

Regarding the statement that "the characteristic of the non-exhaustion of appropriation refers to the seeds of linguistic designation (*nāma-vyavahāra*)": it is because those very seeds increase in accordance with conditions and are capable of giving rise to the causes of linguistic designation and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
"If this were non-existent" means if the ālayavijñāna with its two aspects were non-existent.
"That which has already been done and that which is being done" refers to the wholesome that has already been performed and the unwholesome that has already been performed.

"Regarding 'the exhaustion of the experience of what has been given': this means that what has been given is exhausted through its being experienced; this refutes [the position] if there were no characteristic of the exhaustion of experience.

Furthermore, regarding 'the arising of new linguistic conventions would not be possible': this refers to the fact that there are no worldly linguistic conventions whatsoever that are fundamentally non-existent and newly come into being; all linguistic conventions depend upon seeds of prior linguistic conventions. This refutes [the position] if there were no characteristic of the exhaustion of experience."
Regarding the characteristic of the simile (*dṛṣṭānta-lakṣaṇa*): it refers to the manifestation of the characterized object (*dārṣṭāntika-lakṣaṇa*) by means of similes such as illusions.
Just as illusory phenomena and the like are the causes that give rise to unreal perceptions, so too is the *ālayavijñāna*.

Regarding the phrase "if this were non-existent": it means that if the characteristics of the simile and the object of the simile did not exist, the ālayavijñāna would lack the characteristic of being an unreal, inverted object-condition, and would instead function solely as the characteristic of an object-condition for true vision.
The remaining text is easy to understand and need not be further explained.
The treatise asks:
For what reason do wholesome and unwholesome dharmas produce maturation, yet their maturation fruit is non-obscured and neutral?
Because the maturation fruit (vipākaphala) is unobscured-neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta), it is not mutually contradictory with the wholesome or the unwholesome.

Since the wholesome and the unwholesome are mutually contradictory, if the maturation fruit were of a wholesome or unwholesome nature, the cessation of affliction (saṃkleśa) could not be established. Therefore, the maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna) is exclusively unobscured-neutral.
The commentary states:

Having thus explained all the meanings of the term *ālayavijñāna*, its synonyms, etymologies, essential characteristics, determinations, and distinctions, [the author] now wishes to demonstrate how this [consciousness] accords with correct practice; therefore, he initiates a series of questions and answers.

Regarding the phrase "by what causes and conditions are they non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)": this means they are undefiled and indeterminate. The causes and conditions for being indeterminate are distinguished by way of their maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*) and so forth.

As for why the non-obscured-indeterminate is not mutually contradictory with the wholesome or the unwholesome: it is because they share a common basis; for instance, the commission of immediate transgressions (*ānantaryakarma*) and the attainment of worldly detachment (*laukikavairāgya*) both equally exist [in relation to such a basis].
Therefore, the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, lest it contradict the causal relationship between these two.
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle Three;
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Fascicle Four.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asvabhāva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part Three: The Characteristic of the Knowable. Section One of Part Three. The Treatise says:
The basis of the knowable has already been explained; how, then, should the characteristics of the knowable be viewed?
Briefly, there are three kinds:
first, the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*); second, the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*); and third, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
The commentary states:
"That which has already been explained as the basis of the knowable" means that it shall not be further discussed here.
"This" refers to this characteristic of the knowable (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*).
Briefly, there are three kinds, namely: because all phenomena necessarily possess the distinctions of that which is to be known, that which is to be abandoned, and that which is to be realized.

Regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*): it arises in dependence upon karma and afflictions, through the pervasive conceptualization of the grasped and the grasper, conforming to and arising from others.
What does such a characteristic indicate? It indicates the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*).
As for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*), it is characterized by the perpetual absence of characteristics.

That which is eternally without characteristics is so because it is characterized by the existence-nature of the person (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*), as well as the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), which are all imaginatively constructed (*parikalpita*).
How can that which is non-existent serve as a characteristic?
This is because one discriminates in just this manner. As the Blessed One has said:
"As long as one does not know what truly exists as truly existing, and as long as one does not know what does not exist as not existing..."
In this way, that which truly exists is known as truly existing, and that which does not truly exist is known as not truly existing.

As for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it refers to the very absence of intrinsic nature—whether as the grasped or the grasper, or as self or phenomena—within that [imagined nature]; it is the state of being an object cognized by taking that [absence] as the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Only through such thorough knowledge can one discern that the thoroughly imagined nature is definitively non-existent, because it possesses a contradictory nature and lacks the quality of being an objective referent.
The treatise says:
Among these, what is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?
It refers to all consciousnesses comprised within false discrimination, which have the ālayavijñāna as their seed.

What, then, are these? They are: the consciousness of the body; the consciousness of the self; the consciousness of the experiencer; the consciousness of that which is experienced; the consciousness of that which experiences; the consciousness of time; the consciousness of number; the consciousness of place; the consciousness of verbal expression; the consciousness of the distinction between self and others; and the consciousness of death and birth in good and evil realms.

In this context, the consciousness of the body, the consciousness of the self, the consciousness of the experiencer, the consciousness of that which is experienced, the consciousness of the experiencer [of that], the consciousness of time, the consciousness of number, the consciousness of location, and the consciousness of verbal expression—these arise from the seeds of the perfuming of names and conventions.
If it is the consciousness of the distinction between self and others, this arises from the seeds perfumed by the view of self.
If it is the consciousness of death and birth in the happy or miserable realms, this arises from the seeds perfumed by the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*).

Through these various consciousnesses, all that is comprised within the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*)—the false conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*) subsumed under the defilements of all realms and destinies—is made manifest.

These various consciousnesses are all comprised within false conceptualization; they have the nature of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*), and they serve as the basis for the manifestation of non-existent, unreal objects. This is called the dependent nature.
Among these, what is the characteristic of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva)?
It is the appearance of objects within that which is merely consciousness and devoid of objects.
Among these, what is the characteristic of the perfected (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva)?

This refers to the fact that within that very other-dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), there is an absolute absence of any intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) corresponding to the appearance of objects.
The commentary explains:

"The so-called body, the possessor of the body, the experiencer, and the cognizer" refer, as will be explained later, to the six internal bases (*ādhyātmika-āyatana*) such as the eye, which constitute their nature.

According to what is appropriate: the mental element (*manodhātu*) that serves as the support for the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, is called the "consciousness of the body"; the mental element that serves as the support for the sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness, is called the "consciousness of the experiencer. That which is the consciousness of what is experienced refers to the six external elements, such as form, which will be explained later; that which is the consciousness of the experiencer refers to the six consciousness elements, which will be explained later.
The consciousness of time manifests as if it were the appearance of the three periods [past, present, and future].
The consciousness of number manifests as if it were the appearance of counting, such as one and so forth.
The consciousness of place manifests as if it were the appearance of villages, gardens, and the like.
The consciousness of verbal expression refers to the manifestation of shadows resembling what is seen, heard, sensed, and known through speech.

The consciousness of the distinction between self and others refers to the consciousnesses of the body and so forth; because the grasping at "I" and "mine" continues without interruption, there arises the distinction between grasping at "I" and "mine" versus grasping at "others" and "theirs."

Regarding the consciousness of death and birth in the happy and miserable realms: this refers to the appearance of reflections of death and birth as gods, humans, hell-beings (*naraka*), animals (*tiryagyoni*), and hungry ghosts (*preta*).

In this context, from "the body and the experiencer of the body" up to "consciousness through verbal expression," which arises from seeds perfumed by names and conventions, means that those bodies and so forth are all manifestations produced by the consciousness from seeds perfumed by names and conventions, because there are no separate entities.

If the consciousness that discriminates between self and other arises from seeds perfumed by the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), this means it manifests with the perfuming of the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭa-manas*) as its cause.

If the consciousness of death and birth in the good or evil realms arises from seeds perfumed by the links of existence (*bhava-aṅga*), this means it manifests with the perfuming of the links of existence as its cause.

Regarding the statement that all such consciousnesses are subsumed under false discrimination (*abhūta-parikalpa*): as previously explained, the objects of apprehension and the subjects of apprehension of the various consciousnesses, such as those of the body and so forth, are established as having false discrimination as their intrinsic nature.
That which has consciousness-only as its nature appears as two parts due to false discrimination, yet in reality it is only consciousness.

Although there is no false attachment within dharmas such as the wholesome, because of the power of dependent origination, the two parts appear; these too are only consciousness, appearing as that which does not exist and is not a true reality.

Regarding the basis: that which is apprehended, such as form and so forth, is called "non-existent," while that which apprehends, such as consciousness and so forth, is called "not truly real. Both of these are the thoroughly imagined nature and are collectively termed "objects."

The various consciousnesses subsumed under false discrimination (*abhūta-parikalpa*) are the causal conditions for the manifestation of these two [aspects]; therefore, they are called the "basis" (*āśraya*).

That which is thus termed the "dependent nature" (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) refers to everything previously explained—such as the *ālayavijñāna* acting as the seed—and all such things are designated as the dependent nature.

That is to say, within that which is devoid of objects and consists solely of consciousness, there is the appearance of objects; yet in reality, there is no object to be grasped nor a subject that grasps, for it is comprised solely of false discrimination.
Within the various forms of consciousness, there is the manifestation of objects as they are grasped through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).

This refers to that which, within the dependent nature (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*), is eternally devoid of the nature of appearing as such objects; that is to say, within the reflections manifested by the mind and mental factors arising from conditions, it is the true nature of *tathatā* (suchness) that is never revealed by the characteristics of horizontal conceptualization. This is precisely what is called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, all phenomena arise from causes and conditions and have consciousness alone as their nature; one should know that these are all termed the *paratantra-lakṣaṇa* (dependent nature).
That which appears as objects through inverted and arbitrary conceptualization—one should know that this is all termed the *parikalpita-lakṣaṇa* (imagined nature).
The true nature of suchness, which is eternally non-existent as the imagined nature upon the dependent nature, should be known as the perfected nature.

For example, through the power of its own continuity, the thirst of a deer establishes the false imagined nature of the grasped and the grasper appearing as water; this should be known as the dependent nature.
