The false conceptualization that the appearance of water as a real entity exists should be known as the *parikalpita-lakṣaṇa* (the imagined nature).

Within this very instance of the mirage, the false conceptualization that the characteristic of water is ultimately without intrinsic nature should be known as the *pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa* (the perfected nature).

Furthermore, the imagined characteristic (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa*) is itself the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); the dependent characteristic (*paratantra-lakṣaṇa*) is itself the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), also called the discriminated nature (*vikalpita-svabhāva*); and the perfected characteristic (*pariniṣpanna-lakṣaṇa*) is itself the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), also called the dharmic nature (*dharmatā-svabhāva*). These three types are the teaching of the three things that should be known, abandoned, and realized, respectively.
As it is also said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the Buddha told Maitreya:

"If, regarding various objects characterized by specific modes of appearance, one universally conceptualizes them as form, feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, and even as the basis for all Buddha-dharmas—this is called the universal conceptualization of names, notions, designations, and verbal expressions."

To regard the intrinsic nature of all forms, up to and including the intrinsic nature of all Buddha-dharmas, as being [inherently existent]—this is called "imagined form" up to "imagined all Buddha-dharmas."

Furthermore, regarding those objects of mental aspects, there is only the establishment of the nature of phenomena through conceptualization; with conceptualization as a condition, various proliferations arise, and names, notions, and verbal designations are conventionally established—ranging from what is called "form" up to what is called "all Buddha-dharmas. This is termed the conceptualization of form, up to the conceptualization of all Buddha-dharmas.
Whether Tathāgatas appear in the world or do not appear, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains established and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) remains established.

Because of that form which is conceptually constructed (*parikalpita-rūpa*), this discriminated form (*vikalpita-rūpa*) is at all times and for all eternity the nature of suchness (*tathatā*), the nature of lack of intrinsic existence (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), the nature of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), and the nature of the reality limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). This is called the form of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-rūpa*), and so on, up to the form of the nature of phenomena because of those all-encompassing Buddha-qualities which are conceptually constructed.
This differentiation of all Buddha-dharmas, at all times and for all eternity—even this is called the dharma-nature of all Buddha-dharmas.
The detailed exposition is as in the sūtra.
The treatise says:
Herein, that which is the "body of the body" and the "consciousness of the experiencer" should be understood as the six internal bases, such as the eye and so forth.
That which is the "consciousness of what is experienced" should be understood as the six external bases, such as form and so forth.
That which is capable of receiving [objects] is consciousness; it should be understood as the six consciousness-elements (vijñānadhātu), namely, the eye-consciousness and so forth.
It should be understood that all other forms of consciousness are merely specific distinctions of these [six].
The commentary states:
These various consciousnesses refer to those previously described, beginning with the body and ending with the faculty of sensation.

As for their "differentiation," it refers to the differentiated nature of these various consciousnesses; that is, within these very conditioned consciousnesses, there exists the differentiated nature of what has already occurred, what is currently occurring, and what will occur, based upon which the consciousness of the manifestation of time is established.
Because these various consciousnesses possess distinctions such as "one" and so forth, the consciousness that manifests as number is established based upon them.
Because the consciousnesses of what is experienced possess distinctions such as "superior" and "inferior," the consciousness that manifests as location is established based upon them.
The same should be understood for other categories.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, all these consciousnesses consist of nothing but consciousness alone, because they are entirely devoid of external objects.
By what analogy is this demonstrated?
It should be understood that dreams and the like serve as the analogies; that is to say, just as in a dream there is no objective referent whatsoever, but there is only consciousness alone.
Although various forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, houses, forests, lands, and mountains appear as objective referents, within them there is no objective reality whatsoever.
By means of this analogy, one should understand accordingly that at all times and in all places, there is only consciousness.
By these words, one should understand that there are further analogies such as illusions, mirages, and visual distortions.

If, at all times and in all places during the waking state, everything is like a dream and consists of nothing but consciousness, then just as one realizes upon waking from a dream that everything within the dream consisted of nothing but consciousness, why does it not occur in the same way during the waking state?

The transformation of true wisdom upon awakening is likewise: just as this awareness does not transform while one is dreaming, but only transforms upon waking from the dream, so too this awareness does not transform before one has attained the awakening of true wisdom, but only transforms once that awakening of true wisdom is attained.
The commentary states:
All things are mere consciousness and possess no external objects whatsoever.
The employment of metaphors such as dreams to demonstrate this is because it is established through common consensus.
The passage concerning "being like a dream" and so forth is easy to understand and requires no further explanation.
The treatise says:
For those who have not yet attained the awakening of true wisdom, how can they infer [the nature of reality] within the context of consciousness-only?
This should be understood through both scripture and reasoning.
Regarding scripture, as the Bhagavān said in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*:
"In this way, these three realms are nothing but mind."
Furthermore, the Blessed One’s *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* also speaks in this way.
In that sūtra, the Bodhisattva Maitreya asks the Blessed One:
"Regarding the images that are the objects of various samādhis, should one say they are different from this mind, or should one say they are not different?"
The Buddha told Maitreya:
"One should say they are not different. Why is this?"
"Because that image is nothing but consciousness, I say that the object of consciousness is manifested by consciousness alone.
World-Honored One,
if the image traversed in samādhi is not different from this mind, how can this mind take this very mind as its object?"
Maitreya! There is not even the slightest dharma that can grasp another slight dharma.
However, when this very mind arises in such a manner, there is the manifestation of such an image.

Just as when one uses a physical object as a condition to see that very object, yet thinks, "I am now seeing a reflection," and further thinks that there is a reflection appearing separately from the object.
This mind is likewise; when it arises in such a manner, there appear reflections that seem to differ from one another.
By this very teaching, the underlying principle is also revealed. Why is this so?

Within the state of meditative concentration, all the images of objects of knowledge—such as the various forms of bluish discoloration—that appear according to one's observation are without distinction; these phenomena such as bluish discoloration are seen only as one's own mind.
By this principle, a bodhisattva should infer that within all consciousnesses, there is only consciousness and no external objects.
Furthermore, regarding such things as the livid corpse and so forth, it is not a memory-consciousness (*smṛti-vijñāna*) seeing an object of perception present before one.

The two types of recollective consciousnesses produced through hearing and reflection also take the past as their object; therefore, the images that appear [within them] are established as mere cognition (vijñaptimātra).
By means of this inference, although a bodhisattva has not yet attained the awakening of true knowledge, they should be able to infer the nature of mere cognition.
The commentary states:

"By means of scripture and reasoning" refers to the valid cognition of authoritative testimony (*āptāgama*) and the valid cognition of inference (*anumāna*). Although one has not yet realized the true wisdom of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), one should be able to infer that consciousness-only is devoid of external objects.

The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* is that which, within that very scripture, proclaims the meaning of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva; it consists essentially of the collection of names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*) that establish the characteristics of these ten stages, manifested by consciousness. Specifically, with the images manifested by the consciousness of the noble Vajragarbha acting as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), they appear as reflections upon the consciousness within the bodies of the listeners, resembling those dharma-gates. Thus transmitted in succession down to the present, it is called "the teaching" (*deśanā*).
"Mind-only" means that mind and consciousness are one.
The term "only" (mātra) serves to exclude the object of apprehension (*grāhya*); since that [object] does not exist, the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*) likewise does not exist.
This does not negate mental factors (*caitta*), for they are inseparable from the mind.
As it is said: "If there were no mental factors (caitta), the mind would never arise.
If that is so, why is the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) considered to consist of mind alone?
This is a flaw in their own tenet.
In our Mahāyāna school, wherever there is mind, there must necessarily also be mental factors associated with the mind;
and wherever there are no mental factors associated with the mind, the mind itself is certainly non-existent.
Thus, the three realms are all merely mind; this statement reveals that the three realms are consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
As for the "three realms," it refers to those who, being associated with the fetters of craving such as desire and so forth, have fallen within the three realms.

This statement of "consciousness-only" establishes that there are only the various minds and mental factors, and that there are no objects of perception resulting from the horizontal imputations of the three realms.

This statement does not exclude such objects as True Suchness (*tathatā*) or the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), namely the two kinds of objects—fundamental and subsequently attained—that are subsumed under the Truth of the Path. Because these are not grasped by craving, are not objects of antidotes, and are not delusive, they are not included within the three realms; furthermore, because they are not separate from consciousness, it is unnecessary to state this explicitly.

If that were so, one should likewise speak of these two realms [as being consciousness-only], because in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), according to the Sautrāntikas, there are only mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

This objection is not valid; for since all objects apprehended by consciousness are without objective reality, it is not merely the absence of form that is designated as "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*).
What else is non-existent?
It is the objects apprehended by consciousness, such as space and so forth.

The masters of the Sautrāntika school maintain that the various minds and mental factors of the formless realm are without form, without substance, and without reality, serving merely as the basis for the manifestation of the objects they apprehend.
Fearing that others might hold [these] to be neither mind nor mental factors, it is therefore said that all three realms consist of nothing but mind (*citta-mātra*).
The underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) clarified in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* is as explained in the commentary on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
"Sūtra" refers to the teaching.
"Samādhi" is that which causes the mind to abide in one-pointedness; its essence consists of mental factors.

The object upon which this [samādhi] focuses is called the "sphere of activity" (*gocara*). The original object is called the "substance" (*vastu*), while that which appears as a likeness of it is called the "image" (*pratibimba*).

When I say, "The objects of consciousness are manifested by consciousness alone," I mean that the external objects which are the focal points of consciousness are merely manifestations of internal consciousness; this is the sense that the object of cognition has consciousness as its own nature.
This means that the objects perceived by consciousness are merely images manifested upon consciousness itself and possess no separate substantial entity.
As for the question, "How can this mind take this very mind as its object?"—this demonstrates that such an activity contradicts its own nature.

"Maitreya, there is not even the slightest dharma that can grasp the slightest dharma. This explains the previous objection: because there is no functional activity, for it is established that the activity and the agent of all dharmas are both unestablished.

Regarding such arising: because the power of dependently originated phenomena is great, two reflections arise upon a single substance; in relation to one another, they are neither identical nor separate.
All minds and mental factors arise by their very nature through the power of conditions (*pratyaya*).

This is like seeing a reflection when a physical object serves as a condition; for example, relying upon a physical object such as one's own face, one sees that very object reflected in a mirror or similar surface, yet due to delusion, one says, "I see my shadow."
Because the power of conditions such as a mirror is great, although there is no distinct reflection, an image appears as if it were something separate.

This mind is likewise; when it arises in this way, because the functional capacity of various conditions—such as the mind and mental factors, recollections, and conceptualizations—is great, although there is no distinct object-image of samādhi or the like, an image appears as if it were something separate.
That this scriptural teaching also manifests through reasoning means that within this teaching, the principles of inference (*anumāna*) are also concurrently revealed.

Why is this so? Regarding the phrase "within the concentrated mind" (*samāhita-citta*), it introduces a specific logical meaning found within the teaching: namely, that the [visualized objects] such as the livid corpse (*vinīlaka*) are not separate from the mind, because they manifest according to one's intentional desire, just like the livid corpses seen in a dream.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "within such [states] as the livid-blue and so forth, it is not a consciousness that retains a memory (*dhāraṇā-vijñāna*) and so on," this was said because of the fear of their divergent views.
That is to say, some might hold the view:
"Because he previously saw skeletons and so forth on a desolate road and the like, he now still retains them in memory as the images (*pratibimba*) traversed in samādhi."

To refute this view, it is said: "Furthermore, within such [states] as the livid corpse and so forth, it is not a memory-consciousness (*smṛti-vijñāna*) that perceives the object of focus as being present before one.

If this object of focus were indeed that which was previously remembered, then it would have to be remembered exactly as it was previously perceived, with its location fixed and its qualities received just as they were before.

However, it is not so; the wisdom produced through cultivation is true direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and the objects perceived appear clearly before one, whereas the consciousness that retains memories does not possess such a capacity.

If that were so, then the consciousness associated with the two types of wisdom consisting of hearing and reflection—which recollects and maintains those objects of those two [wisdoms]—would have to exist apart from consciousness itself.

This is not the case; because those two consciousnesses of recollection arising from hearing and so forth take the past as their object, and since the past does not exist, the images of the objects are nothing but consciousness itself.

For example, it is like recollecting one’s own youth; therefore, this consciousness manifests as that which is recollected and maintained, and because it is merely what is remembered by consciousness, it is empty.
It is like the image of a woman as a chain of bones appearing before the mind of a practitioner of meditation who contemplates impurity.
By means of such inference and other methods, the meaning of the words is clear and requires no further explanation.
The Treatise says:

Having thus explained the various consciousnesses through analogies such as dreams, it is established within this very context that the visual consciousness and other consciousnesses are *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only).
Since the various consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and others, possess form, how can it be seen that they too are merely consciousness?
This is also explained as before through scripture and reasoning.
The commentary states:

The "teaching" refers to the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*; the "principle" refers to the reasoning explained within those sūtras—namely, that the images traversed in samādhi, as well as the analogies of dreams and so forth, are all as previously described.
The treatise says:
If these various consciousnesses are also in essence consciousness, for what reason do they manifest as having the nature of matter, appearing as a single class, stable, and evolving in continuity?
Because it serves as the basis for various defiled phenomena such as the perversions;
otherwise, the perversion of perceiving what is non-meaningful as meaningful would not be possible.
If this did not exist, the defilements of the two obstacles—those of afflictions and those of the cognizable—would not be possible.
If this did not exist, all pure phenomena would likewise not exist.
Therefore, the various consciousnesses should transform in this manner.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"The confused appearance and the confused substance Should be admitted as the consciousness of form."
"And as for non-material consciousness, if it were absent, the rest would also be absent.
The commentary states:

If these various forms of consciousness were also essentially consciousness and so forth, this question concerns the cause for the persistence, continuity, and transformation of material consciousness within its own category.

The term "of one kind" (*ekajātīya*) means "similarity. Because it is of one kind from beginning to end, without variation or interruption, it is called "firmly abiding" (*sthirasthāyin*); this is precisely what is described as "continuing in succession" (*saṃtatyā vartate*).

Regarding the phrase "because it serves as the basis for various defiled phenomena such as perversions (*viparyāsa*)," the term "such as" (*ādi*) includes all defiled phenomena consisting of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and birth.
The visual consciousness and other such cognitions serve as the locus of support (*āśraya*) for these various defiled phenomena; here, "locus of support" carries the meaning of "cause."
The word "hence" (*ataḥ*) means "therefore.

Having observed the intent of that question, he offers this answer: within the absence of intrinsic reality (*anartha*), there appear representations resembling the eye-consciousness and the other cognitions; these evolve as a single, stable, and continuous stream, and from this arise such phenomena as the various inversions.
If it were not so, and if it did not function in this manner, then the cognitive inversion that perceives what is non-meaningful as meaningful could not exist.
If such inversion did not exist, the defilements of the two obstacles—those of afflictions and those of the known—could not exist either, as they would lack their causal conditions.
If there were no defilement, there would likewise be no purity, because it is by the cessation of defilement that purity is manifested.
Therefore, when it is said that "the various consciousnesses should transform in this way," it means that the eye-consciousness and the other consciousnesses should transform in this way.
Is it not the case that all phenomena arise without depending on causal power, rather than requiring such power?
No; for the answer was given in accordance with the question.

That question concerned what is required, not the specific types of causes. Since he did not maintain that there are separate material forms (*rūpa*) existing apart from consciousness, he asked only why the *ālayavijñāna* must transform into material forms rather than merely transforming into consciousness itself; therefore, this answer was given.
The delusive appearance is admitted to be a transformation of consciousness resembling matter, while the delusive essence is admitted to be a transformation of consciousness that is not matter.
Because this follows the method of versification, the phrasing is interrupted, yet the meanings remain interconnected.

If there were no causal consciousness that transforms into something resembling form, then a resultant consciousness that is not form could not exist; for if the object does not exist, the subject that possesses the object likewise cannot exist.
The treatise asks:

For what reason do the body-consciousness, the self-consciousness, the experiencer-consciousness, the experienced-consciousness, and the experiencing-consciousness all arise together in conjunction within every body?
"Because it is manifested by the full accomplishment of birth and enjoyment.
The commentary explains:
For what reason are the body and so forth asked about as before?
"Being able to fulfill [the faculties]" and so forth are answered as previously stated.

By means of these five consciousnesses, there is nothing within the entire body that is not fully endowed with and utilized by what they manifest; if even one member were lacking, it would not be complete.
The treatise says: For what reason do the various consciousnesses, such as those of the world and so forth, evolve with differentiation?

It is because the flow of birth and death has been uninterrupted since beginningless time; because the realm of sentient beings is immeasurable; because the receptacle worlds are immeasurable; because the successive verbal expressions regarding all activities are immeasurable; because the distinct apprehensions and experiences of differences are immeasurable; because the experiences of the maturation of the fruits of karma—whether pleasant or unpleasant—are immeasurable; and because the various differences in death and birth experienced are immeasurable.
The commentary states:
For what reason are the world-consciousness (*loka-vijñāna*) and so forth, as well as the consciousnesses of the sixfold manifestation, questioned as before?

The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the consciousnesses of number, place, verbal expression, the distinction between self and other, the good and evil destinies, and death and rebirth—these being the six manifesting consciousnesses.

Regarding the phrase "because from beginningless time until the present, the distinctions of birth and death experienced are immeasurable," this refers to the fruit that must be explained as the sequential manifestation of the world and other consciousnesses.
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, how are these various consciousnesses established so as to constitute the nature of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā)?
Briefly, it is by means of three characteristics.
First, by virtue of being representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), because there are no external objects;
second, by virtue of its dual nature, because there is the distinction between the two consciousnesses of the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*);
third, by virtue of its manifoldness, because it arises with various modes of appearance (*ākāra*).
Why is this so? Because all these consciousnesses lack external objects, they are established as *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

Because they possess the aspects (*nimitta*) and the seeing (*darśana*), they are established as being twofold: for instance, when the visual consciousness and the others take forms and other objects as their aspects, and take the cognition of the visual consciousness and so forth as the seeing, up to the cognition of the tactile consciousness as the seeing.

If it is the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it takes all cognitions—from the eye-consciousness as the first to the cognition of phenomena (*dharmavijñāna*) as the last—as its objective aspect (*nimitta*), and takes the cognition of the mental consciousness itself as its vision (*darśana*).
This is because this mental consciousness possesses discrimination and arises appearing as all the [other] cognitions.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
The two kinds of varieties of consciousness-only— The meditator’s mind can enter them;
By realizing and entering "mind-only," One is also able to subdue and transcend them.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, as to how these various consciousnesses are established, it means that based on the preceding principles, one further employs distinct principles to raise various inquiries.
Because "consciousness-only" means that there are no external objects, it is subsequently stated that "there are no objects.
The term "only" (vijnapti-mātra) is spoken specifically to exclude objects; the principle that there are no objects has been explained in part and will be explained in part further on.
Regarding "by way of two natures," these refer to the image-part (*nimittabhāga*) and the seeing-part (*darśanabhāga*).
Within a single consciousness, both the image and seeing parts arise simultaneously; these two parts, the image and the seeing, are neither identical nor separate.

Beginning from visual consciousness up to tactile consciousness, each according to its respective type, transforms into various objective representations such as form; these are called the *nimittabhāga* (image-part).
The various consciousnesses, such as the visual, discern their objects; this aspect of their capacity for seeing is called the *darśanabhāga* (seeing-part).
Furthermore, the objective aspect is called "characteristic" (nimitta), and the subjective aspect is called "view" (darśana); these are termed the two natures.
It is "various" because it arises through various modes of activity (ākāra).

Within a single consciousness, one portion transforms to resemble the aspect of the apprehended object (*grāhyākāra*), while another portion transforms to resemble the aspect of the apprehending subject (*grāhakadarśana*); these two portions, each possessing various distinct modes of appearance (*ākāra*), arise simultaneously.
If it were not admitted that a single consciousness can possess various aspects simultaneously, there would be no simultaneous cognition of various objects.

As for the statement that the mental consciousness takes all [sensory faculties], beginning with the eye, as its basis, this means that such a mental consciousness is capable of apprehending all objects simultaneously.
With the visual consciousness as the first and the mental consciousness (*dharmavijñāna*) as the last, the established characteristics are its *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect).
This very mental consciousness, in its capacity for discerning objects, is termed the *darśanabhāga* (perceptual aspect).

Because this mental consciousness (manovijñāna) universally discriminates and arises appearing as all [other] consciousnesses, it is therefore called "characteristic" (nimitta), "name" (nāman), and "view" (darśana), and is also termed "the manifold" (citra).

In the verses, the various yogācāras are able to enter into the two natures of mere-consciousness; having ultimately dispelled external objects for the sake of subduing and detaching from them, since the objective referent of the grasping mind does not exist, the consciousness that takes it as an object cannot exist either.
Since there is no object to be cognized, the cognizer also does not exist; it is not the case that there is a cognizer in the absence of an object to be cognized.
Otherwise, the non-conceptualization of objective appearances would also be called a "possessor of an object."

If the mind capable of conceptualization is a supramundane mind, although it is free from the conceptualization of the grasper and the grasped, there still exists the equality of the internal realization of noble wisdom (āryajñāna) as the basis for both the subjective perceiver and the objective perceived.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, within this context, there is a class of masters who maintain that there is but a single consciousness which, as it evolves in dependence upon various bases, receives their respective names—just as mental action (manas-karman) is designated by the names of bodily and vocal action (kāya-vāk-karman).
The commentary states:
Furthermore, regarding the statement by a certain class of masters that there is "only one consciousness," this reveals the differences in the views held by various teachers.

That is to say, there is a certain class of bodhisattvas who maintain that there is only the nature of a single consciousness; when it arises in dependence upon this or that eye and so forth, it receives their respective names—namely, from visual consciousness up to mental consciousness—and within this, there are no other distinct types of consciousness.
How is this so? It is like mental karma (*manas-karman*).

Just as when a single instance of volition (*cetanā*) is activated within the locus of the body and directed toward the body, it is called bodily karma; when activated within the locus of speech and directed toward speech, it is called vocal karma; and when associated with the mind, it is called mental karma.
The mental consciousness is also like this.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, when it operates upon all bases, two kinds of images appear that resemble various characteristics; namely, the image of the object alone and the image of conceptualization.

Furthermore, in all places, it also manifests as an image resembling the tangible; within the realm of form, this very mental consciousness depends upon the body, just as the other material sense-faculties depend upon the body.
The commentary states:

Some might argue that if this were so, such mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) would lack conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), because its support (*āśraya*) is dull, just like the visual consciousness and the others.

For that which depends [on a support] must conform to its support; just as the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) serves as the basis for defilement, the mental consciousness that functions in conjunction with it likewise becomes defiled.
To resolve this objection, it is said that [consciousness] arises in dependence upon all bases (*āśraya*).
"All bases" refers to the eye and so forth.
"When the bases arise" means at the time of their production.
"Manifesting as two images resembling various characteristics" means manifesting as two images resembling the various grasped objects (*grāhya*) and grasping subjects (*grāhaka*).
To explain this, it is further stated: "namely, only the object," and so forth.

In the single consciousness, one part manifests as an image resembling an object, while the second part arises through conceptualization of that object; therefore, there is no fault of non-conceptuality.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "in all places it also arises as a semblance of the tangible image," this means that within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one experiences and discerns tangibles such as lightness and heaviness without distraction, because [the mind] conforms to them.
Regarding "in the realm of form," this does not refer to the formless realm.
Why? Because this very mental consciousness depends upon the body as its support.

Just as other material sense-faculties depend upon the body—just as the other material faculties such as the eye and so forth depend upon the body—they are able to cause benefit or harm to this very body.
Consciousness is likewise; because it relies upon the body within the realm of form, it experiences and discriminates that very body, thereby being able to cause benefit or harm.
The treatise says:
Regarding this, there is a verse:

If one travels far alone, sleeping without a body within a cave, having tamed this mind so difficult to tame—I call him a true brahmin. Commentary: This means that when one departs from the world and wanders alone, there is no physical body remaining; one sleeps peacefully within the cave of the heart. Because the mind is extremely difficult to subdue, one must exert effort to discipline it. Only such a person can be called a true brahmin. It is not by birth, lineage, or clan that one becomes a brahmin; rather, it is through the practice of the Dharma that one attains the name of "brahmin. Just as a fire burns wood and leaves behind only ashes, so too does the practitioner burn away all afflictions until nothing remains. One who has severed all bonds and attained liberation is called a true brahmin. Furthermore, because he has abandoned all worldly desires and is free from the defilements of greed and anger, he is called a true brahmin. Moreover, because he has transcended the cycle of birth and death and reached the ultimate limit of the Dharma, he is called a true brahmin. Finally, because he has realized the supreme truth and attained the state of non-arising, he is called a true brahmin. Thus, it is said: "One who travels far alone, sleeping without a body within a cave, having tamed this mind so difficult to tame—I call him a true brahmin. This concludes the verse. Regarding the term "true brahmin," it refers to one who possesses the four qualities of a brahmin: first, being born of a pure lineage; second, possessing virtuous conduct; third, being endowed with wisdom; and fourth, having attained liberation. Among these, the most essential is liberation. Therefore, the Buddha taught: "One who has cut off all fetters and attained the fruit of arhatship is called a true brahmin. This is why it is said: "I call him a true brahmin. This concludes the commentary on the verse. Regarding the term "difficult to tame": it refers to the fact that the mind is inherently unstable and prone to wandering, making it exceedingly difficult to control. It is like a wild horse that cannot be reined in, or a monkey that leaps about in every direction. Only through diligent cultivation and constant mindfulness can it be brought under control. Therefore, the Buddha taught: "The mind is the master of all phenomena; if the mind is well-tamed, one attains peace. This is why it is said: "Having tamed this mind so difficult to tame. This concludes the commentary on the verse. Regarding the term "sleeping without a body": it means that although the physical body remains, the practitioner has already cast off the "body" of the five aggregates and dwells in the state of emptiness. It is like a bird that has shed its feathers and flies freely in the sky, or like a snake that has cast off its old skin and moves with ease. Because the practitioner has abandoned the body of the aggregates, they are said to "sleep without a body. This concludes the commentary on the verse. Regarding the term "within a cave": it refers to the cave of the heart-mind. Just as a person might dwell in a mountain cave to escape the heat and noise of the world, so too does the practitioner dwell within the cave of the mind, free from the distractions of external objects. Because the mind is tranquil and undisturbed, it is called a "cave. This concludes the commentary on the verse. Regarding the phrase "travels far alone": "far" refers to the transcendence of the three realms of existence; "alone" refers to the absence of the two extremes of existence and non-existence. Because the practitioner has departed from the world and wanders in solitude, they are said to "travel far alone. This concludes the commentary on the verse. Regarding the phrase "I call him a true brahmin": "I" refers to the Buddha; "call" means to designate; "true" means genuine; and "brahmin" refers to one who has exhausted all outflows and attained the fruit of arhatship. Because he has realized the supreme truth and is worthy of offerings from gods and humans, he is called a true brahmin. This concludes the commentary on the verse. To explain that there is but a single consciousness, the Bodhisattva cites scriptural authority, stating:
"Because it travels far and wanders through all objects of cognition, it is called 'Far-Going' (dūraṅgama)."
To further substantiate this meaning, it is said that [the self] wanders alone, for there is no second.
It is called "bodiless" because it lacks physical form or substance.
It is said to "sleep in a cave" because it dwells within.
"To tame this" means to exercise mastery over such a mind.
"The mind that is difficult to tame" refers to its nature being stubborn and unruly.
The treatise states:
Furthermore, as the Sūtra says:
"The objects traversed by these five faculties are each received by the mind; the mind is their support.
The commentary explains:
Furthermore, he cites a second authoritative teaching as proof:

"The objects traversed by these five faculties are each individually apprehended by the mind. This means that the objects traversed by these five faculties are exclusively those which the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) apprehends one by one, individually and separately.
"The mind is the basis for those [consciousnesses]" means that by virtue of its predominance, they arise.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, as it was stated among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the six groups of consciousness are all called the mind base (*manāyatana*).
The commentary states:
Furthermore, a third scriptural authority is cited as proof.
The statement that the six groups of consciousness are all called the "mind-base" (manāyatana) refers to the teaching concerning the activities of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
The Commentary says:

If, in a given context, the *ālayavijñāna* is established as the "object-consciousness" (*artha-vijñapti*), it should be understood that all other consciousnesses therein are its "image-consciousness" (*nimitta-vijñapti*).

If the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and its support are the "seeing-consciousness" (*darśana-vijñapti*), this is because that image-consciousness serves as the causal condition for the arising of this seeing-consciousness; when appearing as an object, it performs the function of providing a basis for the arising of the seeing-consciousness. This is what is called establishing the various consciousnesses so as to constitute the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).
The commentary states:

If, in a certain context, the *ālayavijñāna* is established as the "object-consciousness" (*artha-vijñāna*), then "object" (*artha*) carries the sense of "cause"; thus, it means establishing the *ālayavijñāna* as the "causal consciousness."
"All other consciousnesses" refers to the consciousnesses of the body and so forth.
"Their object-consciousness" refers to the objective aspect (*nimitta*), because it is that which is taken as an object and that which is traversed.

"The mental consciousness and its support" refers to the sixth consciousness and its support—the immediately preceding past mind (*manas*) and the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*)—because these two serve as the basis for the arising of defilement.
Regarding the statement that "the seeing-consciousness is so called because it is capable of discernment":

as for the phrase "because those object-consciousnesses (*nimitta-vijñāna*) serve as the causal conditions for the arising of this seeing-consciousness," it means that the various transformed objects manifested by the *ālaya-vijñāna* serve as the causal conditions for the arising of these two types of seeing-consciousness.
"Appearing as an object" means that the mental consciousness appears as an object.
"Being able to act as the basis for the arising of the visual consciousness" means that the eye and other [sensory] consciousnesses can serve as the basis for the arising of the visual consciousness.
The Treatise says:
Various objects appear before one, manifesting with clear distinctness, yet they do not exist.
How can this be known?
As the Blessed One said:
"If bodhisattvas accomplish four dharmas, they are able to realize and enter into the fact that all is representation-only (vijñapti-mātra) and that no external object exists at all.

First, they accomplish the wisdom that recognizes the characteristics of contradictory cognitions; for example, hungry ghosts, animals, and gods and humans perceive the same single thing, yet there are differences in what they cognize therein."

Second, the accomplishment of the knowledge that consciousness can be perceived even when it lacks an objective referent (*ālambana*), because objects are apprehended within the conditions of the past, the future, dreams, and reflections.

Third, the accomplishment of the knowledge that should be free from inversion without effort, because if there were an external object, the consciousness that perceives that object would have to be non-inverted without relying on effort, as it would know reality as it is.
Fourth is the accomplishment of the sublime wisdom that functions in accordance with the three kinds of superior wisdom. What are these three?

First, attaining mastery over the mind: for all Bodhisattvas who have attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), various objects appear in accordance with the power of their resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
Second, for one who has attained *śamatha* and practices the cultivation of the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmālambana-vipaśyanā*), all objects appear as soon as they direct their attention.
Third, for one who has already attained non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), when non-conceptual wisdom is present before them, no objects at all appear.

By means of these three types of superior knowledge thus explained, the conforming subtle knowledge, and the three types of causal conditions previously described, the principles regarding what is meaningful and what is meaningless are established.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, in order to establish the principle that there is no external object, he cites other teachings and other reasonings, namely that bodhisattvas accomplish the four dharmas and so forth.
Regarding "the knowledge of the characteristics of contradictory cognitions": they are called "contradictory" because they are mutually opposed.
The cognition that is contradictory is termed "contradictory cognition.
The cause for the arising of this cognition is designated as the "characteristic."

Understanding that these appearances are merely transformations of the internal mind and that external objects do not exist, one realizes there is no objective referent; this is what is called "wisdom.

Regarding the statement "as with hungry ghosts, animals, gods, humans, and so forth": it means that due to the predominant power of the transformations of their own karma, hungry ghosts perceive rivers as being entirely filled with pus, blood, and the like;
whereas fish and other animals perceive those same places as houses and pathways for wandering.
Devas see this ground as adorned with various jewels;
humans see this place as having clear, cool water with waves and eddies;
if one enters the meditative absorption of the Sphere of Infinite Space, one sees only empty space in that very place.
It is illogical for a single entity to be both substantially existent and mutually contradictory, such as being the cause for the arising of cognitions of two entirely different categories.
How could it be that within this same river, there is already pus, blood, excrement, and urine filling it, with men bearing swords and staves guarding both banks;
and yet, there are also various fragrant and pure dwellings, clean streets, and ground adorned with many jewels?
The waves of clear, cool, and beautiful water swirl and eddy;
this is the meditative state of empty space.
If one grants that external objects have no real nature and that everything is manifested from the internal mind, then all things are established.
As a verse says: "Regarding the body of a single beautiful courtesan, the renunciant, the lustful man, and the hungry dog— each of these three has a different perception:
as a stinking corpse, as a source of exquisite beauty, and as delicious food."
Regarding the statement, "The cognition that perceives objects of consciousness without an external basis can be directly apprehended," etc.: the past and future are both not substantially existent.
This is established as being commonly accepted by the Sautrāntikas; it is universally understood that dream-objects are entirely non-existent in reality.
It has already been stated that the images which are the objects of various samādhis do not exist, nor are they objects of recollection.
As previously explained, reflections such as faces within the water-element and so forth are entirely non-existent.

In this context, consciousness is established even in the absence of an object; thus, there should be non-erroneous wisdom that transcends effort. Although the original text makes this clear, it is supplemented here with further explanation.
If one were to maintain that the objects as they are perceived exist truly, then all sentient beings would be liberated spontaneously without effort, for they all perceive reality.
One who has attained mastery over the mind is one whose mind is disciplined and compliant, capable of performing its functions.
One who has attained meditative absorption (dhyāna) refers to those such as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have already realized the purity of meditative absorption and one-pointedness of mind.
One who delights in tranquil reflection is called a "dhyāna practitioner.

Regarding the manifestation of various objects through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-bala*): this means that by the force of superior mental resolve, whatever one wishes or desires—such as transforming earth and so forth into water and so forth—all of these manifest accordingly.
"Attaining śamatha" means having already realized the meditative concentration of śamatha, which moistens the mental continuum and causes the mind to become tranquil.

What is called "cultivation" (bhāvanā) refers to being associated with the object of emptiness, or being associated with the objects of the Four Noble Truths; it is termed "associated" because it is the concurrent operation of both śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Because one is associated with this, one is called a "practitioner of the cultivation of the contemplation of phenomena.

This refers to the subsequent attainment contemplation (pṛṣṭhalabdha-darśana) regarding the sūtras and other teachings; when one directs the mind even slightly toward the sublime wisdom of the true Dharma, all phenomena manifest.

This refers to the teaching of the True Dharma, such as the sūtras, wherein one attends to and contemplates, according to its nature, any one of the meanings such as impermanence—for instance, the quality of momentary and rapid cessation.

In this manner, when non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) manifests, all objective referents (*artha*) fail to appear, even though various categories of objects continue to manifest; this will be explained in detail later, following the discussion of non-conceptual wisdom.
If objects were truly existent, this wisdom would not exist; it could not be established as being either with or without conceptual construction.
If objects were truly existent, non-conceptual wisdom, when arising, should not fail to manifest them, because this wisdom takes objects as they truly are.
By means of the reasoning just explained and the three types of causal conditions previously mentioned, it is established through logic that all objects do not exist.
The treatise says:

If the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is in reality nothing but consciousness, serving as the basis for the manifestation of what appears to be external objects, how is it established as "dependent"?
For what reason is it called *paratantra* (dependent origination)?
Because it arises from seeds of its own habitual perfuming and depends upon other conditions for its arising, it is called *paratantra*.
Furthermore, because after the moment of its arising it lacks the capacity to abide spontaneously, it is called *paratantra*.
The commentary states:
"How is it established as the dependent nature? asks about the phenomenon to be understood.
"For what reasons and conditions is it called the dependent nature? asks about the interpretation of the term regarding the categories of the understood and the not-yet-understood.
Because the definitive meaning is understood through these paired questions, the same applies to the two questions regarding the other two natures.
Based on these various questions, answers are given in pairs.

Regarding the phrase "from seeds of its own habitual perfuming" (*svavāsanābījāt*): this means that it arises from seeds of the habitual perfuming of names and conventions belonging to the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature). Because it is produced by another based on its own seed, it is called the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature); this explains that its essence arises in dependence upon others.
The statement that "after the moment of arising, there is no capacity for it to abide spontaneously" means that its essence abides in dependence upon others.
For these two reasons, it is called the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature).
The treatise says:

If the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) is that which, depending upon the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), appears as an object while being actually non-existent, how does it constitute the thoroughly imagined nature?
For what reason is it called "thoroughly imagined and grasped" (*parikalpita*)?

Because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), with its immeasurable modes of activity, thoroughly imagines and gives rise to inverted characteristics, it is therefore called "thoroughly imagined and grasped."

The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not exist in reality; only that which is grasped through the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) can be found. Therefore, it is called "the imagined nature.
The commentary explains:
"Depending on the dependent nature" means depending on the dependent nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*), [which] in reality has no existence whatsoever.
Regarding "that which appears as an object": this means that although it has no real substance, it nevertheless appears with the semblance of an object's characteristics.
If its substance is truly non-existent, how can it be called an "object"?
To avoid this difficulty, it is therefore said that "there is the manifestation of what appears to be an object.

This means that due to the seeds of linguistic habitual tendencies (*abhilāpa-vāsanā*), although there is no substantial reality, there is the manifestation of an appearance resembling an object; thus, objects are said to manifest as if they were real, like illusions, reflections, and so forth.
As for "manifestation," it refers to the clear appearance of that which is non-existent yet seems to exist; thus, it is called manifestation.
This very semblance of an object constitutes its own nature (*svabhāva*), just as in the case of the experience of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-anubhava*).
"Immeasurable modes of activity" refers to the various images of the objects of the self and phenomena.
"The conceptualization of the mental consciousness" means that the mental consciousness itself is designated as "conceptualization."
Regarding the "characteristic produced by inversion": this refers to the grasped and the grasper of the deluded consciousness, as it is the cause for the arising of objective characteristics.

Regarding the term "thoroughly imagined and grasped" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*): this refers to the very objective characteristic that is thoroughly imagined and grasped, which is called the "thoroughly imagined and grasped intrinsic nature."

Regarding the statement that "the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is truly non-existent and only the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is apprehended": this means that within the truly non-existent self and phenomena, only the reflected images and appearances of the imagined nature are apprehended; for this reason, it is called the "imagined nature."
The treatise says:
If the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the perpetual absence of characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), how does it constitute the perfected nature?
By what causes and conditions is it called "perfected"?
It is called "perfectly established" (pariniṣpanna) because it is unchanging;

furthermore, it is called "perfectly established" in the sense of being the ultimate object of purification and the most supreme among all wholesome dharmas. Thus, it is named "perfectly established" by virtue of its supreme meaning.
The commentary states:
Regarding the phrase "it is called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) because it is unchanging," one should understand that this nature is eternally free from transformation.
Furthermore, because it is the object of purification and because it is the most supreme among all wholesome dharmas, its nature is the perfect accomplishment of reality.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, there is that which performs the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) and that which is the object of pervasive conceptualization; it is through these that the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is established.
Among these, what is that which performs the pervasive conceptualization?
What is that which is the object of pervasive conceptualization?
What is the nature of pervasive conceptual construction?
One should know that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is that which performs pervasive conceptualization, because it possesses discrimination.

Why is this so? Because this mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes its own linguistic designations as seeds through perfuming (*vāsanā*), and also takes the linguistic designations of all [other] consciousnesses as seeds through perfuming; therefore, the mental consciousness evolves with infinite modes of activity and conceptualization. It is called "universal imagination" (*parikalpa*) because it universally discriminates and calculates with respect to all things.
Furthermore, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is called the "object of pervasive conceptualization" (parikalpya).
Moreover, that characteristic by which the dependent nature becomes the object of pervasive conceptualization is here termed the "imagined nature" (parikalpita-svabhāva).
"By these characteristics" means "in this manner.
Furthermore, how does the pervasive imagination (parikalpa) perform its pervasive conceptualization?
What is its objective sphere (ālambana)?
What characteristics are grasped?
By what is there attachment?
By what are words produced?
By what means is speech expressed?
What is it that is superimposed?

It refers to taking names as objects; within the *paratantra-svabhāva*, one grasps their characteristics. Through the adherence of views, through the arising of discursive thought (*vitarka*), and through the four kinds of verbal expression such as seeing and hearing, one engages in speech. One superimposes existence upon that which lacks objective reality, and by this means, the *parikalpita* performs its pervasive conceptualization.
The commentary states:

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "there is that which can universally conceptualize" and so forth, this statement is made because one wishes to distinguish the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva); it should be understood that the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is that which can universally conceptualize.
"Because it possesses conceptualization" means that it is intermingled with the conceptualizations of discernment (*nirūpaṇa-vikalpa*) and recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*).

"Taking the habitual perfuming of its own linguistic expressions as its seed" means that the seeds of the habitual perfuming of the conceptual proliferation of linguistic expressions belonging to the consciousness throughout beginningless saṃsāra serve as the cause for its arising.

Regarding the statement that "all consciousnesses take the verbal designations of habitual perfuming as their seeds," this means that they take the seeds of the verbal designations of the habitual perfuming of infinite forms and so forth as their cause; because they arise resembling those [objects], all infinite modes of activity evolve through conceptual differentiation.

Furthermore, regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) being called the "object of pervasive conceptualization" (*parikalpya*): this refers to one portion of it, such as the characteristics of the eye and so forth, which constitute the object of conceptualization (*parikalpa-karma*).

Moreover, if by means of these characteristics the dependent nature becomes the object of pervasive conceptualization, that which is here termed the "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) refers to the characteristics of the conditions belonging to that category; this is what is called the imagined nature.
"Such is the meaning" refers to the meaning of the characteristics of the objects of such categories.

Furthermore, the question "How does the pervasive conceptualization (parikalpa) perform its pervasive conceptualizing? arises in order to explain the distinctions within the nature of the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva).

Regarding the statement that "conditions named as objects," this means that names such as "form" (*rūpa*) or "feeling" (*vedanā*), and so forth, correspond to their respective referents; based on these, various conceptual constructions (*parikalpa*) arise. It is said that consciousness takes the name as its aspect of activity, yet it is not the case that there is no name capable of giving rise to various conceptualizations regarding its referent.
To grasp the characteristics within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is the meaning of grasping at self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Because it can grasp such characteristics, it is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*).
Based on what has been perceived, one engages in verbal expression; or, one grasps the characteristics of the eye and so forth within the dependent nature.
Regarding "due to seeing and attachment": through five types of modes, one engages in investigation and gives rise to various attachments.
Because one has grasped the characteristics and then given rise to attachment, this refers to the sense of firm attachment to those characteristics.
Through seeing, one investigates and reaches a certainty regarding an object; having given rise to attachment, one desires to speak of it to others.
Regarding how speech arises from vitarka (applied thought), as the Sūtra says:
"It is by means of vitarka and vicāra (sustained thought) that one speaks words; it is not without vitarka and vicāra that one can speak words."

Regarding "arising from discourse based on the four kinds of discourse such as seeing and hearing": this refers to arising from discourse based on the four kinds of discourse—seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing.

For example, when one perceives the appearance of a rope that resembles a snake and grasps its various features such as being coiled, one becomes attached to it oneself and, in order to awaken others, speaks these words:
"I have seen a snake."
"I have already seen the snake.
This case is also like this: having heard this, others further reinforce it, asserting that it truly exists.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, regarding these three natures, are they different or not different?
One should say they are neither different nor not different.
That is to say, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is established as the dependent nature by way of different perspectives.
This very same nature, by way of a different perspective, becomes the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva).
This very same nature, by way of a different perspective, becomes the perfected (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
By what perspective does this dependent origination (paratantra-svabhāva) become the dependent?
Because it arises based on seeds perfumed by others,
by what distinct aspect does this very self-nature become the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita)?
It is because it is the characteristic of the object of thorough imagination, and because it is that which is thoroughly imagined by thorough imagination.
By what alternative formulation does this very same nature become the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (the perfected nature)?
Because that which is universally conceptualized (*parikalpita*) never exists in such a manner.
The commentary states:
Regarding "not different," this refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because it is both existent and non-existent in relation to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
One may say they are different when comparing existence to existence; however, this is not the case when comparing it to non-existence, such as the horns of a rabbit.
They are not non-different, because existence and non-existence cannot constitute a single entity.
It is the same with the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*): the former is by nature impure, while the latter is by nature pure.
Now, furthermore, based on another perspective and underlying intention, these three natures may be of a single nature or of distinct natures.

As for the statement, "because they are the characteristics of the objects of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), and because they are that which is pervasively conceptualized," this is because, by virtue of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), [the self] is the basis upon which the pervasive conceptualization of "I" and "form" (*rūpa*, etc. relies.
Furthermore, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is "my form" and so forth, because it is that which is thoroughly conceptualized by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
With this underlying intention, the dependent nature is metaphorically designated as the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Regarding the phrase "because that which is thoroughly imagined is ultimately not so": it means that within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), that which appears is ultimately non-existent. Thus, it is said that the three natures are neither entirely different nor not different, because they are distinguished by their mutual relativity.

When, from the perspective of the objects produced by seeds perfumed through dependence, it constitutes the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it does not, by virtue of that very same [perspective], constitute the other two natures.

When, from the perspective of the objects of universal imagination (*parikalpita*), it constitutes the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it does not, by virtue of that very same [perspective], constitute the other two natures.
When, through dependence, the thoroughly imagined nature is ultimately non-existent, it becomes the perfected nature; yet it does not thereby become the other two natures.
The treatise asks:
Of these three natures, how many types are there for each?
The dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is briefly of two kinds:
first, because it arises based on seeds of habitual perfuming;
second, because its nature as either afflicted or purified is not established independently.
Because these two types depend on others and are distinct from one another, they are called the "dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The "imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) also has two types:
first, the imagined attachment to intrinsic nature; second, the imagined attachment to specific distinctions. For this reason, it is called the "imagined nature."
The perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) also has two aspects:
first, because it is the perfected nature by way of its own essence; second, because it is the perfected nature by way of purity. It is on account of these that it constitutes the perfected nature.
The commentary states:
It is called "other-dependent" (*paratantra*) because it arises based on seeds produced by habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), as it comes into being by depending upon causes and conditions.

It is called "other-dependent" because its nature as either afflicted (*saṃkleśa*) or purified (*vyavadāna*) is not established independently; for when there is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it constitutes an afflicted nature, and when there is no conceptual construction, it constitutes a purified nature—it is thus other-dependent by virtue of these two aspects.
Universal conceptualization of intrinsic nature refers to the general apprehension of the substantial entities of phenomena such as the eye and so forth.
Universal conceptualization of specific characteristics refers to the distinct apprehension of specific attributes of phenomena, such as permanence or impermanence.
The perfected nature as intrinsic nature refers to the *tathatā* with stains;
the perfected nature as purity refers to the *tathatā* free from stains.
The treatise says:

Furthermore, there are four types of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*): first, pervasive conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); second, pervasive conceptualization of distinctions (*viśeṣa*); third, pervasive conceptualization with awareness (*sa-vitarka*); and fourth, pervasive conceptualization without awareness (*a-vitarka*).
"Having awareness" refers to those skilled in linguistic expression; "lacking awareness" refers to those unskilled in linguistic expression.
The commentary states:
Those skilled in linguistic expression are so called because their own intended meaning precedes their speech, and they possess full comprehension; therefore, they are said to have awareness.
That which is contrary to this is called "non-conceptualization.
The treatise says:
Such pervasive conceptualization is further of five kinds. First is the pervasive conceptualization of the intrinsic nature of objects based on names, which means: "Such a name has such an object."
Second, the pervasive conceptualization of names based on objects, which means that such an object has such a name;
third, the pervasive conceptualization of names based on names, which refers to the conceptualization of names whose referents are not yet understood;
fourth, the pervasive conceptualization of objects based on objects, which refers to the conceptualization of objects whose names are not yet understood.

The fifth [point] concerns the two types of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) based on the two natures (*svabhāva*); that is, the pervasive conceptualization of this name and this object as having such an essential nature.
The commentary states:

Regarding "conceptualizing the name based on the name-svabhāva," it refers, for example, to a person born in the Coconut Island (*Tāla-dvīpa*) who, upon hearing the word "cow," does not understand its meaning, yet repeatedly discriminates on the basis of this sound "cow."

Regarding the imagined nature of objects based on objects: this refers to when one who has never previously cultivated the perception of an object encounters a cow's body and, through the mutual correspondence of that perception with the conceptualization of its existence, repeatedly discriminates the meaning of "cow" as such.
Regarding "based on the two, one universally imagines the two natures," this refers to the two kinds of discrimination based on the conventional designations of the signifier and the signified.
The treatise states:
Furthermore, if all forms of discrimination are summarized, there are briefly ten types:
First is fundamental discrimination, which refers to the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
Second is discrimination of the object-aspect, which refers to the consciousnesses of form and so forth.
Third is discrimination of the manifest aspect, which refers to the visual consciousness and so forth, together with their supporting consciousnesses.

The fourth is the discrimination of the transformation of conditions, which refers to the transformations of old age and so forth; the transformations of pleasant feelings and so forth; the transformations of greed and so forth; the transformations of affliction, the passage of time, and seasonal changes; the transformations of the various realms of existence such as the hells; and the transformations of the various spheres such as the desire realm.
Fifth is the discrimination of manifesting characteristics and transformation, which refers to all transformations as previously described.
Sixth is the discrimination induced by others, which refers to the discrimination arising from hearing categories of non-orthodox teachings as well as categories of orthodox teachings.
Seventh is improper discrimination, which refers to the discrimination occurring when various non-Buddhists hear what is not the true Dharma.
Eighth is proper discrimination, which refers to the discrimination occurring when one hears the true Dharma within the true Dharma.

Ninth is the discrimination of attachment, which refers to the class of improper mental attention (ayoniśo-manasikāra) rooted in the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), consisting of the discrimination associated with the sixty-two types of views (dṛṣṭigata).
The ten types of discursive conceptualization refer to the ten kinds of conceptualization of bodhisattvas.
The commentary states:

regarding "fundamental conceptualization," the *ālaya-vijñāna* is the fundamental nature of all other forms of conceptualization and is itself a form of conceptualization; therefore, it is called "fundamental conceptualization."
Discrimination of causal signs (*nimitta-vikalpa*) refers to the discrimination that form and so forth possess such causal signs.

Discrimination of manifesting signs (*lakṣaṇa-vikalpa*) refers to the visual consciousness and its associated supporting consciousnesses, because they manifest appearing as those objects of perception.
The discrimination of the transformation of causal signs refers to the discrimination arising from the transformation of consciousness that appears as reflections of form and so forth.
The transformations such as aging refer to the various transformations arising when the consciousness of form and so forth appears with characteristics such as aging.
Why is this? Because both external and internal forms possess the characteristics of transformation, such as aging and so forth.
The term "and so forth" (等) includes the variations of illness and death.

Regarding the transformation of pleasant feelings and so forth: due to pleasant feeling, the physical appearance undergoes transformation; as it is said, "one who experiences pleasure has a countenance that is dignified and handsome.
The phrase "and so forth" includes painful feeling and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
"Transformation by greed and so forth" means that the physical appearance undergoes transformation due to greed and so forth.
The phrase "and so forth" includes hatred, delusion, anger, and the like; as it is said, anger and the others result in an ugly physical form and so on.

Regarding "alterations caused by affliction, the passage of time, and so forth": this refers to the arising of alterations in the physical characteristics of the body through such acts as killing and binding; furthermore, the passage of time also causes changes in the forms of both internal and external bodies, such as trees and colors, just as it is said that when one is afflicted by cold and other conditions, the body and so forth undergo transformation.

Regarding the "transformations of the various destinies such as the hells" (*naraka*), the term "etc. (*ādi*) includes all evil destinies (*apāya*); the transformations of form (*rūpa*) and so forth in those places are commonly recognized.

Regarding the "transformations of the various realms such as the desire realm," the term "etc. includes the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because in those [higher] realms there is no consciousness that possesses images resembling form and so forth.

Within the various heavens and the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), there are likewise various transformations of the forms of sentient beings and their environments, just as the diverse, pure, and wondrous colors of light transform due to the majestic spiritual power of a mani jewel.

Regarding the discrimination of the manifestation of transformed appearances: this refers to the various transformations of eye-consciousness and the other consciousnesses, which manifest as images resembling form and so forth due to the sense faculties such as the eye acting as their bases;
it is within these very [transformations] that various discriminations arise.
This refers to the aforementioned transformations such as aging, which arise according to their respective conditions.
Why is this? As it is said, because the faculties such as the eye have degrees of sharpness or dullness, and consciousness has degrees of clarity or obscurity.
Just as with non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), when its basis undergoes transformation, it too undergoes transformation;
the same applies to the transformations of pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) and so forth, as it is said that "the mind of one who experiences pleasure is stabilized."
As it is said that for one who suffers, the mind is distracted, so too are the afflictions such as craving, the oppressions, and the seasonal shifts and transformations.

One should understand accordingly that in the hells and in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), consciousness also undergoes transformation due to the transformation of the physical body upon which it depends.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are likewise transformations produced by feeling (*vedanā*) and other factors.

Regarding "the discrimination of consciousnesses based on the discrimination induced by others," this refers to discriminations arising from associating with virtuous or non-virtuous friends, as well as discriminations caused by hearing the true or false Dharma.

This refers to the conceptualizations of non-Buddhist teachers such as Kapila and those of the various *sautrāntikas* within the True Dharma; these are termed "irrational" and "rational" conceptualizations, respectively.
These two types [of views], according to their respective natures, give rise to two kinds of conceptualization associated with wrong view and right view.

The conceptualization associated with the sixty-two views arising from the *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) as their cause is precisely the conceptualization of the past, future, and middle [periods] found in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. It refers to such questions as: "Did I exist in the past? and so forth.
Such distinctions as these are called "clinging distinctions.
As for the term "view-positions" (*dṛṣṭigata*), it carries the meaning of "categories.
Regarding "distraction-based discrimination," it is called "distraction" because it is scattered and agitated.
This is precisely conceptualization; therefore, it is called "distracted conceptualization.
This very state disturbs non-conceptual wisdom. Why is this so?
Because this disturbs the *prajñāpāramitā*, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is itself the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Regarding the ten kinds of conceptualization of bodhisattvas: these refer to the ten kinds of conceptualization by which bodhisattvas are able to produce speech that is induced by others and does not accord with ultimate truth.
Why is this? Because when the realization of ultimate truth is directly manifest before one, it cannot be expressed in words.
The treatise says:

1. Distraction regarding the signless; 2. Distraction regarding signs; 3. Distraction regarding superimposition; 4. Distraction regarding denial; 5. Distraction regarding identity; 6. Distraction regarding difference; 7. Distraction regarding intrinsic nature; 8. Distraction regarding differentiation; 9. Distraction regarding apprehending the object according to the name; 10. Distraction regarding apprehending the name according to the object.
To counteract these ten types of distraction, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is taught throughout all the *prajñāpāramitās*.
Thus, it should be understood that the relationship between the objects to be countered and their remedies fully encompasses the meaning of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The commentary states:
Within all the *prajñāpāramitās*, these ten types of remedies for distraction are fully explained.
For instance, it is said:
“World-Honored One!
How should a bodhisattva practice the perfection of wisdom?
“Śāriputra! [the Buddha replied.]
This bodhisattva truly exists as a bodhisattva, yet does not perceive a bodhisattva as existing.
Why is this? The intrinsic nature of form is empty; it is not by means of emptiness that form is empty, nor is form other than emptiness.
Form is not separate from emptiness; form is itself emptiness, and emptiness is itself form.
Why is this so? Śāriputra!
These are merely names, which are called "form.

Their intrinsic nature is without arising or ceasing, and without defilement or purity; yet, provisional guest-names are established to give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding various phenomena, and provisional guest-names are established to follow along with verbal expression. In accordance with such verbal expressions, one gives rise to attachment in this very way.

All such things are not seen by these bodhisattvas; because they do not see them, they do not give rise to attachment. As it has been said regarding form, one should know that it is the same for everything up to and including consciousness.
