In this context, the objects to be countered are greed, hatred, and so forth; because one wishes to distance oneself from them, they are termed "disgust.

If one perceives the faults of one's own transgressions deeply and swiftly develops weary detachment toward them, one is then able to restrain others from what they ought not to do; this is due to the gravity of one’s authoritative presence, for no other means can effect such restraint.
As the sutra says:
"If one abides in misconduct oneself, one will incur the criticism and debate of others;
such a person will ultimately be unable to restrain the faults of others."
The worldly also say:
"If one commits a transgression oneself, and does not examine it over time,
nor distances oneself from it through proper means, one will be too proud to accept its virtues."

If one harbors anger and resentment while instructing others regarding their transgressions, because this is neither beneficial nor skillful, one’s words will lack authority; consequently, others will become contrary and give rise to various forms of misconduct.
As a verse says: With compassion like that for an only son, He instructs others on their transgressions,
Ensuring they definitely undertake them, So that they shall not commit them again.
"Because one constantly cultivates and purifies the bodhicitta within all modes of conduct" is an explanation of the activity of uninterrupted mental attention (*nirantara-manasikāra-karman*);
for it means that one continuously cultivates and purifies the bodhicitta in all activities whatsoever.
As it is said in the *Caryāviśuddhi-sūtra*:
"When seeing [a Buddha] seated, one should give rise to this thought: 'May all sentient beings sit upon the seat of enlightenment.'"
These verses and others like them explain the sevenfold distinctions of the superior progressive practice,
from "practicing generosity without hoping for karmic maturation" up to "employing the means of gathering through the four bases of sympathy."
That is to say, the six *pāramitās* and the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Being free from the faults to be remedied as previously described, they proceed through the successive stages beginning with the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā*), attaining ever-increasing excellence and tending toward fulfillment; this is termed "activity" (*karman*), because it is that which is performed.
Among these, the four perfections are not explained here because they are easy to understand; however, those with specific distinctions shall now be briefly explained.

Regarding "abandoning the formless realm by cultivating meditative concentration": a bodhisattva is not born within the formless realms, for there they do not perceive the possibility of performing deeds that bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
Furthermore, they do not frequently enter the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), because they do not perceive those states as being the basis for manifold virtues.

For one who cultivates wisdom (*prajñā*) through the skillful means of equanimity—which here signifies the sense of relinquishment—and who cultivates sublime insight (*prajñā*) in conjunction with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), is able to perform all manner of beneficial and blissful deeds for sentient beings.

If this [bodhicitta] were non-existent, the matter of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings would not exist, for it is solely for the sake of this that one seeks the fruit of Buddhahood.
As a verse says: "By practicing wisdom and compassion together, One is able to bring benefit and happiness to others."
Practicing the right path for the benefit of others, one proceeds single-mindedly toward enlightenment.
The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are: giving (*dāna*), pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*), beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), and consistency in purpose (*samānārthatā*).

Through generosity, one is able to gather others; through kind speech, one skillfully provides explanations by teaching the characteristics of the Dharma; through purposeful conduct, one encourages them to cultivate virtue according to their needs; and through shared purpose, at the final stage, one causes them to likewise attain uncommon merit.

Alternatively, through generosity one becomes a vessel for the Dharma; through kind speech one attains resolute conviction in the Dharma; through beneficial conduct one initiates correct practice based on that resolute conviction; and through common purpose the practice thus initiated becomes increasingly pure and more subtle. By these means, the nature of the skillful means is fully encompassed.

"Because there is no duality regarding virtuous friends who maintain or violate the precepts, up to 'because of associating with virtuous friends'"—this is the explanation of the sixfold distinctions of the stage of the practice of fulfillment (*pariniṣpanna-prayoga*).
Because this preparatory application brings [the practice] to completion, it is called "completing preparatory application," which is itself the karma.
By means of the six phrases beginning with "approaching virtuous persons," the eight phrases taught in the sūtra are explained.
Because the merit of mental attention (*manasikāra*) and the merit of its accompanying factors are each explained in two ways:

one possesses virtuous ethical discipline (*śīla*), and is thus called "one who maintains discipline" (*śīlavat*); one possesses unwholesome ethical discipline, and is thus called "one who violates discipline."

Regarding these two types of teachers who can expound the Dharma, for the sake of hearing the Dharma and out of reverence for the Dharma, one should conceive of them as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) without distinction; therefore, it is said that there are no two kinds of spiritual friends.
For this reason, one should not categorically regard those who have broken their precepts as being anything other than virtuous friends.
As a verse says: "If one possesses the feet of ethical discipline, though they may be weak and inferior, yet can eloquently teach and benefit many people,"
Just as the Buddha, the Great Teacher, should be venerated because one loves his excellent teachings, so too should one listen to the True Dharma with a reverent mind.
This means that regarding the extensive meanings and so forth as they have been taught, one should listen to the Dharma by way of the sixteen aspects.
Regarding "dwelling in an araṇya with a sincere mind": an araṇya is defined as being at least one krośa removed from a village; to reside therein is called "dwelling."
To abide as is appropriate without laxity is called "earnestness.

To have no fondness for worldly diversions means not to delight in various worldly matters such as singing, laughter, and dancing; this is precisely to distance oneself from improper discursive thoughts associated with desire and the like.

Regarding the merit of mental attention (*manasikāra*): it consists in relinquishing attachment to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and being associated with attachment to the merits of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the merit of the accompaniments (*sahāya*): it consists in distancing oneself from evil friends, drawing near to virtuous friends, constantly cultivating and purifying the four Brahma-abodes (*brahmavihāra*), and perpetually sporting in the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
"By way of relying on wisdom" is the explanation of the "act of fulfillment.
That is to say, the characteristic of fulfillment is called the act of fulfillment; here, the term "act" (*karman*) is a specific designation for that characteristic.
The three phrases beginning with "immeasurable purity" explain the preceding three phrases beginning with "constantly cultivating the four Brahma-abodes.

The four immeasurables—compassion (*karuṇā*), loving-kindness (*maitrī*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—are called the four Brahma-abodes; because they manifest that all internal virtues have been perfected and purified, they receive the designation of "marks" (*lakṣaṇa*).
To sport with the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) is called "majestic power" (*prabhāva*).

The supernormal power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānābhijñā*) is the wisdom of liberation and is termed "great majestic power"; alternatively, one may take the superior supernormal powers of a bodhisattva as "great majestic power. Such is also called the mark of fulfillment.
Regarding "attaining the qualities," this refers to having already attained manifest mastery. This is explained as follows:
because one relies upon and accords with wisdom, each [aspect] is individually realized within; thus it is called "relying upon and accords with wisdom" (*pratisaraṇa-jñāna*).

It is not only regarding the meaning; because one relies upon consciousness rather than tranquility, this explains the fourfold distinction of the establishment of those activities, such as abiding in right practice and not abiding in right practice.

Based on this, one establishes the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the benefit and happiness of others; this itself is the action (*karman*), and therefore it is called "establishing that action.

Regarding the merit of governing a community: it refers to the expulsion of sentient beings who violate their precepts and the inclusion of those who uphold them, desiring in both cases to lead them out of unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome states; this is termed "not abandoning."

Regarding the phrase "because of decisiveness," it refers to instructions and admonitions that are definitive and free from doubt; this is because his speech is majestic and solemn, whereas if his speech were not decisive, it would lack such majesty and solemnity.

Regarding "valuing truth and reality": this means that the two forms of gathering—wealth and Dharma—are combined into one; having accumulated wealth and Dharma without making any distinction between them, they are distributed equally as previously promised, bestowing them in this manner except for what is currently unavailable.
As a verse says:
Material offerings can cause sentient beings To exhaust their lifespans;
Dharma offerings can cause them To ultimately attain celestial tranquility.
"Because the great bodhicitta is always held as the foremost" is an explanation of the mind free from defilement.
Since it is embraced by bodhicitta, whatever one does, one never seeks after offerings or services from others, but seeks only to realize unsurpassed enlightenment.
The treatise says:
As it is said:
"By virtue of the initial phrase, the various categories of qualities are distinguished."
"By virtue of the first phrase, there is a distinction in meaning between the phrases.
Commentary: The meaning of this verse is easy to understand; there is no need for further elaboration.
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll Five;
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Scroll Six.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asvabhāva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Four: Entering the Characteristics of the Knowable. The Treatise says:
Thus far, the characteristics of the knowable have been explained. How should one understand "entering the characteristics of the knowable"?

The basis for the cultivation of extensive learning is not subsumed within the *ālaya-vijñāna*; rather, like the *ālaya-vijñāna* which functions as a seed, it consists of mental verbalization (*manojalpa*)—comprised of correct attention—which arises resembling phenomena and their meanings, and which appears as an object of apprehension accompanied by a subjective aspect.
The commentary states:

Having cultivated such karma, the Bodhisattva shall now explain the characteristics of what is to be known as they enter into direct realization (*abhisamaya*). Regarding "the basis for the cultivation of extensive learning":

this refers to generating extensive learning within the Mahāyāna; having heard the meaning of the Dharma, it is the basis for the perfuming (*vāsanā*) of the continuum of the mind and mental factors. This is because one who has heard little cannot possibly enter this direct realization.
As it is said in the *Bhagavān-śikṣita-āyuṣmān-Rāhula-sūtra*:
"I pray only that the Blessed One teach me the direct realization (*abhisamaya*.
The Blessed One replied:
"Have you already received and upheld the treasury of the True Dharma? Rāhula replied, "No."
"World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One replied:
'For now, you should receive and uphold the treasury of the Dharma.'"

Those things such as these which are not subsumed under the *ālayavijñāna* mean that because this basis flows from the most pure *dharmadhātu* and serves as its antidote, it is not subsumed under the nature of the latter, as it is contrary to it.

Regarding how the ālayavijñāna functions as a seed: just as the ālayavijñāna can serve as the cause for all defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), this foundational nature (*āśrayatva*) can serve as the cause for all purified phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*).
It is only because they share the same nature as causes that it may be used as an analogy; it does not mean that [the foundational nature] possesses all seeds.
As it is said in a verse:
"To benefit those who are perpetually heedless, And those born blind who do not perceive their own happiness,
The Buddhas descend as spirits into the world To proclaim for them the subtle and wondrous Dharma."
For example, like a priceless maṇi jewel, it can inconceivably eliminate all poisons.
That which resembles the Dharma refers to the sūtras and so forth, such as the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.

Regarding the phrase "resembling the object" (*artha-sadṛśa*): this refers to the selflessness (*anātmatā*) and so forth that are expressed by those [cognitions], because they arise with an aspect (*ākāra*) resembling that [object]. As for the statement that they "arise resembling phenomena (*dharma*) and objects (*artha*), and resemble the grasped entity (*grāhya-vastu*)," it is because they manifest in the manner of that which is grasped.
That which is said to be "accompanied by seeing" refers to that which is concomitant with auditory consciousness.
That which is called "mental discourse" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Alternatively, it possesses the nature of the grasped and the grasper simultaneously with its aspect of seeing; this is precisely the establishment of the self-nature (*svabhāva*) upon which the grasped and the grasper depend, as has been explained previously.
The Commentary states:
Among these, who is able to penetrate the characteristics of that which is to be known?

It is the Bodhisattva whose mental continuum has been permeated by extensive hearing of the Mahāyāna, who has already encountered and served immeasurable Buddhas appearing in the world, who has attained resolutely determined superior understanding (*adhimukti*), and who has well accumulated all roots of goodness, thereby being fully prepared with the provisions of merit and wisdom.
The commentary states:
Since both the action and the instruments of action depend upon an agent, it is asked who is able to enter into this realization.

To answer this question, it says: "The continuum of the permeation of hearing the Mahāyāna, etc. This means that by relying on the Mahāyāna teachings, one initiates the continuum of the permeation of hearing; having already attained the opportunity to serve immeasurable Buddhas appearing in the world, through this very continuum, one is able to actually encounter and serve those Buddhas appearing in the world.

Those who have already attained a resolute and definitive resolve do so by encountering and serving the Buddha, thereby generating deep faith and understanding in the Mahāyāna Dharma; they are not led into hesitation by evil associates.

By virtue of these three causes and conditions—extensive learning and so forth in this Mahāyāna—one is able to skillfully accumulate immeasurable roots of goodness; such a person is called a bodhisattva who has well prepared the provisions of merit and wisdom.
The treatise says:
Wherein can one enter?
It is precisely within that mental verbalization which resembles phenomena and resembles objects, and which is produced by the signs and characteristics of the Mahāyāna Dharma.

In the stage of practice through resolute belief, on the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the ultimate path, one realizes that all phenomena are of the nature of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*) because of resolving in accordance with what has been heard, because of penetrating reality as it is, because of counteracting all obstacles, and because of being free from all obstacles.
The commentary states:
"As for 'where one can enter,' this asks about the realm to be entered and the stage of entry.

Regarding 'that which possesses vision and so forth therein,' this refers to entering this objective realm through mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) that resembles the determined practice produced from the characteristics of the Mahāyāna teachings, wherein the appearance of phenomena resembles the appearance of objects."
The ability to enter is the function; that which is entered is the objective sphere. This is the activity and the sustenance.

Regarding this mental expression, there may be an "ability to enter" while on the stage of conduct through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), because one generates resolute belief merely by following what has been heard regarding the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*) in all phenomena.
There are some who are able to enter into the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) because they penetrate this mental discourse (*manojalpa*) in accordance with reality.

Herein, "penetrating in accordance with reality" means penetrating that [mental discourse] is neither a phenomenon (*dharma*) nor an object (*artha*), and is neither the grasped (*grāhya*) nor the grasper (*grāhaka*).

Some are able to enter the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because by means of this they cultivate the remedies for the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Some are able to enter the ultimate path (*niṣṭhāmārga*), because it is supremely pure and free from all obstructions.
These four types constitute the stages of entry.
The treatise asks:
By what means can one enter?

Because it is sustained by the power of the roots of virtue—namely, by means of three ways of refining the mind, by abandoning four points, and by constant, earnest application and vigilance toward the objects of meditation, which are the meanings of the Dharma, through both calm abiding and insight.
The commentary states:
"By what means can one enter? This question concerns the cause of entry—that is, by what cause one is able to enter therein.

Regarding the phrase "because it is sustained by the power of the roots of goodness," this means that although there is the power of the roots of goodness, the mind might still regress or become discouraged; therefore, it is said that one must exercise three kinds of mental refinement.
The Treatise says:

That in immeasurable worlds there are immeasurable persons and sentient beings who, moment by moment, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment—this is the first way of tempering the mind.

"By means of this aspiration, one is able to practice the perfections such as generosity; I have already attained such an aspiration, and because of it, I shall attain the fulfillment of the perfections such as generosity by practicing them with little effort. This is the second training of the mind.

"If those who have accomplished wholesome qualities that are subject to obstacles are reborn with all desirable aspects of their own bodies complete at the time of death, then since I possess sublime and unobstructed wholesome qualities, why should I not obtain every perfection at that time? This is called the third refinement of the mind."
The commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "immeasurable worlds" and so forth, this indicates the first stage of refining the mind; by citing others as examples for oneself, it causes the mind to become more intense and free from any sense of retreat or discouragement.
"By this intention" indicates the second refinement of the mind.

"I have already attained such an intention" reveals that this intention is free from all fetters; that is to say, this intention is far removed from stinginess, far removed from thoughts of sensual desire, far removed from thoughts of ill will, far removed from laziness, far removed from lethargy and drowsiness, and far removed from ignorance.

Regarding the statement, "By means of this, I shall attain the fulfillment of the perfections such as generosity by expending little effort," this means that having already attained a superior intention (*āśaya*), one is then able to practice generosity and the other perfections spontaneously and swiftly bring them to completion.
Regarding the phrase "if there are those who have accomplished," etc., this reveals the third refinement of the mind.
Those "who possess obstructed virtues" refers to those who have accomplished mundane virtues but have not yet permanently severed the opposing obstacles; therefore, they are said to be "obstructed."

Regarding the phrase "I possess wondrous goodness and so forth," it means that I am able to eternally sever the obstacles that are their opposites; because I have become virtuous through being free from such obstacles, how could I fail to realize the perfect fruit of Buddhahood in the future?
The "cultivation of the mind" refers to uplifting the mind to make it sharp and keen, thereby counteracting despondency.
The treatise states:
Regarding this, there is a verse:
The sentient beings within the human realm are infinite in number;
since they realize perfect enlightenment in every moment of thought, one should not yield to despondency.
With pure mental dispositions, they are able to practice generosity and the other perfections.
This Victor has already attained it, and thus is able to practice generosity and the rest.
When a virtuous person dies, they obtain the fulfillment of their own wishes according to their pleasure;
since this supreme goodness arises from eternal cessation, how could its perfection not exist?
The commentary states:
Furthermore, this meaning is summarized by means of a verse.
Regarding "sentient beings of the human realm," those whose minds are timid and weak are said to be "discouraged"; one should exhort them not to give rise to such discouragement.
To say, "I am unable to realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment," is called a weak and timid mind.
Now, one should encourage such a person not to consider themselves incapable; therefore, there shall be no retreat or discouragement.
As a verse says:
"Infinite sentient beings of the ten directions Have already realized the fruit of the Sugata in every thought-moment;
Since they are great men, so am I— I should not disparage myself or succumb to despondency."

Regarding "those with pure mental dispositions who are able to practice giving and so forth": this means that one practices giving and so forth not with unwholesome or neutral minds, but solely with wholesome minds; therefore, it is called a "pure mind."

Just as there are instances in the world where one practices giving and other virtues even within an unwholesome or neutral state of distracted mind—because of the aspiration for various forms of existence (*bhava*) and wealth and status—the Bodhisattva is not like this;
he seeks only unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Regarding "intention" (*āśaya*): it refers to the ability to cultivate the causes of giving and so forth without obstruction, as previously explained.

As for the statement that "this superior one has already attained [it] and is thus able to cultivate giving and so forth": the Bodhisattvas are called "superior ones"; they have already attained this sublime intention (*viśiṣṭa-āśaya*) beforehand, whereby the perfections (*pāramitā*) such as giving proceed spontaneously. Because they practice according to what has been taught, it is said that they "have already attained" it.
By means of this certainty, one abandons that which is to be countered; because that which is to be countered has been abandoned, one engages spontaneously in giving and so forth without effort.
The term "and so forth" includes the perfections from ethical discipline up to wisdom.
"Those who are virtuous at the time of death" refers to those who, by virtue of worldly virtue, become virtuous and attain [the result] at the moment their life ends.

"Attaining the fulfillment of one's own desires" means obtaining the fruit of worldly fulfillment according to what one loves and delights in; this extends to the meaning of attaining birth even as high as the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
"Supreme virtue by way of permanent abandonment" means that it becomes virtuous through the permanent abandonment of those obstacles.
"How could there be no perfection? means how could there be no sense of attaining the fruit of Buddhahood in accordance with one's aspirations?
The treatise states:
Because one abandons the mental orientations (*manasikāra*) of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas by means of abandoning [all] mental orientations;
and because one resolves doubts regarding the Mahāyāna by being able to permanently sever the doubts of divergent wisdoms.
Because one abandons the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self regarding the dharmas that have been heard and reflected upon, one severs attachment to phenomena;
and because one is without mental engagement or conceptual discrimination toward all manifest, present, and established signs, one severs conceptualization.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
Abiding naturally in the presence [of reality], Establishing all appearances,
The wise do not engage in conceptual discrimination, And thus attain supreme enlightenment.
The commentary states:
Now, the abandonment of the four points shall be demonstrated.
Regarding "the abandonment of mental attention," this refers to the abandonment of the mental attention that induces the stages of the two vehicles.
"Because one can forever sever divergent wisdom and doubt" means that regarding the profound and vast Mahāyāna, one does not give rise to divergent wisdom, inversion, or doubt.

"Because one severs the grasping at phenomena" means that regarding the teachings heard and contemplated, one can forever eliminate the grasping at self and what belongs to self—such as the notions "I am the one who hears," "I am the one who contemplates and realizes," "these are the texts I hear," and "these are the meanings I contemplate. All such attachments are entirely absent, because one has realized direct insight (*abhisamaya*) into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Regarding "the severance of conceptualization": this means that one is able to permanently sever all mental attention and conceptualization regarding the signs of all objective spheres established through pure meditative concentration—such as skeletons—which manifest and persist before one's eyes through spontaneous engagement or through deliberate effort; furthermore, one is able to permanently abandon attachment and conceptualization regarding such signs as all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the *pāramitās*.
The meaning of this verse is clear and need not be further explained.
The treatise asks:
By what means and in what manner does one attain realization and entry?
The commentary states:
Here, both the instrument and the object are questioned.
Since there is an agent who enters into the object of action, one should know that there must necessarily be an instrument by which one enters.
The characteristics of direct realization (*abhisamaya*) constitute that which is to be accomplished; there must necessarily be specific means for accomplishing it in such and such a manner.
Therefore, both shall now be explained.
The Treatise says:

"It is the mental verbalization accompanied by an appearance of the dharma and its meaning, which is comprised of correct attention (yoniśomanasikāra) of the type consisting in the perfuming of hearing.
The Commentary explains:
In this context, first, the term "sound" (*śabda*) refers to the categories of the means for entering [the truth]; that is, verbal expression is the meaning of "cause.
The treatise states:

"By means of the four investigations—namely, the investigation into the provisional designations of names, objects, intrinsic natures, and distinctions—and by means of the four kinds of thorough knowledge of reality as it is—namely, the thorough knowledge of reality as it is regarding the provisional designations of names, things, intrinsic natures, and distinctions—all such [entities] are equally unapprehendable."

Because bodhisattvas thus practice the preparatory application (*prayoga*) in accordance with reality in order to enter into representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), they investigate the mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) that resembles words and resembles meanings, and find that words and names are merely mental verbalization; they investigate the meaning that depends upon these words and names and find it also to be merely mental verbalization; and they investigate the intrinsic nature and specific differences of names and meanings and find them to be merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*).

When one realizes that there is only mental discourse (*manojalpa*), at that time one realizes and knows that whether it be names or objects, their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) and specific differences (*viśeṣa*) are all merely provisional designations; because the characteristics of intrinsic nature and specific difference do not exist, they are equally unattainable.

Through the four types of thorough investigation and the four types of correct thorough knowledge, one is able to penetrate the nature of representation-only regarding these mental verbalizations that appear as words and meanings.
The commentary states:

Regarding "by means of the four investigations and the four kinds of thorough knowledge of reality as it is," this refers to entering into the application of the means for performing what is real, as previously explained. During the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), the investigative search for the characteristics of the means—which are conventionally existent but ultimately non-existent—is called "investigation" (*paryeṣaṇā*). The wisdom of the means that results from this—the definitive cognition that realizes these are conventionally existent but ultimately non-existent—is called "thorough knowledge of reality as it is" (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*).

In this context, "name" refers to such things as form (*rūpa*) and feeling (*vedanā*), which also include the causes of names, the fruits of names, phrases, and so forth. To investigate that these names are of the nature of mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) alone, being merely conventional and not real, without departing from mental verbalization—this is called the investigation of names (*nāma-paryeṣaṇā*).

Regarding the investigation of meaning (*arthaparyeṣaṇā*): one investigates how the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) are designated and expressed by name-groups (*nāmakāya*) and so forth, concluding that their nature is merely conventional and not real.

This is because it is illogical for the relationship between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*) to correspond in the same way that a category (*jāti*) corresponds to its instances (*vyakti*).

Regarding the statement that "seeking the meaning of this name upon which it depends is also merely mental verbalization": one investigates that the external objects signified by the name are of the nature of mere mental verbalization; one reflects that while this meaning manifests as if having an external aspect, it actually exists only within.

Regarding the investigation that the intrinsic natures and specific differences of names and meanings are merely provisional designations: one investigates that the two kinds of intrinsic nature—namely, name and meaning—are merely provisional characteristics. This means that the intrinsic natures of names and meanings such as "form" (*rūpa*) or "feeling" (*vedanā*) do not exist in reality, but are merely provisionally designated, just like the provisional designation of a "person" (*pudgala*). One also investigates that the two kinds of specific differences between names and meanings are likewise provisional characteristics; this is because specific differences of names and meanings, such as "impermanence," are merely provisionally designated.

If both names and their referents—whether in terms of intrinsic nature or specific distinctions—are all merely provisional designations, it is thereby known that the four kinds of false appearances lack the characteristics of intrinsic nature and specific distinctions, and are thus subsumed within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Regarding "the non-apprehension of identity," one thoroughly realizes that the four kinds of objects of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-artha*) are all unapprehendable.

It should be understood that herein, the four kinds of skillful means are called "investigations" (*paryeṣaṇā*), and the four kinds of resultant wisdom are called the "four kinds of thorough knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*).

This means that investigating names as being merely conventional designations and finding them ultimately unobtainable is called "investigation of names" (*nāma-paryeṣaṇā*); when, upon the arising of this resultant wisdom regarding those very names, one definitively knows that they exist conventionally but do not exist substantially, it is called "knowledge of reality as it is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).

In this way, regarding the fact that things exist only nominally and lack reality in terms of their intrinsic nature and specific characteristics, the analytical investigation and definitive conclusion should also be understood accordingly.
The treatise says:
Within this realization of the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), what is it that is realized?
How does one enter into realization?

One enters into the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) by means of the six kinds of meanings—the two natures of appearance and perception, the various natures, whether as names or as objects, as self-nature or as differentiation, and the conventional meaning of self-nature and differentiation—all of which are non-existent; because the nature of the grasped and the grasper manifests before one; and because it arises simultaneously appearing as various appearances and meanings, just as a rope in the dark appears to manifest as a snake.
For example, the snake upon a rope is not real because it does not exist.
If one has already understood that its object is non-existent, although the perception of the snake ceases, the perception of the rope remains.

If one analyzes it according to its subtle categories, since this [snake] has false color, odor, taste, and touch as its characteristics, this cognition should be sublated by the cognition of the rope upon which it depends.

In this way, when the unreal sixfold aspects of meaning are subverted within those mental verbalizations that appear as words and meanings, the cognition of the nature of consciousness-only should likewise be eliminated, just like the cognition of a snake, by means of the cognition of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The commentary states:
Within this realization of the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), in order to clarify both that which is entered and the analogy for the entry, this question is posed:
"If objects do not exist, what is it that is entered within this realization of the nature of representation-only?"
This objection is difficult to answer:
"If this very nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) is itself the object (*artha*), how can it be said that objects do not exist?
To refute this objection, it was previously stated that one "enters the nature of consciousness-only."
This means that the objects of this consciousness also lack the nature of being objects; it is not merely that external objects do not exist.
If they lack the nature of being objects, how can there be the teaching on the twelve bases (*āyatana*)?
What is meant by "worldly discourse regarding objects"?

To refute this objection, it is stated next that although the two natures—of object (*nimitta*) and seeing (*darśana*)—lack any real objective referent, consciousness manifests as if there were internal and external objects. Due to the power of beginningless linguistic conditioning (*abhilāpa-vāsanā*), consciousness evolves in the semblance of an object; its function of discerning [that object] is termed "seeing. Therefore, there is no contradiction.
Is it that one merely realizes and enters into the categories of consciousness that appear as objects and subjects, or is it not so?

To answer this question, [the text] speaks of "realization" and "various natures," meaning that although there is only a single consciousness, it is divided into two kinds at a single moment due to the differentiation between the nature of the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*).
Furthermore, within a single consciousness, three aspects appear: the apprehended object (*grāhya*), the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*), and the self-verifying aspect (*svasaṃvitti*).
These three aspects are divisions of meaning within a single consciousness; they are neither identical nor distinct, as explained in other passages.
Because many aspects appear upon a single consciousness, it is called "various" (*nānātva*).
The statement that the six aspects, such as names and so forth, lack corresponding objects and so on, explains the preceding three types [of selflessness].

To answer the previous question regarding how one enters into realization, it is further stated that it is like a rope appearing in the dark as if it were a snake; by means of this analogy, the penetration of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) is established.
For example, a snake on a rope is not real because it does not exist.

In the same way, the mental verbalization of what appears as names and what appears as objects—namely, the six kinds of imagined natures such as names and so forth upon the dependent nature—is also not real, because they do not exist.

Furthermore, within this context, just as one abandons the cognition of a snake based upon the cognition of a rope, so too does one abandon the cognition of the sixfold object of pervasive conceptualization based upon the cognition of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) as it manifests from consciousness-only (vijñapti-mātra).

Just as the cognition that analyzes color and so forth dispels the cognition of a rope, so too does the cognition of the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) dispel the deluded cognition of the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
As a verse says: "The cognition that takes a rope for a snake, Upon seeing the rope, realizes it is non-existent;
When one perceives its constituent parts, One knows that the cognition of the snake was a delusion."
Regarding the phrase "when one subdues the unreal sixfold characteristics": this means they are non-existent, because the six kinds of unreal characteristics are not the characteristics of existence.
The Treatise says:

"In this way, by awakening to and entering into the characteristic of the semblance of objects within mental discourse, the Bodhisattva awakens to and enters into the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva)."
Because one enters into consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), one enters into the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
How does one enter into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)?

If one has already eliminated the conceptualization of consciousness-only—which is of the same category as the mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) and the permeation of hearing the Dharma (*śruta-vāsanā*)—then at that time, the Bodhisattva has discarded the conceptualization of objects (*artha-saṃjñā*). Since all appearances resembling objects can no longer arise, even that which resembles consciousness-only cannot arise.

By reason of these causes and conditions, abiding in the name that is non-conceptual regarding all meanings, one then attains direct perception within the dharmadhātu and dwells in accordance with it.

At that time, the Bodhisattva’s non-conceptual wisdom—characterized by the absolute equality of the object of cognition (*ālambana*) and the subject of cognition (*ālambaka*)—has already arisen; by virtue of this, the Bodhisattva is said to have realized and entered the pariniṣpanna-svabhāva (the perfected nature).
The commentary states:

Regarding "entering into the imagined nature by way of realizing that mental discourse manifests as the semblance of an object": this means understanding that while mental discourse appears as the semblance of an object, there is no real, substantially existent object as imagined; for this reason, it is called "entering into the imagined nature."

Regarding "entering into the dependent nature by way of entering into consciousness-only": this means that through the realization that consciousness-only is devoid of ignorance, one understands that within the absence of external objects, the appearance of objects manifests; by means of this, one enters into the dependent nature.

In order to manifest the realization of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), it is further stated: "The conceptualization of objects has already been dispelled," which means that one is already able to eliminate the conceptualization of objects.
"Nothing resembling an object can arise" means that there is absolutely nothing that resembles an object capable of arising.

Therefore, that which resembles consciousness also cannot arise; since the grasped object does not exist, the grasping subject likewise does not exist. This is precisely the meaning established by "consciousness-only," and it is also the meaning of non-transformation.

"Abiding in the non-conceptualization of all meanings and names" means that all phenomena (*dharma*) are the basis and domain for the names of the *sūtras* and so forth; these are called "all meanings.
There are ten kinds of names: the first nine kinds of names involve conceptual differentiation, while the tenth name involves no conceptual differentiation regarding any meaning.

Abiding thus in the non-conceptual designation of all objects, as it is said that "everything exists only as its name," that which is capable of giving rise to everything by means of such a name is here metaphorically designated as "name"— referring to consciousness and so forth, which appear as if they were names.
"To dwell in accordance with direct perception within the dharma-realm" means to give rise to resolute conviction through internal realization in accordance with the dharma-realm.

"Perfectly equal" means that just as the object of cognition (*ālambana*) is utterly non-existent, so too is the subject of cognition (*ālambaka*); therefore, both the object and the subject are perfectly equal.

For this reason, a bodhisattva is said to have "already entered into the perfected nature" (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva); however, because their entry into the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) and the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) remains incomplete, there is still an agent, and since their activity has not yet ceased, it is merely called "entry."
Now, herein, when the agent and the activity have ceased and reached their ultimate end, it is called "having already entered into realization.
The treatise says:
Regarding this, there is a verse:
The dharmas and the person, the nature of the dharma and its meaning in brief and in detail,
impurity, purity, and the ultimate— these are called the distinctions of the sphere of activity. Commentary:
As previously stated regarding abiding in the name "non-conceptualization of all objects," this verse now reveals the distinctions between that name and its own respective objects.
First, as for the names of phenomena (*dharma*), these refer to form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth.
The names of persons (*pudgala*) refer to such names as Devadatta and so forth, or those within the Buddhist teachings such as "one who follows by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*) and so forth.
Names of subsequent phenomena (*dharma*) refer to such categories as the *sūtra*, the *geya*, and so forth.
The "meaning-name" refers to that which is expressed, such as the killing of one's parents, the destruction of a kingdom, or its followers.
The "abbreviated name" refers to [the teaching] that all phenomena are devoid of a self and so forth.
The "extensive" designation refers to such things as "form," "non-self," and so forth.
The "essential" designation refers to the various syllables such as *a* and so on, because they are the causes of words and phrases.
The "impure" designation refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), because they are defiled by the stains of the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
The term "pure" (*viśuddha*) refers to the fact that all noble ones (*ārya*) have eternally severed their defilements.

The term "ultimate" (*paryanta*) refers to the general object of focus, namely the *prajñāpāramitā* and the ten stages (*bhūmi*), because these are taken as objects of focus in their general and abbreviated sense.
The Commentary states:
Because such a bodhisattva awakens to and enters the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), they awaken to and enter the characteristics of the objects of knowledge (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*).

By entering this, they enter the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), thoroughly penetrate the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), are born into the family of the Tathāgatas, attain the mind-nature equal to all sentient beings, attain the mind-nature equal to all bodhisattvas, and attain the mind-nature equal to all Buddhas; this is precisely what is called the bodhisattva’s path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
The commentary states:
"One who has thoroughly realized the dharmadhātu" means that one has deeply realized this dharmadhātu.

"Born into the family of the Tathāgata" means that the Buddha-dharmadhātu is called the "family of the Tathāgata"; because one realizes and assembles within it, one is said to be "born. Because the superior wisdom that takes this as its object arises therein, and because the former basis is transformed and another basis is produced, one succeeds to the lineage of the Buddhas, ensuring it is not interrupted.

Just as when one takes rebirth in another *nikāya-sabhāga*, the continuity of that which is produced and that which produces remains uninterrupted as it relies upon the family of the one to be born; so too, when the *prajñāpāramitā* realizes the *dharmadhātu* of the Buddha, it is said to be "born therein" and is called a true son of the Buddha.
Because this Prajñāpāramitā can correctly realize the Buddha-dharmadhātu and bring about the manifest presence of mastery within one's own continuum, it is called "birth."
As it is said: "All those who are heroic and delight in benefiting others are born from and nurtured by both their birth mothers and their foster mothers."
One who attains the mind-nature of equality toward all sentient beings does so by universally perceiving that all are equally devoid of self,
as it is said: "All phenomena are the Tathāgatagarbha," and so forth.
One who attains the state of equality of mind-nature of all bodhisattvas does so because they attain the equality of their resolute intention (*āśaya*).
One who attains the state of equality of mind-nature of all buddhas does so because they attain the equality of the *dharmakāya*.

This is what is called the Bodhisattva’s path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because one sees the supreme dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) not previously seen, just like the path of seeing of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, for what purpose does one enter the nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*)?

By means of supramundane śamatha and vipaśyanā wisdom that takes general dharmas as its object, and by means of the subsequently attained wisdom that cognizes various characteristics, one acts to sever the seeds of all characteristics of the ālayavijñāna, to nurture the seeds capable of touching the dharmakāya, to transform the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti), to desire to realize all Buddha-dharmas, and to desire to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñājñāna) by entering the nature of vijñaptimātratā.

Furthermore, through subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one perceives the nature of all manifestations produced by the *ālayavijñāna* as being like illusions and so forth, without error.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva is like a magician who, regarding the illusory objects and their various characteristics, as well as in explaining cause and effect, is always free from inversion.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "For what purpose, etc.," this asks what is required for entering Vijñaptimātratā. Next, one should answer:

It is for the sake of attaining the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). However, the preliminary expedient means as previously described are intended to reveal the sequence of the teaching and to benefit those types of disciples who are capable of receiving such instruction.

Regarding "taking general dharmas as the object": this means taking as one's object the *tathatā* (suchness) manifested by the general characteristics of all dharmas; that is to say, because according to what is taught in the Mahāyāna teachings, all dharmas have *tathatā* as their intrinsic nature.

Taking *tathatā* (suchness) as its object is precisely to understand the nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; were it otherwise, even after a long period of time, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) would still not arise.
It is called "supramundane" because it is untainted (*anāsrava*) and because it is non-conceptual.
Regarding "by means of the wisdom of śamatha and vipaśyanā," this refers to the non-erroneous wisdom (*aviparyāsa-jñāna*) arising from *samāhita* [meditative equipoise].

"Cognitions of various characteristics" refers to the establishment of the causal nature and resultant nature of all phenomena, as well as their being superior or non-superior; this is precisely the meaning of the divisions of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*).

Regarding "for the sake of severing the seeds of the various manifestations of the ālayavijñāna and its characteristics": this means for the sake of severing the seeds of those phenomena that appear as forms and so forth within the ālayavijñāna, as well as the characteristics of the perfuming agents; this is precisely what is meant by severing the cause and fruit of the seeds.

"To cause that which can touch the seeds of the Dharma-body to grow" means desiring to increase the cultivation of the extensive learning of all Mahāyāna teachings, because by means of this, one first attains the Dharma-body.

Regarding "transforming the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): it is because all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) arise free from defilement through the penetration of *tathatā*, or alternatively, because *tathatā* itself is perfectly purified.
Regarding "desiring to realize all Buddha-dharmas": it is because one desires to give rise to the Buddha-dharmas such as the powers (*bala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
"One who wishes to realize all-knowledge" means one who wishes to realize the stainless and unimpeded wisdom of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, "subsequently attained wisdom" indicates that subsequently attained wisdom possesses functional activity.
"Arising from all ālayavijñāna" here cites the effect in order to indicate its cause.
"Among all aspects of discernment" reveals its result, namely, within the divisions of the grasper and the grasped.

Regarding "seeing the nature of things as being like illusions and so forth without error": this refers to observing the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as it truly is—like illusory phenomena and the like—because there is no delusion.
For example, a magician, with respect to the illusory objects he creates, has no inversion regarding the causes of illusion such as grass and wood, because he sees them as they truly are;
nor does he have any inversion regarding the illusory appearances such as elephants and horses, because he sees them as they truly are.

Thus, when a bodhisattva who perceives reality sees things as they truly are—having realized that there is no nature of grasped object or grasping subject, which is the perfected nature—they give rise to the subsequently attained pure conventional wisdom capable of producing speech; thereby, at all times regarding cause and effect and when teaching the Dharma, they remain forever free from error.
Although those who hear it may still possess distortions, because the hearing-perfuming (śruta-vāsanā) perfumes the mental continuum, they gradually and successively attain freedom from distortion.
Since this brings about what is to be accomplished, the subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) thereafter is likewise undifferentiated and free from defilement.
The treatise says:
When entering into this realization of the nature of consciousness-only, there are four kinds of samādhi, which serve as the basis for the four kinds of aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
How should these be understood?

It should be understood that through the four investigations, when there is receptivity toward the non-existence of objects at a low degree, one attains the samādhi of "attaining clarity," which is the basis for the "heat" stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
When there is receptivity toward the non-existence of objects at a high degree, one attains the samādhi of "increasing clarity," which is the basis for the "summit" stage of the aids to penetration.

Furthermore, by means of four kinds of thorough knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-parijñāna*), one has already entered into representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and attained certainty regarding the absence of external objects; there is an entry into a samādhi that is a portion of the true meaning, which serves as the basis for the patient acceptance in accordance with the truth (*anulomikī kṣānti*).

Immediately following this, one subdues the perception of representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*); there arises the "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) samādhi, which is the basis for the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
One should know that these various samādhis constitute the stage of the "limits of clear realization" (*abhisamaya-antya*).
The commentary states:
In all instances when one enters into clear realization (*abhisamaya*), there are four levels of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), as these are its preceding signs.
Since clear realization has already been explained, it will not be further elaborated upon here.
"By means of the four thorough investigations" refers to taking the provisional designations of names, objects, intrinsic nature, and specific differences as their substance, as previously explained.

"Within the stage of receptivity toward the non-existence of objects at a low level" refers to being within a state of low-level discerning wisdom that delights in the fact that no objects whatsoever exist.
"Clarity" (*āloka*) refers to the wisdom that illuminates the absence of external objects; because the sought-after result is thereby accomplished, it is called "attainment.

Since this meditative concentration first attains the clarity of wisdom regarding the non-existence of objects, it receives the name "the Samādhi of Attaining Clarity" (*ālokopalabdha-samādhi*), just as one first attains fire or the like.
"Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) refers to the roots of goodness belonging to the stage of heat; just as heat is the precursor to fire when drilling for it, so too is this the precursor to true knowledge.
As for the term "basis," it signifies the sense of "cause."
What is called "definitive discernment" (viniścaya) is precisely direct realization (abhisamaya).

This stage consists of the patience regarding the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmyakṣānti); because it draws forth these roots of goodness, it is termed "conducive" (anuloma), and because it stands at the very pinnacle, it is termed "summit" (mūrdhan).

Furthermore, regarding the four kinds of thorough knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-parijñāna*): as previously explained, having attained certainty within the non-apprehension of names, things, and so forth, when one thus transforms, one enters into consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) and definitively realizes that there are no objects whatsoever appearing as names and the like.
Regarding the samādhi that enters one part of the true meaning: it is called "entering one part" because it can only penetrate the non-existence of the apprehended object.

Since, within this state, one has realized the non-existence of objects but has not yet been able to suppress the aspect of the apprehending subject—the representation-only—so as to make it non-existent, this is therefore called the meditative concentration that serves as the basis for the patience that accords with the truth (*satyānulomikī kṣānti*).
"Conformity" means that by relying on the non-existence of the grasped (*grāhya*), one brings about the non-existence of the grasper (*grāhaka*).
One should know that these various samādhis are "at the edge of clear realization" (*abhisamaya-anta*) in the sense that they are proximate to its actualization.
The treatise says:

Thus, having already entered the stages (*bhūmi*), having already attained the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), and having already entered representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*), how does the bodhisattva practice within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?

Regarding the establishment of the ten stages as previously described, within which all sūtras are encompassed and manifest before one, because of the supramundane and subsequently attained wisdom of śamatha and vipaśyanā that takes the universal dharma as its object, and by practicing for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, one attains the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) and diligently practices in order to realize the three bodies of a Buddha.
The commentary states:

Regarding the establishment of the ten stages as previously described, this refers to the ten kinds of stages within their respective conventional expressions of discourse concerning specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding those who take general phenomena as their object, because they take mixed phenomena as their object, there is no taking of distinct phenomena to cultivate correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*).
If this were not the case, the accumulation of provisions for non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) would not be possible.

That which transcends the world is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); that which is subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) is precisely pure mundane wisdom capable of establishing [phenomena]. It is "pure" because it is subsequently attained, and "mundane" because its objects possess characteristics (*sanimitta*).

Regarding "attaining the transformation of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti): it means that after cultivating non-conceptual subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) over many eons, one attains the transformation of the basis, which refers to the purification of the continuum of the mind and mental factors.
Regarding those who diligently practice in order to realize the three bodies of a Buddha, this shall be explained in detail later.
The treatise asks:
What is the difference between the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Śrāvakas and the clear realization of the Bodhisattvas?
It should be understood that the clear realization (abhisamaya) of a bodhisattva differs from that of a śrāvaka by way of eleven types of distinctions.
First, by way of the distinction of the object of focus (ālambana), because it takes the Mahāyāna teachings as its object of focus.
Second, by way of the distinction of sustenance, because it takes the two types of provisions—great merit and great wisdom—as its sustenance.
Third, by way of the distinction of penetration, because it is able to penetrate the selflessness of persons and phenomena.
Fourth, by way of the distinction of nirvāṇa, because it embraces the great non-abiding nirvāṇa;
fifth, by way of the distinction of the stages, because one attains transcendence by relying upon the ten stages.
The sixth and seventh [differences] arise from the distinction of purification, because they purify the Buddha-fields by severing the habitual tendencies of the afflictions.
The eighth arises from the distinction of attaining a mind of equality toward oneself and others, because their application in maturing sentient beings is uninterrupted.
Ninth, by way of the distinction of birth, because of being born into the family of the Tathāgatas.
Tenth, by way of the distinction of taking birth, because of always assuming birth within the great assemblies of all Buddhas.

Eleventh, by way of the distinction of results, because the results consisting of the ten powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the unique Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), and immeasurable merits are fully perfected.
The commentary states:
The distinctions between the clear realizations (*abhisamaya*) of Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas are, in brief, of ten or eleven kinds.

Regarding the distinction of objects of focus (*ālambana-viśeṣa*): in the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of bodhisattvas, the Mahāyāna teachings serve as the objects for the three types of wisdom, such as that derived from hearing; in the clear realization of śrāvakas, the Śrāvaka vehicle teachings serve as their objects.

Regarding the distinctions among the provisions: the provision of merit refers to the three types of application—generosity, ethical discipline, and patience; the provision of wisdom refers to diligence, meditative concentration, and the wisdom derived from hearing, and so forth.
Regarding "provisions" (*sambhāra*), they are so called because they are gathered and accumulated over immeasurable eons.

Within the context of "penetrating distinctions," the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Śrāvaka can only penetrate the principle of the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and selflessness; the clear realization of the Bodhisattva, however, can penetrate both the emptiness of the person and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Regarding the distinctions within *nirvāṇa*: the Bodhisattva’s clear realization (*abhisamaya*) involves gathering the provisions of compassion, wisdom, and skillful means, taking *nirvāṇa* to be non-attachment to both saṃsāra and *nirvāṇa*; the Śrāvaka’s clear realization, however, takes *nirvāṇa* to be abiding solely in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Regarding the distinctions of the stages (*bhūmi-viśeṣa*), the bodhisattva’s clear realization (*abhisamaya*) results in liberation by relying upon the ten stages; such an establishment of stages does not exist within the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Regarding the distinction of purity: the bodhisattva’s clear realization (abhisamaya) forever severs the afflictions along with their residual impressions (vāsanā), and is further able to purify the various jewel-adorned Buddha-fields;
whereas the śrāvaka’s clear realization, though it severs the afflictions, has not entirely eliminated the residual impressions and cannot purify the various jewel-adorned Buddha-fields.
Regarding "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*): although they are free from afflictions (*kleśa*), their actions appear as if they were possessed of afflictions.

Within the differentiation of the mind that regards self and others as equal, the Bodhisattva, through clear realization (*abhisamaya*), attains the equality of the *dharmatā* of self and others, and their application (*prayoga*) in maturing sentient beings is uninterrupted;
whereas the Śrāvaka, through clear realization, discriminates between self and others, cultivating only self-benefit and not the benefit of others.

Regarding the distinction in birth, the Bodhisattva’s clear realization arises within the Dharma-realm of the Tathāgata’s family; he is a true son of the Buddha, just as a Wheel-turning King is born with a son possessing the marks of excellence, unlike the Śrāvaka who is like the son of a low-born, ignorant slave-girl.

Regarding the distinctions in birth, the bodhisattva’s clear realization consists in always sitting cross-legged upon a lotus pedestal within the great assemblies of all Buddhas; furthermore, until the attainment of Buddhahood, they are constantly born through transformation. What is called the "great assembly of all Buddhas" refers to the Buddha-fields within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), and is not like the case of śrāvakas who dwell in a mother’s womb and so forth.

Regarding the distinction of the fruits: the Bodhisattva’s clear realization is adorned by a multitude of immeasurable virtues such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*); it is able to spontaneously perform all activities for the benefit of sentient beings, and takes the attainment of the *dharmakāya* as its supreme fruit, while other functions take the transformation of birth into the untainted (*anāsrava*) state as their fruit.
The Commentary says:
In this regard, there are two verses:
"Name and thing are mutual guests; their nature should be investigated."
One should likewise investigate both [the subject and object]: they are merely cognition and merely designation.
When realized wisdom contemplates the absence of external objects, there is only the threefold discrimination;
since that [object] does not exist, this [subject] does not exist—this is precisely entering the three natures.
The commentary states:
These two verses summarize the investigations (*vitarka*) and the fruits of investigation, making them easy to understand.

Regarding the statement that "name and object are mutually guests, and their nature should be investigated": this means that the name is a guest with respect to the object, and the object is likewise a guest with respect to the name.
This is not like the case of certain [schools] who claim that sound and meaning correspond and arise as mutually connected.

Regarding these two as well, one should investigate that they are merely measure (*pramāṇa*) and merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*); that is, within both the intrinsic nature and the specific qualities, one should seek to find that there is only conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and only conventional designation.
What is this matter?

It means that these two kinds exist only as conceptual constructions and only as conventional designations of distinct verbal expressions; they possess no real intrinsic nature or distinction whatsoever.
"Real wisdom" refers to the four kinds of thorough knowledge of reality as they truly are (*yathābhūta-parijñāna*), which arise from investigation (*vitarka*).
"Contemplating the absence of objects" means contemplating that their objects are fundamentally non-existent.

"Only conceptualization has three aspects" means that one observes and sees that there are only three kinds of conceptualization: namely, conceptualization of names, conceptualization of the designation of intrinsic nature, and conceptualization of the designation of distinctions.
"Because that does not exist, this does not exist" means that because the object does not exist, one observes that these three kinds of conceptualization also do not exist.
"This is the entry into the three natures" means that what has been explained above is precisely the realization and entry into the three self-natures.
This refers to the first half of the initial verse: contemplating that names and things are mutually adventitious is the entry into the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

The second half of the initial verse: contemplating that the distinctions between those two natures consist solely of conceptual construction and solely of provisional designation is the entry into the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The second verse concerns the entry into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Here, one merely eliminates the distinct objects and subjects of mind that are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*); while there is indeed the matter of suppressing and removing conceptual construction, it is not non-existent.
If it were not so, both bondage and liberation would fail to be established, because neither purity nor impurity would exist.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, there are two verses of instruction as explained in the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (Yogācārabhūmi):
When the Bodhisattva abides in the state of meditative concentration, he contemplates that the reflected image is nothing but mind.
Once the conceptualization of external objects has been eliminated, he scrutinizes and perceives that there is only his own mental representation.
Thus dwelling within the inner mind, he knows that the grasped object does not exist.
Next, the grasper is also non-existent; finally, contact is found to be unobtainable.
The commentary says:
Who is it that can thus investigate and attain the fruit?
For whom, then, is this instruction intended?
To answer this question, two verses are spoken.

"The Bodhisattva, in the state of meditative concentration, contemplates that the reflection is nothing but mind" means that he contemplates that all reflections appearing as phenomena (*dharma*) or as objects (*artha*), which are the objects of meditative concentration, are nothing but internal mind.
As the Sūtra says:
"I declare that the object-condition of consciousness is nothing but what is manifested by consciousness.
When it speaks of "bodhisattvas," it refers to those capable of contemplation.
Regarding "one who abides in the state of meditative concentration," it means the mind dwells upon a single object.
"The conceptualization of objects having been eliminated" means that by means of those images, the conceptualization of objects is dispelled.

"Thoroughly observing that there is only one's own ideation" means carefully examining these appearances that resemble phenomena and resemble objects as being merely the manifestations of one's own concentrated mind.
"One who thus abides in the internal mind" means that at that time, this mind abides in the sense of its own nature.

"Knowing that the apprehended object does not exist, one subsequently realizes that the apprehending subject is also non-existent" means that since one has already understood that the apprehended object is non-existent, and just as the nature of the apprehended object is nothing at all, the nature of the apprehending subject cannot be established upon the nature of the apprehended object.
"Subsequently touching upon that which is non-apprehensible" refers to the true suchness (tathatā) attained through the realization of non-duality following this point.
The Commentary states:
Furthermore, there are five other verses on clear observation (*abhisamaya*), as explained in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*:
Having well prepared the two provisions of merit and wisdom to their infinite extent,
and having thoroughly investigated and resolved the nature of phenomena, the Bodhisattva realizes that the ultimate meaning is merely a category of words.
If one knows that all objects are merely words, one abides in the state where they appear as mere mind;
thus, one is able to directly realize the true dharmadhātu, whereby both dualistic appearances are completely eliminated.
Realizing that there is no separate entity apart from the mind, one thereby understands that the mind itself does not exist;
the wise person comprehends that both are non-existent and abides equally in the true dharma-realm where both are absent.
The wise possess the power of non-conceptualizing wisdom, Which functions universally and with equanimity, always in accordance with reality;
It extinguishes the thicket of dependencies and the mass of faults, Just as a great potent medicine neutralizes all poisons.

The Buddha has well established the sublime Dharma; With wisdom and roots settled within the Dharmadhātu, One understands that the movement of thought is but conceptual construction, And with valor, swiftly returns to the shore of virtue.
The commentary states:

Regarding the Bodhisattva who has well-prepared the two provisions of merit and wisdom without limit—namely, the three pāramitās beginning with generosity are called the provision of merit; the sixth, the pāramitā of wisdom, is called the provision of wisdom; diligence is common to both because it cultivates them together; and meditative concentration is likewise.

If they have immeasurable objects as their focal point, they belong to the accumulation of merit; the remainder belong to the accumulation of wisdom. They are called "accumulations" (sambhāra) because merit and wisdom are gathered therein.
The term "well-prepared" (susampanna) carries the meaning of "perfection."
Having perfected the distinctions of incalculable periods of time is called "boundless.

Regarding the phrase "having thoroughly deliberated upon and correctly resolved the Dharma," this means that through the wisdom subsequent to meditative concentration (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), one has reached an extremely firm determination regarding all dharmas such as the sūtras, thereby attaining freedom from doubt.

Regarding the statement that "the comprehension of all meanings and intentions consists solely in the category of mental discourse": this means that one is able to comprehend all meanings and intentions by taking exclusively the conceptualization of mental discourse as the cause.

If one knows that all objects are merely discourse and thus abides in the mind-only nature that resembles those objects—meaning, if one realizes that all objective characteristics are merely mental discourse—one is then able to settle the mind so that it abides within the mind-only nature where various manifestations resembling objective characteristics appear, because one has attained certainty therein.

The first half of this second verse shows that the bodhisattva is at the stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), while the first verse shows the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for this stage.

"Thus, one is able to realize the true dharmadhātu and thereby eliminate both marks" means that because one has previously understood that objects do not exist and abides in *cittamātra* (mind-only), one is able to eliminate the two marks of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*). One realizes the non-dual, true dharmadhātu, because the wisdom of excellent determination arises based upon it.
The first half-verse and the third [verse] following it reveal the stage of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which shall now be explained according to how it was realized.

"Knowing that there is no object separate from the mind, one thereby realizes that the mind itself does not exist" means: knowing that there are no objective spheres of perception whatsoever apart from the mind, and because those [objects] do not exist, the nature of the perceiving mind cannot be established either.
Regarding the statement, "The wise person realizes that both are without intrinsic nature": one is called "wise" because they are endowed with superior wisdom (*prajñā*).
They are said to "realize" because they possess definitive knowledge regarding the absence of intrinsic nature in both.

That which is grasped by conceptual construction—the object of cognition (*ālambana*) and the cognizing subject (*ālambaka*)—is fundamentally without intrinsic nature; this is what is meant by "both are without [intrinsic nature]."

Regarding "equally abiding in the true dharma-realm where the two do not exist": it is called "equally abiding" because one dwells in equanimity; it is said that "the two do not exist" because both the grasped object and the grasping subject are entirely transcended.
Thus, the direct realization that the dharmadhātu is not false is called the "true dharmadhātu.
Regarding the phrase "the power of the non-conceptualizing wisdom of the wise," this refers to the functional capacity of the non-conceptualizing wisdom possessed by all bodhisattvas.
"Universal, equal, and always practiced in accordance" means that because it encompasses both the internal and external, it is called "universal.
Just as the grasped object does not exist, so too is the grasper; therefore, it is called "equal."
To observe in accordance with the teachings of the sūtras and other dharmas as being equal in nature, like space, is therefore called "conforming practice" (*anuloma-carita*).
It is "constant" because it is perpetual.
"Extinction" (*nirodha*) means removal.
The "basis" refers to the cause of all afflicted phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), which is difficult to penetrate, comparable to a thicket of brambles.
All afflicted phenomena are termed "faults.
Because they are an accumulation of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), they are called a "mass."
The meaning of "like a great medicinal herb that neutralizes all poisons" is easy to understand.
Because it can eliminate and penetrate deep into all faults, it is like the agada medicine.
This fourth verse demonstrates the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
"The Buddha taught the sublime Dharma well-established" means that the True Dharma taught by the Honored Muni is extremely well-established.

"Placing wisdom together with its root within the Dharma-realm" means placing that wisdom, along with its fundamental basis, within the Dharma-realm of the True Dharma as well-established by the Buddha's teaching.
"Root" (mūla) means that this is the cause of awakening.
Alternatively, it is called the "root" because it takes all phenomena as its object in their totality; that is to say, all sūtras take the ten stages (daśabhūmi) as their root.
Because phenomena arise in dependence upon that [dharmadhātu], it is called the *dharmadhātu*; this is precisely the emptiness of all phenomena.

To "understand that the movement of mindfulness is merely conceptual construction" means that subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) arises in dependence upon the *dharmadhātu*, understanding that the movement of mindfulness is solely conceptual construction, and that apart from conceptual construction, there are no objects of mindfulness.

This means that because the dharmas such as the sūtras and so forth which are to be recollected, as well as the perfections (pāramitās) and their fruits which are to be recollected, are all entirely devoid of the nature of being conceptually constructed (parikalpita-svabhāva).
