"Those who are valiant and swiftly return to the shore of virtue" refers to those bodhisattvas who, by means of first gradually cultivating the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) of clear realization and subsequently the post-attainment wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), are able to quickly realize and attain the fruit of Buddhahood, which is the perfection of all virtues.
This refers to the stage of the Tathāgata, which transcends the boundless merits of the causal stages and is thus called the "Shore of Virtue. As a verse says:
"When realizing triple awakening, One suddenly achieves the perfect fruition."
Having crossed the boundless ocean of merit, one reaches the stage of the Peerless.
"Swift" means rapid.
Since it takes immeasurable kalpas to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, and the time is so long, why is it called swift?
This argument is not tenable, because the vast duration of eons is merely a mental construction.
As a verse says: "In a dream one may think a year has passed, Yet upon waking, it is but a brief moment."
Therefore, although time is immeasurable, it is subsumed within a single kṣaṇa.
Furthermore, because the Buddha’s diligence is so intensely blazing, even though many kalpas have passed, he regards them as a brief moment.
As a verse says: "Though the fool practices for but a short time, his mind is weary and has long been filled with doubt;
yet for the Buddha, throughout immeasurable eons, diligent effort is but a mere moment."
"Valiant" refers to the power of wisdom; because it accomplishes non-conceptual subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it is called "valiant" as it is free from all timidity or dread.
This verse reveals the ultimate path-stage, which is the most supreme and exalted state of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Fascicle Six;
Commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Fascicle Seven.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asvabhāva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Five: The Section on the Cause and Result of Entering That [Reality]. The Treatise says:
Thus has the entry into the characteristics of the knowable (*jñeyalakṣaṇapraveśa*) already been explained. How is the cause and result of that entry to be perceived?
That is to say, by means of the six perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
How does one enter into consciousness-only by means of these six perfections?
Furthermore, how do the six *pāramitās* constitute the fruit of that entry?

It is said that when this bodhisattva does not cling to wealth or status, does not violate ethical discipline (*śīla*), remains unshaken by suffering, and is untiring in cultivation—such that these causes of distraction do not manifest—the mind becomes one-pointed and is able to discern all phenomena according to reality, thereby attaining entry into consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Having entered into consciousness-only by relying on the six pāramitās, the bodhisattva realizes the six kinds of pāramitās subsumed within the pure superior intention (adhyāśaya).

Therefore, even if one does not currently engage in the practical application of the six perfections, by virtue of gaining resolute conviction in the sacred teachings and through the mental engagements (*manasikāra*) of cherishing, sympathetic joy, and delight, one will constantly and uninterruptedly cultivate the six perfections through the method of meditative union, thereby swiftly attaining their fulfillment.
The commentary states:
Regarding the causes for entering *vijñapti-mātra*, namely the six mundane *pāramitās* during the stage of application (*prayoga*), these shall now be demonstrated.

To say that this bodhisattva does not cling to wealth or status means they have no craving or seeking; thus, it is called "non-clinging. This is the very opposite of attachment, which is the obstacle to be countered by the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*). The same applies to the remaining five perfections.
"Not violating the śīla" refers to the obstacle that is the antithesis of this perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
"Remaining unshaken by suffering" refers to the obstacle that is the agitation of anger, which is the antithesis of the perfection of patience (*kṣāntipāramitā*).
"Being untiring in cultivation" means that laziness is the obstacle to be countered by the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

"The mind being focused on a single object" means that within the causes of distraction—the obstacles to be countered by the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*)—one remains far removed from them and does not engage in them, thereby holding the mind steady and inducing samādhi.
That which is able to discern all phenomena according to reality is precisely the *prajñāpāramitā*.

By means of these six *pāramitās*, one enters into *vijñaptimātratā*; having entered therein, one realizes the six supreme *pāramitās* of the resultant stage, which are subsumed within the pure *adhyāśaya*.

Therefore, if one applies the preparatory effort for the manifestation of the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*), will one not swiftly attain the fulfillment of the six perfections by practicing them constantly and without interruption? Or is it otherwise?
If one were to fail to initiate application toward the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), it would constitute a transgression of the precepts;
however, this is not the case, because there is no initiation of strenuous application.

If one were not to initiate application (*prayoga*) toward ethical discipline (*śīla*), this fault would indeed follow; however, there is no such fault when one does not fail to initiate diligent application.
Because one possesses spontaneous application through the attainment of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) and so forth regarding the Noble Teaching, there is therefore no fault.

In this context, "attaining resolute belief in the noble teaching" means being able to have faith and understanding in the noble teaching associated with the perfections (*pāramitā*), even though it is extremely profound.
The mental attention of cherishing (*priyākarana-manasikāra*) refers to experiencing the flavor of the merits of the perfections (*pāramitā*) already attained.

The mental attention of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā-manasikāra*) refers to rejoicing with a profound heart in the perfections within the continuums of others throughout all worlds in the ten directions, or within one's own individual continuum.
Regarding the mental attention of joyful aspiration (*abhirati-manasikāra*): it refers to the wish for the future that "may I never be separated from this, and may it become even more excellent.
The treatise says:
In this regard, there are three verses:
Having perfected the white dharmas and attained swift and sharp patience,
the Bodhisattva, regarding the profound and vast teachings of their own vehicle,
realizes that all is mere conceptualization and attains non-conceptual wisdom.
Seeking with pure resolute conviction, one’s intention becomes pure.
Through both the preceding and this stream of Dharma, one shall behold all Buddhas;
realizing that enlightenment is near, for it can be attained without difficulty.

These three verses collectively reveal that the purified superior intention (*adhyāśaya*) possesses eight characteristics: namely, by way of the provisions (*sambhāra*), endurance (*kṣānti*), the object of focus (*ālambana*), mental attention (*manasikāra*), the antidote (*pratipakṣa*), the essential nature (*svabhāva*), the auspicious signs (*nimitta*), and the benefits (*anuśaṃsa*).
It should be understood that these verses sequentially reveal [the following].
The commentary states:

herein, there is an explicit exposition of the equipment for the pure superior intention (*adhyāśaya*), as well as its forbearance, objective referent (*ālambana*), mental attention (*manasikāra*), antidote (*pratipakṣa*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), auspicious signs (*nimitta*), and benefits (*anuśaṃsa*).

"Having perfected the white dharmas" means that one has previously fully prepared the provisions on the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*); the perfection of the white dharmas refers to these provisions.

Furthermore, "having attained swift and sharp patience" means that, distinguishing between the inferior and middling levels, one takes up only the superior patience regarding the investigation of the truths (*dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti*); when this patience is active, it is what is meant by "endurance."

Regarding the Bodhisattva’s profound and vast teachings of their own vehicle: this refers to the Mahāyāna’s profound and extensive sacred teachings. Their meaning is subtle and thus termed "profound," specifically referring to the excellence of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
That which is endowed with majestic power is called "vast," namely the various *samādhis* such as the *Gaganagañja*.
This is termed the "object of focus" (*ālambana*).

"Perfectly awakening to [the fact that] there is only conceptualization" means awakening to the realization that all phenomena are nothing but conceptualization; this is termed "mental attention" (*manasikāra*).
The attainment of non-conceptual wisdom is the antidote.

The purity of the intentional disposition (*āśaya*) characterized by aspiration, resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), and pure intention is the essence, because this intentional disposition has faith and desire as its essence.
The phrase "those who, prior to this and within this stream of Dharma, are able to see all Buddhas" refers to auspicious signs.

"Prior" refers to the stage before the purification of one's intention; "this" refers to being within this samādhi; and "the stream of Dharma" refers to the state of being in meditative concentration while abiding in samādhi.

Regarding the statement, "Because one sees the Buddhas, one realizes that bodhi is near, for it is obtained without difficulty": this means that by seeing the Buddhas, one knows that bodhi is near; the phrase "for it is obtained without difficulty" explains this meaning, which constitutes a benefit.

In this stage, one perceives that awakening is near; because one has attained these superior means for its attainment, it is not difficult to achieve, as the power of having cultivated and accumulated the provisions has matured and become capable.
These three verses collectively explain the eightfold distinctions of the pure superior intention (*viśuddhādhyāśaya*).
The treatise asks:
For what reasons and conditions are there exactly six perfections (*pāramitā*)?

The perfection of generosity and the perfection of ethical discipline are established because they counteract their respective obstacles, serve as the basis for realizing all Buddha-dharmas, accord with the maturation of sentient beings, and act as the remedies for the causes of non-entrance [into the path].
The causes for not setting forth are attachment to wealth and status, as well as attachment to the household life.
To counteract these causes for retreating even after one has already set forth, the perfections of patience (*kṣānti*) and diligence (*vīrya*) are established.

The causes for regression refer to the manifold sufferings arising from the transgressions of sentient beings within cyclic existence, as well as the weariness and fatigue resulting from long-term application toward virtuous qualities.
To counteract the causes of ruin that, despite having already set out on the path, lead to regression, the perfections of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are established.
The causes of ruin refer to all forms of mental distraction and erroneous intelligence (*mithyā-prajñā*).
Thus, because the antidotes and the obstacles to be countered are established in this way, only six numbers are established.

Furthermore, the first four perfections (*pāramitās*) are the causes for non-distraction; the next one perfection is the accomplishment of non-distraction. Relying upon this non-distraction, one awakens to the true meaning of all phenomena as they truly are, and is thereby able to realize all the Buddha-dharmas.
Because they constitute the basis for realizing all the qualities of a Buddha, only six are established.
Through the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), one is able to correctly gather in and sustain all sentient beings.
By means of the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), one is able to refrain from harming sentient beings;
by means of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), one is able to endure harm even when it is encountered.
By means of the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), one is able to assist in the performance of what ought to be done.
Through such causes and conditions of gathering and benefiting others, sentient beings are rendered capable of accomplishing the task of maturation.

From this point forward, those whose minds are not yet concentrated shall attain concentration, and those whose minds are already concentrated shall attain liberation; at the time of awakening, they will reach full maturity.
In this way, one should understand that the number six is established solely for the purpose of maturing all sentient beings in accordance with their needs.
The commentary states:
Next, the meanings of the numbers and other characteristics within the final verse shall be elucidated; first, the following statement is made based on the establishment of those numbers.
The establishment of the antidotes and the obstacles to be countered is based on three causal conditions; thus, the number of pāramitās is exactly six, neither more nor less.
First, one should explain the establishment of the antidotes and the obstacles to be countered.

The perfection of generosity and ethical discipline are established to counteract the causes for failing to set out; likewise, up to the perfections of meditative concentration and wisdom are established to counteract the causes for falling away and ruin.
The causes of ruin refer to various forms of mental distraction and the perverted grasping of false wisdom (*mithyā-prajñā*).
Various base and evil cognitions are termed false wisdom; such as those held by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), these are the causes of ruin.
The remaining phrases are clear and easy to understand as they appear in the text.
Regarding the phrase "the basis upon which all Buddha-dharmas depend," this establishes the second reason for the number six:
because these are the causes of all Buddha-dharmas, the *pāramitās* consist of exactly six, neither more nor less.
What is the meaning of this?
It means that the first four pāramitās are the causes for non-distraction, as they cause the distractions that are their opposites to cease to exist.
The dhyāna-pāramitā achieves non-distraction, thereby bringing non-distraction to full perfection.

By means of this perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), one awakens to the true meaning of all phenomena as they really are, because one is able to correctly and universally know the objects of focus.
"The qualities of the Buddhas" refers to the ten powers (*daśabala*) and so forth.
"Realization" means accomplishment.
Regarding "conforming to and maturing all sentient beings," this establishes the third reason for the number six.
This is because through the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), one is able to correctly sustain and gather all sentient beings.
Because through the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), one is able to refrain from harming sentient beings and does not give rise to affliction toward them;

and because through the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), although one encounters harm, one is able to endure it, and by virtue of this endurance, one is able to benefit others without retaliating.
Through the perfection of diligence, one assists in what they are doing;
through the perfection of meditative concentration, one causes those whose minds are not settled to attain stability.
By means of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), those whose minds are already concentrated are led to liberation.
"The time of awakening" refers to the moment when they are instructed and thereby attain realization regarding the objective sphere.
Regarding "one who has attained maturity": such a person has already attained maturity with respect to their objective sphere (*viṣaya*).

As for the term "maturity," it refers to the dissolution and dispersal of the obstacles to be remedied (*vipakṣa*), like an abscess that has ripened; or it refers to the fulfillment of the remedies (*pratipakṣa*) so that they may be put to use, like food that has been cooked.
The treatise says:
How are these six kinds of characteristics to be perceived?
By means of six kinds of supremacy.
First, by way of the excellence of the basis, meaning that it takes the bodhicitta as its basis;
second, by way of the excellence of the activity, meaning that it is fully manifested in practice;
third, by way of the excellence of the objective sphere, meaning that it takes the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings as its objective sphere.
Fourth, it is supreme by virtue of skillful means, because it is embraced by non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Fifth, it is supreme by virtue of dedication, because it is dedicated toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Sixth, by way of supreme purity, meaning that it arises from being free from the obscurations of both the afflictive and cognitive hindrances.
If a gift constitutes a *pāramitā*, [is it so because of this purity?]
Is a pāramitā necessarily giving? There are cases where there is giving that is not a pāramitā; thus, one should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
Just as it is with giving, so it should be understood that the same four permutations apply to each of the other pāramitās as well.
The commentary states:
Based on the characteristics established, it is said, "by way of six kinds of supremacy," and so forth.
These six kinds of supremacy are easy to understand and do not require further explanation.
"Because it is fully practiced" means that one is able to relinquish all types of internal and external things.

"Because it is embraced by non-conceptual wisdom" refers to the purity of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍalapariśuddhi*), as one is completely free from the conceptualization of the giver, the recipient, and the gift.
The remainder of the text is easy to understand.
There are cases where something is a gift (*dāna*) but not a perfection (*pāramitā*), namely, practicing generosity while lacking the six kinds of excellence.
There are cases where something is a perfection but not a gift, namely, the ethical discipline (*śīla*) and other perfections that are gathered through those same six kinds of excellence.
There are cases where something is both a gift and a *pāramitā*, namely, the six kinds of supreme accumulated giving.
There are cases where something is neither a gift nor a *pāramitā*, namely, the cultivation of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and so forth apart from the six kinds of supremacy.
Just as these four propositions were established regarding generosity, they are likewise properly established for the remaining five perfections, such as ethical discipline, as appropriate.
Thus, a verse says: "For the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha], there is no practice of the six pāramitās."
"I alone am the most supreme Honored One, having reached the highest shore.
The commentary asks:
For what reason and by what causal conditions are these six types of *pāramitā* taught in this specific order?
This means that each preceding *pāramitā* conduces to the arising of each subsequent *pāramitā*. The commentary explains:

"Because it conduces to the arising of each subsequent *pāramitā*" means that once one is free from attachment to wealth and status, one is able to maintain ethical discipline (*śīla*); having fulfilled ethical discipline, one is then able to practice patience (*kṣānti*); having attained patience, one is able to endure adversity and thus arouses diligence (*vīrya*); having aroused diligence, the mind attains concentration (*samādhi*); and once the mind has attained concentration, one is able to know things as they truly are (*yathābhūtam*). Therefore, these six are arranged in this specific order.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, how are the etymological explanations (*nirukti*) of these *pāramitās* to be understood?

Because they are the most preeminent among all roots of virtue—such as generosity—belonging to worldly beings, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, and because they enable one to reach the further shore (*pāra*), they are collectively termed *pāramitās*.
Furthermore, because it can shatter stinginess and poverty, and can induce vast wealth, status, merit, and provisions, it is called "giving" (*dāna*).
Moreover, because it can extinguish immoral conduct and the miserable realms, and can attain the happy realms and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called "ethical discipline" (*śīla*).
Furthermore, because it can extinguish anger, resentment, and enmity, and can skillfully abide in the peace and security of both self and others, it is called patience (*kṣānti*).
Moreover, because it can distance oneself from all laziness and evil, unwholesome dharmas, and can give rise to immeasurable wholesome dharmas so that they increase, it is called diligence (*vīrya*).
Furthermore, because it can eliminate all mental distraction and induce the mind to abide in tranquility, it is called *dhyāna* (meditative concentration).
Moreover, because it can dispel all dogmatic views and erroneous wisdoms, and can truly and analytically discern phenomena, it is called *prajñā* (wisdom).
The commentary states:

Regarding the general definition of the term, among all the roots of virtue—such as generosity—in the world of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, these are the most preeminent and are capable of reaching the further shore; therefore, they are collectively termed *pāramitā*.
The name "reaching the other shore" (*pāramitā*) signifies the most supreme meaning.

To explain its specific etymology: it is called "giving" (*dāna*) because at the stage of the cause, it can destroy stinginess and also attract a vast accumulation of merit; and at the stage of the fruit, it can tear asunder poverty and attain great wealth and status.
The explanations of the other specific names are easy to understand from the text.
The treatise says:
How should one know how to practice these pāramitās?
It should be understood that this cultivation is, in brief, of five kinds:

first, cultivation through the application of manifest activity; second, cultivation through resolute belief; third, cultivation through mental attention; fourth, cultivation through skillful means; and fifth, cultivation through the accomplishment of tasks.
Among these, the four types of cultivation have already been explained as before.

Regarding the cultivation of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-bhāvanā*): it refers to the effortless and uninterrupted performance of the Buddha-activities of all Tathāgatas, wherein they further cultivate the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) within their already perfected paramitas.

Furthermore, regarding cultivation through mental attention (*manasikāra*), this refers to cultivating the six types of mental attention comprised within the six kinds of aspiration (*āśaya*): cherishing, sympathetic joy, and joyful delight. These are: (1) the expansive aspiration, (2) the long-term aspiration, (3) the joyful aspiration, (4) the aspiration of gratitude, (5) the aspiration of great resolve, and (6) the aspiration of pure goodness.

If Bodhisattvas were to manifest the realization of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment after even as many countless great eons as there may be, and during each and every moment throughout that duration, were to suddenly relinquish all their bodies and lives, and were to offer to the Tathāgatas worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges filled with the seven precious jewels, continuing in this manner until they sit upon the seat of sublime enlightenment—even then, the Bodhisattvas’ intention for giving would still be without satiety.

Throughout all those moments, at every single instant—even if the great trichiliocosm were filled with blazing fire, and even if one were constantly deprived of all necessities of life during the four postures—one should maintain the constant practice of the mind of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, until finally sitting upon the seat of sublime awakening.
In this way, when a bodhisattva’s aspiration regarding morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom remains insatiable, it is called the bodhisattva’s vast aspiration.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas maintain a resolve free from weariness regarding this very matter, continuing without interruption until they sit upon the seat of sublime awakening, this is called the bodhisattva’s resolve for the long duration.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings through the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and thereby experience profound joy at what they have accomplished—joy that cannot be matched by those sentient beings who receive their benefit—this is called the bodhisattva’s intention of joy (prāmodyāśaya).

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings through the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), they perceive those beings as having great kindness toward themselves, rather than seeing themselves as having any kindness toward them; this is called the bodhisattva’s intentionality of bearing kindness.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas dedicate with a profound mind the roots of virtue accumulated through these six perfections to all sentient beings, so that they may obtain desirable, superior fruits of maturation, this is called the bodhisattva’s great aspirational intention (*adhyāśaya*).

Furthermore, when Bodhisattvas dedicate the roots of virtue accumulated through these six perfections (pāramitās) for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, together with all sentient beings, this is called the Bodhisattva’s purely virtuous intention.
In this way, a bodhisattva cultivates this attention of cherishing, which is comprised within these six types of intentionality.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva deeply rejoices with a sincere mind in the immeasurable roots of goodness associated with the cultivation of the six types of intentionality belonging to other bodhisattvas; thus, a bodhisattva cultivates this intentionality of rejoicing, which is comprised within these six types of intentionality.

Furthermore, bodhisattvas, with a profound resolve, take delight in the cultivation of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) as subsumed within the six types of intentionality toward all sentient beings; they also vow that their own person shall never be separated from this cultivation of the six perfections until they sit upon the seat of sublime awakening (bodhimanda). In this way, the bodhisattva practices this mental engagement of taking delight, which is subsumed within these six types of intentionality.

If anyone, having heard this cultivation of mental attention encompassed by the six types of bodhisattva intention, should give rise to even a single thought of faith, they will still generate an immeasurable mass of merit and all their karmic obstructions of evil will be extinguished; how much more so for a bodhisattva!
The commentary states:
"Cultivation" (bhāvanā) refers to repeated practice.
There are five distinctions, such as the cultivation of manifestation (samudācāra-bhāvanā) and so forth.
Cultivation through the manifestation of application refers to proceeding without error regarding [the perfections] such as generosity.
As a verse says: "The giver is preeminent, Endowed with faith and the like, Reverent and timely."
Giving with one's own hands, and so forth.
As another verse says:
"In applying oneself to the benefit of sentient beings, one makes no distinction between those who are capable and those who are not."
At all times, one should practice universal giving, extensively benefiting others to the best of one's ability.

Regarding the cultivation of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*): it means that through faith and aspiration, one gives rise to resolute conviction, because one deeply seals and accords with the Buddha’s holy teachings and generates a joyful desire for them.
As it is said in a verse:
"Though effortless regarding the activity of gain, One generates resolute conviction in the Buddha’s teaching;
Through the union of faith and aspiration, The mental disposition constantly cultivates [virtue] without slackening."
Cultivation through mental attention refers to cultivation subsumed under the mental attentions of cherishing, sympathetic joy, and joyful aspiration, as previously explained.
Cultivation through skillful means refers to cultivation embraced by non-conceptual wisdom, also as previously explained.

The cultivation of the performance of activities refers to the fact that although all Tathāgatas have attained the ultimate perfection of the dharmas of the *pāramitās*, out of the power of their original vows to benefit others, they act without effort, manifesting the activities they ought to perform—such as generosity—in accordance with the capacities of those beings.
This itself is cultivation; because it is for the sake of that [cultivation], it is also called cultivation.

Furthermore, the word "also" (api) is intended to express that there is a distinction in the cultivation of the preceding mental attention (*manasikāra*), namely, that it is comprised of six kinds of resolute intention (*āśaya*), up to and including the resolute intention that remains insatiable, and so forth.
These words are easy to understand; they are spoken concisely and sparingly.
"Without weariness" means being free from fatigue.

For as long as that duration lasts—in each and every moment—some say that such a duration constitutes a single *kṣaṇa*, meaning that the measure of three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) constitutes one *kṣaṇa*. In this manner, these *kṣaṇas* accumulate until the attainment of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
The meaning of "during that much time, at every single moment" is easy to understand.
"Filled with blazing fire" indicates a lack of superior states.

"Constantly lacking all the various requisites for life" indicates an absence of the requisites for life that serve as antidotes to suffering, because such things are accepted in order to counteract all forms of suffering.
Regarding the four modes of deportment, this reveals the vastness of his resolve.

Although he lacks superior dwellings and the necessities of life, because his mind focused on the practice of the perfections—such as ethical discipline—is constantly present throughout all four modes of deportment.
The intention of long duration refers to the absence of interruption over a prolonged period of time.
The intention of gratitude refers to the profound conviction that those who come seeking are one's spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
This means that one places faith in those who come seeking [gifts], believing that they will bestow upon oneself the ripening of desirable and wondrous fruits; therefore, one bears their kindness.
"Great aspirational intention" refers to an intention associated with a great resolve, being for the purpose of benefiting all sentient beings.

To dedicate one’s own roots of virtue by bestowing them upon all beings—such an aspiration is most excellent; therefore, it is called the "aspiration of great resolve" (*mahāśaya*), which is synonymous with the "purely virtuous aspiration."

Regarding the establishment of a distinct name: if one seeks the perfection of wealth and status within the three realms of existence by dedicating [merit] through giving and so forth, such an intention—desiring the instruments of suffering—is similar to that which possesses fault, and thus is not called "purely wholesome."

If one dedicates acts such as giving, together with all sentient beings, toward the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood, such an intention does not seek out instruments of suffering; because it is entirely free from fault, it is called "purely wholesome."
Cultivating these three types of mental attention, which are subsumed under the six kinds of intentionality, is easy to understand and requires no further elaborate explanation.
As for the statement that "all karmic obstructions of evil deeds shall also be extinguished," this means either causing them to bear no fruit or treating the miserable realms of rebirth.
The treatise says:
How are the distinctions among these various pāramitās to be understood?
One should know that each one possesses three grades.
The three categories of giving are: first, the gift of Dharma; second, the gift of material wealth; and third, the gift of fearlessness.

The three categories of ethical discipline are: first, the ethical discipline of restraint; second, the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas; and third, the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings.
The three grades of patience are: first, patience in enduring enmity and harm; second, patience in accepting suffering; and third, patience in the discernment of dharmas.

The three grades of diligence are: first, the diligence of donning the armor; second, the diligence of application; and third, the diligence that is free from cowardice, free from regression, and free from complacency.
The three categories of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are: first, meditative concentration for abiding; second, meditative concentration for eliciting [supernormal powers];

and third, meditative concentration for accomplishing activities. The three categories of wisdom (*prajñā*) are: first, non-conceptual wisdom of application (*prayoga*); second, non-conceptual wisdom; and third, non-conceptual wisdom attained subsequent to realization (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*).
The commentary states:
Because each of these *pāramitās* has three grades, their distinctions are revealed.
Regarding "Dharma-giving" (*dharmadāna*), it refers to the teaching of the Dharma—such as the *sūtras* and other scriptures—in accordance with reality by means of an undefiled mind.
Regarding the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), it refers to relinquishing the necessities of life with a mind free from defilement.
Regarding the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), it refers to ceasing harm and rescuing others from terror.

Furthermore, the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*) is intended to nourish and benefit the various roots of goodness in others; the gift of material wealth is intended to nourish and benefit the bodies of others; and the gift of fearlessness is intended to nourish and benefit the minds of others.

The ethical discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) refers to the undertaking and maintenance of the practice of distancing oneself from unwholesome states; it is called "restraint" because it protects against all evil and unwholesome actions of body and speech.

This is precisely ethical discipline (*śīla*); it is able to establish the latter two types of *śīla*, because by means of self-protection one can cultivate roots of virtue such as making offerings to the Buddhas and so forth, and because one can benefit all sentient beings.
The precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) enables one to realize all Buddha-dharmas, such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
The precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*) assists sentient beings in their righteous activities by impartially distributing blameless deeds to bring them to maturity.

The patience of enduring harm from others is the cause for the maturation of sentient beings; the patience of accepting suffering is the cause for attaining Buddhahood, because one is able to endure various hardships such as cold, heat, hunger, and thirst without ever regressing.
The patience of discerning the Dharma (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*) is the basis for the former two types of patience, because it is capable of enduring the profound and vast Dharma.

Armor-like diligence (*saṃnāhavīrya*) refers to the initial stage when one exerts oneself, thinking, "I shall perform such-and-such a task"; this explains the phrase "possessing power at the outset" as taught in the sūtras.
Exertion in application refers to diligently practicing application at the time of application according to one's intention; this explains the phrase "there is diligence" that follows in the sūtra.

It is the diligence that is without cowardice, without regression, and without complacency; that is, performing virtuous deeds according to one’s aspiration, never relinquishing them until one is seated upon the sublime seat of awakening.

Not succumbing to discouragement when one’s own mind is weary and suffering is called "absence of timidity"; not wavering in one’s mind when confronted by the afflictions of others is called "absence of regression.
To cultivate wholesome qualities without ever becoming indolent or desisting until the attainment of bodhi is called "absence of complacency."

These three phrases are explained according to their respective order as taught in the sūtras: the phrase "possessing courage, firmness, and vigor, not relinquishing the yoke regarding all wholesome dharmas";
and "abiding in meditative concentration for the sake of attaining happiness in the present life, because one has become pure by being free from conceit, views, and craving."
The meditative concentration that induces [supernormal powers] is for the purpose of inducing superior qualities such as the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

The meditative concentration that accomplishes what is to be done is for the purpose of benefiting all classes of sentient beings by being able to pacify sufferings and afflictions, such as those caused by famine, pestilence, and various fears.
The wisdom of preparatory application without conceptual differentiation refers to the superior skillful means of knowledge prior to true contemplation.
Non-conceptual wisdom refers to the knowledge of true contemplation.

Subsequently attained wisdom without conceptual differentiation refers to the various conventional knowledges at the conclusion of clear realization, which are capable of initiating diverse activities such as preaching the Dharma.
The treatise says:
How can such mutual inclusion be seen?
It is because these are able to include all wholesome dharmas, as they constitute their characteristic, they are in accordance with them, and they are their outflow.
The commentary states:
Regarding the claim that "this is able to encompass all wholesome dharmas," this answer is irrational because it does not correspond to the question.
Previously, the general question was: "How is such mutual inclusion to be seen?"
There is no such fault; it has already been explained that this [classification] is intended to encompass all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*).

As for the statement that "those [wholesome roots] also encompass all these wholesome dharmas," this refers to those beginning with giving (*dāna*) and faith (*śraddhā*), and ending with the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the powers (*bala*).

"Because it is their characteristic" refers to the inclusion of essential characteristics; that is to say, these [virtues] such as giving and those [virtues] such as giving mutually include one another.

"Because it is concordant with them" refers to the inclusion of concordant wholesome dharmas such as faith; for the wholesome mind of giving and so forth is what is cultivated by them, and they function in accordance with giving and so forth within those [wholesome states].
Faith and the other [faculties] are themselves the great gifts of all virtues, as well as the factors of enlightenment such as the foundations of mindfulness.

Regarding the phrase "because they are outflows" (*niṣyanda*), this refers to the inclusion of outflows; that is to say, [qualities] such as the absence of conflict (*araṇā*) and the ten powers (*daśabala*), because they are the outflow fruits (*niṣyandaphala*) of the perfections (*pāramitā*).
As it is said in a verse:
"The stages and the perfections (pāramitās) Are the basis for all Buddha-dharmas;
The dharmakāya and so forth, With their various qualities, constitute the fruit."
The treatise says:
How are the various defilements subsumed under these objects of negation to be understood?
They are to be seen as being of this nature, having this cause, and having this result.
The commentary states:
Thus, regarding the objects of abandonment—namely, stinginess, violation of precepts, anger, laziness, distraction, and faulty wisdom—how do they encompass all forms of affliction?
"Because it has this characteristic" means that it comprises the distinct intrinsic natures of stinginess and so forth, as it is devoid of other natures.
"Because it has this cause" means that lack of faith and so forth serve as the causes for subsequent states such as stinginess, up to and including wrong view.
The Treatise says: How are the benefits obtained from these six perfections (pāramitās) to be seen? They are as follows:

because Bodhisattvas, while transmigrating through birth and death, are encompassed by wealth and nobility; encompassed by noble birth; encompassed by great circles of friends and followers; encompassed by the accomplishment of the application of vast undertakings; encompassed by being free from affliction and harm and having naturally thin defilements; and encompassed by skillful knowledge of all crafts, treatises, and fields of learning. From such superior births that are free from fault, up until sitting upon the sublime seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), they are constantly able to manifest and perform all that is beneficial for all sentient beings. These are called the benefits.
The commentary states:
We shall now clearly explain the meritorious benefits of the pāramitās.
"Because it encompasses wealth and nobility" refers to the benefit obtained from the perfection of generosity (dāna-pāramitā).
"Superior birth without fault" and so forth, up to "this is called the benefit," should be applied universally to all instances.

Regarding "because it is comprised within a great birth": this refers to the benefits obtained through the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); it is called a "great birth" because it is comprised within the superior happy realms (*sugati*).
"Being embraced by a great circle of friends and a great retinue" refers to the benefits obtained through the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
"Friends" refers to kinsmen; "retinue" refers to servants and slaves.
"Because it is encompassed by the accomplishment of the application of vast undertakings" refers to the benefits obtained through the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
"Vast undertakings" refers to such things as the status of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).

Exertion within this context is called "application" (*prayoga*); because all that is to be done is accomplished, it is called "attainment" (*niṣpatti*). Being encompassed by these, one is free from all obstructions.

As for being "encompassed by that which is free from affliction and harm and possesses thin defilements," this is the benefit obtained through the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), for it is by means of meditative concentration that such power is induced.
"Because it encompasses all crafts, treatises, and fields of knowledge that are well-understood" refers to the benefit obtained through the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Regarding "superior birth free from fault": although one attains a most excellent birth similar to those in the world, it is unlike worldly superior births which are accompanied by fault.

Since there is no fault, and since time is boundless and uninterrupted until the attainment of enlightenment, it is not like the worldly pursuit of self-interest alone; rather, one is constantly able to manifest all that is beneficial for the welfare of all sentient beings.
The treatise says:
How are these six kinds of *pāramitās* to be understood as mutually determining one another?

Regarding all these six *pāramitās*, the Blessed One has in some instances spoken of them by the term "giving," in some by the term "ethical discipline," in some by the term "patience," in some by the term "diligence," in some by the term "meditative concentration," and in some by the term "wisdom. What is the underlying intention behind such explanations?
This refers to the underlying intention that within the cultivation of the application of any single *pāramitā*, all *pāramitās* mutually assist and bring one another to fulfillment.
The commentary states:

This means that within the application of practice (*prayoga*) for each and every *pāramitā*, all *pāramitās* mutually assist and accomplish one another. Such an intention implies that within the application of practice for each individual [perfection], there is the presence of all [the others] acting as mutual aids.

That is to say, when practicing generosity, one restrains, endures, exerts effort, concentrates the mind, and is able to correctly understand the causal connection between actions and their results; in this way, there is further transformation within that very act of giving.
When one cultivates ethical discipline, if one remains far removed from stinginess, anger, indolence, distraction, and wrong views, then within such discipline there is further transformation.
The cultivation of the remaining perfections is also explained in this way. As a verse says:
"When giving, there is no greed and no violation of precepts; there is no envy and no malice, but the arising of a compassionate mind."
To all who come seeking, he gives without weariness, without distraction, and without divergent views.
Furthermore, there is a verse that says:
Within the very nature of giving, the six pāramitās are present.
The gift of material wealth and the gift of fearlessness are subsumed within the gift of the Dharma.
The treatise says:
Herein is a summary verse (udāna):
One should know that the enumeration, characteristics, sequence, etymological definitions, cultivation, distinctions,
subsumption, objects of counteraction, and virtues are mutually determined. Commentary:
The preceding text is summarized; its meaning has been explained as above. 6.
The Section on the Differentiations of that Cultivation (*Tat-bhāvanā-prabheda-vibhāga*). The *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* states:
Having thus already explained the causes and fruits of entry (*praveśa-hetu-phala*), how are the differentiations of that cultivation to be understood?
By means of the ten stages of a bodhisattva. What are these ten? First, the Stage of Great Joy;

second, the Stage of Purity; third, the Stage of Radiant Light; fourth, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom; fifth, the Stage of Ultimate Difficult Victory; sixth, the Stage of Manifestation; seventh, the Stage of Far-Reaching Travel; eighth, the Immovable Stage; ninth, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence; and tenth, the Stage of the Dharma Cloud.

How are these stages established as ten? This should be understood as being for the purpose of counteracting the ten kinds of obscurations that are the objects to be remedied by ignorance. Why is this so?
Because there exist ten types of obscurations to be remedied by ignorance regarding the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) characterized by ten aspects.
What are these ten aspects of the dharma-realm that is the object of knowledge?

That is to say: by the sense of universal pervasion in the first stage; by the sense of supremacy in the second stage; by the sense of the superior outflow in the third stage; by the sense of non-appropriation in the fourth stage; by the sense of non-differentiation in the continuum in the fifth stage; by the sense of non-defilement and non-purity in the sixth stage; by the sense of non-differentiation among various phenomena in the seventh stage; by the sense of neither increasing nor decreasing, the sense of the basis for mastery over signs, and the sense of the basis for mastery over fields in the eighth stage; by the sense of the basis for mastery over gnosis in the ninth stage; and by the sense of the basis for mastery over activity and the sense of the basis for mastery over the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of samādhi in the tenth stage.
In this regard, there are three verses:
The meaning of universal pervasion and supreme excellence, And the meaning of the flow of excellence;
Thus, the meaning of non-appropriation, And the meaning of continuity without distinction.
The meaning of being free from defilement and purity, The meaning of manifoldness without distinction,
The meaning of neither increasing nor decreasing, And the meaning of the basis for the four masteries—
These ten meanings exist within the dharmadhātu; They consist of non-defiled ignorance.
In order to remedy these obstacles to be remedied, the ten stages (daśabhūmi) are established.
Furthermore, it should be understood that such ignorance is non-defiled for śrāvakas and others, yet it is defiled for bodhisattvas.
The commentary states:

In order to demonstrate that the perfections (pāramitās), which are subsumed within the causes and results of entering the characteristics of the knowable, can eliminate the obstacles to be abandoned through the paths of seeing and meditation once they have been properly cultivated as appropriate, the distinctions between the stages of cultivation regarding cause and result are explained.

Regarding the ten stages of the bodhisattva: it means that within these stages, the bodhisattvas cultivate clear realization (*abhisamaya*), abandon faults and craving while cultivating the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), and investigate the truths and dependent origination. Whether with effort or without effort regarding the signless (*animitta*), they attain superior eloquence and reach the true consecration (*abhiṣeka*). By eliminating the cognitive and afflictive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa* and *kleśāvaraṇa*), there are thus ten distinct stages within this level of cultivation.
"By means of the ten aspects" refers to the universal [aspects] and so forth.
"The dharma-realm of the objects of knowledge" refers to the dharma-realm as manifested by these ten aspects.

"The presence of the ten types of ignorance as opposing obstacles" means that regarding these ten aspects, there exist ten types of ignorance and ten opposing obstacles that abide as hindrances; in order to sever these obstacles, one cultivates the wisdom of the ten aspects. Through the wisdom of the ten aspects, one attains entry into the stages (*bhūmi*), which are defined as the states of the wisdom of the selflessness of phenomena.

Regarding the meaning of "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*) within the first stage (*bhūmi*): it means that within the first stage all phenomena are empty, and there is not even the slightest phenomenon that is not empty; therefore, it is called "pervasive. By realizing this meaning, one enters the first stage.

Regarding "by way of the most excellent meaning" in the second bhūmi: this principle of emptiness is the most preeminent among all phenomena. Just as it is said that freedom from desire is the most preeminent, by understanding this meaning, one enters the second bhūmi.

Regarding the meaning of "supreme outflow" in the third stage: it means that because the teachings flowing forth from this are most excellent, one does not consider it difficult to seek this well-spoken Dharma even at the cost of body and life; by understanding this meaning, one enters the third stage.

Regarding the meaning of "non-appropriation" in the fourth stage: because attachment to the teachings—such as the sūtras and other dharmas—is severed, one no longer conceives of "mine. One contemplates that these are grasped by neither oneself nor another; by understanding this meaning, one enters the fourth stage.

Regarding the meaning of the non-differentiation of the continuum in the fifth stage: it means that one understands this [continuum] is not like the differentiated continuums of form and so forth; by understanding this meaning, one enters the fifth stage.

Regarding the meaning of "neither defilement nor purity" in the sixth stage: it means knowing that intrinsic nature is fundamentally neither defiled nor pure, because defilement is preceded by the possibility of subsequent purification. By comprehending this meaning, one enters the sixth stage.

Regarding the meaning of the non-differentiation of various phenomena within the seventh stage: while the various phenomena in the sūtras and other scriptures are distinct, this is not so; by understanding this meaning, one enters the seventh stage.

Regarding the meaning of "neither increasing nor decreasing" in the eighth stage: it means that because there is no utility external to phenomena (*dharma*), there is no increase; and because all phenomena are indestructible, there is no decrease. Alternatively, when defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) diminish, this [nature] does not diminish; and when pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*) increase, this does not increase.

Regarding the meaning of mastery over signs as the basis for mastery over the realm (*dharmadhātu*): it refers to the fact that within this very eighth stage, the *dharmadhātu* realized therein constitutes these two masteries. As for the basis of mastery over signs: whenever one desires to manifest any sought-after sign, it can be manifested immediately according to one’s resolute conviction (*adhimukti*); this is called mastery over signs.
Whatever precious lands, such as those of gold, one desires, they can manifest before one according to one’s resolute conviction; this is called mastery over the land (*kṣetra-vaśitā*).
Although this undifferentiated dwelling was also attained in the preceding stages, it was achieved only after applying effort;
in this stage, however, it is accomplished spontaneously and at will, and is therefore termed "mastery."
Having understood this meaning, one enters the eighth stage.

Regarding the meaning of relying on mastery over wisdom in the ninth stage: it means that because one attains the basis for unimpeded eloquence in this stage, one partially realizes the perfection of wisdom (*jñāna-pāramitā*). One is well able to understand the intended meanings of all phenomena without following their literal expressions, and truly brings all sentient beings to maturity so that they may experience the supreme joy of the Dharma. Having understood this meaning, one attains entry into the ninth stage.

Regarding the meaning of the basis for mastery over karma and so forth within the tenth stage: it means that one attains mastery over the activities of body, speech, and mind according to one’s wish; by relying on the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one is able to accomplish whatever actions one undertakes; and because one has attained the power of mastery over the *dhāraṇīs* that retain both words and meanings, one can maintain all the words and meanings proclaimed by the Buddhas without forgetting them.

Furthermore, because one has attained the power of mastery over meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one is able to sustain or relinquish various attainments (*samāpatti*) at will, such that samādhis and samāpattis like the "Space Treasury" (*ākāśagarbha*) manifest before one according to one’s desire.
The dharma-realm realized in the tenth stage is the basis for such masteries as these; by understanding this meaning, one enters the tenth stage.

Thus, ignorance is not an affliction for śrāvakas and others because it is not something to be abandoned; that which is not to be abandoned does not serve as an obstacle to entering the stages that counteract it, nor does it act as a hindrance to their nirvāṇa.

For Bodhisattvas, that which is defiled is that which must be abandoned; and that which is to be abandoned is precisely for the sake of entering the stages (*bhūmi*) that serve as its antidote, because such ignorance acts as an obstacle to the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) sought by Bodhisattvas.
Since one has already attained penetration into the entire dharma-realm upon entering the first stage, for what reason are subsequent distinctions established?
It is because one wishes to demonstrate the manifestation of the various stages that the distinctions of the successive stages are established.

This means that one abides securely in the distinct modes of manifestation of the superior dwelling within the dharma-realm as it has been realized; it does not mean that one merely attains realization and then remains complacent and indifferent.
The Commentary says:
Furthermore, for what reason is the first stage named "Utmost Joy"?
It is because, for the very first time, one attains the supreme merit capable of accomplishing the welfare and benefit of both oneself and others.
Why is the second stage called "Stainless" (vimalā)?
Because it is extremely remote from the stain of transgressing the precepts.
Why is the third stage called "Luminous" (prabhākārī)?
Because it is the basis for non-regressive meditative concentrations and attainments (*samādhi-samāpatti*), and because it is the basis for the great light of the Dharma,
why is the fourth stage called "Blazing Wisdom" (*arciṣmatī*)?
Because all obstacles are incinerated by the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), why is the fifth stage called "Extremely Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjaya*)?

It is because the knowledge of ultimate truth and worldly knowledge are mutually contradictory; this stage is so named because it brings these two difficult-to-unite elements into union and correspondence.
Why is the sixth stage called "Manifestation"?
Because, by relying on the wisdom of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-jñāna*), one is able to bring the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) into manifestation.
For what reason is the seventh stage called "Far-Reaching"?
Because it reaches the ultimate limit of the stage of effortful practice (*prayoga-gati*).
For what reason is the eighth stage called "Immovable"?
Because one cannot be moved by any conceptual signs or by effortful practice,
why is the ninth stage called "Excellent Intelligence" (Sādhumatī)?
It is because of the attainment of the most supreme unimpeded knowledge (pratisaṃvid).
Why is the tenth stage called the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*)?

Because by attaining the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its universal object, it contains within it all *dhāraṇī* gates and *samādhi* gates; it is like a great cloud capable of covering the vast obstructions that are as expansive as space, and because it can bring the *dharmakāya* to full completion.

The commentary states: This statement is made based on the cause for the transformation of the name. It is because, through this, one first attains the supreme capacity to accomplish the welfare of both oneself and others.

That is to say, when a Bodhisattva enters the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they attain the most excellent capacity to accomplish the welfare of self and others; giving rise to extreme joy, they are thus distinguished. When Śrāvakas and others enter the stage of clear realization, they only attain the capacity to accomplish their own welfare and do not give rise to such joy; therefore, that stage is not called the "Ground of Extreme Joy" (*Prāmuditā-bhūmi*).
If it is incompatible with the first stage, it is likewise incompatible with all subsequent stages, because this [first stage] is the precursor.

"By being utterly remote from the defilement of transgressing the precepts" means that because natural morality (*dharmatā-śīla*) is perfected within this stage, one remains remote from all impurities of violating the precepts.

Regarding "that which is based on non-retrogressive meditative concentration and attainment": it means that within this stage, one realizes rarefied samādhi, which can give rise to the light of wisdom that illuminates all phenomena; therefore, it is named "Emission of Light" (Prabhākari).
Having attained them and not losing them is called "non-retrogression. The various dhyāna concentrations are termed *samādhi*, while the various formless absorptions are termed *samāpatti*.
Alternatively, *samādhi* refers to the state of one-pointedness of mind.
Regarding the term "attainment" (*samāpatti*), it refers to the actualization of meditative absorption.

As for being the "basis for the light of the Great Dharma," this means that because one is endowed with meditative concentration in this stage and is free from regression, one attains the light of wisdom regarding the teachings of the Mahāyāna sūtras and other scriptures; since this stage is the causal basis for that [light], it is called "The Radiant" (*Prabhākari*).
Regarding the term "Blazing Wisdom" (Arciṣmatī): it is so called because within this stage there is the flame of wisdom; thus it is named Blazing Wisdom.
Furthermore, all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) are termed "flames," for they burn away all hindrances.
When one dwells extensively in these factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), all afflictions are reduced to ashes.

As for "Extremely Difficult to Conquer" (*sudurjaya*): it is most difficult to conquer. This means that the wisdom of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), whereas worldly knowledge—such as that of scripts, seals, arts, and treatises—is conceptual (*savikalpa*). Since the wisdoms of the ultimate and conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are mutually contradictory, it is difficult to induce them to arise in conjunction with one another. Because this [stage] can harmonize them so that they are no longer contradictory, it is called "Extremely Difficult to Conquer."

Regarding the phrase "manifest before one": it is because the most excellent *prajñā-pāramitā* abiding in the present is manifested. That is to say, within this stage, one realizes and dwells in dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*); by the power of the knowledge of dependent origination, the most excellent *prajñā-pāramitā* abiding in non-conceptuality is brought forth with mastery, whereby one knows that all phenomena are neither defiled nor pure.

Regarding the term "far-reaching practice" (*dūramgamā*), it refers to reaching the very limit of the stage of effortful practice; that is to say, within this ground, all effortful practices are most ultimate. Although one cannot be moved by the characteristics of any phenomena, there is still effort regarding the signless (*animitta*).
Regarding the term "immovable," it means that all signs (*nimitta*) and all conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) are entirely unable to move that mind.
Although in the seventh stage one cannot be moved by any signs because they do not manifest,
one does not yet possess spontaneous mastery because there is still deliberate application (*prayoga*).
In the eighth stage, one proceeds spontaneously (*anābhoga*) without performing preparatory effort (*prayoga*), because it is effortless.
This is called the distinction between the seventh and eighth stages.

Regarding the term "Excellent Intelligence" (*sādhumati*): it refers to having attained the four supreme analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). Since the wisdom of analytical knowledge is the most excellent among all forms of wisdom, and wisdom is itself intelligence, it is therefore called "Excellent Intelligence."
The four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*) are: dharma, meaning, expression, and eloquence.

Through the unimpeded knowledge of dharmas, one spontaneously and thoroughly knows all dharma-terms; through the unimpeded knowledge of meaning, one spontaneously and penetratingly understands all principles; through the unimpeded knowledge of expression, one spontaneously distinguishes all verbal expressions; and through the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence, one spontaneously and appropriately expounds throughout the ten directions according to what is suitable.
On this stage, one first realizes the knowledge of unimpeded analytical insight (*pratisaṃvid*) that was previously unattained; therefore, it is called "Excellent Intelligence" (*Sādhumatī*).

As for the term "Cloud of Dharma" (*Dharmameghā*), it refers to the attainment of the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its collective object; by taking all dharmas, such as the sūtras and so forth, as its collective object, it remains inseparable from *tathatā*.

The cognition that takes the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all these phenomena as its object is like a great cloud; the dharani-doors and samadhi-doors are like pure water. Wisdom can store them within itself, just as a cloud holds water, because it possesses the superior capacity to give rise to them.

Furthermore, just as a great cloud covers and obscures the void, so too does the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its collective object cover and obscure the two obstacles—of afflictions and of knowledge—which are as vast, expansive, and boundless as space.
What is called "concealment" (*paryavasthāna*) has the meaning of obstruction and the meaning of severance.

Furthermore, just as great clouds pour down clear, cool water that fills the void of space, so too does the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its object (*sarvadharma-ālambana-jñāna*) give rise to immeasurable, preeminent virtues, filling the *dharmakāya*, which is the realized and the basis of realization.
The treatise says:
How can the attainment of these various stages be perceived?
It is by means of four kinds of characteristics:
First, the attainment of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), which means attaining deep faith and understanding regarding the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Second, the attainment of correct practice (*samyakpratipatti*), which means attaining the ten types of correct dharmic practices associated with the various stages.
Third is the attainment of thorough penetration, meaning that when one penetrates the dharma-dhātu in the first stage (*bhūmi*), one is able to thoroughly penetrate all stages.
Fourth is the attainment of fulfillment, meaning that one cultivates the various stages until they reach their ultimate consummation.
The commentary states:
Based on the attainment of the various stages (*bhūmi*), it is said that there are four aspects.

First, the attainment of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*): this refers to one who has attained deep faith and understanding regarding the various stages, and who definitively confirms the teachings on those stages as being truly thus.
Second is the attainment of correct practice, which refers to attaining the ten types of correct Dharma-practice associated with the various stages (*bhūmi*), thereby attaining the teachings.

The ten types of Dharma-practice consist of: writing down, making offerings to, giving away, listening to, reading, receiving and upholding, explaining, reciting, reflecting upon, and cultivating the teachings associated with the various stages.

Third, the attainment of thorough penetration: when one thoroughly penetrates the dharma-dhātu at the first stage (*bhūmi*), one is able to thoroughly penetrate all stages universally. This is because, at the very moment of correct penetration in the first stage, one is swiftly able to penetrate all subsequent stages, as they belong to the same category.
As a verse says:
"Just as when the first knot of a bamboo is split, The remaining knots can quickly be split;
Having attained the true wisdom of the first stage, All stages shall be swiftly accomplished."

"Fourth, the attainment of fulfillment refers to those who cultivate the various stages (*bhūmi*) until reaching the ultimate limit; that is, the fulfillment of the fruits within each stage, or the final fulfillment.
The treatise asks:
How can the cultivation of these various stages be perceived?
This refers to the bodhisattvas’ cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā within each stage (bhūmi), which is practiced through five modes.
What are these five? They are:

cultivation by way of synthesis, signless cultivation, effortless cultivation, intense cultivation, and insatiable cultivation. These five modes of cultivation enable bodhisattvas to accomplish five fruits.

That is to say, in every moment of thought, one dissolves all coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*), leaves behind various conceptualizations to experience the joy of the Dharma-garden, and is able to correctly comprehend the great light of the Dharma, which is all-pervasive, immeasurable, and characterized by the absence of limits. One accords with the pure portion, manifests non-conceptualization and the signless, and, in order to bring the Dharmakāya to full completion, is able to correctly appropriate the progressively superior causes.
The commentary states:
Regarding the phrase "in each stage," it is said twice because the stages are not one.
*Śamatha* refers to the meditative concentration that serves as the antidote to all forms of distraction.
Vipaśyanā refers to the wisdom that is able to counteract all inversions.

In each stage (bhūmi), one cultivates these two types [of meditation] by repeatedly practicing through five aspects; these five aspects are namely: the cultivation of accumulation, the cultivation of synthesis, and so forth.

"Cultivation by collecting and synthesizing" refers to collecting all things together into a single aggregate for concise cultivation; likewise, the contemplation of objects such as skeletons and so forth also collects everything into a single aggregate for abbreviated cultivation. To distinguish this from those [other types], it is called "signless cultivation," because one cultivates within the true *dharmadhātu*—which is free from all signs—by eliminating the distinctions between phenomena.

Although there may be cultivation of signlessness that involves effortful application, in order to demonstrate that this cultivation proceeds spontaneously without relying on exertion, it is followed by the explanation of effortless cultivation (*anābhoga-bhāvanā*), because it proceeds spontaneously, free from the application of effort.
Although one practices spontaneously without effort, because the two types—superior and inferior—are not fixed, the fourth stage further describes "intense cultivation.
What is called "intense" refers precisely to increasing excellence.
Even if one practices with great intensity, one may become complacent upon obtaining only slight results, thinking, "I have practiced this much for now; what further use is there?
Therefore, the cultivation of non-complacency is taught last; it is not merely a matter of practicing with intensity through signlessness and effortlessness.
Why is this? One should diligently cultivate [the path] in order to realize the supreme fruit of Buddhahood.

Regarding "dissolving all coarse habitual tendencies (*dausthulya*)": the *ālayavijñāna* is called the basis of coarse habitual tendencies; to destroy that accumulation is what is meant by "dissolving," just as a great medicinal elixir dissolves various masses of disease.
"To leave behind various perceptions and attain the joy of the Dharma-garden" means to abandon perceptions of a self, phenomena, Buddhas, and so forth.

A "garden" (*ārāma*) refers to a place where one may roam and enjoy; "Dharma" refers to the *dharmadhātu*. Because the Dharma is itself the garden, it is called the "Dharma-garden. To take delight therein is called the "joy of the Dharma-garden," and to realize this is called "attaining the joy of the Dharma-garden."
Just as there is a supreme and exquisite garden outside a royal palace where one sports and experiences sublime joy, so too is the *dharmadhātu*.

One who can correctly and thoroughly understand the great light of the Dharma, which is all-pervasive, immeasurable, and characterized by the absence of limits, is said to have correctly penetrated the boundless and measureless characteristics of the ten directions; because it illuminates all conduct, it is called the "light of the Dharma," just as the light of written characters is produced through skillful recitation and study.

Regarding "practicing the signless without conceptualization in accordance with the pure portion": the fruit of Buddhahood in the future is called the "pure portion"; because this [practice] can induce that [fruit], it is termed "in accordance with."
There is no conceptual differentiation, and there is the manifestation of signlessness, such as the Buddha’s white parasol and so forth.

To bring the *dharmakāya* to full completion and to be able to correctly embrace the progressively superior causes is what is called "completion" (*paripūri*) in the tenth stage, and what is called "accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*) in the Buddha stage. The cause that brings about this [state] is most excellent and is thus called the "superior cause" (*viśeṣa-hetu*). Because it is that which has been gathered and accumulated by the preceding causes, it is called "successive" (*uttarottara*).
These five types of cultivation yield five kinds of fruits according to their respective numbers.
The treatise states:
Because they are preeminent, it is said that within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one separately cultivates the ten *pāramitās*.
The six types of *pāramitā* practiced in the first six stages have already been explained as before.

Regarding the four [perfections] practiced in the subsequent four stages: the first is the *upāyakauśalya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means), which refers to dedicating the roots of virtue accumulated through the previous six *pāramitās*, together with all sentient beings, toward the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Second is the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*), which refers to the generation of various subtle and wondrous great aspirations in order to attract and gather the superior conditions for the perfections in the future.

The perfection of the three powers refers to the continuous manifestation of the preceding six perfections through the two powers of analytical investigation (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The four wisdoms are the *pāramitās*, meaning that by means of the preceding six *pāramitās*, one establishes sublime wisdom for the sake of enjoying the dharma-bliss and maturing sentient beings.

Furthermore, it should be understood that these four kinds of pāramitās are subsumed within the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) of the prajñā-pāramitā.
Moreover, throughout all the stages (*bhūmi*), it is not the case that one does not cultivate all the pāramitās.
This Dharma-gate is subsumed within the Pitaka of the Pāramitās.
The commentary states:

Regarding the statement that, due to their predominance, ten distinct types of pāramitās are cultivated within the ten stages—does this not definitively explain the meaning of the distinctions in cultivation?

Since each and every stage (bhūmi) fully cultivates all ten perfections (pāramitā), one should not definitively state that this specific stage cultivates only this specific perfection; for there is no such fault when speaking in terms of predominance.
In this context, only the meaning of "predominant cultivation" is being stated; it does not preclude the cultivation of the others. As the Sūtra says:

"In the first stage, the perfection of giving is most predominant, yet it is not that the other perfections are not cultivated; they are practiced according to one's power and capacity," and so on at length.

Regarding the six types of *pāramitās* cultivated in the first six stages as previously explained: this refers to the cultivation of the six perfections, such as generosity and so forth, within the first six stages beginning with the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā*).

Regarding the four [perfections] cultivated in the latter four stages: this refers to the cultivation of the four *pāramitās*, such as skillful means (*upāya*), within the latter four stages beginning with the Far-Reaching (*dūramgamā*).
As for "skillful means," it means seeking *nirvāṇa* without abandoning *saṃsāra*; this is what is called skillful means.

If one shares the roots of virtue accumulated through the first six pāramitās with all sentient beings, and does not abandon sentient beings out of a desire to benefit them, it should be known that this is precisely not abandoning saṃsāra.

If one dedicates this merit toward seeking unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment for the sake of realizing the unsurpassed Buddha-enlightenment, it should be understood that this is precisely the aspiration for nirvāṇa.

This refers to formulating various subtle and sublime great vows to attract and gather the excellent conditions for the perfections (*pāramitā*) in the future. Seeking the conditions for reaching the other shore in future lives, and for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings as well as swiftly realizing the *nirvāṇa* of Buddhahood, one makes this vow, saying:
"If there are conditions for reaching the other shore in any place, may I be born there in the future."
Such vows as these are immeasurable and boundless; therefore, they are said to be "various.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the two powers of analytical discernment (*cintā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*)," although only two types of power are mentioned here, all other powers are likewise included within them.

This means that the establishment of sublime wisdom—which experiences the dharma-bliss and matures sentient beings—is achieved by means of the first six perfections; furthermore, these six [perfections] are established by means of this wisdom.
That is to say, the various categories such as the calculation of numbers and so forth are called "enjoying the dharma-pleasure.

By means of this sublime wisdom, one correctly understands this generosity, this ethical discipline, this patience, diligence, and so on; according to the Dharma as it has been heard, one benefits all classes of sentient beings—this is called "benefiting sentient beings."

Furthermore, regarding these four kinds of pāramitās being subsumed under the subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna): it means that these four, namely skillful means and so forth as described here, are subsumed under non-conceptual subsequently attained wisdom.
If ten types of pāramitās are established, the sixth, prajñā, is exclusively the fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
If six types of pāramitās are established, the sixth, prajñā, is comprised of two types of wisdom: non-conceptual wisdom and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

Because the four *pāramitās* within subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) are likewise subsumed under the sixth *prajñā*, those dharma-gates that are subsumed within the *Pāramitā-piṭaka*—namely, all the teachings of the Mahāyāna—are called the *Pāramitā-piṭaka*.
