Thus, these dharma-gates of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are subsumed within that *piṭaka*.
Since each and every stage is subsumed within the treasury of all *pāramitās*, it is thereby proven that one cultivates all *pāramitās* throughout all stages.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, for how long must one practice the various stages (bhūmi) before they can be brought to perfection?
There are five types of individuals (pudgala) who require three incalculable great eons (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa).
This means that the individual on the stage of practice through resolute belief (adhimukti-caryā) completes their cultivation after the first incalculable great aeon (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa).

The individual on the stage of pure superior intention (śuddhādhyāśaya-caryā), as well as the individuals on the stages of practice with signs (sanimitta-caryā) and practice without signs (animitta-caryā), complete their cultivation during the sixth and seventh bhūmis after the second incalculable great aeon.
This very person (pudgala) of effortless practice, from this point upward through the tenth stage, completes their cultivation after three incalculable great eons.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"Through the power of pure supremacy, With a firm mind progressing upward,
This is called the Bodhisattva’s initial practice Throughout three incalculable great eons."
The commentary states:

Regarding the five types of *pudgalas* who pass through three incalculable great eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), it should be understood that these five kinds are established solely based on the distinctions within the stages of a single *pudgala*. These are the five, beginning with the "one who practices through resolute belief" (*adhimukti-caryā*) and so forth, as will be explained later.

The practitioner by way of resolute belief (*adhimukti-carita*), though not yet having realized suchness (*tathatā*), diligently cultivates various practices based solely on resolute belief; this person completes their cultivation during the first incalculable great eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

The practitioner of pure superior intention (*viśuddhādhyāśaya*) refers to one who, having attained pure superior intention, diligently cultivates various practices; this is termed "practice with signs" (*sanimitta-caryā*) on the sixth stage and "practice without signs" (*animitta-caryā*) on the seventh stage.
These two types of individuals complete their cultivation during the second incalculable great eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
From this point up to the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), this very practice is renamed "effortless conduct" (*anābhoga-caryā*), and they complete its cultivation during the third incalculable great eon.
In the eighth stage, effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) is not yet fully perfected; it is only in the ninth and tenth stages that this practice attains full perfection.

This is but a single *pudgala*, yet through its association with different states, it is differentiated into five types, just as those such as the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) have undergone the cycle of birth and death since beginningless time.
Regarding the question of when one should say that the initial cultivation of the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) begins, this verse is spoken in order to answer it.
"The power of pure supremacy" means that the power of the roots of virtue (*kuśala-mūla*) is called the power of purity; this refers to one who possesses such power of the roots of virtue.

If the power of great vows is termed "predominant power," this implies that one who possesses the power of great vows has the power of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) by which they can subdue that which is to be countered,
and possesses the power of great vows by which they constantly encounter spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Regarding those whose firm resolve advances: even if they encounter evil friends who employ skillful means to destroy it, they never abandon the mind of great bodhicitta.
The wholesome dharmas they cultivate in the present and future lives increase ever more and never diminish.

Thus, when one possesses the power of roots of goodness and the power of great vows, and the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*) is firm and non-regressive; when the wholesome dharmas cultivated increase in every thought-moment without giving rise to complacency, and one merely accords with what was previously practiced—this is called the initial stage of practicing throughout the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
7. The Section on the Training in Higher Ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*). The Commentary on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, Section Seven: The Training in Higher Ethics. The treatise states:
Thus, the distinctions in the cultivation of cause and effect have already been explained.
In this context, how is the excellence of superior ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*) to be understood?
It is as explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* within the section on the formal undertaking of the bodhisattva vows (*bodhisattvasaṃvara*).
Furthermore, it should be known that this excellence is characterized by four types of distinction.

First, by way of distinction and excellence; second, by way of the distinction and excellence of common and uncommon precepts; third, by way of the excellence of vastness; and fourth, by way of the excellence of profundity.
The commentary states:
It is called the training in higher ethics because one trains by relying upon higher ethics.
As it is explained in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* regarding the formal reception of the bodhisattva vows, that is, as it is extensively explained in the chapter on the *Śīlapāramitā*.
Furthermore, it should be understood that this [bodhisattva precept] is distinguished by four kinds of excellence, which will be explained in detail later.
The treatise states:
Regarding the excellence of differentiation, the bodhisattva precepts consist of three distinct categories:
First, the ethical discipline of restraint; second, the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas; and third, the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings.

Among these, the ethical discipline of restraint should be understood as having the sense of establishing the other two disciplines; the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas should be understood as having the sense of establishing the cultivation and accumulation of all Buddha-dharmas; and the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings should be understood as having the sense of establishing the maturation of all sentient beings.
The commentary states:

Regarding "distinctive excellence," this refers to the fact that bodhisattvas possess three types of ethical discipline (*śīla*): the ethical discipline of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*). Since those of the Śrāvaka vehicle and others possess only the single type of restraint-ethical-discipline, the bodhisattva is therefore superior to them.
The morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*) refers to correctly undertaking the avoidance of all categories of evil and unwholesome dharmas.

The morality of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*) refers to correctly cultivating and accumulating all Buddha-dharmas, such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).

The precept of benefiting sentient beings means that, disregarding one's own happiness, one leads others—according to their capacities—into the three vehicles so that they may abandon the suffering of birth and death and realize the bliss of nirvana.

Regarding the statement that "the discipline of restraint (saṃvara-śīla) should be understood as the basis for the establishment of the two types of discipline," this is because it is the cause of those two disciplines.

That is to say, if one guards the body, speech, and mind, one is able to correctly cultivate and accumulate all pure Buddha-dharmas, and is also able to bring all sentient beings to maturity so that they enter the three vehicles; otherwise, this is not the case.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the distinction between common and uncommon training rules, it means that because Bodhisattvas do not manifest any natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), they share [these rules] with Śrāvakas; however, because they do manifest certain similar prohibited transgressions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), they differ from them.
Regarding these training rules, there are those that a śrāvaka violates while a bodhisattva does not, and those that a bodhisattva violates while a śrāvaka does not.

A bodhisattva possesses the precepts of body, speech, and mind, whereas a śrāvaka possesses only the two precepts of body and speech; therefore, a bodhisattva may also commit violations of the mind, which is not the case for śrāvakas.

In brief, all faultless actions of body, speech, and mind that benefit sentient beings, a bodhisattva should practice and train in them all; it should be understood that this is what is called the distinction between common and uncommon excellence.
The commentary states:

Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and so forth, when produced by greed and other such afflictions, are termed natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*); cutting living grass and the like, which are not produced by greed and other such afflictions, are termed prohibitional offenses (*prajñapti-sāvadya*).
Among these, a bodhisattva should practice everything that is observed to be beneficial and free from fault, whereas a śrāvaka does not.

Furthermore, there are instances where the minds of bodhisattvas commit transgressions that do not apply to śrāvakas; specifically, when they internally give rise to various unwholesome discursive thoughts such as desire, malice, and harm, yet do not proceed to initiate the two types of karma of body and speech.

All blameless actions of body, speech, and mind that benefit sentient beings refers to those capable of bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings, without giving rise to afflictions such as greed in oneself or others.
All such things should be cultivated by Bodhisattvas. The treatise says:

Regarding "vast and sublime," it is further due to four kinds of vastness: first, because of the vastness of various immeasurable training rules (*śikṣāpada*); second, because of the vastness of encompassing immeasurable merit; third, because of the vastness of the intention (*āśaya*) to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; and fourth, because of the vastness of establishing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The commentary states:

Regarding the vastness of the various and immeasurable trainings, this refers to the ethical discipline (*śīla*) in which bodhisattvas train; it is vast because its categories and types are immeasurably differentiated.
Regarding "embracing immeasurable and vast merit": this means that this ethical discipline (*śīla*) can gather immeasurable provisions of merit, and is therefore vast.

Regarding "embracing the vast intention for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings": this means that this ethical discipline gathers all sentient beings, providing them with the intention to benefit them through the abandonment of evil and the adoption of good—whether as cause or fruit—in both this life and future lives, and in both mundane and supramundane realms; it is therefore vast.
Regarding the establishment of the vastness of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment: it is because this ethical discipline (*śīla*) establishes great enlightenment that it is vast.
Since the śrāvakas and others do not possess such a quality, it is therefore superior.
The Commentary states:

Regarding "profound and extraordinary," this refers to how bodhisattvas, through these types of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), may perform the ten kinds of actions such as taking life without incurring any fault, thereby generating immeasurable merit and swiftly realizing unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that the manifestation of the two types of karma—physical and vocal—through the transformative bodies of Bodhisattvas is also profound ethical discipline (*śīla*).
For this reason, they may act as kings, manifesting various actions that afflict sentient beings in order to establish those beings within the Vinaya.

Furthermore, he manifests various *jātaka* tales, demonstrating the practice of afflicting other sentient beings while actually gathering them in; first causing their minds to give rise to deep pure faith, and subsequently bringing them to full maturity.
This is called the profound and supreme ethical discipline (*śīla*) in which bodhisattvas train.
The commentary explains:
"By means of these types of skillful means" refers to the excellent post-attainment wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-prajñā*) of bodhisattvas that is associated with compassion and the vow.

Regarding the statement that one commits the ten types of actions, such as killing, without incurring sin: this refers to those who delight in wholesome dharmas and loathe unwholesome ones; their perception of these [unwholesome states] as being of a false nature is termed the "last three. Because they rely upon this [insight], they may perform the seven [actions] beginning with killing without incurring sin, instead generating immeasurable merit and swiftly realizing bodhi.
Alternatively, while practicing the first seven [unwholesome paths], one does not give rise to the latter three; thus, they are generally said to be ten.

Or, having already suppressed and eliminated them, one may temporarily arouse them in the mind merely to test one's own power; because this cannot summon suffering, there is no fault, and because it can assist the Path, it generates immeasurable merit.

Regarding the manifestation of the two types of karma—physical and vocal—of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*): this refers to the initiation of these two types of karma based upon the transformation body; or, based upon the actual body (*dharmakāya*), the initiation of both physical and vocal karma by means of a transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*). Mental karma, being formless, cannot be transformed.
Alternatively, although instances of greed, hatred, and so forth may currently exist, they are not mentioned because they do not serve a great purpose or benefit for converting sentient beings.

Regarding "establishing sentient beings within the Vinaya," this refers to acting as a king who establishes various laws and regulations, demonstrating the practice of coercion and affliction in order to cause them to abide therein.
Alternatively, because all virtues can extinguish manifold evils, or because Great Nirvāṇa extinguishes and removes birth and death, it is called *vinaya*.

Furthermore, regarding the manifestation of various *jātaka* (birth-story) events: these refer to the *jātaka* deeds of the bodhisattvas manifested by the transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*), or to those who, having already attained Buddhahood long ago, again manifest the performance of various *jātaka* deeds to benefit sentient beings and cause them to train as bodhisattvas; therefore, it is subsequently stated that this is called the *śīla* (ethical discipline) in which a bodhisattva trains.
The Commentary states:
Based on these brief explanations of the four kinds of excellence, one should know that the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) is the most excellent.
One should further understand that there are immeasurable distinctions among these differentiated bodhisattva training rules (*śikṣāpada*), as taught in the *Vinayakauśalya Vaipulya Sūtra*.
The commentary states:
Herein, four kinds of distinctive characteristics are briefly explained; in the Vinayakṣudraka-sūtra, they are explained extensively, with further immeasurable distinctions.
This sūtra is subsumed within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; therefore, it is called Vaipulya.
*Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, Scroll Seven;
*Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, Scroll Eight.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asvabhāva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang under imperial decree.
Section Eight: The Training in Higher Mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*). The treatise states:
Thus has the excellence of higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*) been explained.

How is the excellence of higher mind (*adhicitta*) to be understood? Briefly, it should be known through six types of distinctions: first, by the distinction of the object (*ālambana*); second, by the distinction of variety (*nānātva*); third, by the distinction of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*); fourth, by the distinction of capability (*karmanya*); fifth, by the distinction of induction (*ākṣepa*); and sixth, by the distinction of activity (*karma*).
The commentary states:
Just as the higher training in ethical discipline (*adhiśīla*) differs from that of the śrāvakas, so too should the higher training in mind (*adhicitta*) differ; therefore, this question is raised.
The sixfold distinction provides a brief answer to this question, which will be explained in detail later.
The treatise states:
Regarding the distinction of the object of focus, it means that the Mahāyāna Dharma serves as the object of focus.
The commentary explains:

The Mahāyāna Dharma refers to all the profound and vast teachings contained within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka; since these are certainly not objects that can be perceived by Śrāvakas and others, it is therefore preeminent.
The Commentary states:

Regarding "various distinctions," this refers to the various and immeasurable samādhis, such as the Mahāyāna-āloka (Light of the Great Vehicle), the Saṃbhāra-rāja-samādhi (King of the Accumulation of Merit Samādhi), the Bhadrapāla (Worthy Protector), and the Vīryapāramitā-caryā (Heroic Practice) samādhis. Thus they are manifold and infinite.
The commentary states:

The various distinctions among the samādhis attained by Bodhisattvas are immeasurable; here, they are briefly explained by way of their preeminent representatives. Even the names of these have not been heard by others, such as those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, let alone being able to attain them.
The Commentary states:

Regarding the distinction of the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), it refers to the wisdom that takes the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena as its object; by means of the principle of "using one wedge to extract another," it eliminates all coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the obstructions within the *ālayavijñāna*.
The commentary states:

The suchness that is the object of non-conceptual wisdom is manifested as the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; therefore, this wisdom is called "that which takes the common characteristic as its object."
Concentration can indeed give rise to this wisdom that acts as an antidote, and it is therefore also called an "antidote.
Because the Noble Path is subtle, it is like a fine wedge;
because the seeds of that which is to be countered are coarse and heavy by nature, they are like a coarse wedge.
The Treatise says:
Regarding the distinction of capability, it refers to abiding in the bliss of meditative concentration (dhyāna) and taking birth according to one's own wish.
The Explanation says:

By virtue of this meditative concentration, its nature is disciplined and pliant; thus, wherever one wishes to benefit sentient beings, one proceeds to take birth there without regressing from that meditative concentration.
Such a thing does not exist within the Śrāvaka-yāna; therefore, it is preeminent.
The treatise states:
Regarding the distinction of "inducing," it means being able to induce unimpeded supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) throughout all worlds.
The commentary states:
By means of this power of meditative concentration, one brings forth various unimpeded supernormal powers throughout all worlds.
The treatise says:

Regarding the distinction of activity: it refers to the ability to cause trembling, blazing, pervasion, manifestation, transformation, coming and going, contraction and expansion; causing all forms and images to enter into one’s own body; appearing or disappearing according to the beings one encounters; exercising mastery over actions to subdue the supernatural powers of others; bestowing eloquence, mindfulness, and bliss, and emitting great radiance—because such great supernormal powers are thus elicited.
The commentary states:
By means of this power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are manifested.
"Manifest" refers to making things appear; "hidden" refers to concealing them.
Mastery over actions means, for example, transforming the Māra King into the body of a Buddha and so forth.
Subduing the supernatural powers of others means being able to eclipse and surpass their supernormal faculties.
Bestowing eloquence upon those who lack it, and bestowing mindfulness and joy upon those who lack them.

In order to summon bodhisattvas dwelling afar in other regions who have manifested great radiance and elicited such supernormal powers, he drew forth the various supernormal powers previously described.
Such categories as these do not exist among the śrāvakas and others; therefore, it is preeminent.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, it is able to induce and encompass the ten difficult practices that are hard to perform.
The ten difficult practices are: first, the difficult practice of self-vow, because one vows to undertake the aspiration for unsurpassed bodhi;
second, the difficult practice of non-retrogression, because the manifold sufferings of birth and death cannot cause one to retreat.
Third is the difficult practice of non-abandonment, because one does not forsake sentient beings even though they engage in perverse conduct.
Fourth is the difficult practice of presence, because one manifests all manner of beneficial actions toward those sentient beings who act as enemies.
Fifth is the difficult practice of non-defilement, because although one is born in the world, one is not defiled by worldly dharmas.
Sixth is the difficult practice of resolute conviction, because although one has not yet fully realized the Mahāyāna, one gives rise to faith and understanding toward all that is vast and profound.
Seventh is the difficult practice of thorough penetration, because it possesses the ability to thoroughly penetrate the selflessness of persons and phenomena.
Eighth is the difficult practice of subsequent realization, because it is able to subsequently realize the profound and secret expressions spoken by the Tathāgatas.
Ninth is the difficult practice of non-separation and non-defilement, because one does not abandon cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) yet remains undefiled by it.

Tenth is the difficult practice of application (*prayoga*), because one is able to cultivate the abiding in liberation from all obstacles of all Buddhas, and until the end of cyclic existence, acts spontaneously and constantly for the sake of all benefits and welfare of all sentient beings.
The commentary states:
As it is said that bodhisattvas practice various difficult deeds, all such difficult deeds are manifested through ten aspects.

Regarding the difficult deed of self-vow, which consists of vowing to accept the aspiration for unsurpassed enlightenment: because one disregards one's own happiness and vows to bring benefit to all sentient beings, this is exceedingly difficult.

Regarding "the difficult practice of non-retrogression," which cannot be thwarted by the manifold sufferings of birth and death: because one dwells for a long time within birth and death, being unable to be turned back by such hardships as wind and cold, it is exceedingly difficult.

The difficult practice of not turning one's back on any sentient being, even when they act with perverse conduct, consists in not abandoning them; for it is exceedingly difficult to benefit those such as one’s own parents who commit evil deeds, or even those who, in useless play, seek out one’s eyes or trample upon one’s feet, without regarding their faults.
Regarding "performing all beneficial deeds toward hostile sentient beings in their very presence": although there may be a grave enemy, to manifest benefit toward them is exceedingly difficult.

Regarding "the difficult practice of non-attachment," which refers to being born in the world without being defiled by worldly dharmas: to constantly dwell in the world while remaining untainted by the eight worldly concerns, such as gain and loss, is exceedingly difficult.

Regarding "the difficult practice of resolute belief" (*adhimukti-duṣkaracaryā*) and so forth: although one has not yet fully realized subtle meanings or supreme spiritual powers, to have profound faith and understanding nonetheless is extremely difficult.

Regarding "penetrating the difficult practices" and so forth: it means that one is able to fully penetrate the single meaning of penetration, clear realization, and perfect awakening; for it is extremely difficult to realize that the nature of all phenomena and the *pudgala*—which are conceptually imputed—do not exist at all.

Regarding "the difficult practice of conforming to awakening" and so forth: it is extremely difficult to abandon the understanding of the literal meaning of the Buddha’s secret words and instead awaken to their non-literal meaning.
Regarding "the difficult practice of not being separated from and not being defiled by [saṃsāra]," it is extremely difficult because one does not abandon saṃsāra yet remains undefiled by its faults.

Regarding "the difficult practice of application," although all afflictive obstructions and cognitive obstructions have already been severed and one has already attained liberation, one constantly manifests before others to perform all manner of deeds for the benefit of sentient beings; to joyfully cultivate such a practice without rest until the end of the future is extremely difficult.
The Treatise says:
Furthermore, regarding the "difficult practice of conforming to awakening," what are those secret words of the Buddha that those bodhisattvas are able to conform to and fully comprehend?
This refers to what is stated in the sūtras.
The commentary states:
The meaning of the eighth difficult practice has not yet been fully understood; therefore, it must be explained again.
The treatise says:
How is it that a bodhisattva is able to practice giving?
Although a bodhisattva may have nothing whatsoever to give, they extensively practice giving throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions.
How does a bodhisattva delight in the practice of giving?
If a bodhisattva has no desire for any kind of gift whatsoever,
how can a bodhisattva develop deep faith and understanding regarding the act of giving?
If bodhisattvas practice giving without faith in the Tathāgata,
how can they be said to exert themselves in the practice of generosity?
If bodhisattvas do not exert themselves in the act of giving, [they cannot be called practitioners].
How does a bodhisattva delight in giving?
If a bodhisattva does not give even a small amount for even a brief moment, how can their giving be vast?
How does a bodhisattva’s giving become extensive?
If bodhisattvas are free from the notion of "sorrow" (śalya) regarding giving,
how is it that their giving is pure?
It is when bodhisattvas have completely abandoned stinginess.
How is it that a bodhisattva’s giving is ultimate?
If all bodhisattvas do not abide in the ultimate,
how is it that a bodhisattva’s giving is sovereign?
If bodhisattvas do not exercise mastery over their acts of giving,
how can the giving of a bodhisattva be inexhaustible?
If bodhisattvas do not abide in inexhaustibility, [how can it be so?]
Just as it is with generosity, so it should be understood accordingly for the others, beginning with ethical discipline and ending with wisdom.
The commentary explains:

"If bodhisattvas do not have even the slightest thing to give," etc., means that bodhisattvas incorporate all sentient beings into their own being because they have realized the equality of self and other.
When he practices giving, it is the giving of a bodhisattva; therefore, there is not even the slightest gift that can be called "practicing giving.
Furthermore, because he gives all his possessions to all beings, it is said that there is nothing whatsoever that is not given.
Furthermore, since the gift, the giver, and the recipient are all unapprehendable, the three spheres are pure; therefore, it is said that "there is not the slightest thing given.
If a bodhisattva has no desire or inclination toward any form of giving whatsoever, this negation signifies the meaning of non-attachment.

When those who come seeking alms say, "You should give to me; you should give to me first," they are entirely devoid of desire for such things; rather, desiring only to dwell in the object of focus that is nirvāṇa, they practice the giving of gifts.

If there are bodhisattvas who practice giving without relying on faith in the Tathāgata, it means they bestow gifts having personally realized and gained confidence in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), rather than relying solely on the faith of others.

If bodhisattvas do not exert personal effort regarding generosity, it means that because they are able to practice giving spontaneously and constantly, they have no need for self-exertion; rather, they are able to exert others by exhorting them to give.
If bodhisattvas do not have even a moment’s lack of giving, this is the meaning of "giving at all times" and "giving everything.

If bodhisattvas, in the act of giving, are free from the notion of *sāra* (solidity), the term *sāra* here explicitly refers to firmness and solidity, while implicitly it signifies dispersion; now, taking the implicit meaning, they are free from the notion of dispersion. This is the meaning of practicing giving while the mind abides in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

If bodhisattvas are *udbhūta-mātsarya*, the term *udbhūta* (殟波陀) explicitly refers to arising (*utpāda*) while implicitly signifying uprooting (*uddharaṇa*). Here, taking the implicit meaning, they practice giving by uprooting the root of stinginess.
If bodhisattvas do not abide in the ultimate, they differ from the śrāvakas who are exclusively intent on tranquility and who abide in the ultimate nirvana without remainder.
If bodhisattvas lack mastery over generosity, it means that the obstacles to be remedied by generosity—such as stinginess—lack mastery over them.
If bodhisattvas do not abide in the inexhaustible, it means that although they have attained the perfect, inexhaustible, supreme, and ultimate fruit of Buddhahood, they do not remain settled therein.
What is it that initiates their emanations?
One constantly practices giving for the benefit of others.
Just as it is with generosity, so it should be understood for the other perfections up to ethical discipline; this analogy applies to the remaining five.
As the Sūtra says:
How is it that a bodhisattva is able to be fully endowed with ethical discipline (*śīla*)?

If a bodhisattva does not guard even minor precepts—because they perceive the equality of self and others—then the protection of pure discipline by others is itself their own fulfillment of ethical discipline.
The treatise says:
How can one kill? It is by severing the cycle of birth and death through which sentient beings transmigrate.
What is taking what is not given?
It is when sentient beings take things for themselves naturally, even though no one has given them.
What is sexual misconduct?
If one understands that all sensual desires are false and practices accordingly,
how could one speak falsely? If one can declare falsehood to be falsehood within falsehood itself.
What is meant by being "endowed with *śūnyatā*"?
It is if one can constantly abide in the most excellent dwelling of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vihāra*).
What is meant by a *pārṣada*?
If one is well-established in the perfection of that which is to be known,
what is frivolous speech?
It is the correct teaching of the various categories and distinctions of the Dharma.
How can one be subject to desire?
If one repeatedly seeks to personally realize unsurpassed meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
How can one be subject to hatred?
If one is able to correctly loathe and destroy all afflictions within the mind,
how could one hold wrong views? If one perceives,
in accordance with reality, the pervasive nature of perversion in all places, [one is established in right view].
The commentary states:
Regarding the passage in the sūtra where it says, "O Bhikṣu, 'I' am the one who kills," and so forth, this section clarifies the underlying intention of that statement.
If one cuts off the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra) for sentient beings, "cutting off" carries the meaning of "killing," which corresponds to the question at hand.
"Without a giver, one naturally takes up [the practice]" means that there is no seeking from others, but rather the sense of benefiting oneself through self-restraint.

If, regarding various desires, one understands them to be erroneous and practices correctly, this refers to knowing as it truly is that both objective desires and conceptualized desires are merely perverse disturbances.
As a verse says: The Buddha taught that greed, anger, and delusion All arise from conceptual discrimination;
Purity, impurity, and inversion— These, too, are born of conditions.
The inversions of purity and impurity exist only as conditions;
since their intrinsic nature is entirely non-existent, desire is not real.
If one can speak of the false as being false, then speaking of the false as false is called "false speech."
As it is said in a verse:
"All phenomena are false; The World-Honored One has spoken of them as they truly are.
Among all false phenomena, Conditioned formations are the most false."

If one is able to constantly abide in the most excellent dwelling of emptiness, then according to the principles of worldly linguistic interpretation, one answers the aforementioned question with the word *goṣṇī*.
This term *goṣṇī* explicitly refers to divisive speech (*paiśunya*), while implicitly it signifies the ever-superior emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

The syllable *gu* expresses the meaning of "superior" (*paramārtha*), *śu* expresses the meaning of "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*), and *ni* expresses the meaning of "permanence" (*nitya*). Here, we take the esoteric meaning so that the question and answer correspond;
it is not so in the exoteric sense. The same principle applies to the etymological analysis of terms such as *pāruṣya*.

Regarding this term *pāruṣya*, its manifest meaning is "harsh speech," while its hidden meaning refers to "abiding on the other shore. Here, the hidden meaning is taken; therefore, it is said that one who is well-established in the knowable other shore.
The "other shore" of all that is to be known is omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); because the Buddha is able to dwell perfectly within it, he is called a *pāruṣi*.
If one were to correctly explain the distinctions among the categories of the Dharma, this would clarify the meaning of the term *prapañca*, which is easily understood.

If there are those who repeatedly desire to personally realize the unsurpassed meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), then according to the principles of etymological interpretation as explained above, all meditative concentrations existing within the bodies of the Buddhas are called "unsurpassed."
If one is able to correctly loathe and harm all afflictions within the mind, this "loathing and harming" means that they have already been extinguished and severed.
If one perceives everywhere the pervasive nature of falsity as it truly is, this refers to seeing that all false conceptualizations are by nature delusive and disordered.
The treatise says:
Regarding "the profound Buddha-dharma," what is meant by "profound Buddha-dharma"?
This point should now be explained:
That is to say, the eternally abiding dharma is the Buddha-dharma, because its *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding.
Furthermore, the dharma of cessation is the Buddha-dharma, because all hindrances are forever ceased and extinguished.
Furthermore, the phenomena of arising are the qualities of all Buddhas, because they manifest arising through the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body).
Furthermore, the phenomena of attainment are the qualities of all Buddhas, because the eighty-four thousand types of conduct of sentient beings and their respective remedies are all attainable.
Furthermore, the dharma of greed is a Buddha-dharma, because one vows to embrace sentient beings possessed of greed as one's own body.
Furthermore, the dharma of hatred is a Buddha-dharma; furthermore, the dharma of delusion is a Buddha-dharma; and it should be known that the dharmas of ordinary beings are likewise Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, the quality of being unstained is a Buddha-dharma, because it fulfills true suchness (*tathatā*) and cannot be defiled by any obscurations or impurities.
Furthermore, the quality of being untainted is a Buddha-dharma, because although one is born into the world, no worldly dharmas can defile it.
Therefore, it is called the "profound Buddha-dharma.
The commentary asks:
Regarding the profound Buddha-dharma as taught in the sūtras, what is its meaning?
It is said in other sūtras: "If a dharma is permanent, it is a Buddha-dharma," and so on at length, up to: "Furthermore, if a dharma is undefiled, it is a Buddha-dharma.
The underlying intention (*saṃdhi*) herein shall now be revealed.

Because its *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding, the *dharmakāya* is characterized by the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*); it is the eternally abiding *tathatā* free from all obstacles, for it is without change or alteration.
Alternatively, there is the supreme, wondrous wisdom that is stainless, unimpeded, and non-retributional, like that of the formless realm because it is untainted (*anāsrava*).
This too is subsumed within the eternally abiding *dharmakāya*, for it is without differentiation and cannot be produced by karma or afflictions.

Regarding the statement that "the eighty-four thousand types of conduct of sentient beings and their respective remedies can all be found": this is because eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*) serve as remedies for the conduct of sentient beings who possess greed, hatred, delusion, or an equal proportion of these; thus, there are twenty-one thousand of each of the four types.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the dharma of non-defilement is the Buddha-dharma": it refers to the perfectly pure *tathatā* (suchness), because no obscurations or defilements can stain it.
The remaining meanings are easy to understand and need not be explained further.
What is the fruit of the Buddha’s teaching such secret words?
It is that it enables the speaker to be easily established [in the teaching], because by summarizing the meaning, it is easy to explain it to others.
Precisely because of this cause, it enables listeners to easily receive and uphold [the teaching];
because they uphold the teaching, their provisions are easily fulfilled;
and because their provisions are fulfilled, they easily penetrate the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Because one attains the purity of faith in the Buddha by realizing the Great Self;
the same applies to the Dharma and the Saṅgha, as they are likewise supreme.

By means of this, one realizes dwelling in happiness in the present life and, through that realization, enters the ranks of the wise in the determination of doctrinal discussions before learned assemblies. It is for these ten benefits that the secret words were spoken.
Within the Śrāvakayāna, there are also statements of intentional terminology (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*) regarding the killing of one’s parents and so forth; the ten benefits are likewise [to be understood].
The treatise states:

Furthermore, because it can induce the cultivation of the perfections (*pāramitā*), the maturation of sentient beings, and the purification of Buddha-fields—these being the qualities of a Buddha—it should be known that this is also a specific activity of the bodhisattva’s meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The commentary states: Regarding the various *samādhis* attained by Bodhisattvas, there are furthermore four kinds of distinctions in their functional activities (*karmakriyā*). These are: (1) by relying on these concentrations, they are able to cultivate all the *pāramitās*; (2) they bring all classes of sentient beings to maturity, employing skillful means such as supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) to lead them into the True Dharma; (3) they are able to purify Buddha-fields, manifesting gold and other precious substances according to their wishes; and (4) they are able to correctly cultivate and accumulate all the Buddha-dharmas, such as the powers (*bala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).

Apart from the aforementioned samādhi, one cannot accomplish the four types of activities—such as the cultivation and accumulation [of merit] and the attainment of the perfections—as is the case with the śrāvakas and others.
Chapter Nine: The Section on Higher Training in Wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*) The *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* states:
Having thus explained the excellence of higher training in mind (*adhicitta*), how is the excellence of higher training in wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) to be understood?

That is to say, non-conceptual wisdom—whether by way of its intrinsic nature, its basis, its causal conditions, its object of focus, its mode of activity, its sustenance, its companions, its maturation, its outflow, its departure, its ultimate attainment, its benefits of preparatory application and subsequent attainment, its distinctions, its analogies for non-conceptual and subsequent attainment, or its effortless performance of tasks—one should know that this profound non-conceptual wisdom is called the excellence of superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā-viśeṣa*).
The commentary states:

Since the mind is already in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and is thus able to know things as they truly are, would it not be the case that the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*) is taught immediately following meditative absorption?
If the acquisition of that clear knowledge (*vidyā*) is itself designated as "training," then there should be no distinction between wisdom (*prajñā*) and training (*śikṣā*).
If it is as you say, then according to the interpretation of "relying on the same basis," it means that superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*) itself is the training (*śikṣā*).

If that were so, there would be no sense of "relying" here—that is, training would not arise by relying on a wisdom other [than itself]; therefore, it is called the training in superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).

As with the two preceding trainings, one trains by relying on ethical discipline and by relying on meditative concentration; it is not that one trains here by relying on wisdom, because wisdom itself is the training.

It should be stated thus: the wisdom of application relies on the fundamental training, the fundamental wisdom relies on the subsequently attained wisdom, and the subsequently attained wisdom initiates cultivation by relying on the two types of uninterrupted [wisdom].
What is called the training in higher wisdom? It is non-conceptual gnosis (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Within this context, its essential nature is explained first, and its profound and extensive aspects are explained last.
The treatise states:
Herein, non-conceptual wisdom has as its intrinsic nature the departure from five kinds of characteristics:

first, it is free from the absence of mental attention; second, it is free from the stage characterized by vitarka and vicāra; third, it is free from the tranquility of the cessation of perception and feeling; fourth, it is free from the intrinsic nature of form; and fifth, it is free from conceptual construction regarding the true meaning.
One should know that being free from these five characteristics is what is called non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The commentary states:

It is said to be "free from the five characteristics" by way of describing the intrinsic nature of wisdom; this is explained through the method of negation (*paryudāsa*), because it cannot be expressed through the method of affirmation (*vidhi*).

By eliminating the gateways of conceptual discrimination, the characteristics of non-conceptual wisdom can be understood; if it were different from this wisdom, there would necessarily be conceptual discrimination.
What kind of discrimination?
This will be explained extensively below.

Regarding "absence of mental attention" and so forth: if absence of mental attention were non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), then states such as deep sleep or intoxication, in which no mental attention is exercised, would have to constitute non-conceptual wisdom. However, this cannot be admitted, because one would then attain non-erroneousness without effort.

If that which transcends the stages of vitarka and vicāra were non-conceptual wisdom, then all ordinary beings and śrāvakas in the stages from the second dhyāna upward would possess non-conceptual wisdom; however, they do not possess such non-conceptual wisdom.

If one considers the cessation of ideation to be non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), the essential nature and characteristics of this wisdom are difficult to establish; for within states such as the attainment of non-ideation, there are no mental factors apart from the mind itself. As previously stated, it is said that those states are "mindless" because the mental consciousness has ceased.

If this non-conceptual wisdom were to be [defined] according to its own nature, it could not be established as non-conceptual wisdom, because it would be like derived matter produced from the primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

If one were to conceive of this non-conceptual wisdom through the conceptualization of characteristics distinct from the true meaning, this wisdom would not achieve the state of being non-conceptual; for by conceptualizing characteristics distinct from the true meaning and asserting, "This is the truth," while claiming it is non-conceptual, it is in fact possessed of conceptualization.
The Commentary states:
Within this presentation of the characteristics established for non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), further verses are spoken.
The Explanation states:
Based on the characteristics briefly established for non-conceptual wisdom as previously explained, the following verses are presented in sequence to provide a detailed exposition.
The first verse is spoken in order to reveal its essential nature.
The treatise says:
The essential nature of all bodhisattvas is non-conceptual wisdom, which is far removed from five kinds of characteristics and does not falsely conceptualize reality as being different [from itself].
The commentary states:
In this verse, the first three lines negate five types of characteristics to expediently reveal non-conceptual wisdom, while the fourth line correctly explains its intrinsic nature.

"Not conceptualizing otherwise regarding the truth" means that one does not conceptually construct the true meaning as being something other than its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); there is no distinction between the intrinsic nature and the essential body (*svabhāva*), just as it is said that a ring, a bracelet, and gold have gold as their essential body.
The next verse explains the basis of wisdom.
The treatise says:
"The basis of all bodhisattvas is not mind, yet it is mind."
"This non-conceptual wisdom is not of the nature of mental deliberation.
The commentary explains:

Since wisdom is a mental factor (*caitasika*), it must depend upon the mind. It is unreasonable for that which depends upon the mind to be non-conceptual, because the term "mind" (*citta*) has the characteristic of deliberation (*manana*).
If it were based on what is not mind, such as various forms (*rūpa*), it could not constitute wisdom (*jñāna*).
To resolve these two simultaneous faults, a half-verse is spoken:
"That which is not of the nature of the object of thought" means that the basis of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is not mind, because it is not an object of thought.
Nor is it that which is not of the nature of mind (*citta*) as its support, because it belongs to the category of mind.
It is called "of the nature of mind" because it is induced by the power of repeated cultivation, taking the mind as its cause, and thus attains this state.
This demonstrates that the mind which is the basis of wisdom transcends all conceptualization and discrimination.
Next, there is one verse that reveals the causes and conditions of wisdom.
The treatise says:
The causes and conditions for all bodhisattvas consist of what is called the permeation of hearing,
non-conceptual wisdom, and correct mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*). Commentary:
The meaning of "causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*) and "efficient causal condition" (*kāraṇa-hetu-pratyaya*) is identical.
As for what is called "the perfuming of verbal hearing" (*śruta-vāsanā*): it is so named because there exists the sound of the Mahāyāna teachings from others; hence, it is called "with words."
"Listening" (*śruta*) refers to hearing; it is this and nothing else. The specific functional capacity induced by this [hearing] is termed "perfuming" (*vāsanā*).

Furthermore, regarding "appropriate mental attention" (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), this refers to the mental discourse produced with that [listening] as its cause. It is called "appropriate" because it accords with the purification of reality; for cognition must necessarily have an object.
Next, one verse explains the object of wisdom.
The treatise says:
"The object of focus for all Bodhisattvas is the ineffable nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)."
This is non-conceptual wisdom; it is the suchness of the nature of selflessness.
The commentary states:

"The ineffable dharma-nature" refers to the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) in expressible phenomena; this means it is free from the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) which is expressible.

Regarding the suchness of selflessness (*anātmatā-tathatā*): in order to establish this meaning and bring it to clear understanding, it is the suchness manifested by the non-existence of all persons (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*). It is the objective sphere (*ālambana*) of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) which is liberated from the two extremes of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*), because whenever there is an object of cognition, there necessarily exists a corresponding cognitive aspect (*ākāra*).
The next verse reveals the aspect of wisdom.
The treatise says:
"The aspects of the bodhisattvas' practice, moreover, within their objects of focus..."
"This is non-conceptual wisdom; that which is known by it is signless.
Commentary: It is called an "aspect" (*ākāra*) because it proceeds in a manner similar to its object of focus.
Non-conceptual wisdom operates in a manner that accords with the object of suchness.

Regarding the statement that "the known object is signless," this refers to the mode of activity (ākāra) performed by this wisdom toward the object of suchness; the intended meaning is that non-conceptual wisdom takes suchness as its object, and its mode of activity consists in being free from all signs and mental constructions (manasikāra).
Next, two verses are taught to resolve doubts and difficulties regarding the aforementioned objects of focus and the aspects of gnosis.
The treatise says:
The meaning of the nature of association Is that which is discriminated, and nothing else.
The mutual correspondence of syllables is what is called the meaning of "correspondence.
Wisdom does not operate upon the referent apart from its designator;
because they are not identical, the designator cannot express everything.
The commentary states:
If, in reality, there were no object of conceptualization (*parikalpya-artha*), what would it be that is conceptualized?

Therefore, it is said that the object of conceptualization is the meaning of the "correspondence of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-saṃprayoga*) and not anything else. This means that when various syllables correspond with one another and are proclaimed without interruption, the mind of universal imagination (*parikalpa-citta*) and so forth takes this as a basis for provisional designation, establishing it as the object of conceptualization. There is no separate, real entity that serves as the object of conceptualization; therefore, it is said to be "not anything else."
If there were no sequential proclamation through the medium of syllables, then because conceptualization would be absent, how could it be said that all phenomena are inexpressible?
To clarify this principle, it is stated that [the mind] does not operate upon the signified object apart from the cognizing wisdom that expresses it, and so forth.
If an object existed as a real entity that could be expressed, then even apart from the expressive name, there would have to arise a cognition resembling speech regarding it.
However, such a cognition does not arise with respect to the expressed object for one who has not yet understood the expressive name; therefore, it cannot be said to exist.
Some may claim that although external objects definitely exist as real entities, the cognition that apprehends the signifier and the signified must necessarily arise [in dependence upon them].
To refute this, it is said: "Because the signifiers are not identical."

This means that because their characteristics are distinct, they cannot be real designators; since the designating name and the designated meaning are apprehended as having separate characteristics, their characteristics are each different—how, then, could they constitute a fixed and real expression?
Regarding the fact that "all is ineffable," by this principle, all that expresses and all that is expressed are ineffable.
What, then, does non-conceptual wisdom sustain?
The treatise says:
The various practices undertaken by Bodhisattvas are sustained by non-conceptual wisdom;
these subsequent attainments serve to further progress and increase [that wisdom].
The commentary states:

"The various practices subsequently attained" refers to the manifold bodhisattva practices attained within the non-conceptual subsequently attained wisdom; all these practices take wisdom as their basis.

Regarding "for the sake of advancing and increasing," this means for the sake of increasing the various practices of a bodhisattva; it is said that there is a necessary application of maintenance, because by being free from error, one is able to maintain all practices.
What serves as the auxiliary companion to non-conceptual wisdom?
If it were to exist alone, it would be incapable of accomplishing anything.
The treatise says:
The companions of all bodhisattvas are said to be the two kinds of paths:
non-conceptual wisdom and the nature of the five perfections (pāramitās).
Commentary:

Regarding the two types of paths: first, the path of provisions (*sambhāramārga*); second, the path of reliance (*niśrayamārga*). These have the five perfections (*pāramitā*) as their intrinsic nature.
Among these, the first four perfections constitute the path of provisions, while the fifth, the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*), constitutes the path of reliance.

If one abides in a concentrated mind, the four previously mentioned perfections (pāramitās) serve as virtuous supports that enable the growth of non-conceptual wisdom; this wisdom is termed the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā).
Until the fruit of Buddhahood is attained, in what location does non-conceptual wisdom experience its maturation fruit (*vipāka-phala*)?
The treatise says:
"The maturation of all Bodhisattvas occurs within the two assemblies of the Buddha."
"This non-conceptual wisdom is attained through application.
The commentary explains:
"In the two assemblies" refers to the assemblies of the Buddhas' transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
Regarding "attainment through application," this indicates the sense of being able to bring about a ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*).

This [application] is not itself a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), because it acts as an antidote to that [cause]; rather, it is the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) that is metaphorically designated as "ripened."
Because this nourishes and perfumes other contaminated (*sāsrava*) karmas, causing them to produce maturation (*vipāka*), it is given this name.
When one cultivates the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of non-conceptualization, one is born into the assemblies of the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifested by the Buddhas;
when one realizes non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), one is then born into the assemblies of the enjoyment bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*) manifested by the Buddhas.
What is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of non-conceptual wisdom?
The treatise says:
It is the outflow of all bodhisattvas in their successive future births.
This non-conceptual wisdom, its own essence, becomes increasingly superior.
Commentary:
In successive lifetimes, the non-conceptual wisdom of each preceding life becomes progressively more excellent in each subsequent birth; this is the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).
What is the transcendence of non-conceptual wisdom?
The treatise says:
The transcendence of all bodhisattvas consists in attaining the accomplishment of the corresponding [realization].
This non-conceptual wisdom should be known to exist throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
The commentary states:
When entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) at the first stage, the Stage of Utmost Joy (*pramuditā*), one perceives the principle of non-conceptuality in all stages.
Having first attained liberation, one subsequently attains the non-conceptual wisdom that accords with the accomplishment of the various stages (*bhūmi*) during the practice of the path.
Who is it that reaches the ultimate?
The treatise says:
When the bodhisattvas reach their ultimate goal, they attain the three pure bodies;
this is non-conceptual wisdom, through which they obtain supreme mastery.
Commentary:

Regarding the "purification of the three bodies": although one attains the three bodies within the first stage (*bhūmi*), they are not yet purified; it is only upon reaching the tenth stage that they become purified and are then termed "ultimate. Therefore, it is said that at that time one attains the pure three bodies.

"Attaining supreme mastery" means that at that time, non-conceptual wisdom not only attains the three pure bodies (*trikāya*), but also attains the ten supreme masteries; therefore, it is called ultimate non-conceptual wisdom.
How, from what, and by what means is there non-defilement?
The treatise says:
Just as space is undefiled, so too is this non-conceptual wisdom.
Various kinds of extremely heavy evils, / Arise solely from faith and resolute conviction.
Commentary: To the initial question of how one attains freedom from defilement, the answer is that it is like space, which is undefiled.
Next, when asked from what one attains freedom from defilement, the answer is: "From various kinds of extremely heavy evils.

Subsequently, when asked by what means one attains freedom from defilement, the answer is: "It is solely through faith and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*"; that is, it is attained by taking as causes solely faith and the resolute conviction born of wisdom."
The treatise says:
Just as space is unstained, so is non-conceptual wisdom;
having liberated itself from all obscurations, it attains the fulfillment of its application.
The commentary states:
"Liberated from all obscurations" means liberated from the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
"Attaining the corresponding accomplishment" refers to being in correspondence with attainment on the first stage (*bhūmi*), up to being in correspondence with accomplishment on the Buddha stage.
The Commentary says:
Just as space is unstained, this non-conceptual wisdom constantly operates within the world, yet it is not defiled by worldly phenomena.
The commentary states:

"Constantly acting in the world without being defiled by worldly dharmas" means that although he is born in all places of birth, he is not stained by the eight worldly concerns, such as gain and so forth; thus, like a red lotus, he is categorized as transcending the world.
These three verses demonstrate the benefits obtained through the three types of wisdom.
What is the distinction between the three kinds of non-conceptual wisdom: that of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), the fundamental stage (*maula*), and the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*)?
The Treatise says:
Just as one who is mute seeks to receive meaning, just as one who is mute correctly receives meaning,
and just as one who is not mute receives meaning— the three types of knowledge are illustrated by these analogies.
As a fool seeks to receive an object, as a fool correctly receives an object,
and as one who is not a fool receives an object— the three types of knowledge are illustrated by these analogies.
As the five [senses] seek to receive an object, and as the five correctly receive an object...
Just as the manas experiences its objects, so too are the three types of knowledge (jñāna) illustrated.
Just as one who has not yet understood a treatise seeks that treatise to grasp its meaning, this sequence illustrates the three knowledges;
one should understand them as being equivalent to the preparatory stage (prayoga) and the others.
The commentary states:
To clarify the distinctions between the characteristics and activities of the three types of knowledge, these similes are given.

"Like a mute person seeking to perceive an object" means, for example, that just as a mute person seeks to perceive an objective realm but is neither able to perceive it nor able to speak of it; so it is with the first type of knowledge.
In this way, preparatory non-conceptual wisdom seeks to realize suchness but has not yet realized it; one should know that its silence and ineffability are likewise so.

Regarding the "mute person correctly experiencing the object": just as a mute person correctly experiences an object without any verbal expression, so too should one know that fundamental non-conceptual wisdom, which directly realizes suchness and is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), is likewise so.
Just as one who is not mute perceives objects and, like a person who is not mute, gives rise to speech regarding those various spheres of experience;

so too should it be understood that the subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom, reflecting back upon the true suchness and directly realizing its sphere of experience, is likewise able to give rise to verbal instruction.
By this principle, the verse regarding the "foolish" is explained.

As for the five seeking to experience objects: just as the five consciousnesses seek to experience their respective objects, and though there is that which is sought, there is no conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), so too should one understand the non-conceptual wisdom of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) to be likewise.

Regarding the meaning of the five correct apprehensions (*pañca-samāpattayaḥ*): just as the five consciousnesses correctly apprehend their objects while remaining free from all conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), so too should one understand fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*mūla-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) to be likewise.

Regarding the meaning of the manas as "receiving": just as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is able both to receive objects and to discriminate them, so too should one understand that subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom (*prsthalabdha-nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is likewise.

Just as one who does not yet understand a treatise seeks that treatise to receive its meaning, or just as one who does not yet understand a treatise seeks to recite it but has not yet mastered the recitation;
so too should one understand the preparatory application for non-conceptual wisdom to be.
Just as one who has rehearsed a treatise receives its words, so too should fundamental non-conceptual wisdom be understood.
Just as one who has already studied and mastered the meaning of the Dharma, so too should subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom be understood.
By means of these numerous analogies, the distinctions among the three types of knowledge—namely, preparatory application (*prayoga*) and so forth—are illustrated in their respective order.
Next, the distinctions between the two types of knowledge—the fundamental (*mūla*) and the subsequently attained (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*)—are revealed through analogies.
The Commentary says:
Just as when a person closes their eyes, this is non-conceptual wisdom;
when those very eyes are opened again, subsequently attained wisdom is likewise so.
One should know that it is like space; this is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The manifestation of forms and images within it is likewise the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). Commentary:
These two verses demonstrate the distinction between the fundamental and the subsequently attained [wisdoms].
When the eyes are closed or opened, the images of space and forms appear to both wisdoms; are these non-conceptual or conceptual?
This [wisdom] is equal, yet it is unequal; because the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*) has not yet attained realization, it is omitted here.

Furthermore, the wisdom of application is the cause of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), while the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) is its fruit; therefore, for now, we shall establish the performance of the activities of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

Since the fruit of Buddhahood is accomplished through the cultivation of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), and that wisdom itself is free from conceptualization, how can it perform deeds for the benefit of sentient beings?
The treatise states:
"Like a wish-fulfilling gem (*maṇi*) or a celestial drum (*devadundubhi*), it accomplishes its own tasks without thought."
The various deeds of a Buddha are accomplished, And likewise, one is always free from conceptual thought.
Commentary:
In this verse, the two analogies of the wish-fulfilling jewel (*maṇi*) and the celestial drum (*tūrya*) are cited to establish the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) that has been attained.
Although it is without discrimination and exerts no effort, it accomplishes various tasks, just like a wish-fulfilling jewel or celestial music;
for although they have no such thought as "I shall emit light" or "I shall produce sound," they do so because they are devoid of volition.

Nevertheless, by the power of the merit, karma, and intentions of those sentient beings born there, various lights are emitted and various sounds are produced without waiting for them to be struck or played.

One should know that the non-conceptual wisdom of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is likewise: although it is free from conceptualization and exerts no effort, it can manifest and function as various deeds of benefit and happiness in accordance with the merit and intentions of the sentient beings to be converted.
Next, the profound nature of non-conceptual wisdom shall be revealed.
What is the objective sphere of non-conceptual wisdom?

Does it take the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)—which is the basis of conceptualization—as its object, or does it take another sphere as its object, with its own essence being likewise [non-conceptual]?
Is it wisdom or non-wisdom?
If so, what is the fault?
If it takes the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) as its object through conceptualization, how can it be established as non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*)?
If it takes other objects as its conditions, those other objects must certainly not exist; what, then, would be its object?
If it is this wisdom, it must have something known.
If it is not wisdom, how can it be named non-conceptual wisdom?
To abandon all such faults, the verse says: "Not in this, nor in another;
Not wisdom, yet it is wisdom. The Commentary states: It is not in this [world], nor in another; it is not wisdom, yet it is wisdom.
Because it is no different from its object, wisdom becomes non-conceptual.
The commentary states:
Non-conceptual wisdom does not take the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), which is the basis of conceptualization, as its object, because it is non-conceptual.

It is not that non-conceptualization is established by taking conceptualization as its object, nor does it take anything else as its objective sphere; rather, it takes the very nature of phenomena (dharmatā) within this conceptualization itself as its objective sphere.

Since it cannot be definitively stated whether phenomena (*dharma*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) are identical or distinct, this wisdom cannot be definitively described as having for its object either a conceptualized realm or a non-conceptualized realm.

Its own nature is likewise such that it cannot be said to be definitively wisdom, because, like preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*) and subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), it is devoid of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Nor can it be said to be definitively non-wisdom, because preparatory wisdom serves as its preceding cause.

When cognition is non-different from its object, it constitutes non-conceptualization; one cannot distinguish that "this is the knower" and "this is the known," because the conceptualization of grasper and grasped is absent.
This wisdom is non-different from its object, just as space is non-different from the light within it; therefore, this wisdom is non-conceptual.
In other sūtras it is said that the nature of all phenomena (*dharma*) is non-conceptual; this shall now be explained.
The treatise says:
One should know that all phenomena are, by their very nature, non-conceptual.
Because that which is conceptualized does not exist, non-conceptual wisdom does not exist.
Commentary:

"Because that which is conceptualized does not exist" means that because the objects conceptually constructed as the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) are eternally non-existent, other sūtras state that the nature of all phenomena (*dharma*) is without conceptualization.

If all phenomena have been non-conceptual by their very nature from the beginning, why have all classes of sentient beings not been naturally liberated since the very outset, without having to exert effort?
Because that non-conceptual wisdom does not exist in them;

for while those sentient beings have never previously given rise to the true wisdom that directly realizes the non-conceptual nature of all phenomena, the Bodhisattvas and others have already given rise to such realizing wisdom, taking the lineage of the non-conceptual nature of all phenomena as its cause. By this principle, the Bodhisattvas and others are able to attain liberation, whereas other sentient beings are not.
Next, the threefold and fivefold distinctions of the wisdom of application (*prayoga-jñāna*) and so forth shall be demonstrated.
The treatise states:
"In this context, there are three types of non-conceptual wisdom of application, distinguished by their arising from causes and conditions, from induction, and from repeated cultivation."
The commentary states:
This differentiation in the arising of the wisdom of application (prayoga-jñāna) results from three kinds of power:
first, the power of causes and conditions; second, the power of induction; and third, the power of repeated cultivation.
The power of causes and conditions refers to the power of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*).
There are those whose spiritual lineage, upon encountering powerful conditions, swiftly gives rise to application (*prayoga*); such application arises with the spiritual lineage serving as its cause.

Regarding "lineage" (*gotra*): it refers to the excellence of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) from time immemorial, which constitutes the natural capacity (*dharmatā-śakti*) to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Regarding "the power of induction": it refers to the initiation of preparatory application (*prayoga*) caused by what was previously practiced in former lives.
The power of repeated practice (*abhyāsa-bala*) refers to the frequent cultivation during the present life, initiated through the application of human effort (*puruṣakāra*).
The Commentary states:
Fundamental non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) also has three types, distinguished by being contented, non-erroneous, and free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
The commentary states:

Regarding "contentment and non-conceptuality," this means that one gives rise to contentment with inferior objects and does not seek further superior progress; therefore, it is called non-conceptuality.

For example, having attained the two mundane wisdoms of hearing and reflection, one may become complacent upon merely gaining faith and understanding or reaching a definitive resolution regarding a limited portion of the meaning.

Or, as if having attained mundane meditative wisdom and realized the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), where coarse afflictions have subsided, one may grasp that state as ultimate liberation and thus become complacent.
All such categories as these are termed the non-conceptual wisdom of contentment.

Regarding "non-erroneous non-conceptual [wisdom]": this refers to noble disciples and others who, through their cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), give rise to the four non-erroneous modes of practice—such as impermanence—with respect to the truths of suffering and so forth; because they do not give rise to erroneous conceptualizations such as permanence, it is called non-erroneous non-conceptual wisdom.

Regarding "being without conceptual proliferation and without discrimination": this means that bodhisattvas do not even discriminate regarding impermanence and so forth, up to and including awakening (*bodhi*), as they are free from conceptual proliferation. This is because, through the principle of the non-discrimination of all phenomena, they transcend all paths of verbal expression and surmount the domain of all worldly cognition.

Because the names of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) are subsumed under conventional sounds and conventional knowledge, that which is free from these is called non-conceptual wisdom free from proliferation (*niṣprapañca-nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The treatise states:

There are five kinds of subsequently attained non-conceptual wisdom, distinguished by the differences of penetration (*prativedha*), recollection (*anusmaraṇa*), establishment (*vyavasthāpana*), synthesis (*saṃkalana*), and intentional discernment (*yathābhiprāya-vicaya*).
The commentary states:
Because the functions performed by this subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) differ, there are five types, namely: penetration (*prativedha*), and so forth.
The term "discernment" (*vicaya*) applies to each one individually.
Regarding "thorough penetration through analytical investigation": it is called "thorough penetration" because one attains certainty regarding the truth and realizes the truth.

Through subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), one analytically investigates this very thorough penetration thus: "This matter is exactly as it was internally examined within myself. Therefore, it is called "thorough penetration through analytical investigation."
Regarding "discernment by recollection" (*anusmaraṇa-vicaya*): it refers to the subsequent recollection and realization, thinking, "I previously realized this matter.
For this reason, it is called discernment by recollection.

Discernment of establishment (*vyavasthāna-pratisaṃkhyā*) refers to that which, having emerged from this [state], proclaims to others exactly as it has been realized; therefore, it is called discernment of establishment.

Discernment of synthesis (*saṃgraha-pratisaṃkhyā*) refers to the contemplation of the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena; by means of this contemplation, one advances toward the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*), or, having already undergone the transformation of the basis, one again gives rise to this contemplation; therefore, it is called discernment of synthesis.

"According to one's intention and deliberation" means that when wisdom is present, everything one contemplates occurs exactly as desired; for instance, causing earth and other elements to transform into gold and so forth. Therefore, it is called "according to one's intention and deliberation."
This term "discernment" (vicāra) is intended to mean "wisdom" (jñāna).
It was previously stated that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-conceptual because there is no object to be conceptualized.
How is it known that the objects of conceptualization do not exist in reality?
In order to establish that these [realms] do not exist [as such], many verses are spoken.
The treatise says:
"Ghosts, animals, humans, and gods, each according to what is appropriate for them,"
Because the mind differs regarding such objects, it is admitted that their referents are not ultimately real.
Regarding past events and the like, as well as within dreams and the two kinds of reflections,
although the objects of perception are not real, the appearance of the object is nonetheless established.
If objects were established as having the nature of objects, non-conceptual wisdom would not exist;
if this were absent, the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood would be illogical.
Through the power of resolute conviction, Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery [perceive objects].
Just as the desire realm and so forth are established, so it is for one who has attained meditative concentration.
For one who has achieved discernment, a wise person who has attained concentration,
when contemplating all phenomena, they appear exactly according to their true nature.
When non-conceptual wisdom functions, all objects do not appear;
one should know that there are no objects, and because of this, consciousness also does not exist.
Commentary:
Regarding "hungry ghosts, animals, humans, gods, and so forth": this means that at a place where humans see water, hungry ghosts see it as dry land or high ground;
at a place where humans see excrement and filth, animals see it as pure and excellent food and drink;
and among impure things seen by humans, hungry ghosts and animals perceive them as clean.
What humans perceive as pure and exquisite food and drink, the devas perceive as foul, putrid, and impure.
Since contradictory phenomena cannot exist in the same place, we know that the objects grasped by the parikalpita (imagined) nature do not exist.
If there were no object, how could consciousness manifest in the absence of an external realm?
Why do you pose this challenge?
You Sautrāntikas maintain that past and future objects do not exist; how, then, can cognition arise with respect to them?
