as for that challenge, I see no ground for it—this is my first fearlessness.
Furthermore, I utter these sincere words:
I am one who has truly exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*).
If someone were to challenge me, saying,
"In such and such a way, your outflows are not yet exhausted," [I would respond accordingly].
I see no grounds for such an objection; this is my second fearlessness.
Furthermore, I utter these sincere words:
"I have proclaimed the path leading to liberation for my disciples."
If someone should raise an objection, saying,
"Cultivating such a path is not the correct means for escaping suffering," I see no grounds for that objection; this is the third fearlessness.
Furthermore, he made this sincere declaration:
"For my disciples, I have taught that obstructive dharmas will certainly act as obstructions when one is defiled by them.
If someone should raise an objection, saying:
Although being stained by those dharmas cannot act as an obstacle, I perceive that those challenges lack any basis for valid cognition; this is the fourth fearlessness.

All four of these should be explained in detail: because one perceives those challenges as lacking any basis, one attains great peace and security; because one has attained peace and security, one is entirely without fear.

Regarding the three kinds of non-protection: it refers to the fact that all Tathāgatas possess bodily actions (*kāyakarman*) that are pure in their manifestation; because there is no impure manifestation of bodily action for which they must fear being known by others and thus need to conceal or protect, this is called the first non-protection.
As it was said regarding bodily action, so too should it be said regarding vocal and mental actions; these three are the "unprotected" [states].

Regarding the three foundations of mindfulness (*trīṇi smṛtyupasthānāni*): when the Tathāgatas teach the true Dharma, if there is a class of disciples who listen with respect, abide in a mind intent on following the instruction, practice with diligence, and practice the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, the Tathāgata feels neither pleasure nor joy, and his heart does not exult.

If a class of disciples fails to give rise to reverence, and acts contrary to what was extensively explained above, the Tathāgata does not give rise to resentment or intolerance toward them, nor does he fail to provide them with protection and support.

Regarding a class of disciples who both show respect and do not show respect—and so forth, as explained at length—the Tathāgata’s mind toward them is non-dual; that is, he feels neither delight nor resentment, but dwells in sublime equanimity toward them all.

The eradication of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) refers to the permanent removal of those actions resembling afflictions—such as leaping and so forth—which continue to occur even though the afflictions themselves are no longer present.

The quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣa-dharma*) refers to the possession of correct mindfulness and clear comprehension regarding the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings, such that one does not miss the appropriate time for action.

Regarding "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*), it refers to the great purpose of the altruistic intention to bring about the welfare and happiness of sentient beings, which shall be explained hereafter.
Regarding the "eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha" (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), the meaning of "unique" (*āveṇika*) is the sense of being "not shared" (*asādhāraṇa*).
Thus, the Tathāgatas are free from all error.

For example, although Arhats have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*), when they go out into cities and towns for alms, they may at times dwell together with wicked elephants, horses, oxen, or dogs; or at times their feet may tread upon thickets of thorns or various venomous snakes as they leap about; or at times they may enter such houses and engage in improper speech with groups of women; or in forests and wilds, they may abandon good paths and travel on evil roads; or they may dwell together with enemies, thieves, lions, fierce beasts, or the wives of others.
All such errors as these that belong to Arhats are entirely absent in the Buddhas.
Furthermore, all Tathāgatas possess no harsh or violent sounds.

For instance, an Arhat might at times wander through forests or wilds and lose his way, or enter an empty house and cry out loudly, emitting a great and violent noise; or, due to the fault of unrefined habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), he might clench his lips and bare his teeth to break into a loud laugh.
All such harsh and violent vocalizations found among Arhats are entirely absent in the Buddhas.
Furthermore, all Tathāgatas possess no loss of mindfulness.
For instance, while Arhats may experience non-afflicted lapses of memory regarding things done long ago or words spoken long ago,
such lapses do not exist at all in the Buddhas.
Furthermore, the Tathāgatas have no manifold perceptions.
Just as an Arhat gives rise to a perception of extreme revulsion toward saṃsāra with remainder and a perception of extreme tranquility toward nirvāṇa without remainder,
the Tathāgata has no differentiated perception between that saṃsāra with remainder and nirvāṇa without remainder, abiding in supreme equanimity.
Furthermore, all Tathāgatas possess no unconcentrated mind. For instance,
while an Arhat must first withdraw his mind to enter concentration and becomes unconcentrated upon emerging from it,
the Tathāgata possesses no unconcentrated mind in any state whatsoever.
Furthermore, there are no Tathāgatas who abandon anything without prior discernment.
Just as an Arhat does not abandon the various matters that bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings without first investigating them with wisdom,
the Tathāgata never abandons anything in such a manner without having first exercised discernment.
Furthermore, the Tathāgatas are free from the six kinds of decline, such as desire and so forth.

For example, an Arhat may experience a decline regarding that which has not yet been attained within the capacity for the permanent purification of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); namely, decline in aspiration, decline in vigor, decline in mindfulness, decline in concentration, decline in wisdom, and decline in liberation.
Such sixfold declines do not exist in any Buddha.
Furthermore, the physical, verbal, and mental actions of all Tathāgatas are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom.
Just as an Arhat at one time engages in wholesome bodily action and at another time engages in indeterminate action— and it should be known that the same applies to his verbal and mental actions—
the three actions of a Tathāgata have no indeterminate state because they are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom.
Because it arises together with wisdom, it is called "preceded by wisdom"; because it functions simultaneously with wisdom, it is called "following after wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding the objects of the three times, the Tathāgatas possess knowledge and vision that are unattached and unimpeded.

Just as an Arhat cannot understand the three periods of time merely by momentarily directing the mind toward them—thereby indicating that his knowledge and vision possess attachment—and cannot fully comprehend all things—thereby indicating that his knowledge and vision possess obstruction—the Tathāgata, upon momentarily directing the mind toward those three periods of time, universally understands and knows all objects. Therefore, his knowledge and vision are without attachment and without obstruction.
For these reasons, each of these eighteen types is called an "unshared Buddha-dharma.
Regarding the "sublime wisdom of all aspects," it refers to being thoroughly proficient in understanding all aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).
"Identical in all aspects of conditioned phenomena" means being identical with other immeasurable qualities associated with the *dharmakāya*.
The treatise states:
There are many verses on this point.
The commentary states:
Within these uncommon virtues that serve as the basis for this dharmakāya, they are analytically revealed through the principle of concluding verses by means of the method of eulogy.
The treatise says:
Out of compassion for all sentient beings, you give rise to the intentions of gathering them together and setting them apart;
you never abandon their benefit and happiness—to you, who possess these four intentions, I pay homage.
Commentary:
In this verse, the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are revealed.
"Compassion for all sentient beings" is the general statement.
"Arousing the intention for harmony" reveals the immeasurable of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), because it desires to bring about the harmonious union of sentient beings.
The cultivation of the intention to bring about separation manifests immeasurable compassion (*karuṇā-apramāṇa*), because one desires to cause sentient beings to be separated from suffering.
The cultivation of the intention never to abandon them manifests immeasurable sympathetic joy (*muditā-apramāṇa*), because one desires to cause sentient beings not to abandon happiness.
The phrase "arousing the intention for benefit and happiness" reveals immeasurable equanimity (*upekṣā*), because one desires to cause sentient beings to obtain benefit and well-being.

"Equanimity" means relinquishing; it refers to the desire to cause sentient beings to abandon the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of afflictions such as pleasant feelings, while not abandoning the sentient beings themselves.
Furthermore, abiding in the middle is called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Taking these qualities as one's object, one takes refuge in and pays homage to the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas; thus it is called "taking refuge and paying homage.
All subsequent verses should be understood accordingly.
The Treatise says:
Liberated from all obstructions, the Muni surpasses the world;
his wisdom pervades all that can be known—homage to him whose mind is liberated.
The commentary states:
"Liberated from all obstacles" indicates that the liberation of the Buddhas is superior to that of the śrāvakas and others.
"The Muni surpasses the world" indicates that the state of the Buddhas is superior to that of the śrāvakas and others.

Regarding the phrase "wisdom that pervades all objects of knowledge," this sentence demonstrates that the Buddhas possess a pervasive excellence that surpasses that of the śrāvakas and others; it is not as in the Śrāvaka-yāna and other vehicles, which possess only the eight liberations (vimokṣa), the eight bases of mastery (abhibhv-āyatana), and the ten bases of pervasion (kṛtsnāyatana).

With liberation as the precursor, there are the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*); with the spheres of mastery as the precursor, there are the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*). By means of this gateway, one intentionally contemplates so as to liberate oneself from all hindrances and to surpass all the world.
"One whose wisdom encompasses all objects and whose mind is liberated" refers to one who possesses the three aforementioned virtues and whose mind is free from fetters.
The treatise says:
"Able to extinguish all afflictions of sentient beings without remainder."
"Harmful afflictions and defilements— I always compassionately take refuge in and pay homage to you.
Commentary: This verse reveals the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), which has conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) as its nature.

This differs from the "non-contention" (*araṇā*) attained by the Śrāvakas, who first carefully observe when about to enter a city or town; if they perceive that even a single sentient being might give rise to some form of affliction or contention based upon their person, they will not enter.

The Tathāgata observes that although sentient beings may give rise to various afflictions upon encountering the Buddha’s body, if they are capable of receiving the Buddha’s transformation, he immediately goes to them and subdues them through skillful means, causing their afflictions to be extinguished.

Regarding the ability to extinguish all afflictions of all sentient beings without remainder: this is not like the Śrāvaka who dwells in the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*), employing skillful means to distance himself from becoming a condition for even the slightest affliction to arise in any sentient being; he merely suppresses the manifest afflictions of the desire realm, but not other afflictions.
The Buddhas are not like this; through their skillful means, they are able to extinguish all the afflictions of all sentient beings so that none remain.
One who harms the afflictions harms only the afflictions and does not harm sentient beings.

Regarding those who possess defilements yet are always objects of compassion: if sentient beings are afflicted by the stains of the afflictions, the Buddha always feels compassion for them and does not revile or harm them.
As a verse says: "Just as a skilled physician of spirits treats those possessed by various spirits,"
One merely rebukes and harms the malevolent spirits, not those possessed by spirits;
likewise, the Honored One of Great Compassion treats those possessed by afflictions by merely rebuking and harming the afflictions, not rebuking or harming sentient beings.
The treatise says:
Effortless and unattached, Unimpeded and eternally in tranquil concentration, You are able to explain all inquiries and challenges; I pay homage to you.
The commentary states:

This verse reveals that the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) is superior to that of the śrāvakas and others by way of five characteristics: namely, because it is effortless (*anābhoga*), because it is unattached (*asaṅga*), because it is unimpeded (*apratigha*), because it is always in a state of tranquil meditative concentration (*nitya-śānta-samādhi*), and because it is able to resolve all doubts and difficulties.

The *praṇidhijñāna* (knowledge resulting from aspiration) attained by the śrāvakas and others allows them to enter meditative absorption according to their specific aspirations; however, they can only know this particular object and not others. The Buddha is not like this:

through his effortless wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*), which requires no exertion, he is able to know all objects of experience according to his aspirations—just as a wish-fulfilling gem (*maṇi*) or celestial music responds to wishes. This is because, through his unattached wisdom (*asaṅga-jñāna*), he encounters no obstruction regarding all objects of knowledge; through his unimpeded wisdom (*apratigha-jñāna*), he has severed both the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); and through his eternally quiescent concentration (*nitya-śānta-samādhi*), he has severed the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
As it is said in a verse:
The Nāga walks in meditative composure; The Nāga stands in meditative composure;
The Nāga sits in meditative composure; The Nāga lies down in meditative composure.
By means of this sublime wisdom born of aspiration, one is well able to explain all difficult questions at all times.
The treatise says:
Regarding the basis and that which rests upon it, the spoken words and the wisdom—
To the one who possesses unimpeded wisdom in exposition, Who always skillfully teaches—to you, we pay homage.
Commentary: This verse reveals the four types of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
The "basis of expression" refers to the various teachings, namely the sūtras and so forth.
The "that which depends upon it" refers to the meaning expressed.
Both of these are termed "that which is spoken," because they constitute the activity of speaking.
Both speech and wisdom are "capable of exposition," because they arise from the agent, the instrument, and so forth.
"Unimpeded wisdom" refers to the non-regressive knowledge regarding these matters.
One who always speaks well does so by virtue of possessing the four types of analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*); thus, they are always able to speak well.

If one possesses unimpeded wisdom regarding the basis [of phenomena], it is called the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), because there is no obstruction regarding the various synonyms for phenomena.

If one is unimpeded regarding names and meanings through the unobstructed wisdom that relies upon them—because one is without hindrance concerning the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena, or because one is without hindrance regarding the distinct meanings and intentions of various phenomena.

If one possesses unimpeded cognitive wisdom regarding words, it is called the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); for one speaks without obstruction according to the various expressions and mutually differing conceptions in the diverse linguistic realms of all countries, or because one is unimpeded in explaining the terminology of all phenomena.

The unimpeded wisdom and insight regarding the knowledge that analyzes all phenomena is called the analytical eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid), because it is free from obstruction within the knowledge capable of discerning and analyzing all phenomena.
The Treatise says:
For the sake of those sentient beings, you manifest knowledge of their speech and conduct, as well as their coming and going and their transcendence; to you, the skillful teacher, I pay homage.
The commentary states:
This verse reveals the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
"For those sentient beings" is the general statement.
"Excellent teaching" means that every single word possesses it.
"Excellent" (shàn) means wondrous;
"teaching" (jiào) refers to speech.
Because they speak subtle words to cause others to progress toward excellence, they are called "skilled instructors.

Manifesting as skilled instructors refers to the supernormal power of psychic travel (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*); by going to wherever beings are to be converted according to their needs, they manifest great spiritual transformations to skillfully instruct them.

"Knowing speech and skillful instruction" refers to the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*), because by means of it one hears all sounds and meaningful words spoken by those dwelling at a distance, and accordingly teaches the Dharma to them.

The supernormal power of knowing the thoughts of others and teaching them well is the supernormal power of the penetration of the minds of others, because one knows the superior and inferior states of their minds and thus teaches them skillfully.

The supernormal power of knowing past lives and teaching them well is the supernormal power of the knowledge of recollecting former abodes, because one thoroughly understands the past and thus teaches them skillfully.

Knowing how to skillfully teach regarding the future is the supernormal knowledge of the death and rebirth of beings (*cyutyupapāda-abhijñā*), because it involves thoroughly understanding the future in order to skillfully instruct others.

Knowing how to skillfully teach regarding transcendence is the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*), because it involves knowing how to skillfully instruct others in the severance of afflictions (*kleśa*).
The Treatise says:
When all sentient beings behold the Honored One, they all recognize him as a true spiritual friend;
upon seeing him even for a moment, they conceive deep faith. To this Guide, I pay homage.
The commentary states:

This verse reveals the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*). Since the Dharma-body is the basis upon which these marks and signs appear, one pays homage to the Dharma-body by way of its marks and signs.

Regarding the statement that "all sentient beings who see the Honored One thoroughly recognize him as a true spiritual friend": because all those in the world behold the World-Honored One’s possession of the primary marks and secondary signs, they all thoroughly recognize him as a great and virtuous being.
"All sentient beings" refers to those who, both at that time and in subsequent times, are capable of receiving transformation.

"Those who, upon seeing him for a moment, immediately develop deep faith" means that upon briefly beholding the World-Honored One’s primary marks and secondary signs, they immediately develop profound and pure faith, recognizing him as the one who skillfully guides the world.
The Commentary says:
To the one who possesses mastery over gathering, maintaining, and relinquishing; over manifesting emanations and transformations;
and over meditative absorption and wisdom—homage to you who have realized these attainments.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the four kinds of purity in all aspects.

"Mastery over assuming, maintaining, and relinquishing" reveals the purity of the basis; that is, by relying on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one possesses mastery over the body in assuming, maintaining, and relinquishing it at will, according to one's pleasure, for as long or as short a duration as desired.
"Manifestation and transformation" clarify the purity of the object of focus (*ālambana*).
To manifest various kinds of forms that have never previously arisen is called "manifestation.
To transform various kinds of forms that have already arisen into gold, silver, and so forth is called "transformation."
In this regard, one attains mastery over all categories of transformations.

As for "mastery over meditative concentration" (*samādhi*), it signifies the purity of the mind; according to one's desire, one proceeds with mastery over the gateways of *samādhi*, being able to enter various meditative absorptions at every single moment exactly as one intends.
Mastery of wisdom (*jñāna-vaśitā*) reveals the purity of wisdom; it is the mastery of maintaining the gateways of dhāraṇī according to one's desire.
"In accordance with what is realized" means that one accords with the realization of the four aforementioned purities.
The treatise says:
To the one who deceives sentient beings regarding the skillful means, the refuges, purity, and the transcendence of the Mahāyāna— to that vanquisher of Māra, I pay homage.
The commentary states:
This verse reveals the ten powers (*daśabala*).

That is to say, [the power] regarding the karmic means for rebirth in happy destinies (*sugati*) and miserable destinies (*durgati*), and regarding taking refuge in the mundane and supramundane purities.
Among the four meanings of the Mahāyāna’s transcendence, there is the delusion of sentient beings by Māra; herein, the activity of the Ten Powers that can destroy those Māras is clearly explained.
Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*): expedient means for the happy realms refers to all virtuous karmas, while expedient means for the miserable realms refers to non-virtuous karmas.

When such skillful means for proceeding [to higher realms] are being proclaimed, Māra dwells therein to deceive and delude them, saying that it is not so and asserting the opposite; he proclaims unwholesome karma as the skillful means for the happy realms and wholesome karma as the skillful means for the miserable realms, or he says that everything is without cause, or he asserts that everything has Īśvara and other such deities as its cause.

The power of the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*) is able to refute those [opposing] assertions. Regarding the etymological explanation: "possible" (*sthāna*) refers to a reason (*kāraṇa*), that which provides room for acceptance.
If there is no reason, and nothing is accepted, it is called "impossible" (*asthāna*).
It is impossible and out of the question that any class of sentient beings could come into existence without a cause or from an evil cause.

How so? Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises—namely, with ignorance as the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth. It is not through the agency of a Lord God (*īśvara*) or similar causes that these arise in succession.
Regarding what is called "taking refuge," it refers to all karmic actions.
As it is said: "The world is entirely dependent upon its own karma; karma is the support, and karma is the refuge.
When this karma is discussed, Māra dwells therein, deceiving and deluding beings, as described at length previously.

By means of the second power, the knowledge of the maturation of karma (*karmavipākajñānabala*), one is able to refute their [opposing] assertions without any impediment, namely that the distinctions of high and low, superior and inferior among sentient beings are differentiated by their own karma and do not arise from causes such as non-causality or a creator god (*īśvara*), as explained at length previously.

What is called "purity" refers to mundane purity and supramundane purity; it consists in the temporary and ultimate suppression of all afflictions and the permanent destruction of their latent tendencies (anuśaya) through the various dhyānas, samādhis, samāpattis, and the Noble Path.
When this purity is being taught, Māra dwells therein, deceiving and deluding others, as described extensively above.
By means of the power of knowledge regarding dhyāna, samādhi, and samāpatti, he is able to subdue those [demons] and teach without any obstruction.
Regarding "and the departure via the Mahāyāna," this reveals the activity performed by other powers.

That is to say, when the qualities of the Buddha-fruit—the ultimate departure of the Mahāyāna—are being taught, Māra remains therein to deceive and delude them, saying: "This unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is extremely difficult to attain; you should seek the ultimate departure of the Śrāvaka vehicle instead."
By means of the remaining seven powers, one is able to refute those [wrong views] without any obstruction.
The treatise says:
"One is able to explain knowledge and abandonment, as well as renunciation and its obstacles."
"Benefiting oneself and others, and none other; The outsiders bow down in submission and pay homage.
The commentary states:
This verse reveals the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
One who can speak with wisdom refers to the Buddha’s sincere words:
"I am a truly and perfectly awakened one.
This means that I have thoroughly known all phenomena.
Regarding "the intelligent one speaks of abandonment," this refers to the Buddha’s solemn declaration:
"I am one who has truly exhausted all outflows (āsrava).
This means that the outflows of the afflictions have been eternally extinguished.
These two types are spoken of in terms of self-benefit.
Regarding those capable of explaining deliverance, this refers to the Buddha’s sincere words:
"I have explained the Dharma of deliverance for my disciples."
This is the genuine renunciation.
Regarding that which can create obstacles, it refers to the Buddha’s sincere words:
"I have taught my disciples the dharmas that constitute obstacles."
True obstruction;
these two types are taught in reliance upon the benefit of others.
These four types are called the benefit of oneself and others.
"Not being subdued by other non-Buddhists" clarifies the meaning of fearlessness as being free from dread;
because one cannot be overcome by other non-Buddhists, one is fearless.
The treatise says:
Able to subdue others when preaching amidst the assembly, Distant from the two types of defilement,
Without need for protection and without forgetfulness— I pay homage to you who guide and govern the assembly.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the stationing of mindfulness through non-protection (*arakṣa*).
"Able to subdue speakers while in the assembly" means being able to overcome the arguments of others when situated among a great multitude.

Regarding bodily actions and all modes of deportment, there is nothing unseemly that requires concealment or protection, for fear of being censured by others; therefore, one is able to subdue the arguments of others when in the midst of a multitude. In this way, the three kinds of non-protection are clarified.

Regarding "being far removed from the two types of defilement": this means that because one abides well in mindfulness amidst a group of disciples—both those who listen with respect and those who listen without respect—one remains free from attachment and aversion; in this way, the three applications of mindfulness are clarified.
Because he is thus without lack of protection and without forgetfulness, he is able to skillfully guide and govern the assembly of disciples.
The Commentary says:
In all activities and states of abiding, there is nothing that is not the work of perfect wisdom.
I pay homage to the one who knows all things at all times and possesses the true meaning.
Commentary: This verse demonstrates the eradication of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

"Pervading all modes of conduct and dwelling" means that whether in a village or a town for the sake of alms-seeking, or while walking back and forth under trees and so forth, one dwells in tranquility through the four postures of the body.

"There is nothing that is not the activity of perfect wisdom" means that although Śrāvakas and others have exhausted their afflictions (*kleśa*), they still possess residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Bound by these tendencies, they engage in activities such as restlessness (*auddhatya*) and the like. For example, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was constantly reborn as a monkey for five hundred lifetimes; because he was bound by those residual tendencies, even though he was free from afflictions, he would leap about like a monkey whenever he heard music.
There was once a Pratyekabuddha who, having previously been a courtesan during many lifetimes, would still adorn his face due to the persistence of these residual habits.
Such things as these are not actions appropriate for one possessed of all-knowledge; the World-Honored One is entirely free from them. This is called the unique quality of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the phrase "one who at all times possesses universal knowledge of the true meaning": unlike the non-Buddhists such as the Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and others, who are not truly omniscient, it is therefore said that the Tathāgata is the one who possesses omniscience regarding the true meaning.
This is stated in reverse order for the sake of conforming to the method of verse composition; alternatively, the meanings of these phrases are distinct from one another.
"Omniscient at all times" indicates that the Buddha is the All-Knowing One (*sarvajña*).
Regarding "one who possesses the true meaning": this indicates that the Buddha is one who possesses the true meaning, just as a person holding a staff is called "the staff-man.
The treatise says:
"For the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, his deeds never miss their proper time."
"What is done is never in vain; homage is paid to you who are free from forgetfulness.
Commentary: This verse demonstrates the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣadharma*).

Regarding "acting for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings without missing the proper time": this means that if there are those to be converted by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and if at a particular time there is something that ought to be done for them, he immediately performs what is required for their sake at that very time, never failing to observe the proper timing.
As it is said in a verse:
"Just as the waters of the great ocean, In their surging tides, must respond to the proper time,
So too does the Buddha, out of compassion for sentient beings, Respond to their calls without ever failing."
"His actions are always non-vacuous" means that what the Buddha does is not empty and is never without fruit.
"He is without forgetfulness" means that his actions are timely and he is never forgetful.
The treatise says:
Six times throughout the day and night, you constantly observe all worlds;
endowed with great compassion, I pay homage to your mind intent on their benefit and happiness.
The commentary states:
This reveals great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which has as its essence the intention to benefit and bring peace and happiness.

It is called "great" because it is realized through the perfection of the accumulations of merit and wisdom; because its mode of activity consists in causing liberation from the three types of suffering; because its object of focus is sentient beings within the three realms; because its mind is impartial toward all sentient beings; and because there is certainly nothing superior to it.
"Constantly observing all worlds six times throughout the day and night" reveals the activity and function of great compassion.

This means that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, observes all worlds during each of the three periods of both day and night, [inquiring]: "In whom are wholesome qualities increasing? In whom are wholesome qualities diminishing?"
Who has mature roots of goodness and who has roots that are not yet mature?
Who is a vessel capable of receiving a superior rebirth, and who is a vessel capable of receiving the certainty of a superior rebirth?
Who is a vessel for the Buddha Vehicle, and who is a vessel for other vehicles?
And so forth. The Treatise says:
"By means of practice and by means of realization, by means of wisdom and by means of activity."
"To all those of the three vehicles, I pay homage to the most supreme.
Commentary: This reveals the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma).

Regarding the statement "by way of conduct," this refers to all activities performed during his course of action; that is to say, the Tathāgata is without error, even to the point of being without any unintentional abandonment.
"By means of realization" refers to the six kinds of non-retrogression while abiding, namely: non-retrogression from aspiration, up to and including the sixth, non-retrogression from liberation.
"By means of wisdom" refers to the engagement of unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the three periods of time.
Regarding "and by means of action," this refers to the Tathāgata’s actions of body, speech, and mind, which are preceded by wisdom and proceed in accordance with wisdom.

Regarding "the most excellent among all three vehicles," this demonstrates that the Buddha is the most preeminent among all Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, because he is fully endowed with the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*).
The treatise says:
To the one who, through the attainment of the three bodies, possesses the great enlightenment of all marks;
to the one who dispels the doubts of others in all places—to that most supreme one, I pay homage.
The commentary states:
This verse reveals the nature of the sublime wisdom of all aspects (*sarvākāra-prajñā*).
To correctly and fully comprehend all modes of activity is termed the sublime wisdom of all aspects.

This essence of wondrous wisdom is called the nature of wondrous wisdom of all aspects; it is the objective realm of all that is knowable, the essence of the preeminent wisdom of all modes of appearance.

Regarding the "three bodies," they refer to the nature body (*svābhāvika-kāya*) and so forth; by means of these three bodies, one attains the fruit of great enlightenment, which is the nature of sublime wisdom that is fully endowed with all characteristics, stainless, and unimpeded.
Regarding the phrase "endowed with all characteristics," it means being endowed with all characteristics.
Some say that the sixteen modes of activity, such as impermanence and so forth, are called "all characteristics," because awakening takes them as its primary causes.

Others further state that this and all other phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; they are without arising or ceasing, primordially quiescent, by nature in nirvana, and characterized by non-apprehensibility—this is called "all marks."

Others further state that this does not describe the characteristics of the various categories of remedies and their counter-objects; rather, it describes the perfection of all meanings and benefits, like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) which possesses all attributes.
When I now observe all these characteristics, they are precisely the categories for severing all hindrances.

Why is this? Because they permanently sever all categories of hindrance; that is to say, they sever all categories of cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and sever all categories of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, this Great Bodhi endowed with all characteristics is precisely the correct knowledge of the characteristics of all objects; therefore, it is able to sever all doubts of others.
"In all places" refers to the doubts of others throughout all worlds—that is, all the uncertainties of every human and celestial being—and it is able to sever all such doubts.

By this, the function of severing all doubts and uncertainties among gods and humans is accomplished, manifesting the excellence of the sublime wisdom that perceives all phenomena (*sarvākāra-prajñā*).
The treatise states:

The Dharma-body of the Buddhas is endowed with such virtues as these, and is further endowed with the remaining virtues of essential nature (*svabhāva*), cause (*hetu*), fruit (*phala*), activity (*karman*), association (*yoga*), and manifestation (*vṛtti*). Therefore, one should know that the Dharma-body of the Buddhas possesses unsurpassed virtues.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
The Venerable One has perfected the ultimate reality;
Transcending all stages, he stands above all sentient beings, And brings liberation to all living beings.
Inexhaustible and peerless virtues manifest in accordance with the world and are visible to the assembled multitude, yet they are not seen by humans, devas,
and others. Commentary:
The Dharma-body is associated with these virtues and is further associated with six other virtues; this is the brief indication of the meaning. The two verses provide a detailed explanation.

Regarding "the Venerable One has accomplished the ultimate reality": this means that the Buddha’s Dharma-body has accomplished the ultimate reality manifested as suchness (*tathatā*). This explains the correspondence with the virtues of the Dharma-body's own nature; it is not erroneous to speak of its correspondence with the distinctions of the powers (*bala*), just as when one speaks of fire, one speaks of its correspondence with the virtue of heat.
"Emerging from all stages" means that one emerges from all ten stages, beginning with the Stage of Extreme Joy; this is the cause of the perfected ultimate truth.
"Reaching the pinnacle of all sentient beings" means that the nature of omniscience is the most supreme among all sentient beings; this is the fruit of the perfected ultimate truth.
That which liberates all sentient beings is the activity of the perfected ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

"Endowed with inexhaustible and incomparable virtues" means being associated with and corresponding to all qualities, because it is endowed with inexhaustible and incomparable virtues such as the boundless, unique powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).

That which is visible in the world and within the assemblies refers to the manifestation of the nirmāṇakāya (transformation body) in the world and the sambhogakāya (enjoyment body) dwelling amidst the great assembly; both of these are visible.
"Those who are not able to see [it], such as humans and devas," means that the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* cannot be seen by humans, devas, and so forth.
This explains the distinction between the three bodies (*trikāya*) of the World-Honored One in order to clarify the meaning of transformation.
"Transformation" refers to the differentiation of the transformation of the essential nature (*svabhāva*). Among the three bodies (*trikāya*), two bodies are visible and one is not visible.
*Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Scroll Nine; *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, Scroll Ten.
Composed by Bodhisattva Asvabhāva;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Part Eleven of the Section on the Wisdom of the Fruit: Supplementary Discussion. It is said:
Furthermore, the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is profound, most profoundly profound. How can this characteristic of profundity be perceived?
Regarding this, there are many verses.
The commentary states:

Regarding the profundity of the dharmakāya of all Buddhas: it is said that the intrinsic nature of this dharmakāya is difficult to realize, for even the cognitive wisdom of those in the world who possess worldly brilliance cannot yet comprehend it.
Regarding the "most profound," it is said that the distinctions of this dharmakāya are difficult to realize because the cognitive wisdom of all śrāvakas and others cannot engage with them.
This profundity shall now be briefly demonstrated by means of twelve verses.
The Treatise says:
The Buddha takes non-arising as his birth, and likewise takes non-abiding as his abiding;
all his activities are effortless, and he takes the fourth nutriment as his food.
The commentary states:
This verse reveals the profundity of the abiding of the activity of birth.
That the Buddhas take non-birth as birth means that although all Buddhas are without birth, they manifest birth; this is called the profundity of birth.

"Furthermore, 'dwelling by means of non-dwelling' means that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are characterized by non-dwelling as their dwelling; this is precisely abiding in non-abiding nirvāṇa, which is called 'dwelling in profundity.'"
Regarding "all activities are effortless": performing all activities without relying on effort is like the mani jewel or celestial music of the world; this is called the profundity of karma.
Regarding "the fourth is food for those who eat," there are four kinds of food:
first, food that sustains existence through impure dependence, which refers to those bound by all fetters, whose bodies are maintained by means of edible food and the other types.

Second, the sustenance upon which the pure and impure depend for their maintenance consists of the food of contact, mental volition, and consciousness; that is to say, if one is born in the realm of form or the formless realm, one dwells by means of these three foods, because, having already abandoned desire, there is no food of mouthfuls.

Because those such as the stream-enterer-in-training (srotāpanna-pratipannaka) are still in training (śaikṣa), they subsist upon both pure and impure bases of sustenance; they maintain their physical existence by means of the four kinds of nutriment (āhāra).
Three [types of beings] subsist solely upon pure bases of sustenance; that is, Arhats and others maintain their physical existence by means of the four kinds of nutriment.
The fourth is the mere manifestation of relying on and abiding by nutriment; that is, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, manifests the enjoyment of the four kinds of nutriment, such as edible food.

In reality, when the Tathāgata eats, he does not actually consume food, nor does he rely on food for his own physical maintenance; nevertheless, in accordance with worldly convention, he manifests the consumption of food and manifests reliance on food for the maintenance of his body.
Because one abides by presently partaking of the fourth nutriment, it is called "abiding in profundity.
The treatise says:
Without distinction and immeasurable, without number and a single karma.
Non-firm karma and firm karma— The Buddhas possess the three bodies.
Commentary: This verse demonstrates the profound depth of the establishment of number and activity.
"Non-different" reveals the profundity of the formal establishment (*vyavasthāna*), because it is established without distinction.
"Also immeasurable" reveals the profundity of number; this indicates that the number of its formal establishments is immeasurable.
Regarding "immeasurable yet single karma": although there are immeasurable [manifestations], there is no distinct karma.
Why? Because the karma of transformation and enjoyment is undifferentiated as a single karma, since it accomplishes the benefit of others.
Regarding non-firm and firm karma: the physical karma of the *svābhāvikakāya* (self-nature body) is firmly established, whereas the physical karmas of the other two bodies are not firmly established.
All such cases are termed the profundity of karma.
The treatise says:
Manifest perfect awakening is not existent; all awakenings are not non-existent.
Each and every thought-moment is immeasurable; existence is manifested by means of non-existence.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the profundity of manifest perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).
"Manifest perfect enlightenment is not existent" means that within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not exist.
"All-encompassing awakening is not non-existent" means that within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is truly existent.

"In each and every moment there are immeasurable [Buddhas]" means that throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, immeasurable Buddhas simultaneously manifest perfect awakening in every single moment.

"That which is both existent and non-existent" refers to the fact that all Tathāgatas are both existent and non-existent, for they attain the state of a Venerable One as manifested by emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The treatise says:
"Neither defiled nor free from defilement, one attains liberation through desire."
"Thoroughly knowing desire and the absence of desire, one awakens to and enters the dharma-nature of desire.
Commentary: This verse demonstrates the profundity of detachment from desire.
Why is it not "defiled"?
Because the fetters of greed have been severed.
Why is it not "free from defilement"? Because the latent tendencies of greed have not been swiftly and permanently eradicated.
Those who seek liberation through desire attain great enlightenment precisely because they retain such latent tendencies of craving;
for if they were to sever these latent tendencies of craving, they would swiftly enter nirvāṇa like the śrāvakas and others.
"Knowing desire and non-desire" means knowing that the greed which is imputed by conceptual construction (*parikalpita*) has the nature of being both desire and non-desire.
"Entering into the dharma-nature of desire" means entering into and realizing the suchness (*tathatā*) of the dharma of desire.
The treatise says:
The Buddhas have transcended all aggregates, yet they dwell within those very aggregates;
they are neither identical to nor different from them, remaining perfectly quiescent without abandoning them.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the profundity of the abandonment of the aggregates (*skandha*).

"The Buddhas have transcended all aggregates" means that the Tathāgatas have surpassed all collections of form and so forth that are conceptually imputed (*parikalpita*), because they perceive, in accordance with reality, that such conceptual imputations are unfindable.
"Abiding within the aggregates" means that the Buddha abides within the aggregates of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).

"Neither identical to nor different from them" means that the aggregates of *dharmatā* cannot be said to be different from the aggregates that are conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*), because the nature of conceptual construction is fundamentally non-existent;
yet they cannot be said to be identical, because the conceptually constructed aggregates accord with defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
Phenomena (*dharma*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) are neither identical nor different.

"Not abandoning yet being perfectly quiescent" means that one does not discard the aggregates (*skandha*) which are the nature of phenomena, for they are themselves the sublime and ultimate cessation.
The Commentary says:
The activities of all Buddhas are intermingled, like the waters of the great ocean;
regarding what has been done, what is being done, and what will be done, there is no thought of "this is for the benefit of another."
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the profundity of maturation.

Regarding the mutual intermingling of the Buddha-activities: it means that all the deeds performed by the Tathāgatas for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings are blended together, synthesized into a single flavor, and become indistinguishable.
Question:
How is this matter? Answer:
It is like the waters of the great ocean.

That is to say, just as the great ocean is the destination of all streams, where the water is of a single flavor and cannot be distinguished, and all things alike provide benefit to fish and other creatures.

When I have no such thought as "I am presently acting for the benefit of others," one is free from the mental effort of deliberating on the distinctions between the three times regarding the benefit of others; thus, one is able to spontaneously initiate activities for the sake of others, just as the *maṇi* jewel or the celestial music of Śakra function despite being devoid of volition.
The Treatise says:
When the transgressions of sentient beings are not manifest, it is like the moon in a broken vessel;
yet it pervades all worlds, through the light of the Dharma that is like the sun.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the profundity of manifestation.
Question:
If the body of the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, why does it not appear at all times?
Answer: It does not appear because of the transgressions of sentient beings, just as the moon does not appear in a broken vessel.

Just as water cannot remain in a broken vessel and the reflection of the moon does not appear therein—not because of a fault in the moon, but because of the defect of the vessel—so too, when the clear and moist water of *śamatha* concentration is absent within the bodies of sentient beings, the reflection of the Buddha does not appear; this is not a fault of the Tathāgata, but a fault of the sentient beings.
The water serves as a metaphor because of its clarity and moistening nature.

As it is said: "The Tathāgata is the reflection of truly sublime, wholesome, and untainted dharmas; they appear when there is a response, but if there is no response, he is like one born blind who cannot see."

"Pervading all worlds with the light of the Dharma like the sun" means that the Buddhas, as suns, emit the light of the words of the true Dharma—such as the sūtras—and illuminate the entire world of sentient beings;
those who have the karmic affinity see it, while those who do not see it suffer from their own faults, not from any deficiency on the part of the Tathāgata.
Just as the light of the sun in the world shines everywhere, those with eyes behold it, while the blind do not see it.
The treatise says:
"Sometimes manifesting perfect enlightenment, / Or entering nirvāṇa like fire."
This has never been non-existent, for the bodies of all Buddhas are eternal.
Commentary:
This verse demonstrates the profundity of manifesting perfect enlightenment and parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the statement that they may manifest perfect enlightenment or parinirvāṇa like fire: just as worldly fire burns in some places and is extinguished in others, so it is with the Buddhas.
For those whose roots of goodness are not yet matured, they manifest perfect enlightenment to bring them to maturity so that they may swiftly attain liberation;
for those whose roots of goodness are already matured and have attained liberation, they manifest parinirvāṇa, as there is nothing further to be done for them.
The meaning of "this has never been non-existent" and so forth is easy to understand.
The treatise says:
Regarding non-noble dharmas, the human realm, and the miserable realms, the Buddha...
"Abiding in the supreme self-nature amidst non-Brahma-conduct.
Commentary: This verse demonstrates the profundity of abiding.

Regarding "dwelling in the supreme essence within non-noble dharmas": this refers to dwelling in the supreme essence—that is, dwelling in the supreme abodes—namely, the abodes of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*) with respect to unwholesome states, because one dwells by taking unwholesome dharmas as objects.

Regarding "dwelling in the most excellent self-nature within the human realm and the miserable realms": this means that within the human realm and the various miserable realms, one dwells by means of the most excellent self-nature—that is, by dwelling in the most excellent states, namely the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)—because one abides by taking those realms as objects.

Regarding "dwelling in the supreme self-nature within the dharmas that are not the Brahma-conduct": this means that among the dharmas that are not the Brahma-conduct, one dwells in the supreme dwelling by means of the supreme self-nature; namely, the four immeasurables (apramāṇa) are called the Brahma-dwellings because they abide by taking what is not the Brahma-conduct as their object.
The Treatise says:
The Buddha traverses all places, yet he does not traverse a single place;
he manifests in all bodies, yet he is not within the range of the six sense faculties.
The commentary states:
This verse reveals the profundity of the essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the "essential nature," it refers to the totality of the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding *dharmadhātu* and the qualities realized therein; these are collectively termed the "essential nature."
The Buddha’s practice in all places refers to the subsequent attainment wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) which pervades everything.

What does it pervade? It pervades the various differentiated spheres of objects, namely: the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; the contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava); and the conditioned (saṃskṛta) and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
"Nor does it function in a single location" means that because non-conceptual wisdom is free from conceptualization, it does not function within any differentiated objects.
"It manifests in all bodies" means that the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) manifests by taking birth in all places.

That which is not within the domain of the six sense faculties refers to the ultimate, eternally abiding Dharmakāya, because it cannot be apprehended by sentient beings in any state of birth, such as those in the hells or other similar realms.
The Treatise says:
Defilements are suppressed but not extinguished, like poison neutralized by a mantra;
retaining these delusions until they are exhausted, one realizes the Buddha’s omniscience.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the profundity of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Regarding "the afflictions being suppressed but not extinguished," this means that while in the stage of a bodhisattva, one suppresses the various afflictions but does not yet permanently sever them.

Regarding "being harmed by a poison-spell": it is like various poisons being neutralized by a divinely efficacious spell; although their substance has not yet been destroyed, they no longer cause harm.
Defilements are likewise: through the power of mindfulness and wisdom, the active entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) are suppressed, though the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) still remain.
Why do the latent tendencies of the afflictions still remain?

It is for fear that one might enter parinirvāṇa too quickly, as is the case with those of the Śrāvaka vehicle. By this principle, taking the afflictions as the cause, one attains omniscience upon the exhaustion of those afflictions.
As it is said in a verse:
"Governed by the power of mindfulness and wisdom, Afflictions are realized as bodhi;
Just as poison is neutralized when held by a mantra, Faults are transformed into virtuous qualities."
The Treatise says:
Afflictions become factors of enlightenment, and birth-and-death becomes nirvāṇa;
because they possess great skillful means, the Buddhas are inconceivable.
The commentary states:
This verse demonstrates the inconceivable profundity.

That is to say, that the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are transformed into the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), and that the suffering and affliction of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) are themselves *nirvāṇa*—such a principle of cause and effect cannot be conceived through worldly logic.

The treatise says: It should be understood that these aforementioned profound aspects are of twelve kinds, namely: the profundity of birth, abiding, and the abiding of activity; the profundity of establishment, number, and activity; the profundity of manifest perfect enlightenment; the profundity of detachment from desire; the profundity of abandoning the aggregates; the profundity of maturation; the profundity of manifestation; the profundity of demonstrating the attainment of enlightenment and nirvāṇa; the profundity of abiding; the profundity of revealing the essential nature; the profundity of severing afflictions; and the profundity of the inconceivable.
The commentary states:
These twelve types are all difficult to perceive and realize; therefore, they are called "profound.
Their individual characteristics have already been explained as previously stated.
The Treatise says:
If bodhisattvas are mindful of the Buddha’s Dharma-body, by how many kinds of mindfulness should they cultivate this mindfulness?
Briefly stated, bodhisattvas who are mindful of the Buddha’s Dharma-body should cultivate this mindfulness by means of seven kinds of mindfulness.
First, one should cultivate this reflection: that all Buddhas attain sovereign mastery over all phenomena, because they have attained unimpeded supernormal powers in all worlds.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
Pervading the realm of sentient beings, They possess obstructions yet lack the causes [for liberation].
There are two kinds of definitive transformation, regarding which the Buddhas have no mastery.
Second, one should cultivate the mindfulness that the Tathāgata’s body is eternally abiding, because True Suchness is liberated from defilements without interval.
Third, one should cultivate this mindfulness that the Tathāgata is supremely faultless, because he is completely dissociated from all afflictive obscurations and cognitive obscurations.
Fourth, one should cultivate this mindfulness that the Tathāgata is effortless, because he performs all Buddha-activities without exertion and without cessation.
Fifth, one should cultivate this mindfulness because the Tathāgata experiences great wealth and bliss, due to the great wealth and bliss of his purified Buddha-field.
Sixth, one should cultivate this mindfulness because the Tathāgata is free from all defilements, for while born in the world, no worldly phenomena can stain him.

Seventh, one should cultivate this reflection that the Tathāgata is able to accomplish the great task: by manifesting perfect enlightenment, parinirvāṇa, and so forth, he brings to maturity all sentient beings who are not yet matured, and brings to liberation those who are already matured.
In this regard, there are two verses:
Perfected within one's own mind, Possessing permanence and purity,
Effortlessly bestowing upon sentient beings The great dharma-joy.
Pervasive and without dependence, Impartially benefiting many beings,
The wisdom of all Buddhas— One should cultivate mindfulness of all these.
Commentary:
This reveals the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of mindfulness regarding the merit of the Buddhas’ Dharma-body.

Regarding "mastery over all phenomena": this means that the Tathāgatas, through long-term cultivation, have attained mastery over all phenomena; because they can momentarily give rise to the aspiration for them, all meritorious qualities are able to manifest in their perfection.
If all Tathāgatas possess unimpeded supernormal powers throughout all infinite and boundless worlds, for what cause and condition do all sentient beings not enter parinirvāṇa?
Because of those obstacles and the absence of causes,

whereas previously it was explained in general that the Buddha attains sovereign mastery over all phenomena, this verse is now spoken to specifically demonstrate that the Buddha does not possess sovereign mastery over sentient beings.

Regarding sentient beings who pervade the realm of beings and possess obstructions while lacking the cause: they are said to "possess obstructions" because they possess the obstructions of afflictions, karma, and maturation; these correspond respectively to those with intense afflictions, those who have committed the various immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*), and those who are foolish, dull, and stubborn.
Because there is no cause for nirvāṇa due to the absence of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), it is termed "deficiency of cause.
Regarding the two kinds of certainty of transformation, they refer to the certainty of performing grave karma and the certainty of experiencing its maturation (*vipāka*).

Regarding "the determination of grave karma": this refers to repeatedly practicing an action so that the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) ensures the continuity of its concordant result (niṣyanda-phala), as in the case of Ajātaśatru’s murder of his father, the king.

Regarding those whose experience of maturation is determined: this refers to having performed karma that is certain to produce maturation, such that one is destined to experience various maturational fruits; for example, the Śākyas who were certain to be slain by King Virūḍhaka.
Regarding the sentient beings mentioned above, the Buddhas do not possess the sovereign power to cause them to attain nirvāṇa.

Therefore, although it was previously stated in general that the Tathāgatas exercise sovereign mastery over all phenomena, it must now be specifically explained that they do not possess such sovereignty [in this regard].
The Tathāgata’s body is eternally abiding because its intrinsic nature is the most pure *tathatā* (suchness), and because it is without modification or transformation.
The Tathāgata is supremely faultless because he has eternally severed the faults of all afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Regarding the Tathāgata’s lack of effort (*anābhoga*): this means it is like celestial music, the meaning of which is easy to understand.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s enjoyment of great wealth and bliss: this is because he enjoys the great Dharma-bliss adorned with the merits of vast and pure Buddha-fields.
That the Tathāgata is free from defilement is as easy to understand as the red lotus flower.

That the Tathāgata is able to accomplish the great task refers to his manifesting equal enlightenment, entering parinirvāṇa, and so forth—accomplishing the vast benefit and welfare of sentient beings by bringing them to maturity and liberation according to their capacities.
These seven types of cultivated mindfulness of the Buddha are further summarized in two verses.
The initial phrase "perfectly complete" (paripūrṇa) applies throughout all [the following].
Regarding that which pertains to the perfection of one's own mind, this summarizes the first [point]: the characteristic of sovereign mastery over all phenomena.
"Endowed with the perfection of permanence" refers to the inclusion of the second body's characteristic of permanence.
"Endowed with the perfection of purity" refers to the inclusion of the third body's supreme characteristic of being faultless.
"Perfection of effortlessness" subsumes the fourth characteristic, that of effortlessness.
"Perfection of bestowing great dharma-bliss upon sentient beings" subsumes the fifth characteristic, that of great dharma-bliss.
The perfection of universal activity without dependence subsumes the sixth characteristic: being undefiled by any worldly phenomena.
The perfection of benefiting many beings with equanimity subsumes the seventh characteristic: the ability to accomplish great tasks, because it performs extensive acts of benefit and happiness.
"All Buddhas" refers to the Tathāgatas who have perfected all virtues.
"The wise ones" refers to the great Bodhisattvas.
"One should cultivate all recollections" means that one should cultivate these seven kinds of recollection.
To recollect, maintain, and clearly remember so as not to let it be lost—this is the meaning of mindfulness (*smṛti*).
The treatise says:
Furthermore, how should the characteristics of the pure buddha-fields of all Buddhas be understood?
As it is said in the "Introductory Chapter" of the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* in one hundred thousand verses:

"The Bhagavat dwells in the [palace] of Supreme Radiance, adorned with the seven precious jewels, emitting great light that universally illumines all boundless worlds. It is arrayed with the exquisite decorations of immeasurable locations, circular and limitless, its magnitude difficult to fathom; it transcends the spheres traversed by the three realms and arises from supramundane roots of goodness, having the most supreme mastery of pure consciousness as its characteristic."

It is the capital of the Tathāgata, where the assembly of great bodhisattvas gathers like clouds; it is constantly attended by immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans; it is sustained by the joy and delight of the vast flavor of the Dharma; it accomplishes all that is beneficial for sentient beings; it eliminates all afflictions and calamities; and, being far removed from all māras, it transcends all [worldly] adornments.

It is the locus upon which the Tathāgatas’ adornments depend; it has great mindfulness, wisdom, and conduct as its pathways; it has great tranquility and sublime insight as its vehicle; and it has the gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—as its points of entry. It is a great palace established upon a king of great jewel-flowers, adorned by a multitude of immeasurable merits.

In this way, he displays the pure buddha-field, which is perfect in color, perfect in shape, perfect in dimension, perfect in location, perfect in cause, perfect in fruit, perfect in its sovereign, perfect in its assistants, perfect in its retinue, perfect in its sustenance, perfect in its activities, perfect in its benefit, perfect in its fearlessness, perfect in its dwelling place, perfect in its paths, perfect in its vehicles, perfect in its gates, and perfect in its support.
Furthermore, they enjoy such a pure buddha-field, which is consistently sublime, consistently peaceful and blissful, consistently faultless, and consistently sovereign.
The commentary states:
This refers to the pure buddha-fields of all Buddhas, regarding which it is said that the Bhagavat dwells in "the most excellent radiance adorned with the seven precious jewels," and so forth.

"Most excellent radiance adorned with the seven precious jewels" means that the radiance of the Buddha’s pure land is supreme, being exquisitely decorated and adorned with the seven wonderful jewels; or, it may mean that the seven jewels themselves possess the most excellent radiance.
As for the seven treasures, they are: first, gold; second, silver;
third, lapis lazuli; fourth, crystal; fifth, red pearl; sixth, agate; seventh, emerald.
Fourth, the musāragalva jewel;
fifth, the aśmagarbha jewel—what, then, is this?
It refers to jewels such as the indranīla and mahānīla.
Sixth is the red *muktikā* jewel, which refers to the red pearls produced by red insects;
seventh is the *karketana* jewel.

Regarding the statement that they emit great radiance universally illuminating all boundless worlds, this means that these most excellent, brilliantly shining seven jewels emit great radiance, pervasively illuminating all boundless worlds.
Alternatively, he purifies Buddha-fields and emits great radiance that universally illumines all boundless worlds, and its substance likewise pervades those boundless worlds.
These two preceding lines manifest the perfection of the manifest color (*varṇa*) of the Buddha’s pure land.

"Immeasurable locations adorned with exquisite arrays" refers to the Buddha’s pure land being adorned with exquisite arrays across immeasurable locations, arranged and decorated with wisdom as the precursor; this phrase demonstrates the perfection of form and color.

"Perfectly circular and boundless, its measure difficult to fathom" means that the Buddha’s pure land is perfectly circular and boundless, such that its measure is difficult to fathom; alternatively, because its measure is limitless, it is perfectly circular and difficult to fathom. This phrase demonstrates the perfection of its dimensions.

"Transcending the sphere of activity of the three realms" means that the pure land of the Buddha transcends the sphere of activity of the three realms; for it is not a sphere of activity governed by craving for the three realms, nor is it the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*) of the various fetters and karmas. This phrase demonstrates the perfection of the location.

"Arising from superior supramundane roots of goodness" means that the supramundane roots of goodness serve as the cause, as well as the subsequent superior roots of goodness, which give rise to the pure land;
it is not [the power of] Īśvara or others that serves as the cause of the pure land.
This phrase demonstrates the perfection of the cause.

"Having the supremely sovereign pure consciousness as its characteristic" means that the Buddha-land has the supremely sovereign, purified mind-consciousness as its essential nature; because it consists of consciousness alone, there are no jewels or other things existing apart from consciousness. Rather, the pure mind-consciousness itself manifests in this way, appearing as various jewels and so forth. This phrase demonstrates the perfection of the result.
"The place where the Tathāgata resides" means that the Buddha is the sovereign who presides over this realm and no other; this phrase demonstrates the perfection of the sovereign.

"Where the great assembly of bodhisattvas gathers like clouds" means that only those bodhisattvas who have entered the Great Stages dwell therein to serve as the wings and support for the Tathāgata, and not śrāvakas and the like; this phrase demonstrates the perfection of the supporting retinue.
"Immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and so forth" refers to the various devas and others who dwell therein as retinues; this transformation is not real.
"Makara" here includes the great pythons.
This phrase demonstrates the perfection of the retinue.

Regarding "sustained by the joy and bliss of the flavor of the vast Dharma," this means that in the pure land, the food consists of the joy and bliss of the flavor of the Mahāyāna Dharma; this phrase demonstrates the perfection of sustenance, for food is able to sustain all bodies and lives.

"Acting for the benefit and welfare of all sentient beings" means that after consuming this food, one performs deeds that bring about the various benefits and happiness of all sentient beings; this phrase demonstrates the perfection of activity.

"Eliminating all afflictions and calamities" means that within the Pure Land there are no calamities produced by various afflictions; this phrase demonstrates the perfection of gathering and benefiting [sentient beings].

"Far removed from all Māras" refers to being free from the four types of hostile enemies: the afflictions (*kleśa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), death (*mṛtyu*), and the celestial Māra (*devaputra-māra*); this phrase demonstrates the perfection of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).

"Surpassing all adornments as the locus of the Tathāgata’s adornment" means that it surpasses all the adornments of bodhisattvas as the locus of the Tathāgata’s adornment; this phrase demonstrates the perfection of the dwelling place, for it is the most excellent among all dwellings.

Regarding "taking great mindfulness, wisdom, and practice as the path for wandering": the wisdom accomplished through reflection is called "great mindfulness"; the wisdom accomplished through hearing is called "great wisdom"; and the wisdom accomplished through cultivation is called "great practice."
This phrase demonstrates the perfection of the path; "wandering on the path" is a synonym for the Way (*mārga*).

"Taking great tranquility (*śamatha*) and sublime insight (*vipaśyanā*) as one's vehicle" means that by mounting *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one wanders upon the path of the three types of wisdom to proceed toward the garden of the goal. Because it surpasses the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* mounted by all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, it is called "great."
This sentence demonstrates the perfection of the vehicle.
Taking the liberations of great emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as the gateways of entry, these three doors of liberation constitute the points of entry.
"Door" (*dvāra*) means "passage," the general meaning of which is as explained previously.
This phrase demonstrates the perfection of the door.

Regarding the statement, "established upon a great jewel-lotus king adorned by a multitude of immeasurable virtues": just as worldly ornaments of jewels are adorned with various precious gems, so too this great jewel-lotus king—the support for this Buddha-field—is adorned by a multitude of immeasurable virtues, just as the earth mandala and others rest upon the wind mandala.

Such is the immeasurable merit of this Pure Land, established by the sovereign great jewel-flower adorned by all manner of ornaments; since this red lotus is the most preeminent among all flowers, it is therefore called the Sovereign Great Jewel-Flower.
Alternatively, because the Tathāgata himself is designated as the Great King, the Great Dharma King, this red lotus is the locus upon which the Buddha relies; it is named after its sovereign.
That which is established refers to the Buddha’s pure land, which relies upon this king of flowers and continues in succession for a long time without interruption.
This sentence demonstrates the perfection of the support.
Regarding the enjoyment of such a pure Buddha-field that is consistently sublime and excellent: it is because there is nothing impure and because it is free from filth and excrement.
"Exclusively blissful" means that there is no painful sensation (*duḥkhā-vedanā*) nor neutral sensation (*adukkham-asukha-vedanā*).
"Exclusively faultless" means that there is no unwholesome (*akuśala*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) state.
Regarding "ever-sovereign" (*ekānta-vaśitā*): because it does not depend on external conditions, all matters are accomplished by the mere arising of the mind.
The treatise says:
Furthermore, it should be understood that such a Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) of the Buddhas is able to perform five activities at all times:

First, its function is to provide relief from calamities for all sentient beings; for at the mere sight of them, it is able to rescue those suffering from calamities such as blindness, deafness, and insanity.
Second, its function is to provide relief from the miserable realms (*durgati*), for it uproots sentient beings from unwholesome states and establishes them in wholesome states.

Third, its function is to provide relief from improper means, for it causes those of other paths (*tīrthika*) to abandon practices for seeking liberation through improper means and places them within the Noble Teaching of the Tathāgata.
Fourth, its function is to provide relief from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because it bestows the path capable of transcending the three realms.

Fifth, its function is to provide relief regarding the vehicles (*yāna*), because it rescues bodhisattvas who intend to follow other vehicles as well as śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage, establishing them so that they may practice the Mahāyāna.
Regarding these five activities, one should know that the functional activities of all Buddhas are equal.
On this point, there is a verse:
"Because of differences in cause, basis, object, nature, and practice, the distinction between activities is thus admitted."
This distinct power in the world does not exist without cause; therefore, it is not the Teacher.
The commentary states:
The Dharma-realm of all Buddhas is the Dharmakāya; one should know that it is constantly capable of performing five activities.
Regarding the activity of rescuing all sentient beings from calamities and misfortunes: the suffering of grief and so forth arising from causes and conditions is termed "calamity.
To be able to rescue those with calamities such as blindness, deafness, and insanity at the mere sight of one is as stated in the Sūtra:
"When they see the Buddha, the blind regain their sight, the deaf regain their hearing, and the insane regain their mindfulness," and so forth.
Question:

As it has been taught that the dharmakāya is not an object of the six sense faculties, why is it now said that the blind obtain eyes and so forth, and are able to see the dharmakāya as the activity of the dharmakāya?
Answer:

Those who perceive the Dharma-body do so because the power induced by their past great vows has brought the Dharma-body to fulfillment, thereby sequentially giving rise to the functional activity of the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*); through this, they are able to grant eyes to the blind and so forth.

Through the power induced by the provisions of the past, one realizes the Dharmakāya, which spontaneously gives rise to activity like a mechanical wheel; while it is said that one returns to the source by seeing the Dharmakāya, in reality, one sees only the Nirmāṇakāya.

Regarding the statement that "its function is to rescue beings from the evil realms" and so forth: one is said to provide rescue only when one extracts them from an unwholesome state and places them in a wholesome state, for if the cause does not exist, the result likewise cannot exist.
The phrase "having the function of rescuing [beings] through non-expedient means" and so forth is clear in its wording.
Regarding the statement "having the function of rescuing the *satkāya*," *kāya* means "body" and *sat* means "false"; thus, that body which is false is called *satkāya*.
This refers to those phenomena within which the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) operates; that is, all contaminated (sāsrava) phenomena of the three realms.
Because he teaches the Dharma of deliverance regarding them, it is called "rescue."

Regarding the phrase "having the activity of rescuing those who rely on vehicles," this means establishing indeterminate-lineage bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and others in the correct practice of the Mahāyāna, so that they may realize great enlightenment.
It should be understood that all Buddhas are entirely equal in these five activities; to clarify this meaning, another verse is spoken:

"If one claims that karma differs because of differences in causes, bases, objects, and so forth, as well as differences in worldly causes—meaning that the causes for gods differ, and the causes for humans, ghosts, and others each differ, and therefore karma is different [this is not the case]."
The Buddhas are not like this; because their causes are not distinct, there is no difference in their karma.
