If one were to claim that karma differs based on a distinction in the world, "basis" refers to the physical body, and it is due to its differentiation that their karma would differ.
Just as Devadatta and Yajñadatta have distinct karmas because their physical bodies are different, it is not so with the Buddhas;
since their Dharma-bodies are without distinction, their karma is not different.

If it is argued that karma is distinct because worldly affairs are distinct: "affairs" refers to the differences between what is done and what is used; because these affairs are each distinct, their respective karmas differ.
This is just as ordinary people have distinct affairs such as farming or commerce, and so on for all such cases.
The Buddhas are not like this; because their activity for the benefit of sentient beings is without distinction, there is no difference in their karma.
If one were to claim that karma differs because the natures of worldly beings differ, "nature" here refers to their underlying intention (*āśaya*).
Just as in the world, actions differ because the objects of the intention for benefit and the intention for happiness vary;
it is not so with the Buddhas. Since their intentions to benefit and bring happiness to all sentient beings are without distinction, their actions are not different.

Regarding the claim that karma is differentiated because worldly activities are distinct: "activity" refers to effort. Just as a small effort can give rise to a small karma, while a great effort gives rise to a great karma, it is because efforts differ that their respective karmas are different.
The Buddhas are not like this; all that they do is without effortful application (*anābhoga*), and therefore their karma is not distinct.

As for the statement that they are not "Guiding Teachers" because they lack these five distinct powers: it means that because they lack these five distinct powers—beginning with the cause—they do not possess the fivefold differentiation of karma characteristic of worldly teachers.
The treatise says:

If this perfection of qualities is thus associated with the Dharmakāya of the Buddhas, which is not shared with the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, with what intention did the Buddha teach the One Vehicle?
Regarding this, there are two verses:
"To attract one class of beings, And to sustain the rest,
Because of those of indeterminate lineage, The Buddhas teach the One Vehicle."
Because they are equal in terms of the dharma, selflessness, and liberation, yet differ in nature,
and because they attain two types of mental dispositions and undergo transformation, it is ultimately taught that there is one vehicle (ekayāna). Commentary:
Based on this underlying intention, the Buddha taught the One Vehicle (ekayāna), as demonstrated by two verses.

For the sake of attracting a certain class of beings—namely, those śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage who understand their own state—the Buddha employs the skillful means of leading them toward that liberation; he teaches the One Vehicle so that they may rely upon the Mahāyāna and attain parinirvāṇa.

Regarding "and for the sake of sustaining the remainder": this is intended to sustain those bodhisattvas of indeterminate lineage who might otherwise fall away from their diligence in the Mahāyāna; therefore, it is taught that they abide in the One Vehicle (ekayāna) so that those bodhisattvas do not enter parinirvāṇa by relying on the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Regarding the phrase "because the dharmas are equal": "dharma" refers to *tathatā* (suchness). Although the vehicles of the various śrāvakas and others differ, they all converge upon *tathatā*; since the *tathatā* toward which they proceed is without differentiation, it is called the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Regarding the phrase "because there is no self and so forth," this is because the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) is identical.
If there were actual differences, there could be distinct vehicles for persons, such that one might say, "This is a śrāvaka" or "This is a bodhisattva.
Since there is no real difference between persons, it is therefore said that there is but a single vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Regarding "because liberation and so forth are equal," this means that there is no difference among those of the three vehicles in their liberation from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
As the Blessed One said:
"There is no distinction between liberation and liberation."
It is by virtue of this underlying intention that the One Vehicle (ekayāna) is taught.
Regarding the phrase "because their natures are different," this refers to the distinctions among those śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage.

That is to say, within the person of a śrāvaka who has turned toward enlightenment, both the śrāvaka lineage and the buddha lineage are present; it is by this principle that the One Vehicle is taught.
"Because of attaining two types of aspiration" means that one attains two kinds of aspirations.
The first is the aspiration of all Buddhas toward all sentient beings to regard them as identical to their own self, saying, "That is I; I am that."
Due to these causes and conditions, since this one has already attained Buddhahood, that one shall also attain Buddhahood.
For this reason, it is called "attaining the supreme intention.

Second, at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the World-Honored One bestowed the prediction of Buddhahood upon the śrāvakas, such as Śāriputra and others, in order to cause them to acquire such an intention.
"We are equal to the Buddha, without any difference.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas in this assembly who share the same names as those [in other assemblies], because they have received their respective predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).

A single word from the Buddha contains two kinds of benefit: namely, that the śrāvakas attain an aspiration identical to that of the Buddha’s own essence, and that the bodhisattvas receive their predictions of enlightenment. It is by virtue of this principle that the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is taught.
Regarding the statement "because it is a transformation," as the World-Honored One said: "O Bhikṣus!
I recall that in the past, countless hundreds of times, I entered parinirvāṇa by relying on the Śrāvaka vehicle."
How can one who has already attained Buddhahood enter parinirvāṇa by relying upon a śrāvaka?

Therefore, there is a specific underlying intention here: namely, in order to discipline those sentient beings to be converted who belong to the śrāvaka lineage, he manifests his own body as being of that same vehicle and appears to enter parinirvāṇa.

For this reason, whether it be the Śrāvaka-yāna or the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, these are themselves the Mahāyāna. Regarding the phrase "because they constitute the ultimate consummation of the One Vehicle":
it is based on the principle of ultimate reality that the One Vehicle is taught; it does not mean that there is no distinction between them.
Because there is no other superior vehicle beyond this, and because this Single Vehicle alone is the most supreme, the Buddha taught the Single Vehicle.
The treatise says:
Since all Buddhas possess the same Dharma-body, by what cause can it be seen that there are many Buddhas?
Regarding this, there is a verse:
"In a single realm there are not two; Simultaneously, they are infinite and perfect;
Successive transformation is irrational; Therefore, it is established that there are many Buddhas."
The commentary states:
Regarding "there are no two in a single realm," there are no two Buddhas within a single world-system; therefore, it should be said that there is only one Buddha.

Regarding "the simultaneous perfection of the immeasurable," immeasurable Bodhisattvas simultaneously complete their accumulation of provisions and manifest the fruition of Buddhahood in many world-systems; therefore, it should be said that there are many Buddhas.

Some may say that within a single world-system, immeasurable bodhisattvas attain equal and perfect enlightenment in successive order, rather than many Buddhas appearing simultaneously in multiple world-systems.
To refute this attachment, it is further stated that sequential succession is irrational.

There is no causal basis for immeasurable Bodhisattvas who have simultaneously perfected their accumulations of merit and wisdom to attain Buddhahood by waiting for one another in succession; therefore, there are many Buddhas existing simultaneously.
The treatise says:
How should one understand that within the dharmakāya, the Buddha neither ultimately enters parinirvāṇa nor ultimately does not enter parinirvāṇa?
Regarding this, there is a verse:
Because he is liberated from all obscurations, and because his activities are never-ending,
the Buddha has entered ultimate nirvāṇa, yet he has not entered ultimate nirvāṇa.
Commentary:
There are Mahāyāna followers who maintain that the Buddha never ultimately enters parinirvāṇa, speaking from the perspective of the nirvāṇa-realm without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
Others, conversely, maintain that the Buddha ultimately enters parinirvāṇa, speaking from the perspective of the nirvāṇa-realm with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
These two interpretations based on fixed attachment are irrational.
To speak correctly, one should say that the Buddhas do not definitively and ultimately enter parinirvāṇa, nor do they definitively and ultimately not enter parinirvāṇa.
Because the Buddha has attained liberation from all obstacles, he is ultimately in *nirvāṇa*;
yet because the tasks he must perform have no end, the Buddhas never ultimately enter *nirvāṇa*.
The treatise says: For what reason is the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) not identical to the Nature Body (*svabhāvakāya*)?

It is because of six reasons: first, because the form body (*rūpakāya*) is visible; second, because the distinctions among the assemblies of immeasurable Buddhas are visible; third, because it is visible that the nature [of the assembly] is indeterminate according to the varying inclinations (*adhimukti*) of those who see it; fourth, because it is visible that the nature [of the assembly] fluctuates as individuals see it differently; fifth, because it is visible that various assemblies—such as bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and devas—are interspersed; and sixth, because it would be illogical for the *ālayavijñāna* and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) to undergo the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) [if they were identical]. Therefore, it is unreasonable to claim that the Buddha’s Enjoyment Body is identical to the Nature Body.
The commentary states:

Regarding the phrase "because the form-body (rūpakāya) is visible," this means that the enjoyment-body (saṃbhogakāya) possesses a form that is visible, whereas the essential body (svabhāvakāya) does not possess a form that is visible; therefore, the enjoyment-body is not the essential body.

Furthermore, the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) possesses an infinite assembly of followers and manifests various differentiated forms that can be perceived; such differentiation does not exist in the essential body (svabhāvakāya). Therefore, the enjoyment body is not the essential body.
Furthermore, the nature of the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya) is indeterminate according to one's resolute conviction (adhimukti), as stated in the sūtra:
"There are some who see the Buddha as an Enjoyment Body; some see him as a youth; some see him as a child," and so forth, as explained at length.
The self-nature body (svābhāvika-kāya) does not possess such indeterminacy; therefore, the enjoyment body (saṃbhoga-kāya) is not the self-nature body.

Furthermore, the nature of the enjoyment body is seen to undergo change and differentiation: a single perceiver may at one time see the form and characteristics of the enjoyment body as distinct from another, and at a later time see them as yet different again. Since the essence of the self-nature body does not undergo such change, the enjoyment body is not the self-nature body.

Furthermore, the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is constantly interspersed with various assemblies of bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, and others; such an interspersion of assemblies does not belong to the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*). Therefore, the enjoyment body is not the essential body.

Furthermore, it is because the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is seen to be illogical; that is to say, one attains the svabhāva-kāya by transforming the ālayavijñāna, and one attains the saṃbhoga-kāya by transforming the various pravṛttivijñānas. Therefore, the saṃbhoga-kāya is not the svabhāva-kāya.
Because these six points are contrary to reason, the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) is not the essential body (svābhāvikakāya).
The treatise asks:
For what reason is the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) not identical to the essential body?
For eight reasons:
it would be unreasonable for bodhisattvas, who have long since attained non-retrogressive concentration, to be born in Tuṣita or among human beings.

Furthermore, it would be unreasonable for Bodhisattvas, who have long since constantly recollected their past lives, to lack correct knowledge regarding the treatises on writing, calculation, arithmetic, seals, and crafts, as well as regarding the conduct involved in the enjoyment of sensory objects.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable that Bodhisattvas, having long since understood the teachings of false doctrines and true doctrines, would go to the abodes of non-Buddhist teachers.
Moreover, it is not reasonable that Bodhisattvas, having long since been able to skillfully know the right path of the three vehicles, would practice erroneous asceticism.

Furthermore, it would be unreasonable for Bodhisattvas to relinquish hundreds of millions of Jambudvīpas and instead attain perfect enlightenment and turn the wheel of the true Dharma in only a single location.
If it were permissible to perform buddha-activities in other locations solely through emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) apart from manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment,
then why not establish the simultaneous appearance of Buddhas throughout all of Jambudvīpa, rather than manifesting the attainment of perfect enlightenment only in Tuṣita?
Since nothing is established [as a separate entity], there is no teaching and no principle [for such a distinction].

Although there may be many emanations, this does not contradict the statement that two Tathāgatas do not appear simultaneously in the world, because a single world-system is comprised of one four-continent world (*cāturdvīpaka*), just as two universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) do not appear together.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
The Buddha’s subtle transformation bodies, Entering many wombs with equanimity,
Manifest all aspects [of existence], And turning the wheel after attaining perfect enlightenment.

To claim that one generates the aspiration for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, practices accordingly, realizes great enlightenment, and eventually enters parinirvāṇa, is not logical; for such a vow and practice would be fruitless, resulting in the fault of failure.
The commentary states:
For eight reasons, it is contrary to correct principle to assert that the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is identical to the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*).

This is because bodhisattvas, having long ago attained non-retrogressive meditative absorption (*avaivartika-samādhi*), have never experienced regression; thus, it would already be illogical for them to be born in the desire realm or even in Tuṣita Heaven, let alone to be born among human beings.
It is consistent with correct reasoning that one does not attain the fruit of the desire realm through the cultivation of the non-retrogressive concentration over many kalpas;
therefore, the principle that the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is distinct from the essential body (svābhāvikakāya) is established.

Furthermore, it would be unreasonable for Bodhisattvas, having long since recollected their past lives, to have extensively practiced even false asceticism; this passage is easy to understand and need not be explained further.

Furthermore, it would be illogical for Bodhisattvas to abandon hundreds of millions of Jambudvīpas and attain perfect enlightenment and turn the wheel of the true Dharma in only one location, because all such locations are identical.
By this reasoning, this is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), not the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*).

If it is argued that, apart from attaining manifest enlightenment elsewhere in Jambudvīpa, one truly realizes perfect awakening only here in Jambudvīpa, and that the transformation body performs buddha-activities throughout other places;
why then is it not accepted that the Tathāgata in Tuṣita truly realizes manifest enlightenment, and that his emanation body comes here to these four great continents to perform buddha-activities?
If you think it is not unreasonable for one to attain perfect enlightenment in Jambudvīpa while manifesting emanations in other places,

why would it be unreasonable for one who dwells only in Tuṣita Heaven to attain perfect enlightenment and yet manifest transformation bodies throughout all four continents, including within Jambudvīpa?

If it is not admitted that perfect enlightenment is manifested simultaneously in all four continents, then because there is neither scriptural authority nor logical reason, such a claim cannot be maintained.
There are times when no Buddha appears in Jambudvīpa; this is so as not to contradict those sūtras which state:
"It is impossible and out of the question that two Tathāgatas should appear in the world at the same time, one after another, within a single world-system."
If one were to concede that many Buddhas appear simultaneously in the world throughout all of Jambudvīpa, it would contradict that [scriptural statement].
To avoid this difficulty, it is further stated: "Although there are many emanations, this does not contradict the teaching that two Tathāgatas do not appear in the world simultaneously."
That sutra states that a single world consists of one set of four great continents, not a thousand continents and so forth.
That same sutra further states that, for example, two wheel-turning kings do not appear simultaneously.

If it is not admitted that multiple Buddhas appear simultaneously across multiple four-continent worlds (*cāturdvīpaka*), then it should likewise not be admitted that multiple wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*) appear simultaneously across multiple four-continent worlds.

If it is admitted that two wheel-turning kings do not appear simultaneously within a single four-continent world—rather than across a thousand continents and so forth—it should likewise be admitted that two Buddhas do not appear simultaneously within a single four-continent world—rather than across a thousand continents and so forth.
Furthermore, by means of verses, he manifests many transformation bodies to demonstrate his possession of the marks of enlightenment.

Regarding the Buddha’s subtle transformation bodies and so forth: just as the Buddha’s transformation body manifests entry into a mother’s womb, he likewise creates transformation bodies of Śāriputra and other śrāvakas, each with distinct characteristics, entering their respective mothers’ wombs simultaneously and equally. The Buddha performs these transformations in order to reveal that his awakening in all its aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is most sublime.

Next, it is shown that it is unreasonable for the Tathāgata to enter ultimate nirvāṇa; that is to say, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, he made vows, practiced the path, and realized great bodhi.

It would be unreasonable for this vow and this practice, which are intended solely for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, to enter parinirvāṇa by means of that ultimate nirvāṇa before the task is yet complete; for in such a case, both the practice and the vow would be rendered fruitless.
That which manifests as nirvāṇa is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), not the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*).
The treatise asks:
Since the Buddha’s enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and transformation body are impermanent, why do the sūtras state that the Tathāgata’s body is eternal?
Because the *dharmakāya*, which is the basis for these two bodies, is eternal;

and because the *nairmāṇikakāya* and *sāmbhogikakāya* are constantly enjoyed without cessation and repeatedly manifested without final interruption—just as one might "constantly enjoy pleasure" or "constantly give food"—it should be understood that the Tathāgata’s body is likewise eternal.
The commentary states:
There is a sūtra that says the body of the Tathāgata is permanent.
Since both the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddha are impermanent, how can it be said that the body of the Tathāgata is eternally abiding?
This means that although these two bodies are impermanent, they rely upon the *dharmakāya*; because the *dharmakāya* is eternal, they are also said to be eternal.
Regarding the statement that "the body is eternal," it may mean that its essence is eternal, or that it is called an "eternal body" because it relies upon the eternal *dharmakāya*.

This demonstrates that the *niṣyanda-kāya* (emanation body resulting from outflow) and the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (transformation body) are permanent in the sense of being constant through different modes of manifestation, but not permanent by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body) is like one who constantly experiences bliss, because it perpetually enjoys [the Dharma] without cessation or interruption.

It is just as when people in the world say, "He constantly experiences pleasure. Although he does not experience pleasure in an uninterrupted succession, one may still say that he constantly experiences pleasure. One should know that the Buddha’s Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is likewise:

although it is not eternally permanent, it is sometimes called "constant" because within various assemblies of bodhisattvas, he experiences the great joy of the Dharma without cessation or interruption. Furthermore, the Buddha’s Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) repeatedly manifests emanations without ever being permanently severed; thus, it is called "constant" in a specific sense, similar to the expression "he constantly gives food."

It is just as when people in the world speak of "giving food constantly": although one is not actually giving food at all times without interruption, because the intention to give repeatedly does not cease, it is called "giving food constantly."

One should know that the Buddha’s transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) is likewise: it is not because it lacks arising and ceasing that it is called "permanent," but rather because it manifests repeatedly according to those to be converted and does not cease forever, it is spoken of as "permanent" with intentional meaning (saṃdhāya).
The treatise states:
For six reasons, the emanation bodies manifested by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not abide eternally.
First, because their task is complete; they have already brought sentient beings to maturity and liberated them.
Second, it is to cause the abandonment of a lack of aspiration for nirvāṇa, so that they may seek the eternally abiding body of the Tathāgata.
Third, it is to cause the abandonment of disparaging the Buddhas, so that they may awaken to the teachings of the profound True Dharma.
Fourth, it is to cause one to generate deep longing for the Buddha, fearing that those who see him too frequently might become weary or indolent.
Fifth, it is to cause one to exert diligent effort toward one's own self, knowing that a teacher of the correct teaching is difficult to encounter.
The sixth is for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity as quickly as possible, so that one’s own diligence does not abandon its yoke.
Regarding this, there are two verses:
Because their task is completed, They abandon the lack of delight in nirvāṇa.
To avoid slighting the Buddhas, one should develop deep yearning and arouse internal right effort for the sake of rapid maturation; therefore,
the Buddha’s transformation body is permitted, yet it does not abide eternally.
The commentary states:

"In order to cause the relinquishing of the lack of delight in nirvāṇa, and for the sake of seeking the eternally abiding body of the Tathāgata"—this reveals the intention behind the Tathāgata’s entry into nirvāṇa.

Since the body of the Tathāgata is impermanent, one should take delight in nirvāṇa; yet, if one seeks the eternally abiding body of the Tathāgata, one turns away from nirvāṇa. The World-Honored One manifests his passing into extinction to demonstrate that his body is impermanent, thereby causing beings to delight in the ultimately eternal nirvāṇa.

Regarding the phrase "in order to cause them to abandon the disparagement of the Buddhas and to awaken to the teaching of the profound True Dharma": if one were to claim that the bodies of the Buddhas are eternally abiding, one would fail to apply diligent skillful means toward awakening to and understanding the profound teachings of the Dharma, thinking instead, "I do not awaken now, but shall certainly awaken later."
If he were to interrogate his assembly of disciples one by one, they would immediately give rise to contempt and disparagement; clinging to their own views, they would say:
"Because of this, we shall certainly avoid that questioning."
If he does not remain in the world, where would they find cause to feel contempt or disparagement?
They all said,
"We have not yet grasped his intention."
"When the Blessed One has entered parinirvāṇa, who will be able to correctly awaken us?
Therefore, one should diligently seek awakening into the Dharma.

Regarding "causing oneself to arouse diligent vigor because it is difficult to find one who speaks correctly," this means that knowing the Blessed One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, one then arouses diligent vigor within oneself.
The Buddha is the one who correctly teaches the Dharma in the world; if he were not present, the world would have no refuge.
Having understood this, one exerts diligent effort.

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity as quickly as possible, so that one’s own diligence does not abandon its yoke": it means that in order to cultivate diligence and remain detached from abandoning the good yoke, until the Blessed One has passed into parinirvāṇa, my roots of goodness must certainly be brought to maturity.
For these six reasons, the Buddha’s transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) does not abide eternally.
To summarize the meaning of what has been explained above, the verse beginning with "by what is done" (kṛtya) is spoken.
The treatise says:
The dharma-body of all Buddhas has been non-differentiated and immeasurable since beginningless time; therefore, one should not exert further effort in order to attain it.
Regarding this, there is a verse:
The Buddha’s attainment has no other cause than the immeasurable [virtues];
if sentient beings were to abandon their diligent application, the realization would never become a cause. It is illogical that such a cause should ever be severed.
The commentary states:
Herein there is an objection:

Since the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas has existed from beginningless time, and there is no distinct cause for its realization or attainment, why is it necessary to exert effort in order to seek the fruit of Buddhahood?
Furthermore, there is an objection:

"The Dharma-body of all Buddhas has been non-distinct and infinite since beginningless time; thus, a single Buddha alone is capable of fully accomplishing all matters for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, and it would be unnecessary to exert further effort for their sake."

To answer this objection, it is said that the Buddhas' attainments (*prāpti*) and so forth are such that from beginningless time they have been non-distinct and immeasurable. If sentient beings were to abandon the causes of right effort for the sake of seeking the fruit of Buddhahood, such an attainment would never constitute a cause.
Since this is realized by the Buddha, and it is not the case that sentient beings seeking the fruit of Buddhahood abandon the causes of right exertion, this objection does not apply.
If the fruit of Buddhahood were attained apart from right exertion, then all sentient beings would have already attained it; therefore, one must not sever the causes of right exertion.

Furthermore, the Buddha-dharmadhātu has been without distinction or limit since beginningless time; it universally serves as the cause for all to realize awakening, causing the bodhisattvas’ hearts to be bound by compassionate vows as they diligently seek the fruit of Buddhahood.
In order to bring about the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, one seeks the fruit of Buddhahood and exerts diligent effort.
The treatise states:
This concludes my Asaṅga’s abbreviated commentary on the "Mahāyānasaṃgraha" chapter within the *Abhidharmamahāyānasūtra*.
The commentary states:
I have now briefly explained the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Furthermore, it is said in verse:
Having already resolved upon the lack of intrinsic nature, I have made the sublime vow to seek the fruit of Buddhahood;
regarding the principles and teachings of the pure realm, compassion and wisdom have accumulated within my heart.
Having heard correctly from various masters, I have attained a profound faith and understanding in accordance with reality.
Because focused mindfulness has been brought before me, I have composed this commentary.
Through the merit diligently generated regarding these ten points of profound and vast meaning,
may all the world attain the wondrous wisdom of the [thirty-two] marks.
Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha, Fascicle Ten
